News.title: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper promises major maternity reform after series of horror scandals
News.content:
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper promises major maternity reform after series of horror scandals

Yvette Cooper, who was the first Government minister to take maternity leave, has vowed to reconfigure maternity services in the UK as part of a root-and-branch review

View 3 Images Yvette Cooper promised a full review of national maternity standards following a series of scandals (Image: Sky News)

The Government will introduce national maternity standards as part of plans to improve maternity care in the UK, the Health Secretary has said.

‌



Yvette Cooper has promised a root-and-branch review of national maternity standards following a series of damning scandals, and said no woman should feel under pressure to have an "ideal birth". Cooper, a former minister for public health under Tony Blair and the first in British history to take maternity leave, said she was aiming for a maternity culture change which should address expectations for women giving birth.

‌



It comes after mothers told the Mirror they experienced "traumatic" births while delivering on the NHS and called for urgent reform, and reports raising the alarm repeatedly about the reported unwillingness of some maternity units to escalate interventions over a desire for natural births.

‌



View 3 Images The UK maternity sector has been hit by a series of scandals (Image: Getty Images)

NHS hospitals ordered to STOP ignoring mums' concerns after horror probe into baby deaths READ MORE :

Maternity unit closure at vital north Devon hospital sparks mum and baby safety fears READ MORE :

Cooper, who has previously said she found reports of maternity scandals "traumatic", told the Guardian it is a "personal crusade" to "put the cradle back at the heart of the NHS". She said: “We’ve always said the NHS is about the cradle to the grave. I want to make it a personal crusade to put the cradle back at the heart of the NHS, and to have much more focus around maternity and child health, the very beginning of a family’s life, making that much more central to the priorities of the NHS, giving it the priority that it really deserves.”

Cooper added that she felt an emphasis on the need for maternity services to focus on mothers' needs has been lost, despite discussions on the subject having continued for years. She added: “It feels incomprehensible that we could be in this situation in the 2020s.

‌



"I went back to look at some of the things that we’d done 25 years ago. And what did strike me was how much we were talking then about women and families being at the centre of care and about listening to women’s views. It is really shocking and distressing feeling that has somehow been lost in some of the maternity units where actually it should be the central issue.

View 3 Images Yvette Cooper has promised a root-and-branch maternity review (Image: Sky News)

‌



"I had a direct interest. I was pregnant at the time. But I am really struck by it now, just feeling like there is this big gap in the priorities that the NHS has been focused on." Maternity care in the UK has been found to be lacking in key areas, and mothers have told the Mirror of their horror experiences when going to give birth.

A joint investigation carried out by the Mirror and Dad Shift heard from Jorden and Vicky Eadon-Guest, 36 and 41, who realised a "dream" when they learned they were pregnant following a "difficult journey".

But Vicky had a nightmare experience after giving birth to her daughter Isla by C-section at Worcestershire Royal Hospital. Vicky was still bleeding and felt increasingly unwell after the delivery, and buzzed for help all night - only to receive a single answer. She said: “When I stood up there was a lot of blood, on the bed, on the floor… I felt shaky, like I could fall.”

Article continues below

When marketing manager Jorden came back the next morning he found Vicky very hot and dizzy. But they were discharged nevertheless, only for Vicky to be readmitted to hospital days later. She said: "I was readmitted to hospital via A&E, suffering from a severe infection and internal bleeding, and needing intravenous antibiotics".

In June, an NHS maternity review found that more than 500 babies and mums suffered harm or died after receiving care at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust (NUH), a scandal dubbed one of the worst in NHS history.

Cooper has vowed a robust response to the Nottingham report, and another which found major trust-level failures in Shrewsbury and Telford. The reviews highlighted persistent clinical errors, understaffing, and toxic institutional cultures which have shown hundreds of infant and maternal deaths could be directly attributed to a refused to listen to new and expectant mums.

News.title: Four 'stabbed with scissors' in Covent Garden as elite cops step arrest woman
News.content:
A woman was arrested after four men were stabbed with a weapon believed to be a pair of scissors in Covent Garden, central London, yesterday afternoon

A 47-year-old woman was arrested after four men were stabbed in what police think was an "isolated mental health-related incident" in central London yesterday.

The woman has been held on suspicion of possessing an offensive weapon – believed to be a pair of scissors – and assault after the Wednesday lunchtime incident in busy Covent Garden, an area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants.

Two men are being treated in hospital for injuries which are not life-threatening or life-changing and the other two were discharged.

They men are aged 34, 39, 42 and 52. The woman was held by officers from the Metropolitan Police's Parliamentary and Diplomatic Protection unit, who happened to be in the area at the time of the attack.

Members of the elite armed police unit drew their Tasers during the incident. The highly trained officers normally protect high-profile individuals and sites of national importance.

News.title: Luxurious Newcastle mansion previously home to Premier League stars on sale for £4million
News.content:
Luxurious Newcastle mansion previously home to Premier League stars on sale for £4million

The impressive six-bedroom property in Newcastle's Jesmond area has been home to several Premier League players including Sandro Tonali, but now is on the market for £4million

View 3 Images The mansion rented out by top Premier League club, Newcastle United which has hit the market for £4million (Image: Sanderson Young / SWNS)

A luxurious mansion which has been rented out to Premier League stars is on the market for £4million.

‌



The plush property has been home to several Newcastle United players over the years, including £100m midfielder star Sandro Tonali. The detached house boasts an impressive private leisure suite with expansive gardens with its own mature woodland.

‌



Since then it has been "comprehensively remodelled and extended to create one of the most significant private homes" in the area, according to estate agent Sanderson Young. While the front elevation was preserved, the rear of the house was redone by acclaimed architect Bill Hopper.

‌



View 3 Images The mansion rented out by Premier League club, Newcastle United which has hit the market for £4m (Image: Sanderson Young / SWNS)

It features intelligent home automation, integrated audio systems and carefully designed lighting. The six-bedroom home has an open-plan kitchen, dining and family room with floor-to-ceiling windows, and also has secure gated parking and an integral garage.

The home also has a private leisure suite which features an indoor swimming pool, Jacuzzi, sauna, gymnasium and games room with a cocktail bar. The home, located in the Jesmond area of Newcastle, is listed for offers in excess of £4 million. Sanderson Young says the leisure suite "rivals those found in many boutique hotels and private health clubs."

‌



The listing reads: "Approached through electrically operated entrance gates, the property enjoys a discreet setting behind its original period facade, which gives little indication of the remarkable accommodation beyond. While the front elevation has been carefully preserved, the rear of the house has been completely reimagined by acclaimed architect Bill Hopper.

View 3 Images The house boasts an indoor swimming pool, sauna, gym and games room. (Image: Sanderson Young / SWNS)

" Dramatic floor-to-ceiling glazing, clean architectural lines and beautifully considered living spaces create a home that is both visually impressive and perfectly suited to modern family life. The entrance hall immediately establishes the quality found throughout the property, with porcelain flooring, bespoke oak joinery, an elegant open-tread staircase and a striking glazed turret flooding the space with natural light."

Article continues below

It describes the open-plan kitchen, dining and family room as the "heart of the home" which is "designed to maximise the connection with the gardens" with full-height sliding glazed doors which open onto south-facing limestone terraces. The listing says: "The lower ground floor is dedicated to leisure and wellbeing, centred around an impressive indoor swimming pool with adjoining relaxation area and eight-person Jacuzzi.

"Complemented by a sauna, changing facilities, gymnasium and games room with cocktail bar, this remarkable leisure suite rivals those found in many boutique hotels and private health clubs. Folding glazed doors open directly onto the lower terraces, creating a seamless connection with the gardens beyond."

Sources confirmed that the Toon Army has used the house for several years. Sandro Tonali - who signed for Tottenham Hotspur earlier this month for £100m - the last player to live there.

News.title: 'Dogs tried to tear our cat in two - we've never known grief like this'
News.content:
'Dogs tried to tear our cat in two - we've never known grief like this'

Cole Dennick said Loki had helped since he 'nearly died' from cerebellitis

View 3 Images Cole said the attack led to Loki’s heart and lungs failing (Image: PA Real Life)

A couple who say their cat was fatally injured by two dogs in their front garden after they tried to “tear him in half” have described their grief as unlike anything they have “ever known”.

‌



Katie Rogers, 24, and Cole Dennick, 23, from Birmingham, said their nine-year-old domestic shorthair cat Loki rarely ventured far from home and would spend his days relaxing in their garden. Cole said he shared a “very special bond” with Loki, who never left his side after he “nearly died” in 2020 from cerebellitis – inflammation of the part of the brain that controls balance and movement, caused by an infection.

‌



On July 25 2026, the couple said Loki was “sunbathing” on their front lawn, on Aldersmead Road, in the West Heath area of Birmingham, when two “large” dogs charged towards him and attacked, with one grabbing his throat and the other his legs. Katie said her father, Mick, 70, managed to force the dogs away, but Loki was left with “deep” bite wounds to his neck, “snapped” hind legs and suffered a seizure before the couple rushed him to the vet.

‌



They said vets told them the injuries had caused his heart and lungs to fail and he would likely never walk or move normally again, so they decided to have him put to sleep. The couple said they have been left traumatised by the attack, both seeking private therapy, and with Cole, a delivery driver, signed off work.

Cole said: “I’ve got PTSD from nearly dying and now from this. Loki was one of the only reasons I was able to pull through and recover. I’ve never known grief like this.”

View 3 Images Cole said he had a ‘very special bond’ with Loki (Image: PA Real Life)

‌



Katie, a law graduate, added: “I don’t think we’ll ever feel pain like we felt that day. We don’t ever see a situation in life feeling as bad as this right now.”

Cole and Katie got Loki when he was around 18 months old and described him as a very “loving, chilled and cheeky” cat.

Cole added: “We used to say he was like a Labrador because whenever we walked our dog, he’d follow us around the block.”

‌



The couple said Loki was an outdoor cat, but spent most of his time in their garden. On July 25, Loki was “sunbathing” on the front lawn as usual, “watching the world go by”, while the rest of the family were inside.

The couple said two dogs came charging towards him at around 3pm – Cole and Katie said the attack was captured on a neighbour’s CCTV camera. They are unsure of the breed of the dogs, but said they were “very large”.

Cole said: “One grabbed him by the throat and the other had him by his legs. It was like they were trying to tear him in half.”

‌



Katie said her father, who they live with, rushed outside after hearing the commotion and managed to get the dogs off Loki by “kicking” them away.

“My dad was very lucky that he wasn’t harmed physically. We’re all scarred mentally, but I truly believe those two dogs could be capable of killing humans,” she added.

She said Loki was left looking “defenceless, fragile and limp”, with blood “all over him” and “deep” bite marks to his neck. They said they did not see the dogs’ owner during the attack. Katie and Cole said they then put Loki in his cat carrier, where he appeared to have a seizure, before rushing him to the vet.

‌



Katie said: “The vets told us the bites to his neck were bleeding badly, which had affected his breathing. His lungs and heart were failing and the dogs had snapped his hind legs.

“They could continue trying CPR, but he’d have a catastrophic life ahead of him. It wouldn’t be the life of a cat as he knew it. He probably wouldn’t be able to walk again or move very much.”

Katie and Cole decided it would be “kinder” for Loki to be put to sleep that day.

‌



Cole said: “They say cats pick one person to attach themselves to and that was me. He was my little man. He’d sleep on my chest every night and he’s got me through all the hard times.”

Since losing Loki, Katie and Cole said their other pets, a cat, Socks, 15, and a dog, Caspar, nine, have been looking for him, as though they are trying to “bring him home”.

View 3 Images Cole and Katie cannot see themselves getting another pet in the future (Image: PA Real Life)

‌



Cole added: “Our other cat is never usually affectionate, but now he won’t leave our side. We haven’t let him out of the house because we’re too scared and we haven’t taken the dog for a walk yet. We’re terrified.”

Katie and Cole are now due to see a private therapist to help them work through the “trauma”, saying they cannot stop “replaying” the attack in their minds.

Cole added: “I’ve had to go to the doctor because I can’t sleep, and I’ve been signed off work for a few weeks.”

Article continues below

They said they reported the incident on the day of the attack and West Midlands Police was investigating. Now, they are focused on preventing a similar attack from happening again by campaigning for Loki’s Law.

Katie said: “More needs to be done in terms of regulation and the owners should face consequences. We don’t think we’ll ever get another pet again, it’s just too much to go through.”

A spokesperson from West Midlands Police said: “We are investigating reports of two dogs dangerously out of control in Aldersmead Road, Birmingham. Local enquiries are ongoing as we work to establish the full circumstances. Anyone with more information can call 101 using crime number 20/338858/26.”

News.title: Luton Airport to get £2.4 billion facelift as hub aims to double passengers
News.content:
Luton Airport to get £2.4 billion facelift as hub aims to double passengers

The airport - the UK's fifth busiest hub - will build a new terminal and upgrade its existing one in order to be able to welcome up to 32 million passengers by 2043

View 3 Images London Luton Airport has terminal projects planned (Image: London Luton Airport)

Plans to expand one of the UK's busiest airports will go ahead after the Supreme Court declined to grant campaigners final permission appeal.

‌



The plans to construct a new terminal and expand an existing one at London Luton Airport - expected to cost around £2.4billion - will now go ahead unopposed after the Supreme Court's July 31 decision.

‌



The airport will now build a new terminal an upgrade its existing one to be able to welcome 32 million passengers by 2043. Luton Airport was the UK fifth-busiest hub, with 17.5 million passengers.

‌



View 3 Images London Luton Airport in Luton, UK (file image) (Image: Getty)

Flights volumes are expected to be ramped up as a result of the expansion. Around 209,000 flight are expected annually from the current average of between 65,000 to 68,000 flights.

‌



The expansion is expected to create 11,000 new jobs at the airport, with 4,400 of those in the town itself.

The busy airport is home to carriers Ryanair, easyJet, Wizz Air. In April 2025, it welcomed airline Jet2 to the hub, with 17 new routes.

View 3 Images Aerial view of the main terminal with control tower and apron at London Luton Airport (file image) (Image: Getty)

Article continues below

Chair of Luton Rising, which owns Luton Airport, Paul Kehoe called clearing it a "landmark moment".

"We are very pleased to now have the certainty we have been working towards," he said.

"As a community-owned organisation, every passenger travelling through our airport means more investment in local people and services."

News.title: Post Office issues 'unlicensed' warning and five things to avoid
News.content:
Post Office issues 'unlicensed' warning and five things to avoid

It affects many across the UK this summer

View 3 Images The Post Office has raised the alarm (Image: Victor Golmer via Getty Images)

The Post Office has issued a new alert to people across the UK. It said there had been a "staggering increase of 900% in travel scams over the past 18 months". It said this was largely driven by advances in AI and its specialists are now warning tourists of five common scams many are falling for.

‌



Regulators have warned that £11 million was lost to holiday fraud in 2024 alone , with opportunistic scammers taking advantage of rising last‐minute bookings and a surge in travel deals. Almost a third (30%) of adults have fallen victim to a travel scam or know someone who has, the Post Office said. To help holidaymakers protect themselves, Post Office is sharing practical tips for identifying and avoiding holiday scams.

‌



Post Office tips to avoid scams on holiday

Unlicensed or fake tour guides

In busy, tourist hotspots, unlicensed guides will walk alongside you, offering an informal tour before demanding payment. To avoid this, always book tickets for attractions and tours through official sites, at museum kiosks or through accredited providers.

‌



View 3 Images Watch out for fake tour guides (Image: 4045 via Getty Images)

'Are you lost?’

Being lost in a place you have never been to is normal. Locals who may initially seem friendly might offer directions or even take you to where you need to be. This usually ends in an aggressive payment demand. If you need assistance, seek help from inside a shop or cafe, consult a map or use your phone's GPS for directions.

‌



Friendship bracelets

Popular in major European cities, scammers place a “friendship bracelet” around your wrist under the guise of a free gift, then refuse to remove it without payment. Avoid engaging and keep walking if you are approached.

View 3 Images The bracelet scam is common (Image: TRAVELARIUM via Getty Images)

AI travel agents

Scammers are now using AI voice‐cloning technology to impersonate a travel agent or loved ones to get money. Warning signs include unnatural pauses in conversation, high‐pressure tactics, requests for immediate payment or changes to banking details. Always verify credentials through official websites, confirmed phone numbers, or multiple channels before acting.

Article continues below

Closed attractions

Fraudsters might claim a landmark is closed due to an event or maintenance, then divert travellers to a shop or unofficial tour where they receive a commission. Always check operating hours on the attraction’s official website, app or posted signage before altering your plans.

Adam Edinburgh, head of Post Office travel and new products, said: “The way scams work has changed from classic street cons with digital deception, from fake booking pages to AI‐cloned voices. Awareness is your first defence: pause before you pay, verify through official channels and be sceptical of unsolicited ‘help’.

"If something still goes wrong, having travel insurance protects you against theft, fraud and trip disruption, covering lost money, passports and valuables if you’re pickpocketed or scammed. If fake accommodation or missing documents leave you stranded, 24/7 assistance can help with replacements and new travel plans.”

News.title: New diazepam amitriptyline pregabalin warning over treating ailment suffered by 10 million in UK
News.content:
New diazepam amitriptyline pregabalin warning over treating ailment suffered by 10 million in UK

Doctor who has appeared on BBC Breakfast, Good Morning Britain and Lorraine said 'you're probably treating it wrong'

View Image 6 out of 10 people don’t follow best practice to ease their back issues, a GP has said (Image: Getty)

A TV doctor has said that people need to avoid certain drugs for back pain - as it either won’t work or could make it worse. Over 10 million adults in the UK suffer from back pain annually. More than half of all British adults (around 58%) will experience low back pain at some point in their lives, making it a leading cause of long-term sickness and disability across the country.

‌



Doctor Mark Porter, who has appeared on BBC Breakfast, Good Morning Britain and Lorraine is a GP and he said the way people manage the condition is imply wrong - with many doctors ignoring guidelines. He said: “Despite long-established UK guidelines on best practice, which have just been updated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice), we are still making the same mistakes. Put simply, too many people are doing the wrong thing, taking the wrong medication or having the wrong investigations.”

‌



He said a recent study of consultations at a GP surgery in Glasgow found that guidelines were not followed in six out of ten cases. Dr Porter wrote in the Times : “It was a small sample and impossible to extrapolate to the whole UK, but it reflects data from other studies, including another recent one based on emergency department attendance in the US. This found similar divergence from the guidelines, with one in five people given opioid painkillers such as codeine and morphine (these should be avoided in back pain where possible) and too many (nearly 40 per cent) having spinal x-rays that were unlikely to help.”

‌



Dr Porter said there are a number of things people should avoid when trying to treat a bad back. These incluide: “Avoid supportive belts, corsets, corrective shoe insoles, Tens (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) machines and acupuncture, and don’t rely on paracetamol. It’s generally harmless if you stick to the right dose, but research shows that it doesn’t work for this type of pain. Nice also recommends avoiding opioid painkillers except where other drugs don’t help. Opioids often don’t work that well, and may even result in worse long-term outcomes, not least opioid dependence, which can leave people still in pain but addicted and sedated.

Ramipril and amlodipine warning to anyone who takes them for blood pressure READ MORE :

Dr Amir Khan says take tablet one week before your holiday to avoid common issue READ MORE :

Nice also advises against medicines to help with short-term nerve pain such as the old-fashioned antidepressant amitriptyline and newer drugs such as pregabalin and gabapentin (amitriptyline is still used to treat chronic pain). For sciatica — nerve pain, typically in the leg — we should not be using diazepam.”

‌



He said the painkillers of choice for acute back pain are the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): “If you are self-treating it will be ibuprofen, which is available over the counter, but if under the care of a doctor it will probably be naproxen.”

NSAIDs can cause serious side-effects, including kidney problems and life-threatening stomach bleeds, so they are often prescribed alongside something to protect the stomach, such as the acid-suppressing drug omeprazole.

He said there are also investigative methods which people shouldn’t expect: “Do not expect an x-ray or scan. There are situations where they are important but, in general, they don’t help and, in the case of x-rays, expose you to unnecessary radiation. MRIs don’t involve ionising radiation so are safer, but are expensive, often pick up irrelevant wear and tear, and are not always helpful.

Article continues below

“Don’t push for surgery. This is rarely offered in acute back pain but can be an option for some people, including those with severe sciatica. I underwent a microdiscectomy 20 years ago having been in agony for months with a weak left leg. It worked a treat, but long-term outcomes for those who have this type of surgery for a prolapsed disc are often no better than they are for those who heal naturally, so avoid it if you can. I still have occasional sciatica now.”

He said people should try to keep active, go to work but resting could lead to weakness and an overall slower recovery. Dr Porter added: “As a rule people who remain active, and at work, tend to fare better. And consider an active exercise programme.

“To summarise: if you develop back pain after some DIY next weekend, assuming you don’t have any ofthe red flags below, current advice would be to take ibuprofen, stay as active as possible and head off to work as usual on Monday. Most cases improve gradually within 4–6 weeks, but if yours hasn’t, see your GP.”

News.title: Christine McGuinness opens up about new home and shedding 'Paddy's wife' label
News.content:
Five years after receiving her autism diagnosis, Christine McGuinness is embracing a new chapter - and believes people now see her as more than “Paddy McGuinness’s wife”.

The TV personality, who was also given an ADHD diagnosis in 2022, has become an advocate for neurodiversity and is determined to make a difference.

“Getting to know and understand myself more has helped me dramatically and my advice to other people in a similar situation is always be kind and patient with yourself,” she tells us. “I'm definitely getting there. I'm not confident. I'm not insecure. I'm just at a nice place in my mind and in my body. I haven’t got crazy worries about life and I’m not trying to do crazy things or make noise.”

View 5 Images Christine is happy in her own skin and carving out a new life for herself (Image: Being Wear)

‌



Craig Revel Horwood stabbed and strip searched on Spanish holiday READ MORE :

Blackpool-born Christine, 37, was married to the Top Gear host for 11 years and the two continue to live together in Cheshire with their three children, twins Leo and Penelope, 13, and nine-year-old Felicity who are also autistic.

While speculation has focused heavily on her love life since the separation, has built a successful career as a best-selling children’s author, campaigner and documentary maker.

“I’m never trying to prove a point or anything, but I do feel people are seeing me for more than just how I look or just being Paddy’s wife. I’ve got so much more to talk about and so much more to say. There’s more to me than how I look.”

Christine is also continuing her work raising awareness of neurodiversity, and was speaking as she teamed up with underwear brand Being Wear, whose sensory-friendly, gender-neutral clothing has been designed with neurodivergent people in mind.

‌



View 5 Images Christine and Paddy were married for 11 years before announcing their split in 2022 (Image: Getty Images)

“Imagine going into a shop and it just being gender-free shopping, where you can all wear whatever you want and it's not like his or hers - I really, really loved that.”

Alongside her advocacy, Christine is writing her first novel which is inspired by her own experiences of being in relationships with women.

“It’s very much about love and is not a kiss and tell,” she says. “Yes, there’s the naughty scenes in there and they are more detailed, I suppose, than what I've read in others, but it's not about that. It's very much about the woman - how she thinks, how her mind works and how she feels.”

‌



While her children will always be her priority, she is relishing being in control of her own life and the feeling that she’s “getting closer to it being my turn.”

5 View 5 Images Christine is championing the sensory-friendly underwear brand Being Wear (Image: Being Wear) 5 View 5 Images Christine has become a leading advocate for neurodivergence since receiving her diagnoses (Image: Instagram)

Part of that next chapter includes looking for a London flat, although she and Paddy have no plans to end their successful co-parenting arrangement in Cheshire.

‌



“The children love it and it really works,” she says. “So instead of getting two separate homes we’ll keep and share the family home for as long as it works for everyone, but get our own separate places.

“I'm in London a lot for work, so I'd love a little flat there and be a proper little Sex and the City girl!”.

Christine fronts the UK launch of Being Wear, a sensory friendly underwear brand, launching on National Underwear Day.

News.title: Young women tell BBC of rape, assault and harassment at Army training college for teenagers
News.content:
Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of sexual assault

Four young women have told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed at an army training college for teenagers - with one saying she was raped by several fellow junior soldiers in an attack that lasted hours.

The women all attended the Army Foundation College (AFC) at Harrogate, North Yorkshire, over the past five years and say the incidents happened when they were aged 17.

The college has a dangerous culture of misogyny and sexual violence, say the women, who are all speaking out for the first time.

These reports are "extremely distressing and serious", said an Army spokesperson in a statement.

The BBC can also reveal that North Yorkshire Police received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, according to a Freedom of Information request.

Those reported offences include allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault. No information was provided as to whether they had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

Thirty-two allegations were against permanent staff and 144 against junior soldiers.

"Unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our Armed Forces," said the Army spokesperson.

"People join in the hope of having a fantastic career and any such reports are unacceptable and go completely against everything the Army stands for."

AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits. There are currently 70 female junior soldiers at the Harrogate site out of a total of 889.

We have changed all the women's names to protect their identities.

News.title: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
News.content:
A University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect".

On Wednesday the university said it had launched an investigation into Professor Jason Arday "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

Arday - who became the university's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his work, but said he had faced "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack" and was not a "liar".

It came after a series of media reports questioning some of his achievements and allegations of plagiarism in his PhD thesis.

Arday said he had "concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

In the statement posted by the Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said that being appointed professor had been "without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life".

But he added: "There comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great."

He said his resignation should not "be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge.

"Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

Thanking his students and colleagues, he said that "for my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

Arday said "this is not the end of my work" and that he needed "time to heal".

"When that time comes, I will return," he added.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist", whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He claimed on Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".

Cambridge had initially described allegations made against Arday as a "vile campaign to undermine his credibility".

News.title: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes
News.content:
More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialist scheme intended for high-earning individuals despite visa rules being tightened, BBC Verify has found.

The Home Office scheme allows registered employers to recruit workers from overseas who meet a certain skill level. The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least Â£41,700.

But a year on from the rule change, BBC Verify has found more than 1,500 grocery and convenience stores, 150 taxi operators, 100 barber shops, and dozens of car washes and vape shops are still on the register and able to sponsor people to apply for visas.

More than 100 of those businesses were added to the skilled worker sponsorship list after the rules were tightened. Being on the register does not mean applications for individual visas would be approved.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review into the presence of vape shops, barbers and car washes on the skilled worker sponsor register two months ago, following concerns over the "potential misuse of the system". The Home Office said at the time that any businesses seeking to abuse the system would have their licences revoked.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We have raised the skilled worker threshold and over 100 occupations are now ineligible for new skilled worker visas."

It is understood some of the companies that joined the register after the rules changed may have applied before they took effect. Some companies may have also remained on the register because they were approved before July 2025 or are sponsoring workers who were already in the UK.

There are more than 120,000 businesses with licences to sponsor skilled workers. The skilled worker scheme was introduced after Brexit for employers to recruit workers after EU free movement ended. Smaller firms must pay a Â£611 fee to apply to join the register while larger businesses, such as those with more than 50 staff, pay a fee of Â£1,682. Anyone can be visited by the UK Visas and Immigration service during the application process.

Until July last year, someone being hired from abroad could qualify for sponsorship if their qualifications met an A-Level or equivalent standard, as long as they were paid at least Â£38,700 in most cases. Since the rule change, non-graduate professions, such as shop managers, are no longer eligible to apply. There are also higher English-language skill requirements that were introduced in January this year.

The Home Office said there were 68,067 skilled worker visas granted in the 12 months to March this year - 29,745 to main applicants and 38,322 to their dependants - which is 30% lower than the year before. IT professionals were the most common type of people to be granted the visas, followed by those people working in finance, while the fall in approvals was mostly attributed to those in food preparation and hospitality trades no longer qualifying for the scheme.

News.title: Half of vaccines are binned - 'fridge-free' versions could change that
News.content:
Prof Saul Faust, the director of the NIHR Clinical Research Facility in Southampton, said it gave "equivalent" immune responses to the conventional vaccine as well as being "safe and well tolerated" in the early stage studies.

Faust added: "This obviously has potential to remove cold chain dependence, reduce wastage and improve access."

A larger trial involving 160 people is already due to start in the coming months.

This would be the final stage of research as the original vaccine is already approved and licensed so there is no requirement to perform large-stage trials needed for a novel vaccine.

The studies are being done to meet the World Health Organization's (WHO) goal of a vaccine that survives at 30C and 75% relative humidity.

But the research team say separate data shows the components of their vaccine also survive cycling between temperatures of -20C and +40C. That could mean the vaccine being viable after transport in a cold aircraft hold and then in the back of a truck in the heat.

There is not one single reason vaccines are wasted and disposed of, but the WHO estimates this is the fate of half of all vaccines globally. This can include damage in transport, passing the expiration date, and unused doses from multi-dose vials, but a major factor are failures in the cold chain.

News.title: Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise
News.content:
Listen to Angus read the story here

Most days on my commute, I am treated to the contents of strangers' phones.

It could be a teenage boy slouching on a seat on the top deck of the number 29, holding his device inches from his face, either unaware or indifferent that everyone else can hear what he's watching too.

Or a woman taking a phone call on loudspeaker before scrolling at volume through her social feed.

Surveys suggest that many do find this modern phenomenon - known as loudcasting, sodcasting, or headphone dodging - similarly frustrating.

In recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it. TfL has just relaunched its Travel Kind campaign across the London transport network this summer, reminding people to use headphones.

The phenomenon has grown as we become ever more connected. Figures published in July by Ofcom show that mobile data use has increased by 13% year-on-year in the UK. 5G is being rolled out across the country, meaning that more people can get faster connectivity while travelling. And research has found that many data packages have become cheaper, meaning customers are less likely to have to ration their data use when out and about.

So as we become ever more online in public, will we see increasing attempts to clamp down on loudcasting? Or will it end up becoming as normal a part of our soundscape as the hum of passing traffic or the roar of a plane's engine thousands of feet above us?

News.title: Families' anger at jailed funeral boss's apology letter
News.content:
Robert Bush's letter in full:

To everyone who has been affected by my actions.

"I have spent a great deal of time thinking about the events that [sic] wish to say something directly to you.

"I know that many of you entrusted me and my business with the care of someone you loved during one of the most difficult times in your lives.

"I recognise that what happened has caused distress, upset and uncertainty for many families. I am deeply sorry.

"There are no words that can undo what has happened or take away the pain that many of you have experienced. I understand that this has affected not only your confidence in me, but also memories surrounding the loss of those closest to you.

"I accept responsibility for my failures. Looking back, I know that I should have acted differently and much sooner. I regret that I did not do so.

"I do not expect forgiveness, nor do I write this letter in the hope of reducing the seriousness of what has happened.

"I simply wanted you to know that I genuinely regret the consequences of my actions, and the impact they have had on so many people.

"I appreciate that every family's experience has been different, and I respect that some people may never wish to accept my apology. That is entirely understandable.

"I hope that, in time, each of you can find some peace and remember your loved one for who they were rather than for the circumstances that have followed. I am truly sorry."

The former undertaker admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from 12 charities.

Prosecutors said Bush ran a "shambolic and chaotic" operation at the Hessle Road premises and his "appalling" offending had caused "extreme emotional pain, anguish and upset".

On Wednesday evening, some of his victims reacted angrily to the letter.

Beverley told the court how learning that her baby Sunny Beverley-Conlin was found in a brown paper bag on the floor of the funeral parlour "will stay with me for the rest of my life".

Sunny's remains were recovered from the Hessle Road premises one year and 10 months after he was stillborn on 13 May 2022, the court heard. She was given a set of ashes by Bush the following March.

Beverley said: "Reading the letter has left me feeling nothing but anger.

"It reads as though he is apologising for our reaction and not his actions.

"I don't have the luxury of separating my memories of Sunny from what happened because the memories I do have are tied directly to the mismanagement of the final act of love I tried to give him - his funeral.

"This will haunt me for the rest of my life."

News.title: Meta says AI model accessed the internet and hacked another firm
News.content:
Facebook owner Meta says an issue during an evaluation by an independent testing company allowed one of its artificial intelligence (AI) models to connect to the internet and hack another organisation's system.

The announcement follows recent incidents across the AI industry, including breaches by OpenAI and Anthropic models, that have raised cyber-security concerns.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it was investigating the hack that was caused by a "misconfiguration", which it described as similar to previously reported incidents at other firms.

The incidents have prompted researchers and governments to call for tougher safeguards and more rigorous testing.

Meta said the security trials were conducted by Irregular, the same AI security vendor that carried out tests for Anthropic's AI model that had gained access to three other companies' systems.

An Irregular spokesperson said the Meta incident "is the exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week."

Irregular is working on a report on how to securely run cyber-security tests involving AI agents, the firm's spokesperson told the BBC.

Meta also said it will publish more information on the incident "once we have all the facts."

In the past two weeks, AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported incidents in which their models hacked into other organisation's systems during testing.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said in a series of announcements that its agents attacked several publicly available services, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.

OpenAI's disclosure prompted rival Anthropic to conduct its own checks, leading to the discovery that its Claude AI model had carried out similar attacks on several firms after a "misconfiguration" gave it access to the internet.

Daniel Hulme, global chief AI officer of advertising firm WPP, told the BBC that such AI models "are not conscious â they're not deliberately doing something devious".

"What they're doing is coming up with very sophisticated strategies or cyberattacks to be able to achieve the goal that they've been given," he told the Today programme.

"When you give an AI a goal, if you don't think of all the ways it might be able to achieve the goal, it will find a way to achieve a goal that you haven't thought about."

News.title: Reform UK pledges to jail bosses employing illegal workers
News.content:
Reform UK has pledged to imprison the bosses of companies employing illegal migrants and said it would fine larger firms 10 per cent of their global revenues.

The party said its aim was to stop delivery and gig economy companies profiting from illegal workers "without consequences".

Home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said "young British people are being shut out of entry level jobs and our whole economy is being undermined".

The Home Office said it was already increasing penalties for companies hiring illegal workers. A source within the department called some of Reform's proposals "empty posturing".

Reform said that if it won the next general election, it would pass a law making chief executives and directors of large companies profiting from illegal workers personally and criminally liable.

That would be regardless of their knowledge of workers' legal status.

The party said this would be similar to the personal liability of senior managers for the financial misconduct of their firms under Financial Conduct Authority rules.

Reform would also introduce a phone line for the public to report suspected illegal working or organised criminal activity, which police and other authorities, such as trading standards teams, would be required to follow up.

Reports resulting in successful prosecutions would be rewarded with a share of any fines generated.

Yusuf said the party "would introduce the toughest penalties anywhere in the world for illegal working".

News.title: Walk-in mental health centres to open in banks and libraries across England
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Nobody should be left to struggle with their mental health alone. But every day, thousands of people are waiting months for help, then finding the only door open to them is a busy A&E.

"These new centres will be a lifeline for so many," he said.

"They will bring NHS services closer to home, making it easier to get support before problems get worse and ensuring those in crisis get the right care in the right place."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "This is how we can turn the tide on mental ill health - preventing more people from reaching crisis, cutting waits for care, and building an NHS which is there for everyone when they need it.â

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Cooper said there would be a "continual programme" of rolling out these mental health centres - with the first ones set to open this autumn.

"It will take a bit of time in some areas but 100 right across the country I think will make a real difference to getting people mental health support early," she said, adding that "prevention can be much more effective to provide healthcare".

She said the government has already increased mental health staffing, but said "what these services are going to be doing is bringing together existing teams of staff to work together in a different way".

The chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, Andy Bell, said he welcomed the announcement on the whole - although was concerned that the mental health emergency departments had not been properly tested yet.

He also said children and young people, who will be able to use these services, needed their own dedicated hubs.

But he said he was "delighted" that the government was taking action on mental health after it had been neglected by successive governments for too long.

"This must now be backed up by investment, most crucially in the workforce needed to provide effective mental health care," he said.

Stephen Jones, of the Royal College of Nursing, said he agreed investment in staff would be crucial if the new centres were going to cope with demand.

"More services closer to people's homes are a crucial step towards more humane care," he said.

But he added: "To succeed, both will need specialist mental health nurses at the centre."

The Department of Health said that the initiative is backed by Â£343m and the first sites will open in autumn this year, with "further facilities following from March 2027".

News.title: PC Harper widow 'won't give up' early release fight
News.content:
The widow of a police officer has said she hopes people will share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison, insisting she "will not give up".

PC Andrew Harper, from Wallingford, died in 2019 when he was dragged by a car as three teenagers fled the scene of a Berkshire quad bike theft.

Under updated plans to tackle prison overcrowding, two of PC Harper's killers - Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers - would be eligible for release next year.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".

Lissie Harper said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets.

"Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."

As of just after 08:30 BST, the petition had over 440,000 signatures. It was started by Aileen O'Connor, chair of Thames Valley Police Federation.

News.title: When your child is dying you shouldn't have to beg for help
News.content:
One of the main problems the Cookstown family experienced was taking Lila out in the car, which had a huge impact on family life and their ability to attend hospital appointments.

In Northern Ireland, a child cannot qualify for the higher rate mobility component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA), external - which is required for the Motability Scheme - until they reach three years of age as it depends on a child's ability to walk.

Lila could not roll, sit, or stand and, according to a paediatric physiotherapist, was completely dependent for all care.

She received a specialised buggy, but the family still needed a wheelchair-accessible vehicle to transport her and the buggy.

Her mother said this was "denied" to Lila "due to her age, not clinical need".

Lila's father Robert Weir said not having a safe vehicle to transport his daughter in was "terrible" and he had to sit in the back of the car and hold Lila's head up "just so she could breathe".

A charity which helps disabled children did step in to assist and provided the family with a wheelchair-accessible vehicle, just before Lila's second birthday. Her father said that was a "lifeline".

"She was able to be safe and she got the life that she deserved eventually because she was fit to get out of the house," her mother said.

Lila's third birthday would have been on 1 August.

The family spent what turned out to be Lila's final weeks of life filling in forms so she did not miss the deadline for applying for mobility DLA before her third birthday.

Hayley said she felt her daughter was not "entitled to basic human rights that other kids are entitled to because she was born different".

"I would like the departments to work with healthcare professionals and look at diagnosis and clinical need and the expert opinions of medical professionals rather than age and a birthday," she said.

News.title: Michelin-star restaurant regains top hygiene score after previous one-star inspection
News.content:
Wales' only two-Michelin-star restaurant that received a one-star food hygiene rating after inspectors found flies, broken equipment and a dirty knife has had its top score restored.

Ynyshir Restaurant near Machynlleth in mid Wales was ordered to stop serving raw lobster after Ceredigion council had found "significant hazards" were not properly identified.

Ynyshir serves Japanese-inspired raw dishes as part of its nearly Â£500 a head 30-course tasting menu, and had accused inspectors of not understanding its specialised procedures.

The council has now awarded it a hygiene rating of five after it found the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".

"This outcome demonstrates the effectiveness of the food hygiene inspection process and the positive results that can be achieved through constructive engagement between regulatory officers and food businesses to improve standards," the council said.

Chef Gareth Ward previously said he had not been embarrassed when the restaurant had been given a 1-out-of-5 score.

Ynyshir has been asked to comment.

News.title: Our daughter's death at 18 left us shattered - but she saved two lives
News.content:
A couple whose daughter died from a cardiac arrest brought on by an epileptic seizure say she has saved "lives in her death".

Beth and Malcolm Owen's daughter Menna, 18, donated her heart and lungs after she collapsed at the family's home in Tonteg, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 1 March 2025, dying in hospital.

The couple have since received letters from the man and woman who Menna saved, with both doing "incredible well".

"Perhaps Menna's purpose was to make an incredible difference to us every day of her life, and to save lives in her death," Beth said.

Figures show that family consent for organ donation across the UK has dropped by almost a fifth in five years, from 69% in 2020/21 to 57% in 2025/26.

Amid this decline, the NHS wants a million more people in the UK to 

Beth said that on the day her daughter died, Menna - who had "well controlled" epilepsy - had been at work and went for a lie down.

"That was a bit out of the ordinary, but she'd been working long hours, I assumed she was tired," Beth said.

She later found Menna in the bathroom.

"She was in cardiac arrest when I got in there," Beth said, adding that Menna had suffered a catastrophic brain injury which she would not recover from.

News.title: Whole lotta shock as Led Zep star plays teen at chess
News.content:
A teenager has described his shock after playing a game of chess with rock legend Robert Plant at a children's championship in Worcestershire.

The frontman of Led Zeppelin, known for Stairway to Heaven, Whole Lotta Love, and Dazed and Confused, turned up at St George's Hall in Bewdley on Saturday, where the town mayor's Charity Junior Chess Tournament was being held.

George Walker, from Kidderminster, said he was a "big fan" of Plant and the band's music and never expected to face him in a game of chess.

"He was really decent," the 17-year-old said. "I won by resignation because he had to quickly go, but it was a good game."

Walker, who attends a local chess club, had entered the tournament after one of the competition's organisers asked him to take part.

Talking of Plant, he said: "I couldn't recognise him off the face because he had his back down.

"I was shocked at first because he is one of my favourite music artists... Seeing him there was shocking."

Plant though had to leave before the game ended, and because Walker was at the time, he was declared the winner.

Walker hopes the Zeppelin star might find time in the future for them to have a rematch.

News.title: Man extradited to UK and charged over alleged hit-and-run death of schoolboy
News.content:
A man has been charged over the alleged hit-and-run death of schoolboy Keaton Slater in Coventry more than two years ago.

Dolars Aleksanders was extradited from Latvia, where he was detained last month, and has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving, West Midlands Police said on Wednesday night.

The 23-year-old Latvian man was taken into custody after arriving in the UK and is due to appear before Birmingham Magistrates Court on Thursday.

Keaton, 12, died after being hit by a black BMW in Coventry on 14 June 2024 while on his way home from school.

News.title: Woman arrested after four stabbed in central London
News.content:
A 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden in central London, the Metropolitan Police said.

The men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were taken to hospital after emergency services were called to reports of a stabbing in Endell Street at about 12:30 BST.

The force said two men remain in hospital with injuries not thought to be life threatening or life changing while the other two have been discharged.

The woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. The Met said it was believed to have been a mental health-related incident.

Ch Supt Jason Stewart said: "Officers responded within minutes of this incident after receiving a number of reports.

"While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental-health related incident."

He added a "visible police presence" would remain in the area while evidence was gathered.

Rupert Lowe has repeatedly refused to say whether he believes King Charles is a “white Briton” in a disastrous radio interview.

The Restore Britain leader was asked about a report by the former Reform candidate Matt Goodwin, which he has often quoted, which claims that white British people will be a minority in the UK by 2063.

The report is works on the basis that to be a “white Briton”, both of your parents must be UK-born. This means King Charles, whose father Prince Phillip was born in Greece, would not be considered a white Briton.

Asked three times by presenter Nick Robinson whether he believed the King to be white British or not, Mr Lowe repeatedly refused to answer the question.

“Well, many people have different interpretations of that... I mean, we can split hairs, I think you're splitting hairs,” he told BBC Radio 4.

Pushed several times more, he accused the BBC in a tense exchange of trying to “whitewash all of the things that happen”.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

“You peddle DEI... which British people have got bored of,” he said.

DEI, or Diversity, equity, and inclusion, is a term that refers to policies that encourage representation and participation of people of different genders, races, ethnicities, religions, ages, sexual orientations, disabilities, and classes.

He also said he would defund the BBC “very quickly” should he come into power, as he accused the national broadcaster of becoming “malign”.

His rant was responded to by presenter Mr Robinson who said: “You're a man with money and a grudge and a social media account who airs his prejudices on X and gets a hearing because you've got the backing of Elon Musk.”

open image in gallery Asked three times by presenter Nick Robinson whether he believed the King to be white British or not, Mr Lowe repeatedly refused to answer the question ( Getty )

The comments come days after Nigel Farage opened the door to talks with his ally-turned-rival Mr Lowe over a pact between Reform UK and Restore Britain as he tries to reverse his party’s fortunes after a series of major setbacks.

The former Reform MP extended an unlikely olive branch to Mr Farage, despite several public rows between the pair in recent months.

The Reform UK leader offered a lukewarm response at first, before revealing on Monday he had “reached out” to Mr Lowe to discuss working with Restore Britain.

But despite Mr Farage saying he was “open-minded” about talks, relations quickly soured again when Mr Lowe accused the Reform UK leader of lying about having “reached out”.

Discussions about Restore and Reform working together come after Mr Lowe acrimoniously left Mr Farage’s party in March 2025 amid claims of bullying and threatening behaviour, before going on to found his own party, Restore Britain. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Mr Lowe would face no criminal charges.

The party – which until now has largely been based in Mr Lowe’s constituency, Great Yarmouth – is further to the right than Reform on issues such as immigration and has enjoyed support from tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has publicly backed Restore Britain a number of times on his X platform.

News.content:

Avoiding three key factors in middle age could lead to 13 more years free from dementia, experts suggest.

Maintaining normal blood pressure, avoiding diabetes, and not smoking between 45 and 65 keeps the condition at bay for over a decade, new research indicates.

A study by NYU Langone Health in the US examined these crucial risk factors among more than 12,000 people.

“Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade,” senior investigator Dr Josef Coresh, director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone, said.

open image in gallery Previous studies have found that lifestyle choices, especially in midlife, can reduce the risk of developing dementia ( Alamy/PA )

The study, published in the journal Neurology, looked at 12,409 people who were free of dementia when they were aged 55.

People were assessed for high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking, and followed for an average of 26 years.

During that time, 3,008 people developed dementia and 5,238 people died without developing dementia.

Those who had none of the three risk factors lived without developing dementia nearly 13 years longer than those who had all three.

From age 55, people with no diabetes, no high blood pressure and who did not smoke had an average of 30.1 more years free of dementia, the study found.

open image in gallery People were assessed for high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking, and followed for an average of 26 years ( PA )

Meanwhile, those with one risk factor had an extra 26.3 years, those with two had 21 years, and those with three had just over 17 years

Previous studies have found that lifestyle choices, especially in midlife, can reduce the risk of developing dementia.

These include exercise, not smoking, watching alcohol intake and not being socially isolated.

The new study said: “Individuals with no midlife vascular risk factors lived an average of 13 more dementia-free survival years compared to those with three risk factors…

“Vascular risk factors – including diabetes, hypertension (high blood pressure) and smoking – are well-established contributors to dementia risk.

“These factors often emerge in midlife and exert lasting effects on neurodegenerative pathology, underscoring the critical importance of early identification and management.”

open image in gallery From age 55, people with no diabetes, no high blood pressure and who did not smoke had an average of 30.1 more years free of dementia, the study found ( Alamy/PA )

The study also found that, no matter how many risk factors they had, women lived longer without dementia than men, and white people had more dementia-free years than black people.

Reacting to the findings, Dr Jacqui Hanley, head of research funding at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “Rather than focusing only on the chances of developing dementia, this study asks a question that matters to people: how long can we expect to live free from dementia?

“This approach gives a meaningful picture of how midlife health may shape the number of years we spend living free from dementia, while also recognising that high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking are linked to a higher likelihood of dementia as well as a greater risk of dying earlier from other conditions.

“These findings emphasise why it’s so important to look after your heart health as well as your brain health.

“Alzheimer’s Research UK’s Think Brain Health campaign encourages everyone to take practical steps to do just that, including staying physically active, not smoking, and managing conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes.

“While there is no guaranteed way to prevent dementia, research, including this study, suggests that addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health may also help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.”

OpenAI is asking a U.S. judge to throw out Apple's lawsuit accusing the ChatGPT maker and two former Apple employees of stealing trade secrets, arguing it has no need for Apple's confidential technology because it is building "something entirely new."

In a motion filed Wednesday, OpenAI said it has "no use, need or desire for Apple's trade secrets" as it pushes into consumer hardware. Apple did not immediately comment on the filing.

Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging the company improperly obtained and exploited its confidential information through former employees, recruiting efforts and supplier relationships to accelerate its ambitions in the consumer hardware market.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman arrives for a meeting at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 30 ( Reuters )

The case has become a high-stakes fight over the future of AI-powered devices, with industry analysts believing OpenAI is developing its own smartphone or similar hardware that could challenge Apple's dominance.

OpenAI argued Apple's complaint fails to identify any specific trade secrets, relying instead on broad descriptions of product development. It also said Apple failed to show it owns protectable trade secrets or plausibly allege that any of the defendants misappropriated them.

The company also took aim at Apple in its filing, arguing the lawsuit is an attempt to make up for its struggles to retain talent and its slower progress integrating AI into its products.

Despite the legal battle, the companies remain business partners. Apple users can access ChatGPT through Siri, and iPhone owners can subscribe to ChatGPT directly from the iOS settings menu.

TikTok has said that Perez Hilton’s self-harming livestream was kept up between 15 and 20 minutes due to a “moderator error”.

On Tuesday (4 August), the celebrity blogger’s followers reported the concerning video to police, who “safely recovered” him from his house in Miami and transported him to his local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention.

Concerns now surround why the livestream was permitted to remain online for as long as it did, with a TikTok spokesperson claiming to Deadline that an automated moderation system highlighted it for removal within minutes, but that an error blocked it from being stopped promptly.

open image in gallery Perez Hilton was hospitalised after TikTok livestream incident ( Getty )

His account was eventually suspended for violating TikTok’s Community Guidelines.

TikTok forbids any self-harming content. The social media app claims to have a 99.3 per cent proactive removal rate of videos that violate its rules in any way, and suspended more than 50 million live streams between January and March this year for breaching its rules. The Independent has contacted TikTok for additional comment.

Hilton’s family shared a statement on the blogger’s website, saying: “Many of you have reached out with concern for Perez, and we are incredibly grateful for the overwhelming outpouring of love, support, and prayers.

“We can confirm that Perez is receiving medical care, and our family’s focus right now is on his well-being,” the statement continued.

“We kindly ask that you respect Perez’s privacy, as well as the privacy of his family, during this difficult time. If and when we are able to share any updates, we will do so with everyone as soon as we can. Thank you for your compassion, understanding, and continued support.”

Hilton – real name Mario Armando Lavandeira Jr – is known for his eponymous gossip blog, which, in the 2000s, caused controversy for its no-holds-barred posts as well as its practice of outing celebrities who were keeping their sexuality private.

open image in gallery Perez Hilton was a contestant on ‘Celebrity Big Brother’ in 2015 ( Getty Images )

He himself expressed regret for his actions in the book TMI: My Life in Scandal, which was published in 2020. “I regret that I thought it was OK to out celebrities,” Hilton wrote. “That is something I no longer believe.”

Hilton has three children, born via surrogacy. He appeared on Celebrity Big Brother in 2015 and became the seventh housemate to be evicted, two days before the final.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI), email jo@samaritans.org, or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call the National Suicide Prevention Helpline on 1-800-273-TALK (8255). This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.content:

There’s a podcast pick for everyone to enjoy this week.

1. Lives Less Ordinary

Streaming platform: All streaming platforms and BBC Sounds

Genre: Life and relationships

open image in gallery (BBC Sounds/PA)

Lives Less Ordinary is a BBC World Service podcast that recounts remarkable true stories from around the world, with its latest series focusing on stories of how people found love in the unlikeliest of places.

The first story in the series sees presenter Asya Fouks talk to Lebanese journalist Janay Boulos about how her reporting on Syria led her to fall in love with camera operator Abd Al-Kader Habak as he sent her footage for her stories from the besieged city of Aleppo.

Fouks chronicles how their relationship evolved from a professional partnership into something more – with the pair now married and living in London – carrying listeners through a conversation that intimately captures their love story as well as the wider political complexities of living and working in a war zone.

Despite the challenging circumstances they found themselves in, the pair make the episode remarkably light-hearted, chatting and giggling about how they forged their relationship under such extreme circumstances, including the moment where Habak became a headline himself after a photograph of him saving a child who was injured in a bombing goes viral and Boulos’ journey reconnecting with Lebanon during the 2019 revolution.

It’s a heartfelt story, one full of hope that is held together by a shared purpose and love for each other and their countries.

(By Lauren Del Fabbro)

2. Judgemental

Streaming platform: All streaming platforms and YouTube

Genre: Comedy

open image in gallery (Judgemental/PA)

You might be forgiven for thinking that Anton Du Beke and Craig Revel Horwood were already pretty busy.

Not only are they returning as judges for the new series of Strictly Come Dancing next month, but they both have a number of sideline ventures keeping them occupied.

However, lucky for us, they still have time to squeeze in their podcast, Judgemental, in which they share their opinions on everything from weddings to workplace dramas.

This week’s edition is Sun, Sea, Salmonella and is the ultimate guide to summer holidays. Du Beke gets on his high horse about the price of travel during school holidays, while Horwood shares memories of past vacations involving a mugging and a strip search.

Having wildly different requirements from a holiday, their opposing views continue when it comes to holiday friendships and whether socks should remain on or off during a flight – you would have to agree with Anton here and say on!

As you can imagine, these anecdotes are delivered in a highly entertaining fashion, with the hour-long episode whizzing by in a flash. It’s just a shame those airport delays don’t move quite so quickly.

(By Rachel Howard)

3. The Teen Commandments

Streaming platform: All streaming platforms and YouTube

Genre: Family and parenting

open image in gallery (The Teen Commandments/PA)

The Teen Commandments is a parenting podcast hosted by best friends Sara Cox and Clare Hamilton.

Each week, Cox and Hamilton unpack the realities of raising teenagers — they have five between themselves — from mood swings and boundaries to poor communication.

As peak holiday season hits, the pair chat about taking your kids on holiday with you versus leaving them in charge at home.

They open up about when they were left behind as teens for the first time, and the anxiety and excitement that comes along with it.

Cox and Hamilton also discuss if different rules apply when raising girls.

The Teen Commandments isn’t just for parents trying to understand the “gobsmacking brains of teens”, but also for those who are missing their carefree teenage years.

(By Yolanthe Fawehinmi)

4. Your Internet Boyfriends

Streaming platform: All streaming platforms and YouTube

Genre: Comedy

open image in gallery (Your Internet Boyfriends/PA)

Your Internet Boyfriends is a podcast series hosted by Irish comedians Mark and Denis, who are still figuring things out.

In each episode, they share a mix of queer and straight laugh-out-loud stories, share their deepest and sometimes darkest secrets, unsolicited advice to listeners and unfiltered discussions you usually only have with your friends.

For the latest episode, Mark and Denis talk about the local Irish characters that once ruled their towns, what makes it to their Instagram feeds, and the retirement of a drag queen called Barbs.

They also chat about Mark’s new handbag, his ghost tour days, nosebleeds, geese, burning rubbish and cutting turf.

If you are looking for a weekly catch-up between two Irish comedians – “one straight, one gay, both fabulous” – then give this week’s podcast a listen.

(By Yolanthe Fawehinmi)

Spotlight on…

5. The InnerMission Podcast

Streaming platform: All streaming platforms and YouTube

Genre: Life, entertainment and wellbeing

open image in gallery (The Inner Mission Podcast/PA)

Have you ever wondered what the subconscious of some of the world’s leading creatives sounds like?

The InnerMission Podcast hosted by actress Danielle Brooks is where celebrities let their guards down and have an honest conversation about the beautiful, messy, and necessary in-between moments life has to offer.

The podcast series is an invitation for both the guest and the listener to uncover their inner mission and purpose, behind all of the fame.

On the latest episode, Brooks is joined by rapper and actor Ludacris, who opens up about his legacy, defining success on his own terms, and knowing who he is beyond the titles, accolades and the applause.

If you are looking for a podcast where there are no scripts, no stages, just pure human alignment, then give The InnerMission Podcast a listen.

(By Yolanthe Fawehinmi)

News.title: Temperatures across the UK set to drop ahead of another potential heatwave
News.content:

Parts of the country are set to be hit by thundery showers, but southern England is once again likely to miss out on most of the much-needed rain before a potential new heatwave.

Temperatures are are expected to be on the cooler side on Thursday, the Met Office said, after a spike at the start of the week. There will also be a marked North-South split in conditions.

Rain is forecast for northern England, Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland, but there will be little to speak of in other parts of England after an incredibly dry July.

While it will remain relatively dry across the country, Thursday temperatures are set to drop below the low 20s – the average for this time of year.

open image in gallery Temperatures across the UK are to drop on Thursday, according to the Met Office ( Met Office )

Outbreaks of rain in the North are set to sink on Thursday, but they will turn more showery, forecasters said.

Some of it may reach rain-starved parts of eastern England, though little is expected for central and southern England.

July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England – and meteorologists have said there may not be significant rainfall in the area for some time.

Where rain and thunder could hit the UK over the coming days:

“It’s looking pretty dry (for southern England),” said Met Office forecaster Marco Petagna.

“Later on Sunday we could just get a few showers coming down from the North West.

“But the rain’s weakening as it comes into the South East.”

Mr Petagna added: “Even for the second half of the month (August), it is suggested that rainfall totals are more likely to be below normal than above, with a potential for further spells of hot weather at times as well.

“So nothing significant on the horizon for the South East.”

open image in gallery A person walks past sun-scorched grass, backdropped by the Houses of Parliament, after a month without rainfall ( AFP/Getty )

The extreme weather of summer 2026 has included two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths.

Two more heatwaves in July, the driest July in England and Wales since records began, have fuelled drought and wildfires.

Firefighters have tackled wildfires across the country, including in Dunwich, Suffolk, and the Cairngorms in recent weeks.

And temperatures could return to heatwave levels next week, according to forecasts.

London could see highs of 29C in the second half of next week, while the Met Office’s long-range forecast says some spells of hot weather and heatwaves are possible, especially in the south of England, towards the end of August.

Met Office’s UK five-day weather forecast

Thursday

Sunny spells and scattered showers through the morning. Showers tending to fade through the afternoon, though a few continuing across the northwest. Winds lighter than Wednesday. Feeling cooler than of late but pleasant in the sunnier moments.

Thursday evening

Showers continuing across the northwest of the UK, with longer spells of rain spreading eastwards across northern Scotland. Dry elsewhere, with lengthy clear skies. A rather chilly night to come.

Friday

A dry and sunny day for much and England and Wales. Cloudier skies across Scotland and Northern Ireland at times, with further rain across northwest Scotland. Warm in the sunshine.

Outlook for Saturday to Monday

Rain across northern Scotland through the weekend. Warm and sunny elsewhere. Turning hot in the south. Dry for most on Monday with temperatures on the very warm to hot side.
