Sports.title: Newcastle appoint Jaissle as Howe's successor
Sports.content:
Newcastle have appointed Matthias Jaissle as their new head coach following Eddie Howe's exit.

The German has signed a four-year deal with Newcastle, who paid £9.5m (€11m) compensation to Saudi side Al Ahli, whom Jaissle led to consecutive Asian Champions League crowns over the last two years.

Jaissle has been with his new squad since the weekend and his first match in charge will be a pre-season friendly against Valencia at the Mestalla on Saturday.

"When Newcastle United comes your way, you take notice," Jaissle said.

"The ambition of the club, the vision for the future and the opportunity ahead made this an incredibly compelling place to be. I have followed the club's journey closely in recent years and the progress that has been made is clear for everyone to see.

"I am incredibly excited about the future. I fully and unreservedly believe in this project, the ambition and the direction the club is taking. There is a clear vision, strong leadership and an exceptional platform to build on."

Before his successful spell in Saudi Arabia, Jaissle won two Austrian Bundesliga titles and a domestic cup with Red Bull Salzburg, while also leading them to the UEFA Champions League knockout stages for the first time in their history.

Newcastle described Jaissle as the standout candidate following a "thorough, rigorous and confidential" recruitment process, highlighting his track record of developing players, building high-intensity teams and his alignment with the club's long-term ambitions.

"His track record of success, leadership qualities and relentless drive to improve make him an exceptional fit for Newcastle United," said club CEO David Hopkinson.

Jaissle outlines Newcastle style and 'values'

Newcastle head coach Matthias Jaissle speaking to the club's website:

"They were stressful days, it's behind us now but there were really good honest conversations with the decision makers at Newcastle - and obviously, overall there is only excitement.

"Joining this marvellous club, with this fan base, is something special and a privilege.

"The Premier League is something special by itself, but joining this club is even more special. With that fan base, with that passion the supporters show for the club, it's really interesting to be part of it.

"It comes as a big privilege, but with big responsibility too. I will do my best to live up to it.

"The timing is not easy, it's a challenge but we've said to the staff members we need to really engage and use these three weeks before Liverpool in the best possible way.

"Control the controllables and if everyone is pulling in the same direction - players, staff and fans - it's going to be a really interesting and successful season.

"My football is front-footed, aggressive, vertical in our approach - I think that's a perfect fit to Newcastle, and we've just talked to the staff members about the three values I have always had: trust, respect and pure commitment."

Image: Jaissle has previously managed RB Salzburg

The 38-year-old German played for Hoffenheim before embarking on a coaching career that took him to Denmark and into an academy role at Red Bull Salzburg. His first senior job was at FC Liefering, moving on to the top job at Salzburg in the summer of 2021.

Jaissle won the double in his first season and retained the league in his second. He worked with Karim Adeyemi and Benjamin Sesko at Salzburg, competing in the Champions League, before moving on to Al Ahli in the Saudi Pro League in 2023.

He has spent the past three years there, winning the Saudi Super Cup in Hong Kong last year. But before that he spoke to Sky Sports as part of our Future of Football series for an illuminating discussion of his ideas and how he saw the game progressing.

Read our full feature on Jaissle's philosophy and inspirations here.

Sports.title: Fifa insists Gianni Infantino will remain president after Rabat crisis meeting
Sports.content:
Fifa on Wednesday night confirmed that Gianni Infantino will remain as president after a meeting of its senior executives in Rabat.

In a statement which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team.

Infantino had spent the day in talks with Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, and chief legal officer, Emilio García Silvero, during which he expressed his determination to stay on in the face of mounting criticism from Uefa and the North American confederation Concacaf, both of which have called for a review of Fifa’s governance.

In another indication that he plans to carry on as before, Infantino will fly to Colombia on Thursday to attend the inauguration of the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in the city of Cali.

“Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the Fifa secretary general and members of the Fifa management board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for Fifa president Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 Fifa member associations,” Fifa said in a statement. “In turn, the Fifa president reiterated his full support for the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa administration for their necessary and outstanding work in the delivery of his vision.

“It was discussed and agreed that the processes, communications and interactions between the Fifa president, the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa management board that support the delivery of this vision can and should always be continuously improved in terms of their effectiveness and efficiency.

“In this regard, Fifa’s top management is fully confident that the outcomes of today’s meeting will strengthen Fifa’s governance, help restore confidence in the organisation and enable us to prepare for the major events and challenges ahead in a united and transparent manner while continuing our mission to develop the game around the world.”

While acknowledging that Infantino has apologised for his role in the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, which would have seen 21% of Fifa’s commercial rights sold to private investors, the statement also insisted that Fifa will not tolerate further criticisms of its governance.

Uefa is unlikely to be cowed however, with the European governing body continuing to search for a candidate to stand against Infantino in the presidential election next March, which will also take place in Rabat.

“Mistakes made were acknowledged,” the statement continued. “It was agreed that it was not the intention for the Fifa council and Fifa member associations to feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently. It was further acknowledged that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media.

“In a separate letter to the Fifa council and Fifa member associations, an apology was made for these errors together with a commitment to ensure they do not happen again. A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the Fifa council at its next scheduled meeting.

“As previously communicated, the FFE proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa member associations and the Fifa council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, it was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.

“There are always lessons to be learned, and Fifa will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework.

“Fifa will work closely with the relevant stakeholders to examine how it can further support the development of the game through the Fifa Forward programme for the benefit of Fifa’s 211 member associations, the confederations and the regional associations.”

Infantino and Grafström appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Women’s Africa Cup of Nations group game on Wednesday as a show of solidarity, having also written a jointly signed letter to Fifa council members and vice-presidents echoing the Fifa statement.

Sports.title: ‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakaway
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino held talks about rebranding the ill-fated European breakaway competition the “Fifa Super League”, with negotiations going as far as the term sheet for an agreement that would have changed the face of European football.

The term sheet, whose full contents can be revealed for the first time, is dated October 2020 and proposes renaming any new competition under Fifa’s branding. It outlines the extent to which Infantino’s administration were implicated in a scheme that caused widespread revulsion among fans and excluded clubs in April 2021. It also reveals that Fifa was prepared to sideline its member associations in pushing plans to cut back the number of international windows and outlines how global football’s governing body would have been given special governance and political rights with a “golden share”.

In a week when football is reeling from the fallout after Infantino scrapped his plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, the document shows Fifa’s leadership was deeply involved in another attempt to put the sport’s major competitions under corporate control. It sets out a partnership of at least 12 years between Fifa and the Super League and proposes a joint venture that would have run its commercial operations.

The document also proposes that an iteration of Fifa’s expanded Club World Cup, referred to as the “global club competition”, would be held annually over an enshrined three-week period and tied directly to the Super League. That tournament would have been a straight knockout competition rather than the group-based version that relaunched in 2025. While the term sheet states that the new tournaments would have to be passed by Fifa’s annual congress and the Fifa council, federations around the world are understood to have been bypassed in the plan’s formation.

Infantino was among a number of Fifa staff involved in the project and is understood to have been fully aware of its progression. The term sheet says the founding clubs “want to agree the terms of a partnership” between the Super League and Fifa, leading to the creation of the two competitions. It follows an initial proposal to Fifa by the breakaway clubs, also seen by the Guardian, that sketches the framework for a potential agreement. While non-binding, a term sheet is generally the precursor to a definitive contract and suggests discussions between Fifa and the Super League’s creators were nearing a conclusion at the time.

It is unclear whether Infantino and Fifa progressed their role in the project beyond the term-sheet stage. After a version of the scheme was infamously launched without Fifa’s direct involvement in April 2021, ultimately scrapped following large-scale protests, Infantino addressed Uefa’s congress in Montreux saying his organisation could “only strongly disapprove the creation of the Super League”. Multiple sources have stated that an earlier conversation with the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, convened by a third party, hastened Fifa’s president distancing himself from the new venture. Infantino is understood to have told associates afterwards that he had no wish to work against football’s institutions.

Yet the evidence of Fifa’s outline agreement with the Super League, coupled with Infantino’s disastrous Football Forward Enterprise scheme, casts doubt on that assertion and suggests multiple attempts to reshape the game without consulting its most important stakeholders. The league would have contained 15 permanent members and five clubs qualifying from existing competitions. It also commits to creating a women’s equivalent, using the same clubs, by an unspecified date. The term sheet refers to Fifa under the name “WO1”, which is also the name used in the British army for a high-ranking officer.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino later changed tack in relation to a European breakaway. Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/Reuters

In a section outlining the agreement’s key components, it says the Super League “is open to discuss naming the competition WO1 SL”. It also confirms Fifa would be “granted a preferred equity stake in the Super League”, which would give it decision-making capability on format changes, calendar alterations, distribution of solidarity money and the appointment of a chief executive for the competition.

Senior figures within European football are understood to have been shocked by the plan to drastically shrink the number of international windows, squeezing them into two fortnight-long spaces each year. Member associations, many of whom are being courted for support by Infantino as he battles to save his tenure this week, may have lost the commercial opportunities available from added visibility for their national teams and found themselves at the behest of a privately run club competition.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A separate point in the earlier proposal also notes “reduction of leagues” as a point for discussion. The term sheet states that “a new international match calendar” devised by Fifa, the Super League and “other relevant stakeholders” would be reviewed and implemented with Fifa’s agreement.

Clubs participating in the Super League would have been required to join the World Football Club Association (WFCA), which was a short-lived representative body launched by the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez, in 2019. Real were key drivers of the Super League scheme and only closed the door on the project when announcing an agreement with Uefa in February this year.

Fifa’s close proximity to the Super League proposal adds to the growing number of privately backed ventures brought to the table by Infantino during his 10-year reign. In 2018 he pressed the case for a $25bn offer from SoftBank, the Japanese institution, to create an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. Close allies within Fifa are understood to have cautioned him against the plan, which failed to gain support after opposition from Europe.

Fifa was approached for comment.

Sports.title: How to fix Fifa: what can be done to salvage football’s beleaguered governing body?
Sports.content:
1) Split the governing body up

How can an organisation that runs the biggest sporting event in the world also be the one that sets the rules for the entire game? We saw the reality of such a conflict at the recent World Cup as Fifa ran roughshod over its rulebook – be it over the length of suspensions or the duration of half-time – in an attempt to generate more attention for its competition. One person with extensive knowledge of the inside workings of Fifa puts it like this: “They have shown that they will bend the rules to make them more money. This is a big conflict of interest. Not only should the commercial and the regulatory parts of Fifa be separated, but so should the development part and possibly one or two others as well.”

According to Miguel Maduro, a former chair of Fifa’s governance committee and now one of the leading critics of the organisation, the creation of different corporate entities – even if they ultimately came under its umbrella – would allow for different priorities to take hold. “There would have to be a Chinese wall between these entities and they would have to have different incentives,” he says. “Those who are seeking to maximise commercial income should not be dependent on the regulatory rules and those working on the regulatory side should not be influenced by commercial considerations.”

One insider notes that Gianni Infantino’s aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme would have created such a separation “but for completely the wrong reasons”.

2) Introduce external regulation

The least sexy word in sport might be necessary if a new Fifa – answerable to nobody bar the courts – is to be expected to follow its new rules. “Change needs to be imposed from the outside. It won’t happen from the inside,” says Maduro. He shares the belief with other critics that it would be necessary to create a new equivalent to Wada, the global anti-doping body. It would hold sporting organisations to account on rules related to governance.

“There’s so much money swirling around in football it could easily be funded,” says one Fifa-watcher. The question is under whose auspices the new body would be created. “One way is to do something at the level of the EU,” Maduro says. “Other countries could join, perhaps the UK for example, and that could then evolve into a world sports agency that would exist to review ethical issues and compliance of the sports associations.”

In this context it is perhaps worth noting that Uefa, which is leading the protests against Infantino’s FFE plan, has in recent years been moving closer to Brussels. Meanwhile another body, the European Leagues, has called on the EU’s executive, the European Commission, to intervene over another Infantino plan: to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams. The commission, it said, “should take the necessary action to protect fair competition and ensure compliance with the principles already set out by the court of justice of the EU”.

3) Defang the president

As has been proven by the FFE affair, where the whole scheme was apparently devised without the knowledge of anyone outside Infantino’s office, Fifa’s president has too much power. “The president was not supposed to control the administration, but then he began to control the administration,” Maduro says. “Then the Fifa council was supposed to control the president and be involved in the real big decisions outside the congress, and they weren’t. At the political level itself you need checks and balances.”

One suggestion on limiting executive power would be to remove the president’s power to determine funding. The governance expert Mark Pieth has an alternative proposal, one he says was once mooted by the president of Uefa, Aleksander Ceferin. It would see the heads of Fifa’s six continental confederations taking turns at being president.

“It’s not an outrageous idea,” Pieth says. “I am Swiss and it happens in my country. Seven ministers take turns being the president, but their tenure lasts one year and it’s clear who the next president is because they go around in order. The effect is nobody gets really powerful. Then you ask yourself, well, why would a Fifa president need power anyway? He’s there to organise matters.”

View image in fullscreen Uefa’s Aleksander Ceferin (left) once floated a plan for heads of Fifa’s six continental confederations to take turns at being president. Photograph: Fernando Calistro/AP

4) Greater transparency

For campaigners looking to hold Fifa to account over the world body’s existing commitments, such as human rights, a lack of transparency over decision-making and the existing appeals process are longstanding frustrations.

Equally, what Fifa does with the money it generates and distributes to its member associations can be opaque. Nick McGeehan, the director and co-founder of the not-for-profit Fair Square, has frequently come up against the limits of transparency within Fifa. “Where are the audited accounts?” he asks.

“Fifa have a development budget that is equal to many big development agencies, but not only is there no needs analysis in terms of how that money is distributed but there is literally no evidence of any audits. Go on their website and you can find all sorts of data about what money is spent, but if you actually wanted to verify what that money is being spent on, it’s impossible.”

McGeehan notes that greater transparency would also involve engaging more with the media. “It seems like Infantino only calls a press conference once every four years,” he says. “It shows an authoritarian state-style distrust of the media and a concomitant lack of transparency.”

5) Rethink development

“Fifa is a not-for-profit organisation – the money it makes is reinvested in football.” This phrase has become something of a mantra under Infantino and following the $15bn (£11.2m) generated by this year’s World Cup, each member nation can expect to receive $8m between 2027 and 2030. But not only is there a lack of scrutiny over how the money is spent, the nature of the distribution itself is questionable.

“It’s an issue that one country, one vote is combined with giving everyone the same amount of money,” says the Fifa-watcher. “The money is distributed in proportion to votes, which is completely wrong because Montserrat and Gibraltar have very different needs to Nigeria or India. It’s amazing that he didn’t look to even try and tweak that.”

With money neither distributed according to need nor determined by strategic goals to grow participation in the game, Fifa is undermining its own aims, the critic says. “If Fifa were to be judged on results, then football is more Eurocentric now than it was 20 years ago. You can expand the World Cup, that’s easy. They claim it’s development but if you get into the nitty-gritty it can be a negative. Associations spend all their money on the men’s national team, on a European coach, and there’s nothing spent on the grassroots or technical development.”

View image in fullscreen The recent World Cup generated $15bn but there is a lack of scrutiny over how the money gets spent. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

6) Switch the electorate

The steady funnel of funds shared with associations big and small has kept Infantino popular with his electorate, the heads of his 211 member associations. A change in who gets a say in Fifa’s decisions might be another way to achieve more effective governance.

“When I am at a Fifa meeting and I look around the table, I see very few people who have direct experience of either playing the game, or being a coach or an executive at a club,” says one senior football figure. “I see very few people who actually understand the day-to-day of football.”

The overwhelmingly male makeup of the Fifa electorate is another fact at glaring odds with the real world, while supporters are, as ever, not invited to the party. Ashish Prashar, a political consultant who regularly engages with Fifa on the game’s social responsibilities, says: “What we need is confederations to get together and form a new entity to solidify the game with the values that serve the people. The biggest item for that entity must be fan ownership of the game. The World Cup and its surrounding events should involve the public in its decision making whether that’s fan groups, fan ambassadors or elections for fans.”

For Maduro, a change in the electorate could then unlock further progress. “Currently you have voting syndicates at Fifa, which creates a huge degree of voting control,” he says. “You need to force new mechanisms of representation, and be creative in finding solutions to bring in people that have so far been absent. If you create a diverse electorate that, by itself, will create a mechanism of checks and balances that can help to lead to better decision-making in the interests of football and all its stakeholders.”

Fifa was approached for comment.

Sports.title: Alessia Russo: ‘When you join the club, you take on a part of Arsenal and the love’
Sports.content:
Arms hooked over the bar at the front of the bus, sunglasses on, a drink in one hand and the other pointed towards the fans as she vibed along to the music and joined in with the singing and chanting, Alessia Russo was having a blast.

“I had the time of my life that day,” says the Arsenal forward of the 9km parade through the red smoke-filled streets of north London after Arsenal men’s Premier League triumph and Arsenal women’s Champions Cup success.

It has been a running joke among fans to refer to the 27-year-old as a “childhood Gooner”, a joke which was turbo-charged when the shirt a very small Russo was wearing in a family photo with the FA Cup was Photoshopped from a Manchester United one into an Arsenal one.

While she may not have been a childhood Gooner, she’s fast becoming an adult one.

“I came to Arsenal and I wasn’t an Arsenal fan, but since I’ve joined the club and seen the people around the place, it’s impossible to not become a part of Arsenal and to feel like I support Arsenal,” she says. “I want them to do well, I’m backing them every way, and then the parade was just one of the most amazing things I’ve ever experienced. The fans, the atmosphere, the celebrating the men winning the Prem, something that they’d worked so hard for so many years, I was just soaking it in, having fun and enjoying myself.

“It was just a really really special day. It was nice to experience it with the likes of Lotte [Wubben-Moy] and Leah [Williamson] who are proper Gooners, but I think when you come to Arsenal, and I’m speaking for myself here, you kind of take on a part of it and really start to understand and absorb their love for Arsenal. I definitely feel that and it’s really nice to feel like you’re a part of something like that.

“You pick out moments where you win trophies as the main ones that stand out within your career but that will definitely always stand out for me.”

There were faces everywhere, on every balcony, rooftop, bollard and traffic light, of all ages, races and religions. Young boys, but also, in contrast to the Arsenal parades of the 90s and noughties, so many young girls. Cultivating and supporting that fresh generation of girls interested in watching and playing the game is something Russo is incredibly passionate about.

View image in fullscreen Top: The Arsenal team drive past fans with the Women’s Champions Cup trophy in May. Photograph: Steven Paston/PA

Above: Fans celebrate Arsenal men’s and women’s success during the club’s victory parade. Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/Alamy

That’s the reason she launched her own foundation earlier this year and why she helped launch the fifth year of Starling Bank’s Kick On initiative, which partners local businesses with girls teams desperately in need of sponsorship and subsidises the front of shirt sponsorship.

According to Starling – which commissioned surveys of 1,000 adult female football players, 1,010 11-17 female players, 501 small- and medium-sized business leaders and 1,092 grassroots football coaches – nearly every grassroots female football club (97%) said their team needed more funds, with opportunities for girls suffering as a result.

The survey also found that 76% of female players said they will have to drop out of their team or the sport altogether if more funding isn’t secured in the next five years and 40% of female players said their team doesn’t get the same amount of funding as male teams.

“They are quite damning statistics, which is such a shame considering the growth that we see in the women’s game,” says Russo. “Over the last five or six years, the growth has just been incredible, but there’s still work to do at the bottom to build it up.”

The risk is that women’s football loses its momentum and misses out on great players coming into the pathway.

“I always say you never want to miss out on the next Leah Williamson or Lotte Wubben-Moy, you don’t want to miss out on talented young players just because they haven’t got a local team or the team that they were at folds,” she says. “It seems like such an easy fix as teams don’t need much, but obviously it isn’t because it’s still a problem.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I look back on all the people that I met through my grassroots journey and every single one of them played a part in my career, and I’m still friends with many of them. If local businesses can invest in one team, you never know, you might help produce a superstar who goes on to have an incredible career who will always remember you being a part of it. There’s more to it than just investment, it’s that you can really have a say in a core part of these young girls’ journeys and lives.”

View image in fullscreen Russo scored key goals in Champions League last season, including against Chelsea. Photograph: Harvey Murphy/News Images/Alamy

With no major international women’s tournament this year, Russo has enjoyed a rare summer off, where she has had the chance to focus on these broader issues she’s passionate about, as well as getting in some much-needed rest.

“It was really important that I did have some proper downtime,” she says. “Over the last few years, the minutes and tournaments have really increased, so I needed to look after my body and get myself in a good place mentally. I shut down for about two-and-a-half weeks and just enjoyed time with friends and family, which was lovely, but by the end of it, I was ready to start exercising again, I didn’t know what to do with myself.

“I quite enjoy training on my own over the summer, you get to know your best routines and habits. I often go on holiday with my family too and train out there on the family holiday, which is nice because everyone wants to get involved. I just took time for myself too, being a normal 27-year-old girl, going on holidays. I went to the England v Panama game in New York and got to be a fan and be around that buzz of the World Cup and I had Toonie’s [England teammate Ella Toone] hen do and wedding, which was amazing”.

View image in fullscreen After a few months off, Russo is back at Arsenal for pre-season training. Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

Russo had a standout year in 2025-26, many believe her game moved up a level for club and country. How does she reflect on it after some time off?

“I’m obviously pleased with my season for Arsenal and England from a personal point of view but, ultimately, I’ll always judge it on the trophies that we win,” she says.

“We’ve learned a lot as a team over the last couple of years at Arsenal, but are really hungry for the new season. We’ve made it quite clear that we want to do everything that we can to be the team most capable of winning the WSL and Renée [Slegers] has set the standard really high this pre-season. We’ve got seven new players that have come in, we’ve got a squad that’s raring to go, the competition in it is really high.

“So yeah, I feel happy but now I really want to continue to push on with Arsenal and England and win some trophies.”

Sports.title: Real Madrid agree club-record £115m deal for Yan Diomande and want to keep Vinícius
Sports.content:
Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of €135m (£115.7m) with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of warding off Arsenal’s interest in Vinícius Júnior after offering an improved contract to the Brazil forward.

After several weeks of negotiations that saw Paris Saint-Germain pull out of the race, the deal for Diomande – the 19-year-old who joined the German side from Leganés last summer and starred for Côte d’Ivoire at the World Cup – was finally struck on Wednesday afternoon. It is understood that Madrid will pay an initial €125m plus another €10m in add-ons, a total that would eclipse the fee the Spanish side paid Borussia Dortmund to sign Jude Bellingham in 2023, believed to have been worth up to €134m including add-ons.

Leganés are due a 5% sell-on fee from any transfer. The teenager made only 10 appearances for their first team before being sold to Leipzig for €20m (£17.4m). Diomande, who was pictured arriving at Leipzig’s pre-season training camp in Austria on Wednesday, is expected to sign a contract until 2031 and becomes the most expensive African player in history, surpassing the £72m Arsenal spent on Nicolas Pépé in 2019.

His impending arrival is not thought to have any bearing on whether Vinícius stays in the Spanish capital. The Brazilian and his representatives, Roc Nation, held talks with Madrid officials on Wednesday over a contract extension, with Arsenal waiting in the wings if he decides to depart.

Mikel Arteta’s side are understood to be ready to pay more than £100m for the 26-year-old who has less than a year of his contract remaining. But despite some reports that Vinícius had rejected Madrid’s latest contract offer, it is understood that he is now weighing up an improved deal closer to the €30m a season requested after what sources in Spain have described as positive talks. Vinícius said on Tuesday that Madrid’s new manager, José Mourinho, wants him to be “happy, cheerful ‌and playing my football” after returning to pre-season training following the World Cup.

Arsenal, who have agreed a £75m deal to sign his Brazil teammate Bruno Guimarães from Newcastle, are believed to be exploring other options in attack should Vinícius opt to renew with Madrid.

Barcelona’s sporting director, Deco, held talks with Atlético Madrid over Julián Alvarez on Wednesday in a bid to secure a deal for the Argentina forward but Arsenal are hoping that the 26-year-old could yet be persuaded to join them.

Arsenal, who missed out on Morgan Rogers last month when the England forward joined Chelsea for a British record fee of £117m instead, have also been linked with PSG’s Bradley Barcola, who is wanted by Liverpool and valued at around £145m by the European champions.

Sports.title: ‘Dream come true’: Eva Olid delighted after being named Manchester United’s new head coach
Sports.content:
Eva Olid has described being appointed as the Manchester United Women head coach as a dream come true after signing a two-year contract until 2028 with the option of a further year.

The Spanish coach will replace Marc Skinner, whose surprise departure came on Monday.

Olid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title last season and departing the Edinburgh club by mutual agreement in a five-year spell during which she oversaw a remarkable period of progress.

The 40-year-old’s arrival comes as United are understood to be prioritising developing homegrown players rather than spending large transfer fees rather than spending large fees.

In a statement, the club said: “Olid’s appointment marks the start of an exciting new era for Manchester United Women as the club embarks on a clear vision for long-term, sustainable growth and success.

“Important foundations have already been put in place to further support the development of homegrown talent and young players, as well as senior internationals, and establish a clear football identity. Significant investment has been made into the academy infrastructure and facilities, underlining the ambition to build the leading youth development system in the country.”

Olid told the club’s website yesterday: “The opportunity to become head coach of Manchester United Women is a dream come true. The club has outstanding infrastructure and everything we need to achieve our ambitions. We have an excellent training facility, an academy that is already producing players capable of performing in a competitive first team, and an exceptional group of support staff.

View image in fullscreen Eva Olid signs up for Manchester United. Photograph: Manchester United/Getty Images

“There is already so much talent within our squad and I am excited to work with the players to support them to fulfil their immense potential. I am joining Manchester United at a really exciting time. There is a clear alignment in our shared vision for long-term success. I cannot wait to begin preparing a team that will make our incredible supporters proud.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

United finished fourth in the Women’s Super League last season and reached the quarter-finals of the Women’s Champions League, as well as the League Cup final.

Matt Johnson, United’s director of women’s football, said: “Eva is an outstanding coach with an incredible determination to succeed. Her remarkable achievements at Heart of Midlothian showcased her ability to maximise the potential of individual players, whilst also implementing an exciting style of football.

“Eva is the perfect coach to lead us into an exciting new era. She shares our commitment to developing exciting homegrown and young players, a tradition deeply embedded in our club’s history and culture, as well as improving established senior internationals, both of which form an integral part of our vision for long-term, sustainable success.”

Sports.title: ‘There is a clear vision’: Matthias Jaissle installed as Newcastle head coach
Sports.content:
Matthias Jaissle has described Newcastle “as an incredibly compelling place to be” after finally formalising his managerial move from Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli.

The 38-year-old German has been with his new players at their training camp in La Manga, southern Spain, since last Saturday but, despite also falling under the ownership of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Al-Ahli took time to provide Newcastle with some vital paperwork regarding the release of a head coach they were extremely reluctant to lose.

Jaissle won two Asian Champions Leagues at the Jeddah-based club and, having enjoyed earlier success during a much-vaunted stint in charge of RB Salzburg, is regarded as one of the brightest young coaches in football. He will be installed as the head coach at St James’ Park.

Nonetheless, the task of succeeding Eddie Howe with the start of the new season only a fortnight away is considerable – and particularly as Newcastle have lost three key players this summer in Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and, now, the Arsenal-bound Bruno Guimarães.

Jaissle remains undaunted. “When Newcastle United come your way you take notice,” he said. “The ambition of the club, the vision for the future and the opportunity ahead made this an incredibly compelling place to be.

“I am incredibly excited about the future. I fully and unreservedly believe in this project, the ambition and the direction the club is taking. There is a clear vision, strong leadership and an exceptional platform to build on.”

Under Howe, Newcastle’s motto was “intensity is our identity” and Jaissle suggested he would be following a similar path. “My teams are built on togetherness, hard work and a passion to improve every single day,” he said.

“I believe there is enormous potential within this squad and throughout this football club. I give my complete commitment and total energy to bringing further success to Newcastle.”

With Howe’s coaching staff having departed with him, Jaissle is assembling a new backroom team but it seems David Hopkinson, Newcastle’s chief executive, and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, have full faith in his ability to revive the fortunes of a club that finished a disappointing 12th in the Premier League last season. “Matthias is one of the most exciting and highly regarded young coaches in football and I’m thrilled to welcome him to Newcastle,” Hopkinson said.

Wilson said: “Matthias’s leadership style and football philosophy are strongly aligned with our sporting vision. His teams play high-energy football and we could feel his passion during all our discussions throughout the recruitment process.”

Sports.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns in Chelsea defeat as Real Betis see off Arsenal
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso hailed Mykhailo Mudryk’s “emotional” return from a doping ban as the winger played for Chelsea for the first time in nearly two years in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Juventus in Hong Kong on Wednesday.

Mudryk came on as a substitute for Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute, drawing applause from his teammates and loud cheers from Chelsea fans in the 43,575 crowd at Kai Tak Sports Park.

The Ukraine international has not played a competitive match since November 2024, having been provisionally suspended after returning an “adverse finding” for the banned substance meldonium.

However, the 25-year-old was cleared to return to action after resolving the case with the Football Association. Despite a lively cameo on the left side, Mudryk was unable to stop Juventus taking the spoils courtesy of a wonderful second-half strike from the Kosovo international Edon Zhegrova.

“Really pleased for him. It was emotional for everyone from the club to see him back,” Alonso said of Mudryk.

Arsenal were punished for defensive errors as they slipped to a 3-1 friendly defeat by Real Betis at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The Premier League champions fell behind to first-half goals from Rodrigo Riquelme and Nelson Deossa and although the Gunners hit back through Piero Hincapié, Pablo Fornals struck a third for Betis before the break. Mikel Arteta named an unchanged lineup after his side won Saturday’s opening friendly match 4-1 in Spain against Girona, but they fell behind in the ninth minute when goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga failed to make contact with a corner and Riquelme lashed home at the back post.

View image in fullscreen Piero Hincapié scored for Arsenal but could not prevent their defeat against Real Betis. Photograph: Brian Lawless/PA

Christos Tzolis failed to take advantage for Arsenal when Betis goalkeeper Álvaro Valles passed the ball straight to the Gunners’ summer signing before Deossa put the visitors 2-0 up with a 30-yard thunderbolt into the top corner.

Arsenal reduced the deficit when Valles misjudged a corner from Tzolis for Hincapié to head home, but Betis restored their two-goal advantage before the break as former West Ham midfielder Fornals swept the ball beyond a stationary Arrizabalaga following Kai Havertz’s misplaced pass.

Arteta made wholesale changes at half-time, with the 16-year-old Marli Salmon appearing at centre-half, and neither side created a clearcut scoring chance as the game lost its momentum.

Sports.title: 'We NEED these players': Riccardo Calafiori urges Arsenal to splash the cash ahead of Premier League title defence - with Bruno Guimaraes nearing £75m move and Gunners in the hunt for Vinicius Junior
Sports.content:
Riccardo Calafiori said Arsenal need players like Brazilian pair Bruno Guimaraes and Vinicius Junior to retain their Premier League title.

The Gunners are set to complete their protracted £75million move for Newcastle captain Guimaraes this week, putting an end to a long saga.

The Brazilian is waiting for permission to leave Newcastle’s training base in La Manga, Spain, to finalise the formalities of his move to north London.

Arsenal are also in the hunt for Real Madrid’s Vinicius Junior, whose contract expires next summer. That might prove more of a battle as Madrid fight to keep him.

When questioned about whether Arsenal need the likes of Guimaraes and Vinicius Junior after the 3-1 defeat by Real Betis in Dublin, Calafiori turned to a member of the Arsenal media team and asked: 'Is it official yet?'

Riccardo Calafiori has admitted that Arsenal 'need' new signings to retain the Premier League

The Gunners have been in the market for Brazilian duo Bruno Guimaraes (left) and Vinicius Junior (right) this summer, with the Newcastle midfielder set to sign for £75m this week

He then added: ‘We are on that level now. We are on top. We want to win the league again, we want to be even better than last season if we can. We need these kind of players I think.’

On Guimaraes, he added: ‘It’s not official, so I cannot speak about it.’

Guimaraes, who joined Newcastle from Lyon in 2022, has made clear his intention to join Arsenal as the 28-year-old has emerged as Mikel Arteta's first-choice central midfield target.

Newcastle and Arsenal have been discussing the finer terms of the deal this week with a final agreement now considered a formality.

Guimaraes told Newcastle earlier this summer that he wanted to join Arsenal if a suitable offer arrived.

Meanwhile, Real Madrid are awaiting a response from Vinicius Junior after offering the Arsenal target improved terms in excess of £19million a year.

The Brazil international’s current terms with Madrid expire at the end of next season and Arsenal have made him aware they are willing to step in if he fails to find agreement with the Spanish giants.

Talks between the player’s agents, general director Jose Angel Sanchez and chief scout Juni Calafat took place in Madrid on Wednesday. Jose Mourinho also underlined that the 26-year-old is also firmly in his plans.

The LaLiga giants are believed to be increasingly confident of keeping the Brazilian superstar Vinicius Jnr at the Bernabeu.

Despite the increased confidence at the Bernabeu, the player added to the uncertainty on Wednesday night by deleting his entire Instagram history.

Vinicius' page, which has 63.9million followers, currently displays no images or bio and he's also removed his profile picture.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino REFUSES to resign as FIFA president: Under-fire chief apologises and vows to fight on as he breaks cover after being forced to abandon World Cup sale plans
Sports.content:
Shameless Gianni Infantino has been given the ‘full support’ of FIFA’s top brass - and is set to remain as president - after summoning execs to crisis talks in Morocco.

At the end of another extraordinary day in the World Cup sell-off scandal, which saw Luis Figo become the latest high-profile name to call for Infantino’s head in a blistering attack in Daily Mail Sport, a FIFA statement suggested its under-fire supremo survives, for now.

In a searing 601-word assault Figo had described Infantino’s now-aborted plan to flog a stake in the World Cup to private investors as the ‘lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed’ and a ‘grubby, underhand plot’.

His explosive words ramped up the pressure on Infantino, who had called a crisis meeting in Rabat as he attempted to cling to power.

It would now appear, however, that he has managed to do so. A lengthy statement from FIFA late on Wednesday night admitted mistakes were made, but said they have now apologised in a letter to the various football associations and that a ‘review’ will be carried out.

The statement said that, following the meeting, FIFA’s secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, who had criticised Infantino, and other management board members in attendance ‘reaffirmed their full support for the president’.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (right) and FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström (left) appeared in high spirits while watching a women's AFCON game on Wednesday night

For good measure, it added: ‘FIFA will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.

‘There are always lessons to be learned, and FIFA will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the FIFA regulatory framework.’

Figo, the former Barcelona and Real Madrid star, who initially backed Infantino in 2015, branded the Swiss a ‘relic who should have no part in football’s future’ and accused him of ‘a litany of abuses’.

Aside from the World Cup sell-off, he referenced the decision to suspend the ban for USA striker Folarin Balogun after his red card at the World Cup and the half-time show during the final which ‘broke the laws of the game’.

‘Infantino has debased the office of FIFA president he promised to elevate,’ he wrote.

‘He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve.’

Figo’s comments came after an attack by UEFA, which said it had lost confidence in Infantino, calling his proposal to flog commercial and event operations a ‘shabby, back room, opaque deal’.

Amid heavy criticism and calls for Infantino to go, Grafstrom sent an all-staff memo describing the situation as ‘sad and reproachable’ and adding ‘individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go.’

However, second-in-command Grafstrom was pictured laughing and joking with Infantino at a women’s Africa Cup of Nations game following the meeting, ahead of the release of the statement.

Should he survive, Infantino would face re-election in March, and would need 106 votes from Fifa's 211 members to win another term in charge of the global game.

Infantino arrived at the crunch meeting in Morocco earlier on Wednesday amid mounting pressure.

He had summoned senior FIFA officials to the Moroccan city of Sale for crisis talks after plans to sell £3.1billion in World Cup stakes leaked last week

The Swiss football administrator has since scrapped the proposals after widespread opposition – including an internal rebellion at FIFA.

UEFA and CONCACAF – the body for North and Central America and the Caribbean – are both calling for Infantino to step down, with Europe declaring a lack of confidence in the FIFA president.

Pressure grew further after Jordan FA president Prince Ali bin Hussein accused him of blackmail, becoming the first Asian nation to rebel against the FIFA president.

Jordan became the 91st member association to move against Infantino, assuming all UEFA and CONCACAF nations follow the stance set by their continental bodies. 106 nations are needed to depose Infantino as president.

FIFA President Infantino arrived at an emergency meeting in Sale, Morocco on Wednesday

Infantino is facing mounting pressure over his failed plan to sell off stakes in the FIFA World Cup

Football legend Luis Figo became the latest high-profile individual to call for him to resign, while Arsene Wenger distanced himself from Infantino's plans

A car carrying Infantino was seen arriving at FIFA's Africa regional office in Sale on Wednesday.

The meeting comes hours after Figo became the latest major name in football to demand his resignation.

In an explosive piece for Daily Mail Sport, which further ramped up the pressure on the under-fire FIFA chief, the Portuguese legend described his now aborted World Cup sell-off as the ‘lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed’ and a ‘grubby, underhand plot’.

Across 600 no-holds-barred words Figo, who had initially backed Infantino in 2015, brands the disgraced exec a ‘relic who should have no part in football’s future’ and accuses him of ‘a litany of abuses’, also referencing the now-infamous suspension of the ban behind Folarin Balogun’s red card and the half-time show at the World Cup final which ‘broke the laws of the game’.

‘Infantino has debased the office of FIFA President that he promised to elevate,’ the former Real Madrid, Barcelona and Inter Milan star writes. ‘He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve.’

Figo, now 53, is viewed by many as a potential successor to Aleksandr Ceferin, head of UEFA which is leading the war against Infantino.

Figo and Jordan's Prince Ali had both previously stood against former FIFA president Sepp Blatter in the 2015 elections.

Figo ultimately withdrew from the process, while Prince Ali pulled out after the second round of voting. Blatter announced his resignation four days after re-election amid a vast backlash.

Infantino is facing his own backlash following his World Cup plans, with FIFA’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour saying he was ‘deceived’ by the project and others, including chief of global football development Arsene Wenger, have distanced themselves from the hastily dropped plan.

Figo branded Infantino as a ‘relic who should have no part in football’s future’ in an explosive article for Daily Mail Sport

Figo, who had initially backed Infantino in 2015, claimed the Swiss official has 'debased the office of FIFA President'

With morale among staff said to be ‘rock bottom’ according to insiders, secretary general Grafstrom sent an internal email to staff citing ‘a sad and reproachable series of events’ and perhaps tellingly pointing out that ‘individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go’.

Figo, a former FIFA presidential candidate, starts: ‘I could write 10,000 words on the problems at FIFA. But the solution needs only three: Infantino must go.’

He adds: ‘I have loved football all my life. I was a professional player for 20 years. And believe me, I have met some rogues in my time in the game. But what I have seen exposed in the last ten days is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed. The man who would do that - the man who would try to force through such major changes just to enrich himself and his friends - is a relic of the game’s past and should have no part in its future.’

The Portuguese, who won 127 caps for his country, then rounds on Infantino for a lack of transparency. ’If it was such a good idea, why not tell your members when you had them all in a room before the World Cup Final?’ he asks.

‘If it was such a robust plan, why not tell your members the risks as well as what you describe as the benefits?

‘If the scheme was a no-brainer, why not be honest about the fact that it was going to give you a $30m a year job at the end of it?’

Figo adds: ‘None of this was done. Because it’s not a good idea. It’s not robust when you fail to be transparent about the crippling returns that private equity always seek.

‘It’s not bold when you fail to explain that once you have sold your share it is gone forever and you have disinherited your successors from ownership of the World Cup.

FIFA legends have reportedly declined to publicly support Infantino amid the backlash to his plans

‘And it’s not honest when you fail to mention that, after you have delivered the head of the World Cup on a platter to your mates in DC, they are going to give you a job worth five times your current salary.’

Figo then highlights FIFA’s staggering level of wealth, asking how many shares the $5billion in its reserves ‘could buy in this grubby, underhand plot’.

‘Infantino has debased the office of FIFA President that he promised to elevate,’ he writes. ‘He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve…he should go. Now.’

According to The Times, allies of Infantino had been trying to persuade 'FIFA legends' to publicly support Infantino, but have been unsuccessful.

The FIFA legends are among former international players who have been paid to appear at the governing body's events.

Sports.title: Inside the fall of the Hundred: Attendances down, prices up and locals snubbed as counties fear massive divide once IPL windfall wears off. 'We've seen this all before - it was called LIV Golf. Is the Hundred even going to be here in three years?'
Sports.content:
Inside the fall of the Hundred: Attendances down, prices up and locals snubbed as counties fear massive divide once IPL windfall wears off. 'We've seen this all before - it was called LIV Golf. Is the Hundred even going to be here in three years?'

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

When Harry Brook was wowing those at Headingley on Tuesday night with a no-look six during a record-equalling 50, it felt in that particular moment that everything might at last be coming together for the Hundred.

A competition with multiple launches but a recurring marketing campaign promising to take a new audience to new places – what better than a shot that wasn’t even a thing when 100-ball cricket was dreamt up? – was doing so through one of its homegrown pin-ups.

Undoubtedly, Brook’s 15-ball half century at Headingley just past the midpoint of the Hundred’s sixth season ticked all the boxes, fulfilling the pledges to make this competition second only to the Indian Premier League in short-form stature and to feature England’s premier players at its forefront.

The strength of the attack the 27-year-old was up against spoke of the quality on show this year: six of the London Spirit bowlers were internationals and the seventh was James Coles, the Hundred’s most expensive auction purchase ever at £390,000.

Yet that snapshot also exposed two sporting spheres colliding. In South Asia and North America – the territories from which this year’s new money in a £975million Hundred upgrade has come – franchises pop up, move cities and disband with minimal fuss while supporters are more willing to change allegiance depending on where their favourite players move.

Here in the UK, though, we are a parochial bunch and one trick that the newly owned teams either missed, or brazenly disregarded, was signing local county players to their respective Hundred teams to boost identity.

When Harry Brook was hitting a no-look six during a record-equalling 50, it felt in that particular moment that everything might at last be coming together for the Hundred

Australia stars Marcus Stoinis (left) and Adam Zampa (batting) are two of the international stars cementing the Hundred as the second-strongest short-form competition behind the IPL

Nowhere in the country is as insular as Yorkshire and it felt wrong during the early stages of this year’s auction that SunRisers Leeds were not going all out to recruit one of Joe Root, Jonny Bairstow or Adil Rashid. It left Brook and his former Burley-in-Wharfedale club mate Matthew Revis as the only familiar faces to relate to on Tuesday.

Southampton-based Southern Brave have just one Hampshire player in their ranks in teenager Manny Lumsden, a squad player rather than a first-choice pick and could not retain their local hero and captain James Vince in this season’s auction.

Somerset’s England Twenty20 international Tom Banton has played for three Hundred franchises, but has spent the past three seasons at Trent Rockets and admits continuity in squads is needed to deepen connections with fans.

‘If they're coming every year and there's new faces, I guess it's hard for people to get behind the team and support, isn't it?’ says Banton. ‘Whereas if you've been playing for a few years, they can kind of relate to you, get to know you and want to come and watch you.’

In contrast to the majority of their new-money rivals, the table-topping Rockets have also maintained the same colours and badge following the tournament’s unofficial relaunch. Five seasons of familiarity has been removed elsewhere.

Until recently, Headingley was full of purple-shirted Northern Superchargers fans. Overnight, following the complete buyout of Yorkshire’s stake in the competition by Sunrisers Hyderabad, they were being asked to form an orange army, and support Leeds rather than band together as the North. Best of luck.

Colours and identities are important to a British supporter base. Recall the anger when Cardiff City switched from blue to red shirts and ditched the bluebird for a dragon or when Hull City’s former owner Assem Allam applied to change the club’s name to Hull Tigers.

The Sunrisers are one of three teams to have changed names, along with Oval Invincibles becoming MI London and the Manchester Originals being renamed Manchester Super Giants. All have badges and kits to reflect their IPL links, although MI have retained the colours of the reigning three-in-a-row champions Invincibles for training.

‹ Slide me ›

Oval Invincibles won the last three men's titles wearing a turquoise strip, before being taken over by Mumbai Indians and becoming MI London, playing in royal blue

‹ Slide me ›

Meanwhile, the Old Trafford-based franchise have gone from being Manchester Originals in black kits to Manchester Super Giants in red and navy stripes

Southern Brave have gone from green and black to blue and red. Birmingham Phoenix have moved from orange shirts to black. To their credit, both Manchester and Leeds teams have begun schemes to make the switch easier, giving out replica shirts to every ticket holder at their early matches.

MI London launched a shirt amnesty in which turquoise 2025 Oval Invincibles shirts could be exchanged for the new royal blue ones. Additionally, they produced a club T-shirt for £20 under their ‘Twenty’s Plenty’ campaign.

Vikram Banerjee, the Hundred’s managing director, says that 40 per cent of those through the turnstiles are Under 16s and that ‘as we look to deepen and accelerate fandom, merchandise sales are a great barometer. Southern Brave and London Spirit are already having to restock, and nearly 40,000 fans are wearing the new jerseys of Manchester Super Giants or SunRisers Leeds.’ Presumably referencing the freebies.

Filling their grounds with a shirt-donning, flag-waving, family-oriented crowd has been championed as a success by the host counties too, but there are sceptics from within the county game about the real impact underneath the veneer, with one executive telling Daily Mail Sport: ‘The rebranding is utterly ridiculous. They’ve alienated the local people, and now they've whacked the prices up that nobody can afford it. And the sales are through the floor.

‘I don't know about anybody else, but I'm just looking at the Hundred right now and thinking we've seen this before – it was called LIV Golf. So, is the Hundred even going to be here in three years’ time?’

Whether it is the impact of the cost-of-living crisis, increased ticket prices or the rebranding that has proved a turnoff remains to be seen, but the Hundred is proving a hard sell in 2026. The first block of matches saw attendances down around 20 per cent on last year, the second block dropping by 27 per cent.

Crowds have generally picked up across the competitions since, but with ticketing operations now run by the organisations themselves rather than centrally, entrance fees hitting a high of £55 is an issue, even if you do get access to both parts of the men’s and women’s double-header for your money.

That is some hike for a competition that spent its first iteration between 2021-25 dishing out complimentary seats to its target audience of mums and kids. The problem with freebies, though, comes when you ask people to start paying instead.

The first block of matches saw attendances down around 20 per cent on last year, the second block dropping by 27 per cent

Brook’s blockbuster knock was watched by just over 9,000 spectators this week, a few hundred down on the 9,438 that turned out for the Leeds v Manchester contest. By comparison, the established Roses Twenty20 Blast fixture, promoted with a fraction of the budget, drew 11,300 at Headingley in June.

Kaviya Maran, part of the Sun Group that owns the SunRisers said the first signs at Headingley were ‘a good beginning’, adding: ‘Obviously it's a new brand for them.’

It was a similar story across the Pennines at Old Trafford, scene of a 16,500 sellout for the reverse Blast match. The cheapest tickets were £30 with £8 concessions for that, and while those for Super Giants matches cost less, starting at £24 and £5 in advance, their average men’s Hundred crowd has been under 12,000.

There have been some misjudgments. A huge proportion of Yorkshire fans will refuse to support a team with Leeds in its name, especially after the woeful attempt to incorporate Leeds United’s Marching On Together as the club song via a (swiftly deleted) social media post.

There have been highs, such as Welsh Fire setting attendance records for any women’s match in Wales and in the men’s competition on July 25 for the visit of the MI London teams. And the women’s game is benefitting with a higher percentage of people turning up earlier to stadia. Eighty per cent of fans that watched Southern Brave’s men on July 27 had been there early doors to see the women’s game too.

While the cash-rich Hundred stumbles, the county game it has kicked into the side verges has witnessed a series of triumphs. Helped by the presence of Ben Stokes, Durham sold out Jesmond when hosting Glamorgan in the MetroBank One-Day Cup and had to warn ticketless supporters not to turn up on matchday. There were 2,300 present to witness a thrilling match that saw Durham recover from 97 for six to knock off their 327-run target with three balls to spare.

Stokes was also in the Durham team that played to almost 5,000 in defeat by Yorkshire at York last week, 48 hours after the same venue accommodated 4,500 for the visit of Worcestershire.

Gloucestershire have had to expand their capacity for their visits to Cheltenham this year because of demand and although these numbers are more modest than the Hundred, full outgrounds are aesthetically pleasing to see and provide a county’s emerging players with an entry level for professional cricket.

By contrast, the Roses T20 Blast match drew a sell-out crowd of 16,500 - despite prices being higher than the Hundred

Peter Matthews, chairman of Gloucestershire, is an advocate of taking 50-over cricket to venues ‘that don't normally see cricket,’ adding: ‘It has echoes for those of a certain generation of some of the Sunday League grounds. Gloucestershire used to play a Sunday League game at a number of different grounds – Lydney, Moreton-in-Marsh, Gloucester – which we can't do now because it doesn’t work economically.’

Matthews says the lack of an obvious Hundred competitor in the region has helped footfall during the period between the World Cup and the start of the Premier League in a fortnight. And non-host clubs like his have been able to plan for more sustainable futures thanks to the £25million individual windfalls from the ECB’s big sell-off.

In addition to paying off their debts – ‘we got ourselves into a bit of a muddle,’ says Matthews – Gloucestershire ploughed £3million into a project codenamed Dressing Rooms, which drastically improved player and match official facilities plus general infrastructure at their Nevil Road headquarters.

Leicestershire are another to have been dragged out of the red by the Hundred’s millions, and they have begun feasibility studies on adding further non-cricket earnings to their annual income.

They have already been creative in this space on a smaller scale, holding drive-in cinema days last weekend and planning to install a 4G multi-sports pitch alongside the country’s largest playing area to be hired out during the winter. Their decision to allow children in free this month has resonated with their following, coming during the school holidays.

Chief executive Emma White says: ‘We're in the middle of a cost of living crisis, so I think there’s a ridiculous squeeze on the leisure pound. Are we getting a true reflection of the Hundred effect? I'm not entirely sure we are, if I'm totally honest. We're seeing a true reflection of the fact that people can't afford to do much at the moment.

‘The massive positive is that it's given quite a lot of counties more than you would imagine, the breathing space needed to kind of reset a little bit and almost future-proof cricket in their area by investing in revenue-generating projects.’

With the £25million lump sums viewed as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to become less reliant on ECB annual handouts, counties – particularly the non-hosts – are taking their time to assess how best to invest. Durham recently received planning permission for an on-site hotel that they first discussed pre-Covid and will now employ a project director to produce a report on profitability, given the rise of costs in the hospitality industry.

Counties – particularly the non-hosts – are taking their time to assess how best to invest. Durham received planning permission for an on-site hotel that they first discussed pre-Covid

But there is a fear that however smartly the money is used, the disparity between those that have taken the finite sum and those still with skin in the Hundred game is only going to widen

The IPL might be a behemoth now but it took the expansion of the league from eight to ten teams in 2011 to truly realise its potential

But there is a fear that however smartly the money is used, the disparity between those that have taken the finite sum and those still with skin in the Hundred game is only going to widen.

‘Host counties are going to become wealthier and more able to attract the best players,’ said one county chair. ‘Fundamentally you're talking about those grounds having tradition, history and scale. It's very difficult to argue against tradition, history, and scale. They’re always going to generate more revenue than elsewhere.’

To back up the theory, the Lord’s-based Spirit have been valued at £300million – two and a half times more than the field. Suspicion remains around the shires that while this year’s competition will not return profits for the new investors, they are biding their time until expansion. Teams based in Bristol and Chester-le-Street would be the most obvious additions.

It was not until the IPL increased from eight to ten teams that the original set hit a goldmine, as the fee paid for the rights to own a new franchise would be distributed among the rest of the existing teams. And that with half the teams now controlled by powerful IPL owners, it is only a matter of time before Indian players are allowed to feature in a league outside of their own, significantly increasing its value in television and commercial rights on the subcontinent.

At which point, Hundred teams would potentially need fewer Englishmen and counties would be re-stocked with some of their primary talents, opening the chance to play the County Championship throughout August once more and easing a schedule already past saturation point. Unlike Brook’s shot in Leeds, all eyes are on what direction the Hundred will go now.

Sports.title: Atletico lead chase for Cristian Romero, Aston Villa braced for fresh Arsenal bid for Ezri Konsa, Mikey Moore set for Cologne loan... and Mo Salah mobbed in Turkey: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Madrid wait for Vinicius Jr decision

Real Madrid are awaiting a response from Vinicius Jr after offering the Arsenal target improved terms in excess of £19million a year.

The Brazil international’s current terms with Madrid expire at the end of next season and Arsenal have made him aware they are willing to step in if he fails to find agreement with the Spanish giants.

Talks between the player’s agents, general director Jose Angel Sanchez and chief scout Juni Calafat took place in Madrid on Wednesday. Jose Mourinho also underlined that the 26-year-old is also firmly in his plans.

Atletico lead chase for Romero

Atletico Madrid are ready to firm up their interest in Tottenham defender Cristian Romero after he held talks with Inter Milan.

Atletico are in talks to sell left-back Matteo Ruggeri to Aston Villa in a deal worth £19.7m if the 24-year-old agrees to go. They are also selling Nahuel Molina to Roma and the combined fees will go towards a £30m bid for Romero.

Tottenham's Argentina defender Cristian Romero has suitors in Spain and Italy

Spurs yet to approach Liverpool about Gakpo

Tottenham remain keen to sign Cody Gakpo from Liverpool, as reported earlier this week, but, as of this afternoon, the Reds have yet to receive a formal approach.

Liverpool want to keep Gakpo but are exploring the possibility of signing Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris Saint-Germain as well as Bradley Barcola. But they are not in for Pedro Neto at Chelsea, who is a target for Manchester City.

Liverpool do not want to sell Cody Gakpo, with Spurs interested in a move

Toon working on replacement for Bruno

Newcastle are working to find a replacement for Bruno Guimaraes, who is set to have a medical at Arsenal after a £75m deal was agreed.

They have asked about Dortmund's Felix Nmecha, Angelo Stiller at Stuttgart and Luka Sucic at Real Sociedad, among others. as they try to find a solution swiftly with new boss Matthias Jaissle being announced tonight.

Norgaard's Everton move a done deal

Arsenal midfielder Christian Norgaard has completed a £7m move to Everton.

Ait Boudlal in talks with Fulham

Fulham have opened talks with Rennes for centre-back Abdelhamid Ait Boudlal. The 20-year-old Morocco international is valued in excess of £25m.

Spurs' Moore off to Germany

Tottenham winger Mikey Moore has accepted a loan move to Cologne in Germany. The 18-year-old spent last year on loan with Rangers.

Tottenham’s teenage striker Mason Melia has undergone his medical at Lincoln today ahead of finalising his loan move. The 18-year-old is a Republic of Ireland international.

Mikey Moore is set for another second loan spell after spending last year at Rangers

Villa working on £14m Ruggeri deal

Aston Villa are continuing to discussing a £14m deal with Atletico Madrid for Italian left-back Matteo Ruggeri but they are awaiting approval from the 24-year-old. Daily Mail Sport reported their interest yesterday.

Atletico looking to utilise funds towards their planned bid for Cristian Romero at Tottenham.

Burnley go for keeper Amos

Burnley have signed free agent goalkeeper Ben Amos.

The 36-year-old had taken part in the PFA training camp for free agents this summer after leaving Port Vale at the end of last season. He has signed a one-year deal with Burnley.

Amos has over 360 appearances with a host of EFL clubs after beginning his career at Manchester United.

Ben Amos spent time at Charlton, among several EFL clubs

Chalobah arrives for Como medical

Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah has arrived in Italy for his medical with Como. The deal is worth an initial £25.7m plus a further £5.1m in potential add-ons.

Spanish defender Pep Chavarria is in London to complete his £16m deal from Rayo Vallecano.

Trevoh Chalobah is closing in on a move to Como

Coventry aim to break transfer record AGAIN
