World.content:
The eye-catching strip celebrates another historic chapter in Sundowns‘ history after lifting the CAF Champions League title for a second time.

The new away strip features a blue jersey, white shorts and blue socks. The shirt also includes two stars above the club badge to commemorate Kabo Yellows‘ second African crown, secured in May 2026.

MAMELODI SUNDOWNS CELEBRATE CHAMPIONS

PUMA supports the launch with a campaign titled “Fueled by the Sun.” The campaign highlights Mamelodi Sundowns’ attacking identity and winning mentality.



According to PUMA, the design captures the fearless ambition and relentless intensity that have become synonymous with Masandawana.

The jersey features striking geometric graphics inspired by the power of the sun. Shades of royal blue, deep navy and the club’s famous yellow complete the modern design.

“PUMA drew inspiration from the powerful energy that defines Mamelodi Sundowns when designing the new away kit. It is a bold expression of the Masandawana spirit and embodies the Club’s ambition and the momentum that drives every performance,” said Brett Bellinger, PUMA SA’s Marketing Director.

KIT GOES ON SALE NEXT WEEK

Supporters will have two versions to choose from. The Authentic shirt is the same version worn by the players and features PUMA’s ULTRAWEAVE fabric for lightweight performance. It also includes dryCELL and ThermoAdapt technologies to help keep players cool and dry.

The Replica jersey is made from recycled polyester and is designed for everyday supporters.

The new away shirt will officially go on sale on 13 August 2026.



Pricing has been confirmed as follows:

Authentic jersey: R2,399

Replica men’s and women’s jersey: R1,299

Replica kids’ jersey: R1,199

Supporters will be able to purchase the new strip from PUMA retail stores, PUMA.com, the Mamelodi Sundowns online store, the club’s pop-up store, as well as JD Sports, Totalsports, Sportsmans Warehouse, Takealot and Studio 88.

World.title: Zimbabwe moves to reform intersex laws after landmark court challenge
World.content:
The Zimbabwean government has begun reviewing laws affecting intersex people following a court challenge.

Officials say existing legal and administrative systems do not adequately cater for people whose biological characteristics do not fit traditional male or female classifications.

The Ministry of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs convened a high-level breakfast meeting in Harare on Wednesday, bringing together government ministers, legal experts, healthcare professionals, development partners and civil society organisations to discuss legal recognition and the protection of intersex persons.



Justice Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi said the process was initiated after the government received a court challenge relating to intersex rights.

“Basically what we have done is we have received a court challenge regarding this issue (intersex) and we referred it to the Attorney General,” Ziyambi said.

“After that we decided as a Ministry that we need to undertake research.”

According to the minister, the research was carried out by the Law Development Commission with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), while the stakeholder meeting was organised to gather expert opinions and lived experiences before recommendations are submitted to Cabinet.

Court challenge prompts Zimbabwe’s intersex law review

Ziyambi said Zimbabwe’s Constitution recognises two sexes, but acknowledged that government systems must also respond to people whose biological characteristics do not fit neatly within the country’s binary legal framework.

“The research and this meeting are part of work in progress,” he said.



“We have presentations and testimonies and lived experiences, and we believe that out of the meeting, we will be able to come up with concrete measures.”

Although government has not yet outlined specific legislative amendments, officials indicated that recommendations emerging from the consultation process will guide future policy and legal reforms.

Zimbabwe government identifies legal gaps affecting intersex people

Public Service, Labour and Social Welfare Minister Edgar Moyo said the meeting exposed significant gaps in Zimbabwe’s laws.

“There is a real gap in our statutes to address those issues because we are basically classified as male and female and then there are people falling in between,” he said.

Moyo said stigma and cultural beliefs have contributed to intersex issues remaining largely hidden, leaving many affected individuals facing discrimination and exclusion.

He said some intersex people experience repeated difficulties when official documents do not accurately reflect their biological characteristics, creating obstacles when accessing government and private sector services.

Documentation challenges facing intersex Zimbabweans

Participants at the meeting highlighted several barriers encountered by intersex people, including challenges obtaining birth certificates and national identity documents where biological characteristics do not align with existing binary sex classifications.

Officials also noted that documentation challenges can affect access to education, healthcare, employment, banking services and voter registration.

The meeting heard that many families continue to struggle with limited public understanding of intersex variations, with stigma often discouraging parents from seeking support or discussing the issue openly.

Government officials said greater public awareness, family support and improved child protection services would form part of a broader response.

Government to submit recommendations on legal reforms

The Ministry of Justice said the consultation process will continue through validation of the research findings before drafting legal and policy recommendations for Cabinet consideration.

Officials also pledged to maintain engagement with intersex persons, healthcare professionals and civil society organisations throughout the reform process.

The ministry said any future reforms would be informed by expert advice as well as the lived experiences of intersex Zimbabweans, with the aim of creating a more inclusive legal and administrative system.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies Foley, Phipps rejoin Waratahs ahead of home World Cup
World.content:
MELBOURNE - Former Wallabies Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps signed for the NSW Waratahs with the veteran duo returning home after long stints in Japan.

The pair, who steered the Waratahs to their maiden Super Rugby title in 2014 under coach Michael Cheika, reunite seven years after they last took the field together.

Their return to the Sydney-based side where both made their debuts in 2011 comes barely a year out from a home World Cup.

Fly-half Foley, who has played 76 Tests, the last in 2022, is reportedly keen to press his case to make an international comeback for the global showpiece.

"I'm so grateful to have the opportunity to rejoin the Waratahs for 2027," said the 36-year-old, who has spent the last five seasons with Kubota Spears in Japan.

"I feel very lucky to have the chance to finish back at the club where it all started."

Scrum-half Phipps, who has been capped 72 times, plied his trade with London Irish under current Australia coach Les Kiss when he left the Waratahs in 2019.

The 37-year-old joined Foley in Japan four years ago with the Green Rockets Tokatsu.

"I'm super excited to be back home at the Waratahs," he said.

"The chance to return and give something back to the club and the players is an opportunity I simply couldn't pass up."

The Waratahs are currently without a coach after Dan McKellar quit in June with a year left on his contract after two underwhelming Super Rugby seasons.

Names touted as his replacement include former Wallabies and Argentina coach Cheika and ex-Australia international Stephen Hoiles.

World.title: Environmental disaster looms as tanker leaks off Oman
World.content:
DUBAI - Oman is facing an impending environmental catastrophe as an alleged Russian shadow fleet tanker leaks oil across hundreds of square kilometres near a nature reserve, NGOs warn.

The ship was rocked by explosions, a maritime security firm told AFP, but the cause of the blasts is unclear.

Russia has built up a ghost fleet of old ships with opaque ownership to get around Western sanctions since its 2022 Ukraine invasion, and experts have said the vessels' poor condition increases the risk of oil spills.

Satellite imagery verified by AFP showed what appeared to be an oil slick spreading from a ship that has been stranded for over a month near al-Qibliyyah island, off Oman's southern coast.

It is far from the Strait of Hormuz, which has seen regular tanker attacks in the Middle East war.

"With oil apparently continuing to leak and the vessel stranded in a difficult location, the risk of an even larger environmental disaster remains serious," Nina Noelle of Greenpeace told AFP.

She warned of a "severe and long-lasting" consequence.

Greenpeace said the oil sheen had expanded from up to 20 square kilometres on July 24 to an estimated 600 on August 4, according to satellite imagery it reviewed.

Environmental open-source investigator Wim Zwijnenburg, from Dutch peace organisation PAX, gave the same estimate for the August 4 sheen.

Kpler data showed that the Caroline Bezengi, which is believed to be the ship leaking off Oman, loaded one million barrels of crude oil at the Russian Black Sea terminal of Sheskharis on May 11.

It still had the oil when its last signal was recorded a month later.

World.title: Baby hippo from Escobar's feral herd dies after rescue
World.content:
BOGOTA - A baby hippopotamus descended from creatures that belonged to Pablo Escobar died Wednesday after being rescued in northwestern Colombia, an environmental organisation told AFP.

Colombia has around 200 invasive hippos living in the wild, according to the Environment Ministry, all of which stemmed from a colony brought to South America by the late cocaine kingpin. It is the largest hippo colony anywhere outside Africa.

Authorities earlier Wednesday rescued the roughly 15-day-old malnourished creature, which had been discovered by fishermen on the banks of a river without its mother.

The infant hippo "was admitted with chronic signs of dehydration, malnutrition, and an acute gastrointestinal condition that complicated its entire clinical picture," said a vet working for the environmental organization Cornare.

Despite rescue and rehydration efforts, "the animal did not respond adequately to treatment and died," the vet said.

The animal was earlier transferred to a hippo sanctuary at Hacienda Napoles, the estate previously owned by Escobar, is now a theme park.

Escobar imported four hippos in the 1980s for his private zoo at the hacienda.

After the Medellin cartel leader's death in 1993 as he tried to elude capture by police, the animals escaped and settled along the banks of the Magdalena River, where they have disrupted the ecosystem and even attacked local residents.

They are now considered an invasive species and are destabilizing native ecosystems, prompting the government this year to approve a plan to cull around 80 of them after attempts to curb their reproduction through sterilization failed.
