A battle over a lobster diving spot off the Florida coast allegedly escalated into an underwater nightmare after a man was accused of shutting off another diver's air supply, a confrontation that landed him behind bars on an attempted murder charge.

Michael Joseph Simpson, 51, surrendered Tuesday to the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center in Miami-Dade County, where he was booked Tuesday evening on an attempted murder charge, according to Miami-Dade jail records. His bond was set at $10,000.

According to Local 10 News, the incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. on July 29 about a half-mile east of Fisher Island during Florida's annual lobster mini season.

Citing the arrest affidavit, Law&Crime reported that Simpson allegedly approached another boat at a high rate of speed and circled the vessel several times before anchoring about 10 feet away.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED FOR DUI AFTER TROOPERS ALLEGEDLY FIND 34 OPEN ALCOHOL CONTAINERS IN VEHICLE

Investigators say the confrontation began after Simpson claimed the group was diving in "his spot" and warned that a larger boat was on its way before it arrived and anchored nearby.

Authorities allege Simpson then threatened to turn off the surface-supplied air system providing oxygen to an 18-year-old diver searching for lobsters. Investigators say Simpson jumped into the water and intentionally shut off the unit.

As the confrontation unfolded, witnesses yelled, "We have a diver down there you a--hole!" according to the arrest affidavit cited by Law&Crime.

The diver's boat owner jumped into the water and pulled him to the surface. The diver was gasping for air and appeared disoriented but was not injured, Local 10 reported.

FLORIDA MAN GIVES AN INCREDIBLE INTERVIEW ABOUT HOW HE FOUGHT OFF AN ALLIGATOR WITH A FISHING POLE

Investigators allege Simpson left before deputies arrived. After authorities identified him as the suspect, Simpson voluntarily surrendered Tuesday, according to Local 10.

Simpson's attorney, Howard Srebnick, strongly denied the allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing investigators ignored evidence and witnesses he says support his client's account.

Srebnick said Simpson was diving from his own boat with friends and his two young children and "never disabled anyone's diving equipment."

Srebnick said video shows one of the accusers becoming entangled in the Brownie's Third Lung air system while Simpson "was nowhere near it."

AMERICAN TOURIST ATTACKED BY SHARK IN VACATION HOT SPOT

He also disputed investigators' allegation that Simpson fled, saying his client instead idled his boat away from the immediate area to avoid escalating the confrontation before cooperating with responding Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers and providing a statement.

Srebnick said numerous eyewitnesses aboard two separate boats corroborated Simpson's version of events and criticized the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for arresting his client before interviewing what he described as exculpatory witnesses.

"We are optimistic that the State Attorney's Office, after reviewing the video and interviewing all the eyewitnesses, will dismiss the charges, clear his name, and restore the reputation he has spent a lifetime building," Srebnick said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for additional comment.

SEMITRUCK DRIVER IN DEADLY INTERSTATE CRASH FRAUDULENTLY OBTAINED LICENSE, CITIZENSHIP: OFFICIALS

The body camera footage shows a deputy questioning Swanson about her identity after she said she was visiting Florida from New York in a rental vehicle.

VIRAL BODYCAM CAPTURES FLORIDA DEPUTY'S TRAFFIC STOP UNRAVEL AS HE ACCUSES ONE-HANDED DRIVER OF HOLDING PHONE

World.title: Federal judge acknowledges Supreme Court ruling clearing path for Trump to end Haiti TPS
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump on Wednesday notched a major immigration victory after a federal judge acknowledged that the court order blocking the administration from ending temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of thousands of Haitians is no longer in effect after the Supreme Court's ruling in Mullin v. Doe.

The ruling marks the culmination of a yearslong legal battle over the Biden administration's expansion of Haiti's TPS designation and delivers a significant immigration victory for Trump, who repeatedly campaigned on ending the Biden administration's expanded TPS protections for Haitians.

The issue became a centerpiece of the 2024 election after Trump and running mate JD Vance blamed the Biden administration's Haiti TPS policies for the influx of Haitian migrants into Springfield, Ohio, where residents raised concerns about traffic safety, strained public services and cultural clashes.

BLUE STATE LEADERS ERUPT AFTER SUPREME COURT’S DECISION ENDING TPS PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIANS, SYRIANS

The controversy later exploded onto the national stage after Trump referenced residents' claims that migrants were taking ducks and geese from parks and eating household pets.

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment by publication time.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote Wednesday that her earlier order staying the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) termination of Haiti's TPS designation "is no longer in effect" after the Supreme Court's decision and the D.C. Circuit's subsequent mandate.

While the underlying lawsuit will continue, the administration is no longer barred by the injunction from moving forward with ending TPS protections for an estimated 330,000 to 350,000 Haitians living in the U.S.

The remaining litigation centers on whether the administration acted with unconstitutional racial animus in terminating the designation.

LIBERAL COURT STUNS WITH RULING THAT HANDS TRUMP MAJOR IMMIGRATION WIN

The Supreme Court ruled in June that the TPS statute bars judicial review of the administration's non-constitutional decisions to terminate TPS designations and found the plaintiffs' equal protection challenge was unlikely to succeed. The court reversed the lower courts and remanded the case for further proceedings.

DHS General Counsel James Percival pushed back on reports suggesting Wednesday's order itself ended Haiti's TPS designation, arguing the protections effectively expired when the Supreme Court's mandate was issued July 27 and that Reyes' order merely acknowledged that legal reality.

"Haiti TPS ended when the Supreme Court mandate issued on July 27," Percival wrote on X. "I will give Judge Reyes kudos though for taking the L with grace and not doing something bonkers like many of her colleagues."

Haiti first received TPS after the country's devastating 2010 earthquake, but the designation remained in place for 16 years through multiple administrations. The Biden administration later expanded and extended protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians already living in the U.S.

MORE THAN 100 HAITIAN IMMIGRANTS WITH VIOLENT OFFENSE AND SEX CRIME CONVICTIONS DEPORTED: DHS

After reviewing conditions in Haiti, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem determined the country no longer met the statutory requirements for TPS and announced the administration's decision to terminate the designation, arguing the humanitarian program had been extended well beyond its intended temporary purpose. The move triggered the legal challenge that ultimately reached the Supreme Court.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

After the SCOTUS decision, the DHS announced Haiti's TPS designation would be terminated, effective July 27, and that employment authorization documents issued under the designation were no longer valid. The department instructed employers to reverify the work authorization of affected employees.

The State Department maintains a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" advisory for Haiti because of widespread gang violence, kidnappings and civil unrest.

Fox News Digital's Danielle Wallace and Michael Lee contributed to this report.

World.title: Progressive Democrat scores narrow victory in Michigan primary
World.content: Abdul El-Sayed's projected victory over Rep. Haley Stevens delivers another win for progressives in the battle over the Democratic Party's direction, setting up a closely watched general election in Michigan. NBC News’ Shaquille Brewster reports.Aug. 5, 2026

World.title: Trump-backed John James wins Michigan’s GOP primary for governor
World.content:
Rep. John James has won Michigan’s Republican nomination for governor, NBC News projects.

James, who represents the Detroit suburbs, prevailed in the primary despite being vastly outspent by his opponent, wealthy businessman Perry Johnson.

President Donald Trump, despite harboring early concerns that a bid for higher office would put the two-term congressman’s competitive House district at risk, endorsed James and last week traveled to the state to campaign for him.

James, 45, will face Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary, this fall in one of the most fiercely contested battleground states. Term limits prevent Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, from seeking re-election.

An Army veteran who lost two Senate races before winning his House seat in 2022, James presented himself throughout the race as a capable public servant with applicable business experience, given his work with his family’s logistics company.

“This is an amazing state with all the great ingredients, but for the past seven-and-a-half years, under Gretchen Whitmer, we’ve been led to higher taxes, more crime on the roads — and frankly, the roads we have aren’t fixed yet,” James said during a televised debate last month, throwing back to Whitmer’s 2018 campaign vow to “fix the damn roads.”

“We’re going to work together to make sure that our children can read, to make sure that we put criminals in jail, and we hold those accountable who continue to let them back out,” James added. “And we’re going to be making sure that we come together to accomplish the mission of increasing hope and purpose with tested, positive leadership that has actually been tested from the battlefield to business to delivering for you right now.”

Johnson, 78, pounded the state with more than $31 million worth of ads, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm. He drew on his work in quality control and improving business efficiencies while campaigning on a plan to eliminate the state’s income tax. Johnson also drew on his personal wealth, self-funding his run while declining political donations.

“In the state of Michigan, people are really tired of the politicians,” Johnson told NBC News in an interview last month. “I am an outsider. Nobody denies this fact. I’m the outsider of outsiders.”

James’ campaign spent a fraction on advertising — $2.8 million, according to AdImpact.

One potential factor in the results was the absence of former state Attorney General Mike Cox, who dropped out of the primary on July 17 and threw his support to James. Several polls had shown Cox grabbing a substantial share of the Republican vote and raised the possibility of an unpredictable three-way split that could have benefited Johnson.

Meanwhile, the general election challenge eased a bit for Democrats in May when former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan ended his independent bid for governor. Duggan, a longtime Democrat, had expressed disappointment with both major political parties but caught attention — and grief — from Democrats who noted his reluctance to aggressively criticize Trump.

Michigan voters have not elected a Democrat to succeed a Democrat as governor in more than 65 years.

Benson deputy campaign manager Alyssa Bradley wrote in an email that the secretary of state “begins the general election with something no other candidate can claim: a record of delivering.”

An accompanying campaign memo took a parting shot at both Republican candidates for governor.

“John James and Perry Johnson spent this year lobbing personal attacks at each other and competing for Donald Trump’s attention, not talking to Michigan families about the cost of housing, healthcare, or keeping the lights on,” the memo read. “Both Republican candidates focused on election denying and Donald Trump, while Jocelyn has stayed focused on the issues affecting Michigan families every day.”

World.title: FDA approves 1st mRNA flu shot, from Moderna
World.content:
The Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday approved the U.S.’ first flu shot that uses mRNA technology: mFlusiva, from drugmaker Moderna.

The FDA granted approval for two age groups, adults 50 to 65 and adults 65 and up, on the condition that Moderna run an additional clinical trial in the older group, the company said in a release. In a late-stage trial, mFlusiva was found to be about 27% more effective than a standard flu shot.

Many scientists and public health experts have touted the idea of an mRNA-based flu vaccine, which uses the same messenger RNA platform as the Covid vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer. That’s because mRNA vaccines can be manufactured much faster than traditional vaccines, allowing scientists to better match circulating influenza strains.

Moderna said it takes two to three months from picking the strain to rolling out its flu shot, compared with about six months for traditional flu shots.

“If you’re choosing the strain half a year before, how good can we be at sharpshooting?” said Dr. Ofer Levy, director of the Precision Vaccines Program at Boston Children’s Hospital.

The flu puts hundreds of thousands of people in the hospital every year, according to the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and there can be tens of thousands of deaths. Young children and older adults are more likely to get very sick from the flu.

The traditional flu shot ranges in effectiveness from 22% to 56%, according to the Mayo Clinic. “We wish it were higher, quite frankly,” Levy said.

Even though mFlusiva outperformed the traditional flu shot in a late-stage clinical trial, its approval was not a sure thing.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — an anti-vaccine activist — has repeatedly criticized mRNA technology, calling the Covid vaccines “the deadliest vaccine ever made.” Last year, HHS under Kennedy canceled nearly $500 million in funding for mRNA vaccine research.

The FDA initially refused this year to review Moderna’s application before it reversed course a week later. Agency officials said they wanted more data because Moderna had compared its vaccine with a standard flu shot in adults 65 and older, even though the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a high-dose flu vaccine for that age group. Moderna has said the FDA previously signed off on the trial design.

In June, the FDA’s independent vaccine advisory committee unanimously recommended approving the vaccine.

That decision was based on a late-stage clinical trial of more than 40,000 older adults across 11 countries, including the U.S. Rates of side effects — such as injection-site pain, fatigue and headaches — were more common in the mFlusiva group but still mild to moderate.

A combination flu and Covid vaccine from Moderna, which also uses mRNA, was approved by the European Union in April. Moderna withdrew its application for U.S. approval for that shot last year despite positive late-stage trial results.

Moderna said mFlusiva will be available for this fall’s flu season.

Vaccines, however, are typically formally recommended by the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee — called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) — before they are used. But a federal judge has blocked the committee from convening.

Levy said mFlusiva could still be legally prescribed in the U.S. without ACIP’s sign-off.

However, he said, patients most likely would not be able to get insurance coverage, as private insurers generally cover only ACIP-recommended shots, and the public distribution of the vaccine would be severely limited with no official federal guidance on whom the shots should go to. Federal programs, such as Vaccines for Children and Medicaid, also rely on ACIP’s guidance.

“That is a serious concern,” he said.

World.title: Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeños at Chipotle and Qdoba expands to 27 states
World.content:
Federal health officials are investigating a salmonella outbreak tied to jalapeños that has sickened 345 people in 27 states, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Wednesday.

The jalapeños were supplied by California-based Coast Citrus Distributors and sourced from Mexico, the CDC said. They were served at Chipotle, Qdoba and other restaurants.

Minnesota and Colorado account for the vast majority of cases, with 110 each. Illinois has reported 30 cases and Kansas 13. The remaining states are Alabama, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Thirty-six people have been hospitalized, the CDC said. No deaths have been reported.

Chipotle said Tuesday that it had removed jalapeños from its menu “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, Qdoba said it had “proactively removed jalapeños from all our restaurants.”

The CDC said there is no ongoing risk at either restaurant because the jalapeños were removed from their menus.

Coast Citrus Distributors has agreed to issue a recall, the CDC said.

The Food and Drug Administration said it began investigating “multiple ingredients” tied to the outbreak on July 22 but has not named any restaurants or suppliers.

The CDC said the FDA is working to determine whether the jalapeños went to grocery stores.

The FDA did not respond to requests for comment.

Minnesota state officials said the majority of people sick in the state reported having eaten at Chipotle from June 14 to July 14. The remaining people reported having eaten at a variety of other Mexican-style restaurants, said Carlota Medus, a senior epidemiologist supervisor in the state Health Department’s Foodborne Disease Unit.

Salmonella infection is a foodborne illness usually caused by eating raw or undercooked produce contaminated with salmonella bacteria, according to the Mayo Clinic. Symptoms include diarrhea, stomach cramps and fever.

More than a dozen states are experiencing a surge in cases from another foodborne illness, cyclosporiasis. That outbreak has been traced to lettuce served at Taco Bell that was supplied by Taylor Farms and sourced from central Mexico. More than 22,000 people have confirmed or suspected illnesses, and 517 people have been hospitalized in that outbreak, according to the CDC.

Byron Chaves, a food safety expert at Rutgers University, called the dual outbreaks “coincidental” and most likely the result of increased testing.

However, he said the CDC’s response to the salmonella outbreak was “delayed,” noting that Minnesota first began reporting cases of salmonella earlier in the summer.

“Why is the response so broken?” he asked.

World.title: Cyclosporiasis outbreak has expanded to six more states
World.content:
A massive cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce has expanded to an additional six states, according to a source familiar with the matter.

The outbreak, caused by a microscopic parasite found in human feces, is responsible for hundreds of hospitalizations and two deaths since early May.

The newly linked states — Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina — join Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, said the source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services has reported 1,095 cases as of Sunday — nearly double the number of cases it reported last week.

The agency’s update marks a significant expansion in the outbreak of cyclosporiasis, a foodborne illness that often leads to watery, sometimes explosive, diarrhea.

The additional states, however, do not necessarily mean the outbreak is continuing to spread, said Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting Food and Drug Administration commissioner.

The majority of the cases have been traced to lettuce at Taco Bell that was supplied by Taylor Farms and sourced from central Mexico. Last month, the produce giant issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce supplied from central Mexico, which the company said was distributed to restaurants and retail stores in 27 states.

The FDA hasn’t yet identified other potential sources beyond Taylor Farms.

The newly linked cases, Ostroff said, may involve people who ate the recalled lettuce weeks ago but were only recently diagnosed and reported to health officials.

“With an incubation period up to two weeks, there should no longer be people newly getting sick from that product,” Ostroff said. “But it takes a while for people to seek health care after onset, get tested and diagnosed, reported to state health departments and then to CDC.”

“Think of it like solving a jigsaw puzzle,” he added. “You have all these pieces sitting there, and the longer you work on it, the more likely it is you’ll figure out where each piece fits into the puzzle.”

More than 22,000 people have confirmed or suspected cyclosporiasis, and 517 people have been hospitalized in the multistate outbreak, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said late Tuesday.

On Monday, health officials in Michigan — which has the most cyclosporiasis cases — confirmed the first deaths linked to this outbreak in the United States. Both people had underlying health conditions that may have been affected by the illness and dehydration, the officials said.

Ostroff said the key question about the newly added states is when their patients became sick.

The recalled Taylor Farms lettuce should no longer be available in the U.S., and its use-by dates ended Aug. 3, Ostroff said. If people were exposed after that, investigators may need to look for another source.

“We may have solved the Taylor Farms shredded lettuce piece, but that’s unlikely to explain everything we’re seeing,” he said.

World.title: Firefighters are working 16-hour shifts as they battle the Spokane Complex Fire
World.content:
SPOKANE, Wash. — Hundreds of firefighters are working long shifts to slow the Spokane Complex Fire ahead of hotter and drier conditions this weekend.

More than 1,500 firefighters from two dozen states are battling the conflagration, which has damaged or destroyed nearly 850 structures since it ignited Saturday.

Temperatures were expected to climb from the 80s the last two days into the upper 90s later this week with no rain on the horizon.

Still, “tremendous progress” has been made, said Tom Stokesberry, spokesman for the California Interagency Incident Management Team that is coordinating the multiagency response.

The fire has grown by only 2 acres since Monday, and fire lines are being established on the three fires that make up the Spokane Complex. About 67,000 people have been displaced, officials said, adding that the number could climb.

No deaths have been reported.

“If our lines hold through the weekend, I think we’re going to be on the path to not having this fire move anymore,” he said. “But it’s still going to be a long recovery phase.”

The Old Trails and Autumn Lane fires were each 13% contained Wednesday, and the Fairview Fire was 5% contained, according to fire officials. The fires had burned 10,546 acres by Wednesday evening.

Firefighters are embroiled in what Stokesberry called a “search and destroy” mission. Elite Hotshot crews are stationed within acres of one another in an effort to mitigate all hot spots as they emerge, he said.

The crews are sleeping just five to seven hours a night, and they are working 16-hour shifts. Their deployments are typically two weeks before they are replaced by fresh crews, Stokesberry said. Additional support is expected to arrive this weekend.

“It’s trying on them, but they’re here for the long haul,” he said.

Michael Kelly, a spokesperson for the Washington State Department of Natural Resources, said that with more than 800 structures lost, the fire is “likely one of the most destructive in state history.”

The 2023 Grey and Oregon Road fires outside Spokane destroyed 350 structures, Kelly said.

Wildfire smoke in Spokane on Saturday. Tyler Vanwert via Reuters

Progress was thwarted this week when 40 drones entered restricted airspace and forced aerial crews to land until flight paths were cleared, Stokesberry said.

“If you fly, we can’t,” he said. “It puts crews at risk. It puts life and property at risk, the infrastructure at risk. It puts everything at risk.”

Drones have interrupted firefighters in the past, including in the Palisades Fire last year. A Southern California man was charged with recklessly operating a drone that crashed into a Super Scooper firefighting aircraft. He pleaded guilty, the U.S. Justice Department said.

It was not immediately clear whether any drone operators have been identified or questioned in connection with the recent incidents. Stokesberry said the skies have remained free of uncrewed aircraft since Monday, which has allowed fire crews to attack from above and below.

A man suspected of arson in one of the fires is expected to be arraigned Thursday.

Aaron Farinacci, 37, who is accused of starting the Old Trails Fire, was charged Monday with first-degree arson. An attorney for Farinacci did not immediately respond to a request for comment after normal business hours Wednesday.

Dozens of homes are burned to the ground after a wildfire hit the northern part of Spokane on Monday. Lindsey Wasson / AP

People also started the two other fires, investigators have said, though not necessarily intentionally. The exact causes remain under investigation, officials said. No one else has been arrested.

On Saturday, Paul Child, 64, was driving along railroad tracks in his rural neighborhood northwest of Spokane, he told The Associated Press. He saw a man standing and looking toward nearby trees.

“He was bent over in the brush, acting nervous,” Child said. “You get the feeling this guy’s up to something.”

After they got home, his daughter told him there was a fire, he said.

She called 911 with a description of the man. A responding sheriff’s deputy saw a man matching the description and detained him, according to court records related to Farinacci’s arrest. Officials said the man, identified as Farinacci, was released because a cause had not yet been determined, but he was later arrested and charged.

Alicia Victoria Lozano reported from Los Angeles and Morgan Chesky from Spokane.

World.title: Three state attorneys general subpoena Anthony Fauci over Covid guidance
World.content:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Wednesday that his office is joining two other states in issuing a subpoena to Dr. Anthony Fauci, alleging that he “profited” from the recommendations he gave during the handling of the Covid pandemic.

Uthmeier, joined by West Virginia Attorney General John McCuskey and Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, said in a news release that he was issuing an investigative subpoena to Fauci for “an official investigation into awards, professional opportunities, financial incentives, grants, and Covid-19 guidance that impacted Florida businesses and consumers.”

“Government officials have a certain level of immunity in their official capacities, but if Fauci personally profited off of the ‘guidance’ he issued, that very well could have broken Florida law,” Uthmeier said.

The move comes as Fauci has faced renewed scrutiny from some lawmakers on Capitol Hill over his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Uthmeier cited the journal entries recently released by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., that revealed Fauci’s near-daily account of the pandemic as it unfolded during both the Trump and Biden administrations.

“Fauci’s diary focused more on self-promotion than the legitimate safety concerns from the mRNA vaccines,” Uthmeier said. “While Fauci was pushing for book deals, awards, and fortune and fame, Floridians were being deceived and harmed by his misrepresentations.”

“The public deserves answers to about a million questions related to the pandemic, its origins, and the government’s actions in response,” he said.

Uthmeier said Fauci’s entries detail “substantial awards,” including grants, book deals and board positions, linked to his public recommendations as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases that affected Florida.

Fauci’s journal entries were written during his time as a federal government employee, and they were written on government-owned devices. Fauci has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing related to his handling of the Covid pandemic response.

Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, did not immediately return a request for comment.

The subpoena asks Fauci to provide documents that relate to the alleged “self-dealing” from Jan. 3, 2020, through the present day by Aug. 31.

The list includes grants, awards and book deals Fauci was considered for or received, as well as his interactions with Florida businesses, media outlets and communities about Covid recommendations. The subpoena also asks for documents “concerning vaccine efficacy and boosters, natural immunity, potential adverse events including myocarditis risks, messaging strategies, and communications with vaccine manufacturers.”

At a contentious hearing last week before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering questions from Republicans about the handling of the pandemic.

McCuskey called his refusal to answer the questions “concerning” in the release Wednesday.

“The American people deserve to know if they or their elected leaders were misled or manipulated. Both my Office and I support Attorney General Uthmeier’s efforts to uncover the truth,” McCuskey said.

The committee is scheduled to vote Thursday morning on whether to hold Fauci in contempt for his refusal to answer its questions. The resolution is expected to be approved, as it requires a simple majority vote from the Republican-led committee to pass.

Paul, the chairman of the committee, said he plans to send the resolution to the Justice Department immediately if it is approved.

The Justice Department will decide whether to act upon the resolution, as the committee’s recommendation does not force any action.

President Joe Biden issued a pre-emptive pardon for Fauci just before he left office in January 2025.

But the proposed resolution argues that Paul “found the privilege of the Fifth Amendment unsupported as applied to questions pertaining to the period of the pardon and directed Dr. Fauci to answer.” It added that Fauci “waived his right” to invoke the Fifth Amendment since he included “subject matter pertinent to the questions under inquiry” in his opening testimony to the committee.

At the committee hearing, Republicans attacked Fauci’s past recommendations about Covid and accused him of providing harmful advice and not being honest about the origins of the virus.

Fauci said in his opening testimony that his decision to invoke his Fifth Amendment right stemmed from Paul’s repeated attacks against him, citing Paul’s “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution.”

World.title: Trump denies U.S. running low on some munitions, says vast resupplies being made
World.content:
President Trump is taking issue with recent reports of significant U.S. munitions shortages due to the war with Iran.

In a post on his Truth Social platform early Thursday, Mr. Trump said, "The U.S. has massive amounts of 'munitions,' especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country's history. The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!"

CBS News reported Tuesday that the U.S. has used nearly all of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the war, according to two sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

The sources said the U.S. has used virtually all of its Army Tactical Missile Systems, known as ATACMS, and Precision Strike Missiles. Reuters was first to report that the U.S. had used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during Operation Epic Fury.

CBS News previously reported that the U.S. has dwindling stockpiles of defensive interceptors and long-range missiles, which has become a pressure point within the administration, and that the U.S. cannot sustain the rate at which it expended precision munitions early in the war with Iran.

U.S. officials said there are limited inventories of the ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, and that the most pressing concern involves the number of Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors, which have been used faster than the industry can replace them.

A July report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that before the war began, the U.S. had 2,330 Patriots, and at the end of July, was down to between 759 and 827 of them. The report also estimated that before the war, the U.S. had 452 THAAD interceptors, and as of July 27, was down to between 234 and 278. Another recent CSIS report estimates it could take until at least mid-2029 to return to pre-war inventory levels for both.

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement to CBS News that, "America's military is the most powerful in the world and has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the President's choosing. We have executed multiple successful operations across combatant commands while ensuring the U.S. military possesses a deep arsenal of capabilities to protect our people and our interests."

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously dismissed concerns about the U.S. stockpile.

"That is a manufactured story that the media wants to peddle and ultimately our stockpiles are great, and they're only getting stronger," Hegseth said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on June 14.

World.title: Man carrying ammunition arrested near Trump National Golf Club before president's visit
World.content:
A man was arrested near the Trump National Golf Club in Los Angeles County over the weekend after authorities found ammunition and a gun inside his car, just days before the president's planned Southern California visit for a Republican National Committee event on Tuesday.

In a news release shared by the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, deputies said that plainclothes federal agents reported a suspicious individual on the property at 1 Trump National Drive in Rancho Palos Verdes on Saturday afternoon.

"The individual was observed walking throughout the golf course grounds taking photographs and videos and appearing to monitor security-planning activities," the release said.

Legal complaint against Jeanine John Taele Page of

When deputies approached the man, who has been identified as 38-year-old Downey resident Jeanine John Taele, they determined he was already under investigation by the El Segundo Police Department for an alleged robbery at an AT&T store in November 2025.

"Deputies detained Taele and located his vehicle in a parking lot on the golf course," the release said. "During the detention, deputies recovered a 16-round magazine containing hollow point ammunition from Taele's pants pockets."

While searching his vehicle, deputies said they also recovered a loaded pistol with a round chambered and an additional loaded magazine that also had hollow point ammo. Federal authorities also noted that a pair of binoculars and a badge that read "security protection agent" were also found.

Taele, a former U.S. Marine who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan, was arrested and booked on charges of carrying a concealed firearm and possession of armor-piercing/prohibited ammunition, deputies said.

"Recognizing the potential security implications surrounding the incident, detectives ... obtained and executed a search warrant yesterday afternoon for Taele's residence," the release said.

Investigators said an illegally modified AR platform rifle, a 1911 .45 caliber pistol, an AR platform upper receiver, body armor, high-capacity magazines, bulk pistol and rifle ammunition, two radio signal devices and multiple notebooks containing "concerning statements" were recovered from the home during Monday's search warrant.

The statements referenced the White House, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

"With respect to this defendant, we do not comment on the specifics of protective intelligence matters," the Secret Service said in a statement. "However, the U.S. Secret Service thoroughly investigates any information or activity that may reasonably be perceived as a protective intelligence concern or indicate a potential threat or directed interest toward any individual under Secret Service protection."

Taele received multiple commendations during his eight years in the Marines, including for good conduct. After leaving the service, he was a licensed armed security guard, according to a public records search.

Jeanine John Taele, the Downey man who was arrested near the Trump National Golf Club over the weekend after authorities found a firearm and ammunition in his vehicle. U.S. Department of Justice

Deputies said the investigation is being conducted with the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force and the U.S. Secret Service.

"Additional charges could be added as the investigation continues. Taele remains in custody," the release said. "The investigation is ongoing."

Law enforcement sources tell CBS News that Taele had initially approached employees at the golf course and falsely identified himself as a U.S. State Department employee who needed to see Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Secret Service personnel, who were already on the property to conduct advanced security preparations, were then alerted to Taele's presence by staff.

Deputies said the case was presented to the LA County District Attorney's Office for filing consideration on Tuesday morning. He was scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday morning, but his hearing was postponed. No rescheduled date was announced.

Sources tell CBS News that Taele has no known prior history with the Secret Service and that he was not on their radar. Investigators said they would be reviewing the material and items recovered from Taele's home, contacting friends and family members and reconstructing his activities before the arrest to determine his intentions.

"With respect to this defendant, we do not comment on the specifics of protective intelligence matters. However, the U.S. Secret Service thoroughly investigates any information or activity that may reasonably be perceived as a protective intelligence concern or indicate a potential threat or directed interest toward any individual under Secret Service protection," a statement provided to CBS News from USSS said.

The firearm and badge that were allegedly recovered from the suspect's possession by federal authorities. U.S. Department of Justice

U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said on X that his office and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives were also investigating the incident, and that they would be providing information as soon as possible.

He later said that Taele was also federally charged for the incident, and that he now faces up to 10 years in federal prison after he was charged with possession of an unregistered short-barreled rifle. Taele still faces charges in a Los Angeles Superior Court for the incident, Essayli noted.

"While we are still investigating the motives of this individual, we are thankful he was apprehended before the President's visit," a statement from Essayli said when federal charges were announced. "Federal and local law enforcement stepped in early and prevented what could have been a dangerous situation from occurring. This investigation remains ongoing."

Authorities said that Taele visited the golf course twice before the president's visit, once on Friday and again on Sunday when he was arrested.

President Trump was briefly in Southern California on Tuesday for a Republican National Committee fundraising dinner hosted at his Rancho Palos Verdes golf course. He departed a little before 9 p.m. as he heads to Las Vegas, Nevada.

Victim of alleged 2025 robbery speaks

The alleged victim of Taele's November 2025 robbery spoke with CBS LA the day after his arrest was announced.

"The way he was talking, he was reporting something to someone. Like, he was recording or doing some sort of voice talk to someone," said Pavish Patel, the AT&T store employee working at the time of the alleged robbery. "I don't know what that was."

Patel said that Taele accused him of recording with his Meta glasses while he was inside the store trying to transfer his phone number.

"I said, 'I'm not recording you,' and then I went back to mind my own business. Then he also starts saying, 'If you're recording me, it won't be good for you.'"

He also alleged that Taele then followed a female customer to the door and started acting strangely, by reciting everything that was happening inside the store and documenting how many people were inside, where the exits were and how many security cameras he could see.

Once Taele left, Patel says he came back and demanded that all of his personal information be deleted. After again leaving for a short time, Patel then said that Taele returned to the store and took his Meta glasses before leaving in his pickup truck.

Taele pleaded not guilty to charges in the robbery case.

World.title: Meta says its AI model breached a third-party company during testing
World.content:
Tech giant Meta revealed Wednesday that one of its artificial intelligence models hacked another organization during testing, the third time in recent weeks that an AI model has improperly accessed a third-party company.

In a statement provided to CBS News, Meta said that "a misconfiguration by Irregular, an independent testing company Meta uses, inadvertently allowed one of our models access to the internet during evaluation."

In its statement, Meta did not name the AI model in question, but sources told the tech outlet The Information that it involved Meta's Muse Spark 1.1, according to Reuters.

"The model subsequently exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party service, in a manner similar to previously-reported instances with other companies," Meta said Wednesday. "Meta learned of this when Irregular notified us, and we are currently investigating and will issue a full retrospective once we have all the facts."

Last week, Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing. The revelation came just days after ChatGPT maker OpenAI disclosed its rogue models had also hacked another company.

Anthropic, the San Francisco-based AI company behind Claude, posted on its website July 30 that it discovered the three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs.

It had launched a "large-scale" cybersecurity review which specifically looked for evidence whether its AI models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off, in response to the OpenAI incident, Anthropic said.

Anthropic said the models involved in the incidents were Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model. The earliest incidents date to April, the AI company said.

"Claude compromised the impacted organizations' infrastructure using basic techniques," Anthropic said, such as exploiting weak passwords.

In all three incidents, the AI models were tasked with a "capture the flag" cybersecurity challenge, which Anthropic said has been one of the ways it assesses a model's cyber capabilities.

The models were given a fictional scenario and told a piece of secret information, or the "flag," had been hidden on a different machine on the network with the objective of breaking in and retrieving it, it said.

It added that it had already reached out to the affected organizations, which it did not name. Two of them said they had not previously detected the activity. Anthropic said it was "continuing to reach out to the third."

Anthropic also said it conducted its review with Irregular.

"Addressing these risks will require closer cooperation across the AI ecosystem," Irregular said in a July 30 post on X.

Last month, OpenAI said its AI models went rogue during an evaluation of its models, breaking into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face. OpenAI described it as a "significant security incident."

These incidents have highlighted the vulnerabilities in AI security and controls and raised questions over how AI can be safely kept under human control as the technology's usage becomes more widespread globally.

World.title: Perez Hilton hospitalized after livestreaming acts of self-harm, officials say
World.content:
Celebrity gossip journalist Perez Hilton was taken to a hospital in Miami on Tuesday night after livestreaming "acts of self-harm" on social media, police said.

The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said it received multiple calls about the incident and responded to the scene. Deputies spoke to family members and learned Hilton was alone inside the home.

In the TikTok livestream, which has since been taken down, Hilton appears to be bloodied and in a distressed mental state.

Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, was taken to a local hospital for medical attention, law enforcement said.

"The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office Crisis Response Unit and Licensed Mental Health Professionals are also on scene providing support and resources to the individual's family," the sheriff's office said.

In a statement posted to his website Wednesday evening, his family said it was "able to confirm that Perez is able to communicate, which has given our family hope."

In an earlier statement, the family said it could "confirm that Perez is receiving medical care, and our family's focus right now is on his well-being. We kindly ask that you respect Perez's privacy, as well as the privacy of his family, during this difficult time."

Hilton, 48, grew to prominence in the 2000s when he started a controversial celebrity blog. The journalist has courted many controversies over the years for his unfiltered take on celebrity life, not hesitating to criticize those celebrities who he disliked.

TikTok said the video was flagged by its automated moderation system and sent to its team for review, but an error by a moderator caused a delay in its removal. The steam remained up for about 15 minutes, according to TikTok.

The company said it alerted law enforcement immediately and banned the account.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: FDA approves Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine after initial pushback
World.content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a new seasonal flu vaccine from Moderna that uses mRNA technology, the drugmaker announced Wednesday.

mFLUSIVA, approved for adults ages 50 and older, is the first influenza vaccine using mRNA technology to receive FDA approval.

"This approval also reflects the ongoing potential of our mRNA platform to help address important public health challenges through continued scientific innovation," Moderna said in a statement. "We are grateful to the clinical trial participants, investigators, regulators and Moderna teams whose contributions made this milestone possible."

The FDA is part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the approval comes despite repeated criticism of mRNA technology by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Last year, Kennedy canceled 22 vaccine development projects that use mRNA technology.

The FDA had earlier this year said it would refuse to consider Moderna' application. But it reversed course about a week later and stated it would allow the vaccine to proceed to review after discussions with Moderna "led to a revised regulatory approach and an amended application, which FDA accepted."

The dispute had centered on a 40,000-person clinical trial that found Moderna's new vaccine was more effective in adults aged 50 and older than one of the standard flu shots used today. In a refusal-to-file letter sent to Moderna though, FDA vaccine director Dr. Vinay Prasad faulted the trial for not including another brand specifically recommended for people 65 and older.

Moderna subsequently revised its application to seek full vaccine approval for adults aged 50 to 64 and accelerated approval for adults aged 65 and older. The drugmaker also agreed to conduct an additional study of the drug's use by older adults.

Moderna said it expects to have mFLUSIVA available for the 2026-27 flu season.
