World.title: Germany's brigade key to deterring Russia, Lithuanian FM tells Euronews
World.content:
"We are not interested in having the extension of Russia on our borders for many reasons," Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said of neighbouring Belarus.

 

Those concerns are part of the reason for the Bundeswehr's first permanently stationed combat brigade abroad in its 71-year history.

By the end of 2027, around 5,000 German soldiers will be permanently stationed in Lithuania, just a few kilometres from the Belarusian border, to help protect NATO's eastern flank.

The Lithuania Brigade – officially Panzerbrigade 45 – will be the Bundeswehr's first permanent overseas deployment since it was founded in 1955.

Budrys added there are some independent actions they see coming from Belarus, which are often connected to hybrid activities against Lithuania, such as instrumentalising migration, using meteorological balloons to violate the country's airspace, as well as Belarussian security services harassing the exiled opposition.

Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys speaks with the media as he arrives for a meeting of EU foreign ministers at the European Council building in Brussels, 16 March, AP Photo

Belarus 'a military backyard of Russia'

Belarussian exiled opposition politician and president-elect after the 2020 elections, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, also told Euronews, that Russia has turned the country into "a military backyard of Russia".

"They are deploying nuclear weapons, deploying Oreshnik. They are using our infrastructure. They have logistic capability to use Belarus. Lukashenka actually militarised our economy, about 300 Belarusian enterprises are producing military stuff for Russia," she told Euronews.

"It's a tough neighbour," Budrys added, arguing that Lithuania has learned the value of strong alliances.

Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya in Berlin, 01.04.2026 Franziska Müller

"Our recipe and what we learned throughout these years is that regional partnership and partnership through EU and our NATO membership really helps in these situations," he said. Those partnerships, he added, "not only come in the form of political solidarity, but also in providing some collective instruments that we can apply."

The permanent deployment of Germany's battletank brigade is one of those instruments, albeit Berlin's military presence being not entirely new. Since 2017, the Bundeswehr was part of NATO's Enhanced Forward Presence (eFP) mission, contributing troops to a multinational battlegroup designed to deter Russia. Those deployments were temporary, though, with troops and equipment rotating in and out of the country.

That changed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Vilnius called for stronger security guarantees and then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz pledged to permanently station a brigade in the country.

"I have promised our friends in Lithuania that Germany will lead a robust Bundeswehr brigade that will also be permanently present in Lithuania and, in the event of a crisis, be reinforced immediately by forces from Germany. This is solidarity in action between friends and allies," Scholz told the Bundestag in June 2022.

Outgoing German Chancellor Olaf Scholz in the first voting process at the German federal parliament in Berlin, 6 May, 2025 AP Photo

Germany had initially intended to station only a brigade headquarters in Lithuania, while combat units would continue to deploy from Germany for exercises or if required, as part of NATO's already existing rotational model.

According to the German Bundeswehrverband, this strategy shifted in the summer of 2023, after Wagner group chief Yevgeny Prigozhin's failed mutiny against Russia's military leadership when thousands of his fighters moved to neighbouring Belarus, bringing heavily armed mercenaries to NATO's eastern border.

While the German government insists the Wagner mutiny and the relocation of Wagner fighters to Belarus were not the sole drivers of the permanent deployment to Lithuania, it has acknowledged that the events gave the decision additional momentum.

Weeks later, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius and Chief of Defence General Carsten Breuer travelled to Lithuania to announce a major change: for the first time since the Bundeswehr was founded, Germany would permanently station a fully operational combat brigade outside its own territory. "It is our mission to play a decisive role in protecting NATO's eastern flank," Pistorius said later that autumn.

FILE - Yevgeny Prigozhin, the owner of the Wagner Group military company, looks from a military vehicle leaving an area of the HQ of the Southern Military District in a street AP Photo/File

'No one here is preparing for war'

Lithuania's foreign minister Budrys told Euronews that "deterrence should start from the border," effectively defending every centimetre with "very exact forces" rather than hypothetical capabilities.

"We're so thankful for Germany taking this leadership and increasing its presence in Lithuania," he added, pointing out that he sees it as an "example for others to follow."

Budrys called this the "key to peace and success."

"No one is preparing here for war. We're preparing here to have a stable country, environment, secure for people to be, for the business to flourish," Budrys told Euronews.

Alongside NATO, each Baltic country has one acting security guarantor: the UK leads NATO's enhanced Forward Presence battlegroup in Estonia, while Canada is responsible for the combat-ready NATO Multinational Brigade Latvia and Germany provides protection with the eFP and the Lithuania Brigade.

Kęstutis Budrys Franziska Müller

According to the minister, "more than 80% of the population In Lithuania trust Germany" and the country's decision to permanently deploy a battletank brigade to NATO's eastern flank.

A public opinion poll carried out by Spinter Research company in November 2023 at the request of the Strategic Communications Department of the Lithuanian Armed Forces supports Budrys' point, suggested that the overall approval of the German Brigade stationing in Lithuania was at 82% with a "positive view on the German military" at 83%.

In Germany, just 49% of respondents supported Pistorius' plan to deploy the Lithuania Brigade, a YouGov poll commissioned by the German Press Agency (dpa) from 2023 suggested.

World.title: Younger children who use social media heavily get worse grades, study finds
World.content:
Children who start using social media at a young age appear to struggle more at school than those who open social media accounts only once they are older, a new study has found.

 

The study was published in Nature Human Behaviour and analysed more than 5,000 pupils from northern Italy aged 7 to 16.

The paper was built on a combination of data from a questionnaire on digital media habits with longitudinal standardised exam scores collected in grades 2, 5, 8 and 10 in Italian, mathematics and English.

Specifically, when tested in grade 8 (usually the age range from 13 to 14), students who joined social media at 11 or 12 did worse than those who waited longer to get on social media in both Italian and maths.

And when tested in grade 10 (ages 15-16), the impact not only persisted but widened, particularly in mathematics and for those exposed to social media before 13.

The negative impact is tied to smartphone distractions at key moments of the day, according to the researchers.

While the use of social media from an early age appears to be linked to lower performance in Italian and maths, the same cannot be said for English, which Italian students generally learn as their first foreign language, the study highlighted.

The authors of the study suggest that this discrepancy might be related to the high quantity of English content on social media, which can potentially offer informal learning to its users.

Research on the relationship between social media and children is on the rise and this study aligns with results from recent analyses exploring the impact of social media use on the educational and cognitive performance of school-aged children.

Based on their results, the authors of the study emphasise the need for digital literacy programmes in schools, suggest regulating engagement mechanisms on platforms used by minors, and note the need for policies delaying social media access for children.

A timely study

This study comes at a particularly sensitive time for the debate around social media.

After Australia became the first country in the world to ban social media for users aged under 16, the discussion reached European countries and the European Union (EU) institutions.

Earlier this summer, French lawmakers approved a bill prohibiting social media access to children under 15, and similar measures are being discussed in Spain and in the UK.

At the EU level, debates are also moving in the direction of more restrictive rules over children’s social media use. In July, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, presented an expert report on this topic and said the evidence increasingly supported introducing a minimum age for accessing these platforms.

The report, however, did not back a blanket ban on social media platforms like the one in Australia, but rather underlined the necessity of a “safe by design” approach, putting part of the responsibility onto digital platforms.

Despite the social media debate being in the spotlight, Italy, the country where the study was conducted, was not particularly central to the discussion.

In June, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said her government will not push for a social media ban as the measure can easily be circumvented.

This argument is often put forward by critics of the measure and is backed by some studies conducted in Australia, which show that age verification methods are not effective.

World.title: City breaks without the crowds: Europe’s top ‘second cities’ to visit
World.content:
Congested capitals, tourist taxes and unending queues to see iconic landmarks are enough to make any traveller rethink taking a much-needed holiday altogether.

 

Rather than flocking to Europe’s popular capitals, many tourists are turning to the so-called “second cities” that are growing in appeal.

Observers of this trend have said that travellers are on the lookout beyond familiar itineraries. Instead, they are searching for places that feel more personal, connected and rewarding to explore.

Whether you’re someone who is looking for a quieter alternative to Barcelona, or want to swap London's bustling streets for a slower, more relaxed pace of travel, these destinations offer a stronger sense of local life, the country’s rich heritage, culture and food – but without the crowds.

What is a ‘second city'?

These are the destinations that sit outside of a country’s most popular city, region or area, that may be overlooked by visitors, despite offering a chance to connect with local culture and discover unique experiences.

While the term suggests that it refers to a country’s second most famous or populous city, HuffPost said that it has expanded more generally to “lesser-known destinations”, too.

Think more family-owned places to eat over chain restaurants, smaller art galleries, local food markets offering farm-to-table delicacies – all with the backdrop of stunning landscapes.

While the bright lights of the major destinations have their own allure, travelling to second cities avoids crowded streets and struggling to get a table at the local favourite restaurant. There are also more opportunities to explore untouched neighbourhoods rather than generic tourist hubs.

Second cities are also typically friendlier on travellers’ wallets. Accommodations, meals and entertainment can often be less expensive.

Split in Croatia Photo by Spencer Davis on Unsplash

Europe’s top second cities to visit

From culinary and creative hubs, to scenic coastal destinations, here are our top 10 picks for the second cities in Europe that should be your first choice to visit.

Split, Croatia

Centred around the stunning architecture of the preserved Diocletian’s Palace, Split blends 2,000 years worth of history with an Adriatic lifestyle. Here, visitors can wander alleys from the Roman Empire that lead to waterfront promenades and casual cafés.

For views of the city, climbing the reconstructed bell tower of the Cathedral of Saint Domnius is an unmissable experience.

The coastal Croatian city also offers no shortage of beaches, cycling paths, spas and centres for wellness, making it easy to combine experiences all in one trip.

Cork, Ireland

Located in the southwest of Ireland, Cork packs plenty into a walkable city centre.

Visitors can shop for local produce at the historic Cork English Market, which was created in 1788. Here you’ll find freshly caught fish, confectionery, spices and fruit and veg. From there, you can stroll along St Patrick’s Street all the way to Fitzgerald's Park, which is also a stone’s throw away from the Cork Public Museum.

Cork is also a gateway to Ireland’s southern coastline of colourful harbour towns and scenery of the Atlantic, including dramatic sea cliffs.

Graz, Austria

Graz is a melting pot of Renaissance courtyards, eclectic architecture and a bustling gastronomy scene.

Aboard the Schloßbergbahn, the iconic cable funicular running since 1894, a €3.30 ticket unlocks unbeatable views of Graz, including of the Old Town.

Meanwhile, the futuristic Murinsel, a floating island, connects visitors to the river Mur and houses an amphitheatre and a café.

Hamburg, Germany

Hamburg is Germany’s largest port city and pairs its maritime heritage with a lively street art scene. There are plenty of murals and installations across neighbourhoods like St Pauli, Schanzenviertel and Karoviertel.

While Berlin may have its currywurst and Bavaria has its pretzels, the fish sandwich reigns supreme in Hamburg.

Whether the humble herring, mackerel or crab, freshly caught fish sandwiched in between a roll is a very popular snack. Hamburg Tourismus recommends stopping by the Goedekens Kombüse restaurant for this local popular snack.

Brno in Czechia Photo by Leonhard Niederwimmer on Unsplash

Brno, Czechia

Often overshadowed by Prague, Brno’s medieval landmarks and hidden underground passages pack centuries of history into a walkable city.

From the top of Špilberk Hill, you'll be able to see Špilberk Castle, which is home to the Brno City Museum. Concerts, theatrical performances and festivals are also held there.

Beneath the streets, you can also explore the city’s labyrinths and underground reservoirs, including the Žlutý Kopec Water Tanks where an excursion is split into three experiences, unpacking the histories from the oldest to newest water tanks.

Ypres, Belgium

Steeped in First World War history, Ypres is in Belgium’s Dutch-speaking region of Flanders.

The Yper Museum explores 11 centuries of Ypres and the surrounding Westhoek's history through a collection of archeological finds, maps and handicrafts. The museum also offers a playful cat hunt through the city centre.

Cyclists and hikers can also relish in its sophisticated network of routes that weave past preserved trenches, memorials and green landscapes.

Cambridge, England

Best known for its centuries-old university, Cambridge offers much more than just a day trip from London.

The River Cam runs through the city and boasts views of the famous Cambridge College Backs while leisurely cruising in a punt vessel.

The city is brimming with independent bookshops, museums and greenery – making it ideal for wandering on foot.

Visitors can also explore lively markets including the All Saints Garden market, where you'll find wares from art, jewellery and pottery every Saturday.

Thessaloniki in Greece Photo by Miltiadis Fragkidis on Unsplash

Thessaloniki, Greece

Think Byzantine churches, Roman ruins and a picturesque waterfront with a relaxed atmosphere.

There are plenty of must-see landmarks to be explored, including the Arch of Galerius, Aristotelous Square and the White Tower of Thessaloniki which journey through the city’s history.

When in Thessaloniki, some must-try bites include koulouri, sesame bread rings, bougatsa, a filo pastry snack, and trigona which are crispy friend pastries filled with a velvety cream.

Basel, Switzerland

Located right where Switzerland meets France and Germany, Basel is home to one of the continent’s finest art scenes.

Home of the Art Basel fair, which featured 90 galleries and attracted 16,000 visitors in its inaugural edition in 1970, today, visitors can still attend the illustrious gathering of creative minds.

Meanwhile, the Kunstmuseum Basel museum boasts the oldest public art collection in the world, dating back to 1661, with a collection of more than 300,000 works.

While on the banks of the Rhine river, the city also provides easy access to neighbouring countries.

Lille, France

Lille’s unique Flemish heritage is seen throughout the city’s architecture and cuisine. Elegant squares, colourful townhouses and a bustling art scene also add to its charm.

Meanwhile, the cobbled streets of Vieux-Lille are perfect for a stroll to the picturesque Quai du Wault, a great waterside setting for a picnic or watching the sunset after a day of sightseeing.

World.title: Hungry for cash: where will the EU find the money?
World.content:
In the coming months, European governments will intensify their efforts to establish how the EU's long-term budget for the period 2028-2034 should be financed, with new revenues, called "own resources", at the centre of the debate.

 

The discussion on own resources is not new. During the last long-term budget negotiations, the 27 member states failed to agree on any resources at all, and the budget was eventually financed by a national contribution, each country contributing 1.13 percent of its gross national income.

But given the bloc has grand ambitions to make large new investments in strategic sectors such as AI and defence while maintaining investments for sectors such as agriculture and fisheries, it is clear that the EU needs its own money collected and spent in a coordinated manner, rather than fragmented across 27 different national budgets.

European governments are therefore trying to source fresh money – but finding an agreement on new taxes is not easy, and none of the proposals currently on the table are to everyone's advantage. Member states will have to find a compromise and make the right trade-offs to leave all 27 governments happy – or at least, equally unhappy.

The central problem is that no government welcomes the prospect of new taxes on citizens. This is the central concern EU diplomats expressed to Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity: how can governments convince their publics to accept a new tax?

After all, taxes introduced at the EU level are often perceived as being “imposed” from above, making them a powerful political issue. They can easily become a focal point in election campaigns and may even contribute to the rise or fall of governments.

There are some countries that are setting their negotiating position even higher. Sweden, for instance, is against any form of own resource, arguing that the EU's wealthiest member states would have to shoulder a disproportionate financial burden.

At the same time, any new EU-wide taxes will also face significant technical challenges, since they often require a harmonisation of the bloc's tax law and would have to be set up at lightning speed to start contributing to the budget as of 2028.

Here, Euronews weighs up the proposals currently on the table. This analysis is based on conversations with EU officials and diplomats as well as documents seen by our newsroom.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)

What you need to know: Conceived as complementary to the Emissions Trading System (ETS),the CBAM applies an equivalent carbon price to imports of selected carbon-intensive goods (currently including iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen), preventing producers from relocating emissions abroad and ensuring a level playing field.

Pros: EU countries largely support CBAM in principle. Finland, Austria, Portugal and Poland are among its most vocal backers, and Franceis also in favour.

Cons: Similarly to the ETS, CBAM does not create a new tax but simply redirects revenues from an existing tax towards Brussels. And while it is relatively non-controversial, the revenues it would generate are modest.

Odds: ★★★★★

Value: €1.4 billion annually.

Parcel handling fee

What you need to know: The Commission proposed introducing a Union handling fee on low-value e-commerce parcels imported from outside the EU, mainly targeting Chinese platforms such as Shein and Temu. The rationale is to cover the growing costs incurred by customs authorities in processing billions of small consignments.

Since 1 July, the bloc has levied a temporary €3 flat tax on small parcels under €150 of value. This temporary levy will be in place until the EU implements its tax reform, including the set up of the new EU Tax Authority based in the French city of Lille, which will serve as a so-called Tax Data Hub to improve the speed and efficiency of tax administration across the bloc.

Pros: The proposal aligns with the EU's broader effort to "rebalance" economic relations with China, confronting a widening trade surplus driven by a flood of cheap Chinese goods that often do not respect European safety standards or counterfeit laws.

Cons: There is still no clarity on how much revenue the handling fee will actually generate, and it also creates an economic disincentive to order low-value parcels. Circumvention is another major problem, with e-commerce platforms likely to respond by increasing their warehouse capacity within the EU.

Odds: ★★★★☆

Value: No official estimate. According to the latest figures, close to 5.9 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2025. However, the new fee might shift the share of parcels shipped directly to consumers, which would be charged €2, in favour of parcels shipped from warehouses located in the EU, for which only a €0.50 fee applies.

Online gambling tax

What you need to know: EU officials are focused on two ongoing trends in the gambling world: the shift from physical to online, and the growing proliferation of illicit activities. Data on the market is scarce, and an online gambling tax might take some time to set up.

Pros: The new tax might help address several ongoing issues related to online gambling, such as underage gambling, betting on illicit subjects and organised crime. It might also increase the revenues for countries where most gambling websites are located, among them Malta.

Cons: Malta in particular remains fiercely against an online gambling tax, a major obstacle given the EU budget can only be adopted unanimously. The question is what Valletta might be offered in return for concessions. Besides this, there are also questions about disparity between the treatment of online gambling activities and offline ones.

Odds: ★★★★☆

Value: €1.9 billion annually.

Tobacco excise duty

What you need to know: The exact baseline for the tobacco tax is still a moving target since EU countries are discussing a revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive, and have already reduced the scope and ambition compared to the initial proposal.

Pros: A tobacco tax could generate significant revenues and is being harmonised at the EU level. It also discourages tobacco usage, especially among poorer users, with positive impacts on health. Opposition is not seen as insurmountable.

Cons: The tax faces opposition from southern European countries, in particular Bulgaria, Czechia, Luxembourg, and Slovenia. There are fears it could fuel the black market and put jobs at stake, and there are disagreements over whether alternative products like e-cigarettes should be taxed on the same level as traditional products.

Odds: ★★★★☆

Value: €11.2 billion annually.

Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE)

What you need to know: The CORE would be an annual lump-sum contribution paid by big companies that operate and sell in the EU with a net annual turnover of €100 million.

Pros: Taxing big companies, particularly Chinese or American, might be easy to sell to the public, and EU officials point out that the amount companies are asked to pay is typically lower than bonuses for top executives. While CORE in its original form is unlikely to survive, officials insist it "isn't dead yet" since it could be recalibrated to overcome Washington's opposition to the EU's digital taxation, since a corporate tax is not sector-specific.

Cons: The idea of creating an EU-level corporate tax is facing significant ideological opposition, as it runs counter to the competitiveness agenda. Although the percentage floated is considered minimal, countries like Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands are against the move in principle, saying it could create a dangerous precedent.

Odds: ★★★☆☆

Value: €6.8 billion annually.

Non-collected e-waste

What you need to know: The Commission proposed to introduce a contribution based on the application of a call rate of €2/kg (annually adjusted for inflation) to the weight of non-collected e-waste.

Pros: A new incentive to collect and recycle e-waste would have environmental benefits whilst making a strategic contribution to grappling with China's dominance in critical raw materials supply chains.

Cons: The amount would be paid by the member states as a national contribution based on the non-collected e-waste that the capitals declare to Eurostat. This might provide a perverse incentive for governments to under-report the actual volume of e-waste rather than reducing it.

Odds: ★★★☆☆

Value: €15 billion annually.

EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)

What you need to know: Since 2005, the EU's ETS1 has operated as a “cap-and-trade” scheme aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It sets a limit on the total emissions that companies can produce and requires firms to purchase allowances to cover their pollution, either from the EU or from other companies.

Pros: The European Commission proposed a targeted adjustment of the revenues generated from ETS1 to go to the EU budget**.** Austria is backing the proposal. The overall ETS is aligned with the EU's green agenda, as the revenues generated are intended to support green transition initiatives.

Cons: Poland is viscerally against the proposal, as are other central and eastern European countries like Estonia, Slovenia, and Bulgaria, who consider it regressive. In addition, the Commission has recently proposed a reform of the ETS1 over industrial competitiveness concerns, with a slower reduction of emissions caps after 2030.

Odds: ★★☆☆☆

Value: €9.6 billion annually.

Digital levy

What you need to know: Introducing a levy on digital services is one of the main ideas floated by the European Parliament. It has yet to be fully developed in terms of design and scope, though the digital taxes already present in France, Spain and Italy could provide a significant precedent.

Pros: The EU countries that already have a digital services tax might support moving it to the European level to avoid direct retaliation from Washington. The tax would also largely fall on non-European businesses, and tech companies pay notoriously low taxes in Europe.

Cons: Washington has already warned it might retaliate if the initiative moves forward. Ireland, the current chair of the EU Council, is also against the proposal, hosting as it does the European headquarters of many of the world's largest tech companies.

Odds: ★★☆☆☆

Value: €5 billion annually.

Tax on crypto assets

What you need to know: Even though it might be politically viable for the member states to back a cryptocurrency assets tax, getting it up and running and preventing tax avoidance present big problems. "It might be a lot of work for nothing," EU officials say.

Pros: Cryptocurrencies are facing increasing regulatory pressure due to their use in black market activity, money laundering and other illicit purposes. There is political appetite for further scrutinising this market and better tracking the revenues coming from it.

Cons: Among all the revenue ideas floated at the European Parliament, this might be the least viable. The market it would be focused on is very volatile and fundamentally decentralised, allowing users to escape the scrutiny of public authorities. Some countries already have a capital gains tax that covers crypto, but most users simply do not report it.

Odds: ★☆☆☆☆

Value: €3-4 billion annually for a crypto transaction tax, €1-2.4 billion for a capital gains tax.

World.title: Exiled PM Sheikh Hasina vows return to Bangladesh
World.content:
Sheikh Hasina vowed to return to Bangladesh despite facing a death penalty, telling supporters that fear could not decide her "duty to the people."

Ousted former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said Wednesday that she plans to return to Bangladesh from exile in India in December. She faces a death sentence at home over a deadly crackdown on protesters in 2024.

Hasina spoke during a media event in New Delhi hosted by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia. It marked the second anniversary of the uprising that forced her out of power. It was her first time speaking to the media since she fled the country. While she had been expected to appear on video, she only delivered an audio message from behind a blank screen.

It remains unclear why she chose not to show her face, since other Awami League leaders and her son, who had spoken earlier, had appeared on camera.

Sheikh Hasina delivered a virtual address with audio only Image: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

Sajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of Sheikh Hasina, addresses reporters via video link Image: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

What did Sheikh Hasina say?

"I will return to my people," Hasina said. She added that she would share the exact date and details of her return at a later time. "I know that they may put me in jail, or they may kill me, or anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she said. "Fear cannot decide my duty to the people."

Hasina fled to India in 2024 after student-led protests ended her tenure as prime minister, a role she had held for a total of 20 years spread across two terms.

In 2025, a Bangladeshi court convicted her in absentia of crimes against humanity for her role in the violent crackdown on student-led protests in 2024. The United Nations said close to 1,400 people were killed.

She was sentenced to death. Hasina denies the charges and calls the case politically motivated.

How has it impacted Bangladesh-India relations?

Relations between Bangladesh and its neighbor have been strained since Hasina fled there. Dhaka has repeatedly sought Hasina's extradition, while India said it had received the request and was reviewing it.

Bangladesh's foreign ministry criticized Wednesday's event, calling it an insult to the country's sovereignty. It said letting Hasina speak publicly to the press was "deeply hurtful" and that Bangladesh was "outraged."

The government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had also warned local media a day earlier not to publish her remarks, citing a 2024 court order that prohibited the broadcasting or publication of her statements. As a result, no media outlets in Bangladesh covered the event, but it was shared widely on social media.

Rahman is the son of former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia and a longtime rival of Hasina. He won power in a February election overseen by the country's interim government. Hasina's Awami League was barred from taking part in that vote.

Hasina calls charges politically motivated

During her address, Hasina also called on the government to lift its ban on her party and to free political prisoners, arguing that what began as protests over public job quotas turned into a coordinated effort to remove her government and undermine the constitution.

She also claimed Bangladesh's economy had worsened since she left office, citing slower growth, weaker investment, and more than 20 million newly unemployed people.

As Hasina spoke to the media, protesters in Dhaka burned an effigy of her. August 5 marked two years since Hasina fled to India by helicopter after her government fell.

The government of Bangladesh has turned the official residence of Sheikh Hasina into a museum commemorating the 2024 student-led protests that forced Hasina from power Image: Samir Kuman Dey/DW

Also on Wednesday, Bangladesh inaugurated a new museum dedicated to the 2024 uprising. The July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum sits inside Hasina's former official residence in Dhaka. It includes audio and video displays, personal items belonging to victims, and newspaper clippings from the time, along with material documenting alleged abuses during Hasina's years in power.

The museum was launched under the interim government of Nobel Peace Prize winner Muhammad Yunus, who took office three days after Hasina's removal. Yunus attended Wednesday's opening alongside Rahman.

Bangladesh and India recently signaled interest in improving ties, but Bangladesh's foreign ministry said allowing Hasina to speak to the press would hurt that relationship.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: What's behind the Algeria-Morocco rivalry?
World.content:
Morocco and Algeria have been at odds for decades, chiefly over the territory of Western Sahara. But their rivalry now extends far beyond the territory.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez traveled to Algeria on July 20 for talks with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb.

The meeting's aim was to resolve a diplomatic row that erupted between both countries in 2022 after Spain sided with Morocco's autonomy proposal to resolve the Western Sahara conflict — much to Algeria's dismay.

It is a matter of debate whether Spain's rapprochement with Algeria outraged Morocco so much that it deliberately allowed tens of thousands of migrants to storm the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, even though both countries have improved their relations enormously in recent years. Spanish daily El Pais has certainly entertained the possibility of Moroccan meddling.

"Ceuta tensions coincided with Pedro Sanchez's trip to Algeria, a regional rival of the [Moroccan] Alawite Kingdom," an opinion piece in the Spanish paper notes. The article later states that "any attempt to use immigration as a bargaining chip is unacceptable."

Moroccan interior ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi has rejected such accusations, saying the incident resulted from "the malicious exploitation of the digital space," as well as "misleading information" and misinterpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on the rights of arriving migrants.

Red Cross personnel were on the scene to support migrants who had entered the Spaish exclave Image: Iván Zambrano/Europa Press/dpa/picture alliance

Experts interviewed by DW say that while potentially deliberate inaction by Moroccan border guards contributed to the breach, it's unlikely the country intended to instigate such a major diplomaticincident.

Algeria and Morocco's deep-rooted rivalry

The recent Ceuta incident and subsequent accusations point to the deep-seated rivalry between Algeria and Morocco. At its heart lies the conflict over Western Sahara, which began when Spain withdrew from the territory in 1975. A conflict between the Polisario Front, which fights for the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination, and Morocco ended in 1991 with a UN-brokered ceasefire. A planned referendum to allow Saharawis to determine its future has never taken place, and the UN considers it Africa's last non-self governing territory.

Morocco, relying on historical claims, considers the region an indispensable part of its own national territory, and has sought international recognition for its integration as a semi-autonomous province. Algeria, in contrast, supports Western Sahara's independence and backs the Polisario Front.The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Morocco and Western Sahara are distinct territories.

The Western Sahara conflict has long since become a symbol of a deeper rivalry between Algeria and Morocco over influence in the Maghreb region, according to a paper by the Research Unit on International Security and Cooperation (UNISCI) , an independent Madrid-based research group.

The dispute connects to both countries' domestic politics in the sense that Morocco regards the Western Sahara issue as a matter of territorial integrity, whereas Algeria favors self-determination as it sees itself as an anti-colonial state. This constellation means reaching a compromise in the Western Sahara conflict is becoming increasingly difficult. Indeed, the "Western Sahara conflict has evolved into a struggle for regional hegemony in the Maghreb," says UNISCI.

These tensions have hindered North Africa's economic integration for decades, according to UNISCI experts. Institutions such as the Arab Maghreb Union have been largely paralyzed, with regional economic and security projects making little progress. This diminishes the region's economic momentum and international standing, UNISCI analysts say.

Relations with Israel

The Algeria-Morocco rivalry took on added significance in 2020 when Morocco normalized relations with Israel, after Israel recognized Morocco's claims to Western Sahara.

Algeria began viewing Israel's increasingly close ties with Morocco as a threat to its own security, according to an analysis by the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank . Algeria's concern centers less on diplomatic normalization with Israel per se and more on the prospect of long-term military and intelligence cooperation, which could shift the regional balance of power to Algeria's detriment, the ICG finds.

A Sahrawi refugee woman is seen standing at the door of her home in the Boujdour refugee camp, Algeria, in 2021 Image: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/picture alliance

ICG analysts describe the relationship between Algeria and Morocco as a classic security dilemma, with both states viewing own their military and foreign policy actions as defensive moves, yet perceiving the other's actions as a threat. This gives rise to a growing arms buildup and deepening mistrust, even though neither government has an interest in open war. It is precisely this logic, ICG scholars write, that makes the conflict so dangerous, as even minor incidents or miscalculations can trigger an escalation.

Relations with Europe

Their rivalry is no longer limited to the Western Sahara conflict. Indeed, the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) writes that Morocco and Algeria's strained relationship has evolved into a broader competition for international partners and political influence that includes ties with the European Union . Both nations are striving to underscore their strategic importance to the bloc by leveraging their respective foreign policy strengths, says the ECFR.

While Morocco is positioning itself as a key partner in the areas of migration, counterterrorism and economic cooperation, Algeria is emphasizing its role as an energy supplier and security influence in the Maghreb and Sahel region.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament
World.content:
On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.

Japan on Thursday commemorates the 81st anniversary of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima.

On August 6, 1945, the US dropped an atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima during the last days of World War II, killing close to 80,000 people in the initial blast. Three days later, the US dropped a bomb over Nagasaki.

"Japan adopted a pacifist constitution in reflection on World War II," noted Masako Wada, assistant secretary general of Nihon Hidankyo, or the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers' Organizations.

Japan "earned the trust of the international community as a country that promised never to wage a war again," added Wada, who survived the Nagasaki bombing as a 1-year-old.

The dropping of the atomic bomb on August 6, 1945, flattened more than two-thirds of Hiroshima [FILE: September 8, 1945] Image: Stanley Troutman/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, in recent years, Japan has increased defense spending, eased restrictions on weapons exports and expanded the role of its military, citing growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia.

"The current administration is destroying that [trust]," Wada told DW, referring to Japan's recent efforts to pivot away from decades of strict postwar pacifism.

"Japan's recent military buildup is no different from recreating the arms race that led the country toward World War II," said 84-year-old Masashi Ieshima, who survived the Hiroshima bombing at the age of 3.

Survivors warn against rearmament

Ieshima was playing in the entrance of his house, just 1.2 miles (2 km) from the hypocenter, when the blast shattered all the windows in the house, sending shards of glass into his mother.

Hiroshima 'successors' keep telling atomic bomb stories To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Seventy years later, he underwent surgery for thyroid cancer, which was officially recognized as an atomic bomb-related illness. His father, who was also exposed to the Hiroshima atomic bombing, died of laryngeal cancer.

"It makes my blood boil to see Japan justify its military buildup and the easing of arms export restrictions over the possibility of a Taiwan conflict," said Ieshima, who serves as the chairman of Toyukai, the Tokyo affiliate of Nihon Hidankyo.

"If Japan continues down this path, it could lead to war. And if another war breaks out, I believe it will be a nuclear war."

The average age of Japan's atomic bomb survivors, known as "hibakusha," has reached almost 87. They face the urgent challenge of passing on their testimony and calls for peace to younger generations, including their children, grandchildren, and supporters.

Takako Nakamura, a second-generation atomic bomb survivor from Nagasaki, began working actively as a family testimony speaker in February 2026, following her career retirement.

"People were killed without a trace, not even their bones remain. That is the true nature of the atomic bomb," the 73-year-old told DW, her voice breaking.

Wada urged people around the world to recognize that the danger of nuclear weapons is "not something in the past, but in front of us right now."

She said she does not want sympathy for survivors, but empathy. "I want people to think of it as their own issue."

Japan pushes for military buildup, non-nuclear principles at risk

On Tuesday, Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the country needs to strengthen its military with a "sense of urgency and crisis" as a new government assessment again highlighted growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

In the preface to Japan's latest annual defense white paper , Koizumi said it was "imperative that Japan further reinforce and transform its defense capabilities with a stronger sense of urgency and crisis than ever before."

An atomic bomb explodes after being dropped by a US Air Force B-29 bomber over Nagasaki [FILE: August 9, 1945] Image: U.S. Army Air Forces/Library of Congress/REUTERS

The Defense Ministry told DW that Japan must strengthen its defense capabilities to enhance deterrence while maintaining its exclusively defense-oriented policy.

It cited an increasingly severe security environment, including China's military expansion and activities in the East and South China seas and around Taiwan.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has introduced a series of measures to strengthen Japan's defense capabilities. Her

Her government also relaxed restrictions on arms exports in April 2026, allowing exports of lethal weapons.

It is also considering revising Japan's long-standing commitment to the three non-nuclear principles of not possessing, producing or permitting the entry of nuclear weapons onto Japanese territory.

In November 2025, Takaichi said that a Chinese military attack on Taiwan could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its legal right to collective self-defense.

Many Japanese Gen Zers are opposed to Japan's military expansion Image: Daiki Tateyama/DW

However, the argument that Japan must strengthen its military because China might invade Japan or Taiwan is "not convincing" to the Japanese public, said Koichi Nakano, a professor of political science at Sophia University in Tokyo.

China's military activities, including its maritime expansion, remain limited compared with Russia's war in Ukraine and US attacks on Iran, he told DW.

"Japan is being skillfully drawn into the narrative that it must fall into line with Europe and the US to confront so-called rogue states such as China, North Korea and Russia."

"Japan must responsibly pursue disarmament and establish dialogue," Nakano said. "It must stop demonizing China and recognize it as a country with which meaningful dialogue is possible."

Youth in Japan take to the streets in anti-war protests

Meanwhile, around 27,000 people gathered on July 10 outside the Japanese parliament building in Tokyo, holding colorful illustrated placards with messages such as "No war," and waving glow sticks in the dark.

Reina Tashiro, 36, a member of a civil organization "We Want Our Future," told DW that they aim to "make it as easy as possible for people to take that first step and join a protest."

"It is different from the traditional image of demonstrations, where people raise their fists and shout slogans," Tashiro added. "Our protests may even look stylish."

Nahoko Hishiyama, who has been involved in civic activism for 24 years since the age of 13 and now serves as co-chair of another activist group, pointed out that recent protests have increasingly been led by people in their 20s to 40s, and more women are taking part.

"Japanese women are often said to be too mindful of how others perceive them. In activism, however, that has been turned into a strength, thinking about how to present our message in a way that resonates with the public."

Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: FIFA president Infantino to stay on after crisis meeting
World.content:
FIFA's leadership has apologized for the controversial plan to open the World Cup to private investment. The plan has since been scrapped.

FIFA's leadership on Wednesday apologized for President Gianni Infantino's plan to open the World Cup to private investment, in a crisis meeting held after growing outrage at the plan and Infantino.

In a statement, the FIFA management board acknowledged "that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media." Infantino has since scrapped the plan.

The football body stressed it supported Infantino in staying on as president.

FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did FIFA say?

"Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the FIFA Secretary General and members of the FIFA Management Board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 FIFA Member Associations," the statement added.

FIFA added that a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologizing and promising a review.

But the football body stressed it would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, ‌good governance and due process" with the plan now withdrawn, vowing to take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Calls for Infantino to step down have grown since he abandoned the controversial plan on Saturday.

What was the controversial World Cup sellout plan?

The backlash was centered on a proposal to sell a 20% stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion (roughly €3.6 billion). The plan also came under fire over the involvement of a company with family links to US ‌President Donald Trump, who is considered a close ally of Infantino.

European soccer's governing body UEFA had threatened to boycott the World Cup over the plan.

After the plan was abandoned, UEFA as well as CONCACAF, which runs the game in North and Central America plus the Caribbean, said it had lost confidence in the 56-year-old Swiss Italian’s leadership.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) was also critical of the way the proposal was pushed without consultation.

Additionally, European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect not just clubs and players, but also fans.

The "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament was also heavily criticized.

Infantino faces a re-election bid in March at FIFA's next Congress, which will also take place in Morocco — co-hosts of the 2030 World Cup.

Until recently, him claiming a fourth term seemed a formality.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: US: Abdul El-Sayed wins contentious Michigan Senate primary
World.content:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated moderate Haley Stevens in a contest seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the Democratic party.

US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed scored an important victory against incumbent House Representative Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic primary, a closely watched contest that pitted progressives against moderates of the US party.

El-Sayed, who represents the leftwing progressives, narrowly defeated the moderate leaning Stevens 48.5% to 47.5%.

He will go on to face Republican incumbent Senator Mike Rogers in a seat that Democratic party must win if they hope to take control of the US Senate this November in the midterm elections.

If he defeats Rogers in November, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

Trump insults El-Sayed after primary race

The race between El-Sayed, who was endorsed by the likes of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and Stevens, who had the backing of the Democratic party establishment was seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the party.

Stevens was also backed with a big fundraising effort of the pro-Israel lobby American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

Democrats "have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the US Senate," El-Sayed said after winning the primary.

Stevens conceded to El-Sayed, saying she would "offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers."

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump reacted to the news by calling El-Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel."

Israel at the center of campaign

The 41-year-old doctor focused his campaign on domestic issues like affordable healthcare, the economy and working class people's needs, but he also was vocal on his advocacy to end unconditional military aid to Israel.

The Michigan primary became a battleground between progressives and moderates over US support for Israel, something that has been seen in other Democratic primaries nationwide this year.

Stevens outspent El-Sayed, receiving over $60 million (€51 million) from outside Michigan groups, with more than $30 million coming from AIPAC and its affiliates.

After his primary win, AIPAC signaled said it would oppose El-Sayed and “his radical anti-Israel agenda" in November by supporting Rogers.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic, Rana Taha

World.title: Will Russia start a fresh mobilization drive?
World.content:
Russian authorities are planning to "expand mobilization" in autumn this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, citing intelligence services. According to Zelenskyy, Russian President Vladimir Putin is reportedly preparing to recruit additional Russian soldiers to fight in the war against Ukraine.

"He is concealing his intention behind different words and signals, but he is making preparations," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that we, together with our partners, exert sufficient pressure on Russia so that the idea of ending this aggression — the idea of peace, rather than further Russian mobilization — prevails," he added. The Ukrainian president also said Russia's army was losing more fighters at the front than it can recruit, even though Putin wants to intensify the attacks and expand the war.

Putin issued a decree in autumn 2022 launching a "partial mobilization," which remains in effect to this day, as confirmed by the presidential administration in 2023. The document, it said, "regulates additional measures necessary to ensure that the armed forces fulfill their objectives."

Scores of Russians fled abroad after the Kremlin announced a partial mobilization in September 2022 Image: AP/picture alliance

What points to a possible new mobilization drive?

Independent Russian exile media outlet Verstka and Latvia-based Russian-language news portal Vaschnyje Istorii published an investigative report in late June stating that Russia's leadership was secretly "discussing mobilization" given the difficulties in recruiting new conscripts. One source quoted by Verstka said figures by Moscow's mayoral office show the city sent 1,708 people to the front in April of this year and 1,378 in May — around 1,000 fewer people than during the same period last year. This low recruitment rate reportedly continued in June as well.

Vaschnyje Istorii reported that the recruitment rate for soldiers serving on fixed-term contracts more than halved in the last quarter of 2025 compared with the same period the previous year. The outlet said the recruitment rate had dropped even further in early 2026. The news outlet also cited sources from different Russian regions revealing that the number of people applying for army contracts was falling.

Military personnel interviewed by Verstka said that contract soldiers being sent to fight this year were "unfit for combat," with many new arrivals fleeing the front lines. One conscript told the news outlet that "units are staffed at 30 to 40%, at best."

Droves of Russian fighting-age men made also their way to Georgia in 2022 Image: Daro Sulakauri/Getty Images

The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported in late July that the Kremlin is laying the groundwork for a fresh mobilization drive. ISW analysts wrote that such a move would be "a personal decision for Putin that is contingent on his personal perception of the battlefield situation and his perception of the stability and integrity of the Kremlin." They added that it "remains unclear whether or how Putin will decide to implement mobilization."

A few days ago, Verstka reported that demand for Armenian rental apartments had shot up, driven by Russian interest — just as it had in 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The outlet said rents in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, have risen by about 30% in recent months. According to the report, Russians are planning to leave the country ahead of the State Duma election, scheduled to be held from September 18 to 20.

One landlord told the outlet that in recent years most of his clients had been Russians who had already been living in Armenia for quite some time. Now, however, 80% of inquiries were from Russians who had recently moved to Armenia or were planning to relocate there.

What has Russia said?

Speaking at a press conference in late July, Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov chose not to comment on Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's remarks regarding a possible new mobilization drive, saying "it is not Zelenskyy's job to talk about our plans."

Andrei Klishas, a member of the Russian Federation Council, told Russian-language media outlet RTVI in early summer 2026 that a new mobilization was not currently being discussed in the country as it was unnecessary.

Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, dismissed rumors about a possible new mobilization, calling them "pre-election propaganda." The former Russian president also claimed that in the first half of 2026, some 200,000 people had enlisted in the Russian army.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has refused to comment on rumors of a looming mobilization Image: Ulf Mauder/dpa/picture alliance

"Of course, you can't blindly trust information provided by the Russian authorities," military expert Yan Matveyev told DW. "Information is adjusted to align with their objectives," he added, with regard to Medvedev's statements on the number of new Russian contract soldiers. That said, figures provided by Russian officials are not too far off when compared with analyses by independent researchers, Matveyev said. "Instead of Medvedev's nearly 200,000 new soldiers, that number would probably be closer to 170,000 or 180,000 over six months."

In his view, the current recruitment rate is not sufficient for Russia to secure a military victory over Ukraine. A new mobilization drive would not change that, Matveyev added. "Even if they doubled the size of their army, Russia would not be able to defeat Ukraine, but as can be seen from the statements made by Putin and his officials, that is precisely their goal."

Matveyev believes that, given the losses on the front lines, the strength of Russia's army will dwindle unless a fresh mobilization is launched. This decline, he believes, will continue slowly at first but then accelerate. "Losses are growing and will continue to rise given current trends."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: WHO's Tedros visits DR Congo as Ebola outbreak accelerates
World.content:
The head of the World Health Organization warned that "we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts" against the latest Ebola outbreak, with new cases doubling in some hotspots in the past week alone.

The head of the World Health Organization visited Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), on Wednesday, warning that the Ebola outbreak in the east of the country was "spreading faster than our scale-up of the response."

The 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC's history is already the fastest-spreading and the second-most deadly outbreak on record.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has now visited twice this summer since the public health emergency, centered in the eastern Ituri province, was first declared in mid-March,.

His visit coincided with a health scare in the Maluku municipality in northeastern Kinshasa. A passenger on a crowded ship died with Ebola-like symptoms and authorities were rushing to isolate it and conduct checks.

The presence of Ebola was not yet confirmed in the latest scare involving a timber-transporting boat Image: Wendy Bashi/DW

DW correspondent Wendy Bashi reported that the boat was mainly transporting timber, but that roughly 200 people were also on board. The barge had come from Kisangani originally, far to the east in DRC. Bashi reported that the isolation measures were a precaution and that the deceased had not yet been tested for or diagnosed with Ebola.

What did Tedros say in Kinshasa?

WHO's Tedros said that he was holding meetings with health and humanitarian partners supporting the Ebola response in the DRC to "discuss the challenges we face." He noted new cases were "doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone."

"We all agree that we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts across all pillars of the response and by all partners," he wrote in an online post. "That means reaching every affected community despited insecurity and displacement, strengthening coordination under the Government's leadership, ensuring health workers ahve the protection, training and support they need, and accelerating access to care, surveillance, and safe, dignified burials."

He also said it was crucial that communities be "at the center" of the response, saying the outbreak could only be stopped with their "trust, leadership and partnership."

What are the latest figures on the DRC Ebola outbreak?

According to the most recent data from Congo's Ministry of Health, it had confirmed 3,874 cases, including 1,751 deaths, as of Monday. At least 717 patients were in isolation while 749 patients have recovered.

The vast majority of cases, somewhere in the region of 90%, have been recorded in the eastern province of Ituri bordering Uganda. Only a handful of cases are on record outside DRC's borders.

Authorities and aid groups are racing to construct health care and screening facilities in DRC's eastern regions, as here in North Kivu Province [FILE: July 22, 2026) Image: Xinhua/picture alliance

As Tedros visited on Wednesday, the US State Department pledged another $242 million (roughly €210 million) in funding for a combination of immediate response, preparedness efforts and humanitarian assistance related to the outbreak.

The State Department also said its Travel Advisory status for the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan "remains at Level 4 — Do Not Travel."

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What other problems are responders encountering?

Medical charity Doctors Without Borders warned on Wednesday that the rare strain was still "spreading at an alarming and unprecedented rate" in a remote area of DRC with poor infrastructure.

"The response is expanding but is still not reaching communities quickly enough to break transmission chains," the group said.

Reports of many front line health workers going on strike, either in disputes over pay levels or non-payment, or a mixture of the two, have only worsened already inadequate access to healthcare.

Health officials are trying to enforce epidemic prevention protocols in a country whose funeral customs lay great value on open coffins and laying hands on the dead Image: Xin Huashefa/Xinhua/picture alliance

Dr. Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa Centers for Disease and Control, warned that "contact tracing is not working" and more and more cases were detected late, reducing the chances of survival.

The rare Ebolavirus strain in this outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved treatment or vaccine. Hurried trials of candidate vaccines and treatments have since begun.

Researchers believe the outbreak started in remote areas several months before it was identified and officially declared, with early deaths being misdiagnosed as conditions like peritonitis.

Local funeral practices, often involving open coffins and laying hands on corpses, helped the virus to spread.

World.title: La acogida de menores por la crisis de Ceuta pone a prueba los pactos de PP y Vox en las comunidades
World.content:
Los cuatro últimos pactos de gobierno de PP y Vox en las comunidades donde se han celebrado elecciones comparten un mismo punto. “No más menores no acompañados”. Así lo acordaron ambas formaciones en Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León y Andalucía. En el resto de territorios donde los populares mandan en solitario, además, la resistencia a acoger más niños y jóvenes extranjeros es total bajo el pretexto de que los recursos están ya desbordados, y también con los ultras presionando desde la derecha.

Sin embargo, pese a las declaraciones políticas en público, la derivación de los menores migrantes desde Ceuta a la Península ha seguido funcionando fuera de los focos mediáticos hasta mediados de julio. Días después, se desató la gran crisis humanitaria en la ciudad autónoma con la entrada de 72.000 personas y la consiguiente llegada de más de un millar de menores, que ha excedido con creces los medios del Ejecutivo ceutí. Su presidente, Juan Jesús Vivas, del Partido Popular, clama “socorro” mientras, enfrente, Santiago Abascal aprieta exigiendo no destinar ni un euro para estos chicos. Todos esos elementos nacidos de la emergencia ponen a prueba el segundo matrimonio de conveniencia de PP y Vox en los recientes gobiernos autonómicos, tras un primero que acabó abruptamente en verano de 2024 cuando el líder de Vox dio la orden de romper todos los acuerdos con la excusa de que los populares aceptaban el reparto no obligatorio de 345 menores migrantes.

Hoy Ceuta está atendiendo en este momento a 1.200 menores migrantes, según su presidente Vivas, muy por encima de sus 29 plazas disponibles de ordinario. Presidentes autonómicos del PP reconocen en privado que cumplirán la ley que les obliga a la acogida de los menores, aunque peleen contra la norma con uñas y dientes en la línea de los pactos suscritos con Vox. “Cumpliremos la ley y los acuerdos firmados”, señala un presidente autonómico. “Los decretos se impugnan y se pueden parar”, añade otro. En público, portavoces del Partido Popular de otros territorios han recibido con todo el recelo la noticia de nuevas derivaciones, pero tampoco se han opuesto de plano. “Lo valoraremos todo”, dijo este miércoles la consejera de Servicios Sociales, Familia e Infancia de la Generalitat Valenciana, Elena Albalat. “Eso lo hablaremos”, expresó el vicepresidente de la Xunta de Galicia, Diego Calvo, que asumió que “habrá que atenderlos”.

En cuanto a la posición de Génova, Alberto Núñez Feijóo evitó responder cuando fue preguntado el sábado, durante su visita a Ceuta. También su secretario general, Miguel Tellado, este martes. “No tiene nada que ver con situaciones anteriores, no es una crisis migratoria, es una crisis de seguridad”, afirmó el número dos de Feijóo. Sin embargo, con el paso de los días, la dirección nacional ha pasado del silencio oficial a clarificar su posición, y además en el mismo sentido al que apuntan los dirigentes territoriales: asumirán el acogimiento, aunque lo combatan. “Las comunidades autónomas del Partido Popular siempre van a cumplir la ley. Lo que no van a hacer es aceptar las consecuencias de la irresponsabilidad de un Gobierno que ha llevado a miles de niños a jugarse la vida”, resumió Alma Ezcurra, vicesecretaria de Coordinación Sectorial del PP, “Ese reparto, en caso de producirse, tendrá que ser justo, con datos, bien dotado, planificado y con el Gobierno de España asumiendo la responsabilidad”, añadió Ezcurra al día siguiente.

El presidente de la Junta de Andalucía, Juan Manuel Moreno, y el líder de Vox andaluz y hoy vicepresidente, Manuel Gavira, el 4 de julio en Sevilla. PACO PUENTES

Mecanismo de derivación

El mecanismo de derivación de menores extranjeros no acompañados se reguló en marzo del año pasado a través del decreto 2/2025 de “medidas urgentes para la protección de la infancia y la adolescencia migrante, modificando la ley de extranjería y estableciendo criterios de reubicación”. En él se establece una tabla de datos que adjudica a cada comunidad un determinado número de plazas y que entró en funcionamiento el pasado agosto. La lista se estableció en función de las capacidades de cada territorio, que estableció el Ministerio de Juventud y que se tradujo en un número determinado de estos niños y adolescentes, cuya tutela compete a las autonomías como cualquier otro menor de edad que esté en suelo español. Desde que el mecanismo empezó a funcionar y hasta mediados del mes pasado, más de 1.750 menores han sido realojados en comunidades de la península o Baleares desde Canarias, Ceuta y Melilla, según fuentes del gobierno ceutí. Por tanto, y pese a las declaraciones de muchos cargos públicos, el sistema ha estado funcionando.

La ministra de Juventud e Infancia, Sira Rego, viajará a Ceuta el viernes con “el objetivo de activar todos los mecanismos disponibles para dar una acogida digna a todos estos niños, niñas y adolescentes”. A su vez, la responsable de Migración, Elma Saiz, ha anunciado 25 millones de euros salidos del Gobierno central para dar respuesta a la situación extraordinaria de los menores en la ciudad autónoma. La Moncloa informó este miércoles de que 528 menores que llegaron el pasado jueves ya han sido identificados por la policía y trasladados a centros de la ciudad autónoma, pero que todavía hay menores que permanecen en las calles. “Vamos a reforzar la oficina de extranjería de la delegación del Gobierno para poder tramitar cuanto antes los expedientes”, avanzó el delegado del Gobierno en Ceuta, Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano.

Tras los últimos pactos, los ultras tienen las competencias sobre los menores migrantes en tres comunidades: Extremadura, Aragón y Castilla y León, donde sus consejeros están al frente de esa cartera. Y desde donde han ido aprobando medidas muy controvertidas, como la supresión de la asignación personal de 17 euros que recibían los menores extranjeros no acompañados residentes en Aragón. La dirección nacional de Vox ha salido en tromba contra los anuncios de La Moncloa sobre Ceuta. “Los ha enviado Marruecos en un acto de guerra sin precedentes, con la sumisión de Sánchez, que no protege nuestras fronteras. Los falsos menas, deportados; y los niños, a casa con sus padres. ¡El dinero de los españoles, para los españoles!“, proclama la formación Vox en un comunicado. ”Ni un euro de los españoles para menas, para ilegales, para invasores, para mafias del tráfico de personas, para Marruecos. Para NADA que no sea el bienestar de los españoles", proclamó Abascal.

En la memoria reciente está la mencionada ruptura de hace dos años de Vox con el PP en cinco gobiernos autonómicos después de que los populares aceptaran el reparto no obligatorio de menores migrantes. Pero el de ahora es un momento político muy distinto, y también lo son las circunstancias que rodean a esta crisis humanitaria de Ceuta, por lo que, según fuentes consultadas, Vox no se plantea llegar a ese escenario por más que la coyuntura pueda generar tensiones y sobre todo servir a la extrema derecha para amplificar su mensaje. De hecho, en la Junta de Extremadura —que el martes pasado ya anunció que irá a los tribunales contra el mecanismo legal de reparto—, la Consejería de Desregulación, Servicios Sociales y Familia, en manos de Vox, cargó este martes contra el Gobierno por asegurar que en Extremadura hay 257 plazas disponibles y alegó que son muchas menos (12). Pese a ello, no dijo que esas 12 no fueran a ponerse a disposición de los menores.

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Bol and De Bijenkorf warn customers of possible data leak
World.content:
Online retailer Bol and department store chain De Bijenkorf have emailed customers to warn that their personal details may have been exposed in a cyberattack on a logistics company both firms use.

Hackers may have gained access to systems at CEVA Logistics, which handles deliveries for both companies. Names, addresses, postcodes, and phone numbers are among the details that may have been taken, broadcaster NOS reported.

Bol said its own systems were not affected and that the incident involves orders from a single distribution centre. Neither company has said how many customers may be affected, and De Bijenkorf has commissioned an external investigation into the breach.

Bol said there is no indication that payment details, passwords, or login credentials were affected and has taken part of its range offline – products handled by the logistics company – cancelled some orders, and stopped exchanging data with the firm as a precaution.

De Bijenkorf blocked access to the systems involved and added further security measures. It says customers may face delays to orders, returns, and refunds, and that email addresses and product information may also have been taken. The chain said it was certain no bank account numbers or passwords had been exposed.

CEVA told Bol about the possible breach on August 1 and the Dutch data protection authority AP was informed on August 3, but customers were only emailed on Wednesday.

A Bol spokesperson told NOS the company wanted to establish first what had happened and who was affected, rather than contacting people repeatedly.

World.title: Business confidence rebounds despite geopolitical fears
World.content:
Confidence among companies in the Netherlands has recovered sharply after a slump earlier this year, national statistics office CBS said on Thursday, though most firms also say they are operating in a more uncertain economy than a year ago.

It was the biggest quarterly improvement since 2021, but businesses remain more pessimistic than optimistic overall, and confidence is still below its long-term average.

Almost four in five companies said economic uncertainty had increased over the past 12 months. Wars and trade tensions were the main cause, cited by 42%, ahead of changes in demand and difficulty finding staff, suppliers, or materials.

Confidence improved in almost every sector. Construction and farming saw the biggest turnaround, though both still remain among the most pessimistic, along with bars, cafes, and restaurants.

Only the tech and media sector and the culture, sport, and leisure sector were positive outright. Car dealers and garages were the only sector to become more downbeat.

Nearly three-quarters of firms facing more uncertainty have changed how they operate, most often by making staff and working methods more flexible. Around one in five delayed or cut back investment.
