World.title: Remembering Three Young Croatian Soldiers Who Fell in the Final Battle of Operation Storm
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – As we mark the 31st anniversary of one of the most important events in modern Croatian history, we remember the thousands of defenders who fought for freedom. That includes three young Croatian soldiers of the 4th Guards Brigade who tragically lost their lives in the very final hours of Operation Storm.

Ivan Svalina, Stipan Dundović, and Miroslav Vođera all lost their lives killed on the 5th of August, 1995, in a small hamlet not far from Golubić, as Croatian forces advanced toward Knin and the final victory of Operation Storm. Their deaths came on the very day when the operation was reaching its historic conclusion, a reminder that even in the final moments of victory, Croatian soldiers continued to face fierce fighting and sacrifice.

The Final Battle Near Knin

Ante Brekalo, commander of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, led the advance across Dinara toward Knin. When his unit reached Golubić, they encountered very strong resistance.

“I was honoured to have such men in my company, men I could lead,” Brekalo later recalled. He said the three young soldiers lost their lives during intense close combat. Miroslav Vođera, who had previously served in the Yugoslav Army before joining the Croatian Army, was killed near a house during the fighting. His fellow soldier Ivica Bošnjak remembered him as a true example of what a soldier should be.

“His life ended only a few hours before it was announced that everything was free,” Bošnjak said. He also recalled the intensity of the battle, describing how fighting continued with gunfire and grenades exchanged between the two sides. Vođera, he said, attempted to call for surrender but was killed while trying to enter the building.

Remembering Young Comrades

Miro Moro was among those who discovered the bodies of Stipan Dundović and Ivan Svalina. These three soldiers were only 20, 22, and 23 years old. Moro, who had witnessed many difficult moments during the war, said that this particular memory remained especially painful. He especially remembered Svalina, a young man from his own village.

“That was a child from my village. That morning I saw him with a smile on his face,” Moro recalled. Svalina had joined the unit as a teenager, and his commanders remembered him as a cheerful, friendly and very dependable soldier. Brekalo described him as someone who always helped others and inspired confidence among his fellow soldiers. “He was a true fighter who never, ever left anyone behind,” he said.

A Tradition of Remembrance

Every year on the anniversary of Operation Storm, veterans gather at the site where the three soldiers fell, where a memorial has been built in their honour. Veterans from across the region, including Zadar, Split, Sinj, Imotski, Šibenik, and parts of neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, come together to remember them.

They also honour other fallen defenders from those final days, including Dražen Kuduz, who died in an accident on the approach to Knin on the same day. “They will never be forgotten for as long as we’re alive,” said Josip Bebek, president of the Association of Veterans of the 4th Guards Brigade in Šibenik-Knin County.

A Legacy That Lives On

In Crivac, the hometown of Ivan Svalina, the memory of their youngest fallen soldier remains especially strong.

Around 150 residents of the small village joined the Homeland War, almost half of the local population at the time. Svalina was the youngest from the village to lose his life. His sister Marija Vučić said losing him left a permanent emptiness. She and her other sister also served during the war, spending four years on front lines across Croatia, from Zadar to Dubrovnik. A monument dedicated to Ivan Svalina was unveiled in the centre of the village last year, created by sculptor Petar Melvan. His fellow soldiers plan to visit it every year in remembrance.

For those who knew them, Ivan Svalina, Stipan Dundović, and Miroslav Vođera represent more than names from history, they are remembered as young men whose courage and sacrifice became part of Croatia’s story of independence. The Municipality of Muć also plans to open a memorial room this autumn dedicated to all those from the area who lost their lives during the Homeland War and Croatia’s fierce struggle for independence.

World.title: 31 Years Since Operation Storm: Veterans Recall the Battle for Knin and the Moment History Changed
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – 31 years have passed since Operation Storm (Oluja) altered the course of the Croatian War of Independence, and veterans have recalled the fierce battle for Knin.

Today, Croatia marks Victory and Homeland Thanksgiving Day, the Day of Croatian Defenders, and the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, the military and police operation that became a turning point in the country’s modern history. Launched on August the 4th, 1995, Operation Storm saw Croatian forces manage to regain control of areas that had been held by rebel Serb forces, opening the path toward the final stages of the Homeland War.

Over three decades later, those who took part in the operation continue to remember the days that changed the course of Croatia’s modern history. Among them is Perica Prpić, president of the Association of Special Police Units from the Homeland War “Sharks”, who recalled the moments before the operation began while stationed with fellow soldiers on Velebit Mountain.

He remembers hearing the announcement from Croatia’s first president, Franjo Tuđman, before the operation began, while artillery fire could already be heard in the distance. “The moment I remember the call from President Tuđman, I still get goosebumps. We heard the artillery preparation in the distance. It had begun. You cross yourself, hug your fellow soldier, and start moving down Velebit. It’s just a unique feeling when you know there’s no turning back now,” Prpić said in an earlier interview.

The Battle for the “Igla” Position

Josip Bebek, a member of the 4th Guards Brigade who participated in Operation Storm, also recalled the beginning of the operation.

His unit advanced toward Knin from the direction of Bosansko Grahovo in the early hours of August 4, but encountered heavy resistance along the way. The obstacle was a strategically important hill known as “Igla” (“Needle”), which was held by rebel Serb forces. “We got about halfway there and then we stopped. We faced strong resistance. They held a position called Igla. It was extremely difficult to capture. Once we took Igla, everything moved forward more smoothly,” Bebek recalled. Taking control of that position became a key moment in the advance toward Knin.

Entering Knin

The following morning, after artillery preparation, Croatian forces entered Knin. “We literally walked into Knin,” Bebek said, describing the city at the time. He recalled that the city was largely empty and that his unit encountered no significant resistance after entering. “The 7th and 4th Guards Brigades never killed anyone, there was no resistance, and thankfully there was no need for it,” he said.

Bebek also remembers a personal encounter that stayed with him. He helped an elderly man and brought him to the military barracks, where he was later able to choose whether to remain in Knin or leave for Serbia. “I don’t know what he eventually decided, but later I met his brother, who actually told me their life story,” he said.

From Adrenaline to unbelievable levels of Pride

Although 31 years have passed since Operation Storm, Bebek says the emotions connected to those days remain strong and the memories vivid. “The dream of every Croatian soldier was to reach Knin. After every liberation operation we were happy, but we knew entering Knin would mean the end. That was the finish line,” he said.

At the time, he remembers the feeling of adrenaline and youthful determination. Today, those memories are replaced by pride and gratitude. “When I think about it today, I feel happiness and tears still fill my eyes with pride. We have our own country; we achieved that dream. May God ensure this never, ever happens to anyone again,” Bebek said.

After the war, Bebek remained a professional soldier. In 2003, he moved from Split to Knin, where he still lives today. For him, life in Knin is now simply everyday life.

As Croatia marks 31 years since Operation Storm, veterans continue to remember not only the military victory, but also the experiences, sacrifices, and personal stories behind one of the most significant events in the country’s history.

World.title: Croatia to Experience Peak Heat on Thursday With Temperatures Up to 42 Degrees
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – Croatia is currently under a particularly strong heat dome, with the peak of that heat set to beat down on the country on Thursday. In some areas, the temperatures could reach a dizzying 42 degrees.

Index reports that a very powerful “heat dome” traps extremely hot air over southern and southeastern parts of the continent. According to meteorologists from Severe Weather Europe, the hottest conditions are expected over the Balkans, Italy, Greece, and parts of the western Mediterranean, with some locations forecast to reach or exceed 42 degrees.

For Croatia, the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue climbing through the week, with Thursday expected to be the peak of the heatwave. Inland parts of the country face the highest temperatures, potentially approaching 42 degrees, while the Adriatic coast will also experience very hot weather, although sea breezes should keep coastal temperatures somewhat lower than inland areas.

a high pressure system from north africa

The extreme heat is being driven by a strong high-pressure system stretching from North Africa into southern and central Europe. This atmospheric pattern allows very warm air from the Sahara to spread northward while preventing cooler Atlantic air from moving into the region. As a result, the hot weather is expected to persist for several days.

Meteorologists warn that the prolonged high temperatures significantly increase health risks, especially for older adults, young children, and people with chronic medical conditions. Authorities advise people to stay hydrated, avoid all kinds of more strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, seek shade or air-conditioned spaces whenever and wherever possible, and check on vulnerable family members and neighbours.

The article also highlights an increased wildfire risk all across southern Europe. The combination of extreme heat, dry vegetation, and periods of gusty winds creates conditions where fires can ignite easily and spread rapidly. Fire services across several Mediterranean countries remain on heightened alert.

a colder front is coming!

Looking beyond the peak heat, the forecast suggests that a cold front will begin moving into central Europe later in the week, bringing thunderstorms to some regions and a noticeable drop in temperatures. Croatia is expected to see this change after Thursday, although forecasters caution that any storms accompanying the front could be locally severe, with heavy rain, strong wind gusts, hail, and frequent lightning possible.

Overall, the article’s main message is that Thursday is expected to be the most dangerous day of the current heatwave in Croatia, with temperatures possibly reaching 42 degrees in some inland areas before a cooler, more unstable weather pattern arrives later in the week.

World.title: Bizarre Medieval “Vampire” Found in Pakrac Cemetery
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – An extremely bizarre Medieval “vampire” has been found in a Pakrac cemetery, with archaeologists believing that the particular method of burial was to “prevent the vampire returning among the living”.

Index reports that a very mysterious medieval burial discovered at the Stari Grad Pakrac archaeological site has once again brought attention to ancient beliefs about vampires and the fear of the dead returning among the living. Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a person buried face down, an unusual burial position that experts believe may have been an intentional ritual. According to archaeologist Krešimir Vacek, the way the body was placed suggests that people of the time wanted to prevent the deceased from returning after death.

The “vampire” burial likely dates back to the late 13th century and was found at a medieval cemetery connected with the former settlement around Stari Grad Pakrac. Archaeologists have been researching the site for years, uncovering numerous graves and important historical remains.

This is not the first unusual discovery of its kind at the location. Earlier excavations revealed another so-called “vampire” burial, a skeleton inside a valuable sarcophagus that was missing its human head. Instead, researchers found animal remains believed to be part of a horse skull. Such practices were linked to medieval beliefs that certain people could return from the grave and harm the living.

In medieval Europe, fears of supernatural forces were widespread, and communities sometimes carried out unusual burial practices when they believed someone could become a threat after death. The latest discovery in Pakrac offers another rare insight into the beliefs, fears, and rituals of people who lived more than 800 years ago.

World.title: Erik Gamzejev: What will happen to Ida‑Viru County after the 340 million euros are spent?
World.content:
Researchers at the University of Tartu note in their study that although the Just Transition Fund has initiated new activities in Ida‑Virumaa, the question remains of what will happen once the fund's money has been used up, writes Erik Gamzejev.

A group of University of Tartu researchers presented part of their findings to the public this week. In simple terms, the study examines how satisfied Ida‑Virumaa residents are with their lives.

The official name of the research and development project is "The socio‑economic well‑being of Ida‑Viru residents and labor‑force monitoring." Observing and studying Ida‑Virumaa residents will continue for years and costs nearly 1.5 million euros.

The funding comes from the Just Transition Fund, intended as an elixir to preserve life in Ida‑Virumaa after the region's main industry, oil shale, becomes effectively taxed out of existence by European climate policy. The fund also provides work and income for researchers, consultants, trainers, communications specialists and others outside Ida‑Virumaa. Hopefully for the benefit of Ida‑Virumaa.

The survey results published so far about residents' expectations did not reveal much new. The main conclusion is that if there are jobs with decent pay, schools, healthcare options and affordable prospects for establishing a home, people will stay. If not, they leave. High unemployment and lower income create insecurity and increase anxiety.

These facts apply to all regions far from Tallinn and Tartu. If residents of South or West Estonia were surveyed, the results would be similar.

Ida‑Virumaa's specific situation is that the exhaustion of the oil‑shale industry through EU carbon‑trading rules has accelerated negative trends. If, for example, the European Commission decided that spas must buy water‑use quotas on a fluctuating market, making their survival uncertain, then a Just Transition Fund would also be appropriate for Pärnumaa and Saaremaa.

"Ida Virumaa's specific situation is that the exhaustion of the oil shale industry through EU carbon trading rules has accelerated negative trends."

In Ida‑Virumaa, many positive developments have emerged thanks to the fund, and more are expected. The first stage of the Narva magnet factory has been completed. Last week, a grand and unique nature spa opened on the shore of Lake Peipus, becoming a new landmark for the region. The Jõhvi film studios will soon be finished. Companies are being established in the Kohtla‑Järve business park. Construction of an oxygen plant is underway in Auvere.

With the fund's support, dozens of small businesses have built new facilities and purchased equipment. Local university colleges have strengthened their footing. Municipalities also have their "department" in the fund: Alutaguse renovated the old post office in Iisaku into a new municipal building, Jõhvi is building a new social‑services center, and Kohtla‑Järve is giving new life to the Punamütsike kindergarten. The same fund has also covered costs for cultural festivals and sports events.

Compared to how much employment and tax revenue oil‑shale companies previously provided to local residents, municipalities and the state, the one‑time 340‑million‑euro fund is still only a garnish on the plate.

The Just Transition Fund has turned out to be a slower‑acting painkiller than hoped. Creating new businesses does not happen as quickly as politicians would like. Several companies that received support a year or two ago have not yet begun construction. Some have withdrawn due to high risks. The fund helps significantly with building facilities and acquiring equipment, but entrepreneurs must also convince lenders and investors to put their own money into the idea.

The shutdown of an industry can happen quickly through political decisions. Restructuring an economy and creating new businesses is more like an ultramarathon, where not all participants reach the finish line.

"The Just Transition Fund has turned out to be a slower acting painkiller than hoped."

Given past experience, Estonian politicians should strongly defend the interests of local industry during the ongoing reform of the EU emissions‑trading system. We should avoid repeating the situation from about ten years ago, when a still‑functioning heavy industry was strangled first, and only afterward was a long‑term plan created. New‑generation companies should be successfully launched before considering the downsizing of fossil‑based industry.

University of Tartu researchers note in their study that although the Just Transition Fund has initiated new activities in Ida‑Virumaa, the question remains: what happens when the fund's money is gone?

How can we ensure that the good initiatives already started do not collapse before gaining momentum and producing results? Preparations should already begin for a second and possibly third stage of the Just Transition Fund. A strong Ida‑Virumaa with a diverse economy benefits all of Estonia.

--

World.title: Outgoing Language Board chief: We have managed to enforce language rules without conflicts
World.content:
Ilmar Tomusk, who has headed Estonia's Language Board for 30 years, tells ERR in an interview he considers one of the agency's greatest achievements to be helping Estonia avoid any major language-based conflicts.

Your time as head of the Language Inspectorate is coming to an end and you don't plan to apply for the position again. How did you come to that decision?

It's actually a fairly logical decision. I've been in this position for more than 30 years — on October 5, it'll be 31 years. I'd like to do something else with my life as well. A little calculation shows that I've spent exactly half my life doing this job. While following some of the recent competitions for leadership positions at other institutions, I've read that it's generally considered normal for someone to stay in a position for maybe seven years, perhaps 10, and then move on to something else. My career as the head of this agency has been unusually long. I don't think there's another agency head in Estonia who's been in office this long, although State Archivist Priit Pirsko is catching up with long strides — I think he's already reached 25 years. I hope he'll catch up with me. That's really the reason: I'd like to do something different. And I still have some time before retirement. We'll see what life brings.

Your 31 years at the Language Board have certainly been dynamic and unique. Looking back, how would you sum up that time, if it's even possible in just a few sentences?

You put it very well — they've been extremely dynamic. Over those 31 years, there hasn't been a single day that was like another and probably not a single workday when I didn't have to learn something new. It's not as if you complete your master's and doctoral degrees and suddenly you're ready to be a senior civil servant. That's when the real learning begins. Even yesterday and today, I've had to learn something new. Circumstances change, legislation changes and new court rulings come out on a wide range of issues, so you have to stay on top of them. It's been an incredibly intensive period of learning — very fascinating, but also mentally and emotionally quite demanding.

What has been the Language Board's main role and mission in Estonian society and what impact has it had and will continue to have in the future?

The primary role is exactly what our statutes say: supervising compliance with the Language Act. The requirements set out in the Language Act are, in essence, the same principles laid out in the preamble to Estonia's Constitution. The preamble states that the purpose of the Estonian state is to ensure the preservation of the nation, the language and the culture through the ages, and safeguarding the Estonian language is what the Language Board is responsible for.

In other words, our task is to ensure that, amid internationalization and globalization, Estonian remains present in every area of life, so that people are able to conduct their affairs in Estonian wherever they are. That isn't always the case. Given the composition of our population and our history, it's a difficult goal to achieve, and it has fallen to the Language Board's officials to enforce these requirements. That has been our core mission.

When I was writing my doctoral dissertation in 2002 and 2003, I also analyzed the implementation of language requirements and considered what the education system might look like 10 years later, in 2012 and 2013. At the time, I argued that if Estonia successfully transitioned to Estonian as the language of instruction — which, even then, was supposed to happen — the Language Board's work in the education system would decrease significantly. I was badly mistaken. The transition to Estonian-language instruction was postponed for years. It began in upper secondary schools only in 2011 and in basic schools only in 2024 when the transition to Estonian-language instruction started on a grade-by-grade basis. My conclusions from 2002 turned out to be completely wrong and in recent years the greatest workload for Language Board officials has come from verifying educators' Estonian-language proficiency and enforcing the language requirements.

What does the Estonian language need to be protected from and how should it be protected?

One cliché that people often repeat — and one that is actually true — is that the Estonian language also needs to be protected from Estonians themselves. In democratic Estonia, the pressure from foreign languages is quite strong and at different times Estonians have tended to favor various foreign languages over their own. Right now, the attraction of English is especially strong. You see it in the business world and also in the way young people communicate with one another.

As a children's author, I spend a great deal of time meeting readers, teachers and librarians and they tell me that Estonian children read a great deal of fiction exclusively in English. On the one hand, being able to read in English carries a certain prestige. On the other hand, reading also develops language skills. If we don't develop our command of our native language through reading, it gradually begins to deteriorate. Young Estonians' ability to express themselves becomes weaker and weaker.

I've said on several occasions that, of course, we need to pay close attention to the transition to Estonian-language instruction in schools that are making the change. But when it comes to preserving the Estonian nation, language and culture, the most important decisions are made in Estonian-language schools, in Estonian language classes. That is an area that unquestionably deserves much more attention and should feature far more prominently in the public debate than it does today.

How does a foreign-language sign in the urban environment without an Estonian translation threaten the Estonian language?

It doesn't so much threaten the Estonian language as it conflicts with people's language rights. The basic principle is that you have the right to understand what is written on a public sign, regardless of whether you know the foreign language used. We've become accustomed to seeing foreign-language signs — previously in Russian, now mostly in English — and we tend to assume that everyone knows English. But in cities across Europe, and increasingly in Estonia as well, signs in Chinese and Arabic are beginning to appear alongside the more common English-language ones. In those cases, we obviously can't assume that everyone understands them.

Ilmar Tomusk. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Regardless of which foreign language is used, the information on a sign must also be provided in Estonian because the Constitution states that everyone has the right to freely receive information intended for the public. In Estonia, information directed at the public must first and foremost be available in Estonian. A translation may also be included and the Language Act does not restrict which languages that translation may be provided in.

If, at some point, our streets are filled with signs in Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Arabic and we can no longer understand any of them, then things have probably gotten out of hand. At the moment, we deal more often with English than with those other languages, although we have also issued compliance orders to businesses displaying what we would consider more exotic signage — signs that neither you nor I can understand because we don't read those writing systems. That's why those businesses are required to provide the information in Estonian as well.

What if it's art or some other form of creative expression?

That's very difficult to assess. As a consumer walking past a café or restaurant, do I have enough knowledge to judge whether those characters are a work of art or whether they're conveying information? I certainly don't.

Has Estonia's language policy ever been too strict on some issues or too lenient?

In my view, Estonia's language policy has been very balanced and consistent. Perhaps this is a consequence of having spent so many years in the position, but I've seen all the developments in language policy over the years — both the tightening and the easing of requirements. I would say that, in some cases, we could have eased the rules a little less than we did. Overall, though, our language policy has been very balanced.

Despite the composition of our population and the existence of an agency like the Language Board to enforce language requirements, Estonia has not experienced a single interethnic conflict over language proficiency or language requirements since regaining independence — something that has occurred in some of our neighboring countries. We've managed to shape our language policy and implement language requirements in a sensible and balanced way. That's one achievement I can take with me from this institution: we've been able to enforce the language requirements without any major conflicts.

During your time in office, has the Russian-speaking population's attitude toward the Estonian language and learning it changed significantly — for example, become more positive?

It has definitely become more positive. There's much greater awareness of its importance now. Back in the mid-1990s, when I started working here, many people, including teachers at what were then Russian-language schools, were literally astonished by the idea that they were now expected to learn Estonian. For many of them, Russian was the only language in which it was possible to express anything meaningful and many didn't even regard Estonian as a real language.

In reality, attitudes toward Estonian have become much more positive and Estonian-language proficiency among non-Estonians has improved significantly. That said, the long delays in transitioning to Estonian-language instruction have had negative consequences. Although the decision was made in 1993, the first years, and even decades, were marked by repeated postponements of the deadlines. The transition that is now underway — to Estonian-language instruction in upper secondary schools, basic schools and preschools — is somewhat painful. Even today, we see news reports about shortages of assistant teachers.

But we'll get through it and eventually we'll reach a point where a Russian-speaking young person graduating from school has sufficient Estonian-language skills to continue their studies in any field in Estonia and find a job. It won't be like it was years ago when someone could graduate from high school but be unable to work even as a cashier because they didn't know Estonian. Those situations are absurd. The whole purpose of the transition is to ensure that Russian-speaking people have equal opportunities to compete in the labor market and find decent jobs.

What impact will the transition to Estonian-language education have on the Language Board in the coming years? Will the board's role remain as relevant as it has been until now?

It will change somewhat. If we look at the statistics, teachers — people officially employed as teachers — are required to have C1-level Estonian proficiency. Already now, 97 percent formally meet the language requirement. That means the results have been very good. However, among that 97 percent, there are still teachers whose actual language skills in one area or another need improvement. Formally meeting the requirement is an excellent outcome, but in practice we still need to work with those teachers and encourage them to further develop their language skills, whether in writing or speaking.

It's no longer a matter of an inspector showing up and ordering someone to take a language exam — the exams have already been passed. Now it's a question of improving language proficiency. Those kinds of supportive measures in the education system will probably continue. During the upcoming school year, we'll likely need to devote considerable attention to assistant teachers in preschools because there is a shortage of teachers and assistant teachers are required to have B2-level Estonian. We'll need to continue working with them.

So the focus of the Language Board's work will likely shift. But yes, the board will certainly continue to have a role in the education system through around 2029 or 2030. I believe that within four or five years, we'll reach the point where the overwhelming majority of teachers and assistant teachers meet the language requirements and are able to do their jobs confidently in Estonian.

What do you feel will remain unfinished?

That's a difficult question. One area that has been especially important to me is language law and its development. One of the Language Board's responsibilities has been to propose amendments to legislation concerning language and over the past 31 years we've made quite a number of such proposals. Some have become law, while others have not, and those are probably the ones that will remain unfinished for now. But the ideas are there and I believe that the vision I've had for language law will, in one way or another, eventually be realized.

For me — and for many heads of regulatory agencies — legal clarity is essential. That means different laws should speak with one voice and that voice should reflect the principle set out in the preamble to the Constitution: the preservation of the Estonian nation, language and culture through the ages. It shouldn't be the case that one law says Estonian must be used in a particular context while another law ignores that principle. Legislation concerning language, the nation and culture should be consistent and coherent.

Ilmar Tomusk. Source: Screenshot

World.title: Tartu schools to offer drone training this fall
World.content:
Tartu plans to add a drone studies course to its upper secondary school curriculum as an elective in the upcoming academic year.

Throughout August, representatives from the City of Tartu, upper secondary school administrators and the Estonian Defense Resources Agency will meet to discuss the content of the drone studies course and what equipment will be used to teach it.

According to Kaisa Keisk, chief specialist for education management for Tartu city government, one reason for creating the course is the growing need for national defense.

"We would like to see young people become interested in these topics and pursue not only drone technology but engineering more broadly. Giving them hands-on experience at an earlier age could encourage them to consider careers in these fields later in life," Keisk told ERR.

Urmo Uiboleht, head of Tartu Private School, and Lembi Loigu, vice principal for academics at Jaan Poska High School, agree that creating the course is important from a national defense perspective and that schools must adapt to technological advances. However, Uiboleht is critical of the plan, questioning whether there is room for it in an already crowded curriculum.

Keisk said several schools already have teachers with the necessary qualifications, including certification to operate drones and teach related subjects.

"We still need to discuss what kind of equipment is needed, whether we can purchase it and how we would provide it to schools — whether drone simulators or some other type of equipment," Keisk said.

Students at Jaan Poska High School have been able to participate in an extracurricular drone studies club since 2017. According to Loigu, the club is offered only if enough students sign up. So far, it has been held every year and Loigu said student interest remains strong.

Keisk said it is unlikely that other upper secondary schools will begin offering drone studies in September. She added that schools will be allowed to introduce the course gradually. It also remains undecided what form the instruction will take, since drone flights are subject to certain restrictions. Keisk said the most likely approach is for students to train using simulators.

Drone. Source: Olev Kenk/ERR

"Another option that has been proposed is that it could take place indoors. We have also discussed, though to a lesser extent, whether there may be locations in Tartu where schools could cooperate with another institution or a company that has facilities where students could fly drones in a real-world outdoor environment," Keisk said.

Developing drone education capacity is part of the City of Tartu's engineering action plan, which aims to strengthen technology and engineering skills in both schools and kindergartens.

World.title: Sirje Potisepp: Changing who pays the bill will not make the environment cleaner
World.content:
Under the planned amendment to the Waste Act, producers who place single‑use plastic packaging on the market would compensate local governments for litter‑cleaning costs. In its current form, the system does not encourage cost control or reduce littering, and therefore the draft needs changes, writes Sirje Potisepp.

Estonian food producers and other packaging producers have fulfilled packaging‑related producer‑responsibility obligations for more than twenty years. Packaging companies finance the collection and recycling system for packaging waste and meet notification and reporting requirements.

The planned amendment to the Waste Act expands this responsibility further, and producers would also have to cover costs related to single‑use plastic packaging that arise from servicing public trash bins and cleaning public spaces. This principle comes from the so‑called SUP Directive, the directive on single‑use plastic products.

More precisely, the change concerns two types of costs. First, it covers the servicing of public trash bins, such as removing a yogurt cup, sandwich wrapper or drink container thrown into a city or municipal bin. Second, it includes costs that arise when plastic packaging is thrown into a park, onto a street or into the forest and must be collected from there.

While the first type of cost is understandable, the second raises a fundamental question: should responsibility lie with the producer who placed the packaged product on the market, or with the person who decided to throw the packaging on the ground? In the case of food, plastic packaging is often not a voluntary choice by the producer but an unavoidable part of ensuring food safety and shelf life.

The principle "the polluter pays" is cited, but who is the actual polluter? When a person throws a drink cup or salad container onto the street, it is deliberate misconduct, and societal responsibility should not shift from the person who committed the act to the producer. The "producer pays" approach sends exactly that signal, reinforcing rather than reducing the real problem: littering.

Who controls the costs?

If the state creates a new financing system, it must be clear how costs are determined, who verifies their justification, and how unjustified cost increases are prevented. In the current draft, these questions remain largely unanswered.

Regarding projected costs, the Ministry of Climate has said that "there is no precise overview, because local governments have not been required to separate such costs, and practices differ across Estonia." The ministry has estimated the cost of the new system at 2–10 million euros per year, illustrating how unclear the picture is. Many local governments currently lack an overview of how much is spent on cleaning public spaces or servicing trash bins, because these costs are part of broader maintenance services.

"The ministry has estimated the cost of the new system at 2–10 million euros per year, illustrating how unclear the picture is."

Although the draft requires local governments to establish such cost accounting by 2028, it lacks a substantive oversight mechanism that would allow producers to verify the justification of costs. Essentially, producers would receive an invoice and be required to pay it, with no regulatory possibility for control. Such a system does not motivate finding cost‑effective ways to maintain public spaces or reduce littering; instead, it lacks incentives to manage costs or address the root causes of the problem.

In several EU countries, this extension of producer responsibility has already been implemented. Their experience shows that additional costs are significant; for example, in Germany, producer‑responsibility costs related to plastic packaging roughly doubled after the changes. These costs inevitably affect product prices and ultimately reach consumers.

It is also important to consider that implementing the SUP Directive is far from the only packaging‑related change that Estonia's food industry must adapt to. Alongside it, the waste reform will take effect and a new EU packaging regulation will be enforced. Both bring major investments and ongoing costs for companies, amounting to tens of millions of euros annually. This makes it even more important that every new requirement is well‑considered, purposeful and provides real environmental benefit.

What should be done differently?

The Estonian Food Industry Association does not oppose the goal of reducing the environmental impact of single‑use plastic products. The EU SUP Directive also aims for this. The question is how to achieve this goal most effectively and how to avoid unintended side effects of regulation.

If producers are required to cover public‑space litter‑cleaning costs related to certain products, the system must be transparent and verifiable. Cost formation must be clearly understandable, and producers must have the ability to ensure that only actual and justified costs are compensated. This requires a clear oversight and control mechanism in the law.

Even more important is focusing on solving the underlying problem. Local governments and other public‑sector institutions should carry out consistent awareness‑raising and more effective supervision to reduce littering.

One example is Singapore, where littering is treated much more strictly than in Estonia. Violations are followed by swift and severe penalties, including large fines and the possibility of requiring offenders to clean public areas. Such strict consequences may not fit our legal or cultural environment, but reducing littering certainly requires a comprehensive set of measures.

The authors of any new regulation should constantly ask themselves one simple question: does this help solve the problem for which the regulation is being created? Changing who pays the cleaning bill will not solve the problem of littering in public spaces; the environment becomes cleaner when less litter ends up there.

World.title: Health Board: Lyme's disease and tick-borne encephalitis cases picking up in Estonia
World.content:
Peak tick-borne disease season has arrived. According to the Health Board, cases of tick-borne encephalitis and Lyme disease are on the rise.

Anyone who has had a tick-borne disease knows these tiny creatures can be a real menace. Musician Ruslan Trochynskyi knows that firsthand. In late June, while making birch whisks for the sauna, he found a tick on himself and soon developed Lyme disease.

"I went to bed, and by the next morning I already had a headache. Then my joints started hurting and I had a fever of 37 degrees Celsius — not very high," Trochynskyi said.

After completing a two-week course of antibiotics, however, his condition worsened.

"Then I felt really terrible. My fever was 39 degrees and my family doctor told me to go to the emergency department immediately. That's where they discovered I already had encephalitis and meningitis. Fortunately, I reacted very quickly and the encephalitis didn't affect my brain itself — only the tissues around it," the musician said.

This is currently the peak season for these diseases, although people can become infected at any time of year.

"If we look at the long-term trend, unfortunately the number of cases has generally been increasing. But if we compare this year with the same period last year or the year before — from January through the end of June — the figures are generally the same," said Julia Geller, head of the Health Board's Department of Communicable Diseases.

Geller added that comparing only two years does not provide an accurate picture because many variables are involved, including people's outdoor activity and weather conditions. More than 1,200 people have contracted Lyme disease in Estonia this year, while more than 50 have been diagnosed with tick-borne encephalitis.

There is no place in Estonia that is completely free of ticks.

"Saaremaa is particularly tick-rich, as are Hiiumaa and Vormsi. More generally, the west coast is also affected, partly because migratory bird routes run along the western coast, bringing both ticks and the pathogens they carry," Geller said.

Although Lyme disease is often associated with a red ring forming around the bite, in reality about one-third of infected people never develop this characteristic rash. If left untreated, the disease can also cause symptoms much later.

"Whether several months later or even a year later, secondary symptoms can develop. As a rule, these patients do recover. Sometimes fatigue and weakness can persist after the infection, but those symptoms should generally resolve over time," family physician Reet Laidoja said.

It should be noted that Ruslan is still recovering from the illnesses he contracted more than a month ago.

World.title: Estonia's Maarika Lepik crowned women's world champion in axe throwing
World.content:
Maarika Lepik is now women's world champion in double-bit axe throwing after reaching those heights in Bollnäs, Sweden.

Otto Peet claimed the junior crown for Estonia too.

Double-bit axe throwing is a precision target sport which has its roots in North American logging camp history. Competitors stand several meters away from a wooden target and throw a symmetric, dual-edged axe. To score, the axe must complete a single rotation in the air.

A total of 145 hopefuls from 12 countries took part in the three-day World Championships. In addition to Estonia and the host nation, competitors from Canada, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Italy, the United Kingdom, the United States and Switzerland attended.

Lepik is a math teacher at a school in Viimsi by day, and she had posted her previous world championships best result four years ago, with fourth place. Two years ago, she narrowly missed the final, finishing first outside the cut.

This year was Lepik's year, however, as she scored 48 out of a possible 60 points in the semifinals, tying for second and third place and making it to the final.

That final involved eight women, down to three, one of them Lepik, after five rounds – the competitor with the poorest throw in each round was eliminated.

An Irish axe thrower had already made it to the final with 11 points, but Lepik tied on 9 points with a Canadian competitor, meaning a throw-off beckoned. The first two of these were a tie, but Lepik made the better third throw, to secure her place in the final.

Despite reaching that final second, the Estonian went on to win 12:11, claiming her first world title.

Of other Estonians taking part, Sirje Leini narrowly missed the final, finishing 10th with 40 points. A score of 41 would have been enough to reach the top eight and qualify for the final.

Karol Raidma, the women's silver medalist at the last event, scored 37 points in the semifinal and finished in a tie for 14th-16th place.

In the junior final, Peet was clearly dominant, defeating his opponent 8-0 in the throws for the gold medal. Also, Emma Liisa Toikka finished fourth for Estonia after posting the second-best result in the semifinal.

None of the Estonian representatives reached the men's semifinal, reserved for the top 27 competitors, from a field of 96 entrants, though two of these, Kristiar Papstel, tied for 28th-29th and Roland Peet, who came 30th, almost made it.

Marek Peet, one of the driving forces behind axe throwing in Estonia and who also took part in the Bollnäs event, said there is a chance that Estonia will be awarded the right to host the next World Championships in double-bit axe throwing, which take place in 2029.

World.title: OMD's Andy McCluskey: Even our best friends hated our first songs
World.content:
Speaking to the ETV show Ringvaade suvel, the band's singer and co-founder Andy McCluskey said he is looking forward to the Tallinn concert. The band last performed in Estonia in 2020, and has been in existence around half a century, becoming prominent in their home country at the beginning of the 1980s. OMD also had a huge following in Estonia almost from the outset, something which the weight of Soviet oppression could do little to squelch.

It's an honor to talk to you because I have to give you a quick personal story – I grew up as a teenager listening to OMD and it was behind the Iron Curtain, during the Soviet era so all the Western music was like a symbol freedom for me. So for me it's actually incredible to sit down and talk to you. You're going to be back in Estonia in August. What do you remember from your last gig, and what kind of memories do you have?

You're always a bit nervous when you play in a new country, because you think how many of these people have ever seen us before? Probably not many, so they don't know what to expect, and we don't know what to expect from them. Having played once, and remembering the concert was great, I'm looking forward to August 29th.

There is kind of a unique bond between OMD and the fans of Eastern Europe. Why do you think your music resonated so deeply with the people from our neck of the woods?

One of these things perhaps I've always thought about our music is that most of our songs, particularly in the early days, the chorus was not words, it was a melody, so you didn't have to speak English to sing along with OMD. Maybe that's it. Since the end of the Cold War, we'd been able to come and play in some of the countries that we couldn't play in in the 1980s.

Unfortunately with that we have made a bunch of bootleg copies of your albums and you never got royalties from that – sorry about that!

It's ok. You're forgiven, just tell everybody to buy a ticket and come and see the gig [Laughs].

What about the name Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, it's quite a mouthful and it's a strange name for a pop band. What's the story behind that?

Well we weren't supposed to be a pop band: Paul [Humphreys] and I were writing music from when we were 16 years old, and frankly even our best friends hated it. So we finally dared, in 1978, almost 48 years ago, we finally dared to go on stage and play our songs.

What we didn't realize was we were actually writing very pop melodies, but wrapped in experimental ideas, and so the name of the band just came from – I used to write things on my bedroom wall, and we decided to do this one-off concert, we just thought well we need a weird name, as it was a weird idea, you know, two guys with a tape recorder playing songs that their friends don't even like [Laughs].

OMD's Paul Humphreys and Andy Andy McCluskey. Source: Press materials.

You guys kind of swam against the current, with a different style - even though you had some synth bands starting at the time as well.

I think the first two British synth bands that started were Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and the Human League, and it was before the internet, so we didn't know the Human League were there, and they didn't know that we were there; I think both of us had found our alternative music just before punk, because I got into German music in 1975 with bands like Kraftwerk and La Düsseldorf and Neu, and so that was my alternative. The good thing about punk was that there were lots of new clubs opened up all around Britain, and they had a policy of letting anybody come and play, so we didn't have to be punk – we could play our synthesizers and take a tape recorder.

But yeah it was pretty different at the time, we were definitely not a punk band.

What was crazy was that we started in '78, the Human League started just a bit before us, and neither of us I think thought we were ever going to be pop groups – we were just making our music, it was our hobby really. But suddenly when Gary Numan had hits, then everybody was talking about electronic music, and there was more and more and more electronic music and suddenly something that seemed a crazy idea in 1978 was the new international pop music in 1980.

I read about how much guys you have been influencing different styles of music, it's pretty amazing how many different bands have named the influence by you guys. I can understand the electronic music – Moby's going to be in Estonia as well. But then the Red Hot Chili Peppers have mentioned you, U2, and the craziest for me would be ZZ Top – totally different style and everything.

ZZ Top is my favorite one, and it's true – one of the first TV shows we ever did in England was at the beginning of 1980, we did a program called the "Old Grey Whistle Test", and they have live bands; we were live in the studio, ZZ Top were live in the studio, and we were all like 19 and 20, and thought we were the new thing, and we thought they were old-fashioned, beardy Texas blues rockers and we didn't want anything to do with them, but they loved us. We didn't know this, but years later someone said 'I was reading a book about ZZ Top and they credit you with helping them go electronic, to make the Eliminator album which is the biggest album they ever made, and they used drum machines and synthesizers, and also the way I move with my bass guitar, swinging the bass guitar, they copied that in the videos, and years later in the 1990s I got into a lift in a hotel in Paris with Billy Gibbons, and I went '"hey Bill I'm Andy from Orchestral Manoeuvres," and he was "Hey Dustin, this is the guy that gave us the move we ripped off," so I heard it from Billy's mouth – they did copy OMD; can you believe that?!

You've built such a massive legacy from the 1980s. When you decided to get together, did you feel any pressure writing any new material to live up to this iconic OMD reputation of the eighties.

The first thing was really just to play live and have fun and see if people wanted to watch us play live again, and it's been great – you know, people have been really coming to see us, and they have enjoyed the gigs and in fact our live audience now is probably bigger than it was 40 years ago. But after two years, we were kinda like "OK is this it now, we're just going to play the old songs over and over again. Are we basically just a tribute band to ourselves?" And that's when we decided to do the crazy, stupid thing and write some new music; we're going to work hard on it and make it good, and actually I think the four albums that we've made in the last 17 years, people have been saying that they're actually as good as the albums from the early 80s. The last one got to number two in the U.K. – that woman Taylor Swift stopped us from being number one [laughs].

Your own personal influences – who have been the main idols for your music?

When I was a kid there was not much music I liked to be honest. It was the Düsseldorf bands, Kraftwerk and Neu, David Bowie, Roxy Music and Brian Eno, and the Velvet Underground, and that was it. I really didn't listen to anything else than that. Those were the people that influenced me, and I still listen to that music. The music you listen to on your journey from childhood to adulthood, the first part of your life where you grow into being an adult, that music becomes a soundtrack to your life forever.

OMD are appearing at the Birgitta Convent ruins (Pirita Klooster) on Saturday, August 29.

World.title: Concert organizer: world‑famous artists want to feel at home while on tour
World.content:
Liina Tammepõld, marketing manager for the large‑concert agency L Tips Agency in Estonia, says that world‑famous artists want to feel as comfortable as possible while on tour, and therefore their requests are not caprices or difficult demands.

"I studied advertising and imagology at Tallinn University and worked in a record store at the same time. My love for music started in childhood; I recorded songs from the radio onto cassette tapes and went to various summer tours in Estonia, I was a fan of many artists. Then I volunteered at the Positivus festival, and from there I was invited to do marketing and communication," said Liina Tammepõld, marketing and communications manager for the Estonian branch of L Tips Agency, which organizes large concerts in the Baltics.

L Tips Agency is organizing concerts by Moby, The Cure and OMD this August.

The stress level in this work can be very high at times, but the adrenaline and the experience you get when the concert is finally over are worth it. "The coolest moment is when the concert begins and I send photographers right to the front of the stage to shoot, and I can spend the first songs right at the stage myself. The energy that arises when the artist comes on stage always gives me chills," Tammepõld said.

"The choice of artist mainly comes down to logistics and dates, not so much thinking about the audience reaction. When we do something in Estonia, Latvians and Lithuanians also come," said Tammepõld, who works at a Latvian agency. "For very big artists, we treat Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania as one region."

Tammepõld works in a small company with four Latvians, one Estonian and one Lithuanian. "We talk a lot about artists among ourselves, and the final decision is made by the company's director, who also carries the risk."

It can also happen that an artist's tour is cancelled. "I gave my husband Neil Young concert tickets in Italy as a gift. We also bought flights and accommodation, but already in spring he cancelled the entire tour. Thanks to the fact that I had a credit card from a bank that included travel insurance, the insurance covered the costs because the purpose of the trip was the concert. It's worth checking these things," Tammepõld noted.

Moby had no surprising requests. "Moby's personal assistant on this tour is an Estonian, with whom we have been in close contact to make sure the artist feels very comfortable in Estonia," Tammepõld said. "Artists want to feel as much at home as possible while on tour. This week we have at both concerts a backstage helper who works with Andrea Bocelli. Estonians are capable people," she smiled.

American multi‑instrumentalist, producer and singer Moby released an album earlier this year that includes a track titled "Tallinn." "I did a bit of research and found that the song is a tribute to Arvo Pärt," Tammepõld said.

Tammepõld also organizes community concerts and wants to help Estonian artists reach big stages.

"I feel that a big part of my heart belongs to Estonian artists and Estonian music. Working at Tallinn Music Week is very close to my heart, and contributing to helping Estonian musicians reach big stages. In my hometown Elva, I organize a couple of concerts myself. At the end of July, Mikk Tammepõld and Lauri Räpp performed in the garden of the Verevi Motel. At the end of August, Mari Jürjens will perform," Tammepõld said.

World.title: Iraqi security delegation to visit Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein and his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, discussed on Wednesday arrangements for the upcoming visit of an Iraqi security delegation to Saudi Arabia.

The Iraqi Foreign Ministry mentioned that the two ministers convened in Amman, the capital of Jordan, during the Arab ministerial meeting focused on Jerusalem.

The meeting addressed the importance of enhancing ties between the two countries, issues of common interest, preparations for the upcoming Arab summit, and the security developments in the region.

The two sides also reviewed plans for the Iraqi security delegation’s future trip to Saudi Arabia, as well as mutual visits between the two countries to strengthen cooperation.

As Hussein discussed the Iraqi government’s initiatives to bring weapons under state control, Farhan conveyed Saudi Arabia’s backing for the new Iraqi government and its efforts to enhance security within the country and uphold regional stability.

The two sides reviewed security development in the region and their impact on oil export routes and energy security. They also discussed regional initiatives and potential agreements focused on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to facilitate maritime traffic.

Both parties stressed the significance of ongoing collaboration within the Arab League framework to promote common interests and improve regional stability.

World.title: US dollar slightly rises against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar compared to the Iraqi dinar rose on Wednesday in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, and the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Erbil.

The US dollar exchange rate slightly rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,521.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,519.5 Iraqi dinars on Wednesday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,525 Iraqi dinars and 1,515 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also rose, fluctuating between 1,524 and 1,523.5 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq, Jordan, Egypt discuss cooperation mechanism, energy partnerships
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq, Jordan, and Egypt highlighted on Wednesday the importance of activating the trilateral cooperation mechanism via specialized committees and enhancing coordination in the economic, investment, industrial, and energy sectors.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein, Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty met in Amman, the capital of Jordan, to discuss the trilateral cooperation mechanism.

The meeting was held on the sidelines of the foreign ministers’ participation in the Arab ministerial meeting on Jerusalem, according to a statement released by the Iraqi Foreign Ministry.

The three parties agreed to activate the tripartite system through specialized technical committees and organize periodic discussions at various levels to monitor the progress of joint projects.

The three ministers reviewed cooperation in the energy sector, including oil and electricity interconnection projects, as well as measures to broaden partnerships in these areas to enhance economic integration and improve energy security.

The meeting addressed the latest developments in the region, particularly efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to strengthen regional stability.

The foreign ministers highlighted the need to halt military operations, reduce tensions, and adopt diplomatic means to resolve crises in the region.

World.title: Graham Arnold extends Iraq contract ahead of Gulf Cup and AFC Asian Cup 2027
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq national team head coach Graham Arnold has officially signed a contract extension with the Iraq Football Association (IFA), ensuring he will remain in charge of the Lions of Mesopotamia for the country’s upcoming major international tournaments.

The renewal secures Arnold’s position on the sidelines as Iraq prepares for the Gulf Cup and the 2027 AFC Asian Cup, providing continuity as the national team continues its long-term development.

According to a source within the Iraq Football Association, Arnold finalized the agreement on Wednesday, extending his tenure as head coach of the Iraqi national football team.

The new deal confirms that the Australian manager will oversee Iraq’s preparations and participation in the upcoming Gulf Cup before leading the team into the AFC Asian Cup 2027.

The contract extension reflects the federation’s confidence in Arnold’s leadership and its desire to maintain stability ahead of two of the region’s most important football competitions.

Keeping the same coaching staff allows Iraq to continue building tactical consistency, squad cohesion, and long-term planning without interruption.

The upcoming Gulf Cup will provide valuable competitive experience before the national team shifts its focus to the AFC Asian Cup, where Iraq will aim to compete for continental honors.

Coaching continuity is considered an important factor in international football, particularly as teams prepare for major tournaments.

By extending Arnold’s contract, the Iraq Football Association signals its commitment to maintaining the current technical project while continuing preparations for future regional and Asian competitions.

Further details regarding the duration and financial terms of the renewed agreement have not yet been officially disclosed.

World.title: Iraq, Jordan, and Egypt agree to boost trilateral cooperation
World.content:
Amman (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq, Jordan, and Egypt have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening trilateral cooperation by activating specialized technical committees and expanding coordination across key economic sectors, including investment, industry, and energy.

The agreement was reached during a trilateral ministerial meeting held in Amman, where the three countries also discussed regional developments, the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, and the importance of diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions across the Middle East.

According to a statement from Iraq’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein participated in the meeting alongside Jordanian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty.

The meeting took place ahead of the Arab ministerial meeting on Jerusalem and focused on accelerating implementation of the Iraq-Jordan-Egypt cooperation mechanism.

The ministers agreed to activate the partnership through specialized technical committees and hold regular meetings at various levels to monitor the progress of joint initiatives.

The three countries emphasized expanding cooperation in strategic sectors that support long-term economic growth.

Discussions focused on increasing collaboration in:

Economic development

Investment projects

Industrial cooperation

Trade facilitation

Infrastructure development

Officials said stronger coordination would help deepen regional economic integration while creating new opportunities for sustainable growth.

Energy cooperation was a central topic during the talks, with ministers reviewing ongoing and future projects involving:

Oil cooperation

Electricity interconnection

Regional energy security

Cross-border energy infrastructure

The three governments stressed that expanding joint energy initiatives would contribute to improving energy security and strengthening economic ties between Iraq, Jordan, and Egypt.

The ministers also exchanged views on regional developments, particularly the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.

They welcomed ongoing efforts aimed at reopening the strategic waterway as quickly as possible, highlighting its importance for regional stability, international trade, and global energy markets.

The meeting concluded with a joint call for an end to military escalation across the region, emphasizing that dialogue and diplomatic engagement remain the most effective means of resolving regional crises.

The ministers reiterated their shared commitment to peaceful solutions and closer regional cooperation in addressing common political and economic challenges.

World.title: Al Qaim Cement Plant expands exports to Syria
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Al-Qaim Cement Plant has reached its full designed production capacity of 840,000 tonnes annually, strengthening domestic cement supplies while increasing exports to neighboring Syria, the Ministry of Industry and Minerals announced on Wednesday.

The achievement marks a significant milestone in Iraq’s efforts to boost local industrial production, reduce reliance on imports, and expand the country’s non-oil exports.

According to the ministry, the Al-Qaim Cement Plant is now operating at its full design capacity, producing approximately 70,000 tonnes of sulfate-resistant cement each month.

The output is sufficient to meet demand across Anbar Province and other Iraqi governorates while supporting the government’s strategy to enhance domestic industrial self-sufficiency.

In addition to serving the local market, the plant currently exports around 7,500 tonnes of cement per month to Syria, reflecting growing cross-border trade and regional demand for Iraqi construction materials.

General Company for Iraqi Cement Director General Zuhair Dawood Ahmed said the facility is operated through a partnership with Al-Maysarah Cement Industry Company.

He explained that the plant features a fully modernized production line equipped with advanced machinery and internationally sourced equipment, alongside a modern centralized control system that manages production processes efficiently.

The factory also includes advanced laboratories for testing both raw materials and finished products, ensuring quality standards are maintained throughout the manufacturing process.

To ensure uninterrupted production, the Al-Qaim Cement Plant operates its own 30-megawatt power station, providing stable electricity independent of the national grid.

This dedicated energy supply enables the plant to maintain around-the-clock production, minimizing operational disruptions and supporting consistent output.

Officials said continuous operations are essential to meeting domestic demand while expanding Iraq’s presence in regional cement markets.

The Ministry of Industry said increasing production at state-owned industrial facilities remains a key objective in supporting economic diversification beyond the oil sector.

By achieving full operational capacity and maintaining exports, the Al-Qaim Cement Plant contributes to strengthening Iraq’s manufacturing base, creating greater industrial resilience, and expanding opportunities for Iraqi products in foreign markets.

The ministry added that efforts will continue to increase cement exports while supporting the country’s infrastructure and construction sectors through reliable local production.

World.title: Iraq lawmakers scrutinize Karbala Refinery contracts amid government anti-corruption drive
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi lawmakers have begun reviewing government contracts suspected of containing inflated costs, as Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi intensifies efforts to tighten oversight of public spending and prevent corruption before contracts are approved.

The renewed scrutiny comes a day after Al-Zaidi ordered the Federal Board of Supreme Audit to establish a specialized team responsible for conducting pre-contract financial audits within 10 working days. The initiative aims to identify high costs before agreements are finalized, marking a shift from investigating corruption after it occurs to preventing it at the contracting stage.

MP Haider Mohammed Al-Mutairi, a member of the Ishraqat Kanoun bloc, called on the prime minister to review several contracts related to the Karbala Refinery, arguing that some agreements warrant immediate investigation due to their financial burden on the state.

Al-Mutairi urged the formation of a high-level investigative committee to examine a consultancy contract involving 49 advisers, claiming it costs the Iraqi government approximately $52 million annually.

He also highlighted an operational contract for the refinery valued at $180 million per year, which he said amounts to nearly 750 million Iraqi dinars in daily expenditures.

The MP called for greater transparency in reviewing major state contracts, particularly those involving strategic infrastructure projects.

The parliamentary review follows a broader government campaign to strengthen financial oversight across ministries and state institutions.

Prime Minister Al-Zaidi directed the Federal Board of Supreme Audit to implement mandatory pre-audit procedures for government contracts, including setting financial thresholds that determine which agreements require advance scrutiny.

According to the prime minister, inflated contract values and weak oversight have long been among the primary channels through which public funds were lost.

He stressed that Iraq’s next phase of anti-corruption efforts should focus on preventing irregularities before contracts are signed rather than relying solely on post-contract investigations.

The government says the new oversight framework is intended to improve transparency, accelerate contract reviews, and safeguard public finances without delaying legitimate development projects.

The initiative forms part of a wider reform agenda aimed at enhancing accountability, improving governance, and restoring confidence in public procurement procedures.

No official findings regarding the Karbala Refinery contracts have been announced, and any investigation would be subject to the legal and auditing procedures established by Iraqi authorities.

World.title: Iraq studies oil pipeline network to Turkey, Syria, Jordan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Oil Ministry is working on diversifying oil export outlets by constructing a pipeline network that will be extended to ports in Turkey, Syria, and Jordan.

The spokesperson for the Iraqi Oil Ministry, Salim al-Rikabi, told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) on Sunday that the government is studying the construction of the Basra-Haditha-Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline as a new route, with branches from Haditha to the Syrian port of Baniyas and the Jordanian port of Aqaba.

Fluctuations in the global oil market have a significant impact on Iraq’s revenue. However, the most significant impact is the decline in daily export volumes, which have been severely affected by the ongoing war in the region, according to al-Rikabi.

The current conflict in the region has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which is a strategically important waterway that transports the majority of Iraq’s oil shipments.

Al-Rikabi explained that the pipeline from southern Iraq to the port of Ceyhan on the Mediterranean will raise oil export volumes via Turkish territory.

The Iraqi official said earlier that the Basra-Haditha oil pipeline needs to be carried out first to transport crude oil to Haditha in the western province of Anbar, and then preparation for the alternate pipeline takes place.

The project’s feasibility study is presently underway, and if completed, the pipeline will serve as an alternative for oil tankers now transporting oil to the Syrian port of Baniyas.

The Iraqi cabinet decided in April to move forward with the implementation of the Basra-Haditha oil pipeline.

According to reports, the project is an Iraqi venture estimated at $4.6 billion aiming to transport crude oil from the southern Iraqi province of Basra to Haditha.

The pipeline’s capacity is projected to be approximately 2.25 million barrels per day using 56-inch diameter pipes. This design aims to enhance domestic transportation and establish connections to future export facilities.

The pipeline will be 685 kilometers long and will serve as the initial phase in the construction of a pipeline network that might eventually extend to Jordan and Syria.

The state-owned Basra Oil Company (BOC) and State Company for Oil Projects (SCOP) are building the project, which is funded by the Iraq-China Framework Agreement.

The pipeline provides a direct path to both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and, subsequently, to European markets.

Once completed, the project will improve flexibility, as Iraq studies alternative routes to its present seaports to expand export capacity.
