The survey has been conducted every five years since fiscal 1995 to grasp the awareness of peace among children. As the survey was canceled in fiscal 2020, the latest one, conducted on 3,630 students, was the first in a decade.

World.title: FIFA apologizes to members and affirms support for president Gianni Infantino
World.content:
FIFA ⁠apologized to its members for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to sell commercial rights to the World Cup as the body’s leadership reaffirmed its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino after a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday.

The proposal to sell a 20% stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion provoked a fierce backlash and was withdrawn last Friday. Infantino bore the brunt of the criticism, including some from inside FIFA, which raised questions over his reelection as president next March.

“Following a ​meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the FIFA Secretary General and members of the FIFA management board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino,” the statement said.

World.title: In Taiwan drill, armored carrier takes president to command center
World.content:
Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te made a late-night dash in the back of an armored personnel carrier to a command center as part of annual war games ​designed to show how the government would continue to work in the event of a war.

Taiwan kicked off the Han ‌Kuang ‌exercises on Wednesday. Lasting 10 days, the drills are designed to bolster preparations should China, which views ​the democratically governed island as its own territory, ever make good on its vow to take Taiwan by force if necessary.

The presidential office said on Thursday that Lai and a group of senior officials had been taken the previous night to a command center, ⁠and showed images of him wearing body armor and a helmet getting into the back of an armored personnel carrier.

World.title: U.K. mansion where ‘listeners’ spied on Nazi generals becomes museum
World.content:
Upstairs, Nazi generals enjoyed wine and lounged in elegant rooms. Downstairs in the basement, a team of covert listeners followed their chatter, gleaning vital insights into Germany’s war plans.

During World War II, Trent Park, a country house north of London, was turned into a camp for high-ranking German prisoners of war.

Now it has become a museum called Trent Park House of Secrets, which highlights the role of the team of German speakers, most of them Jewish refugees, who transcribed tidbits from the prisoners’ bugged conversations.

World.title: Hong Kong police to merge Tin Sum division with Sha Tin and Ma On Shan
World.content:
Hong Kong police will merge the Tin Sum division into the Sha Tin and Ma On Shan ones from August 30 to improve operational efficiency amid population changes and infrastructure development.

A briefing was held at Ma On Shan police station on Thursday morning for members of the Sha Tin district Council, the Fight Crime Committee and area committees, as well as representatives of government departments and community partners.

“The Police Force regularly reviews resource deployment based on local policing demands and demographic changes. Over the past two decades, the force has restructured its resources through division mergers on multiple occasions to support community development,” a spokesman said.

The Shek Kip Mei, Tsz Wan Shan and Waterfront divisions, for example, were merged into nearby divisions in 2004, 2006 and 2010, respectively. The Tseung Kwan O division was also upgraded to a full police district in 2017 to meet growing demand.

“Given the significant population growth and infrastructure development in Sha Tin over the past two decades, the Police Force determined, following a careful evaluation, that police resources needed to be reallocated across the district to maintain high-quality services,” the spokesman said.

“Consequently, the jurisdiction currently covered by the Tin Sum Division will be absorbed by the Sha Tin and Ma On Shan divisions. The police have fully considered emergency response times, geographical terrain, major landmarks, traffic black spots and major annual events to ensure frontline officers can respond swiftly to incidents.”

World.title: CLP posts HK$5.73 billion underlying profit in first half of 2026
World.content:
CLP Holdings , the parent company of a top Hong Kong energy firm, has posted a HK$5.73 billion (US$730.49 million) underlying profit in the first half of 2026, a 9.7 per cent year-on-year rise, driven by growth in its local regulated business.

Its chairman also said the company planned to invest in boosting the electricity supply for the Northern Metropolis megaproject.

Including one-off gains, mainly from the sale of the Jhajjar Power Station in India, the company’s net profit grew 6.6 per cent year on year to HK$5.99 billion, according to a statement issued on Thursday.

CLP Holdings chairman Michael Kadoorie outlined proposals to support the city’s inaugural five-year plan, accelerate decarbonisation in line with national targets, and invest in strengthening the power supply to the technology-driven Northern Metropolis project.

“We are committed to contributing to a low-carbon, resilient and sustainable energy future that Hong Kong needs for its next phase of growth,” he said.

For the first time, Kadoorie shed light on high-level meetings held earlier this year between CLP and Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, as well as He Yang, deputy director of China’s National Energy Administration.

“These meetings provided an important opportunity to reaffirm CLP’s long-term commitment to Hong Kong and the Chinese mainland, and to exchange views on the evolving energy landscape, including CLP’s role in safeguarding electricity supply amid a complex international environment, and supporting the national energy blueprint set out in the 15th national five-year plan,” he said.

World.title: MTR passengers face up to 30-minute delays after Hong Kong signal fault
World.content:
Passengers travelling between Hung Hom and Tuen Mun faced delays of 25 to 30 minutes on Thursday afternoon after a signalling fault at Kam Sheung Road station, Hong Kong’s rail operator said.

The MTR Corporation said at around 2.23pm on Thursday that the glitch had been repaired and train services on the Tuen Ma line were “gradually returning to normal”.

At around 1pm, the MTR said it was repairing the faulty equipment near the tracks and urged passengers to allow extra time for their journeys.

Trains on the Tuen Ma line towards Tuen Mun and Wu Kai Sha remained in service, but were travelling slowly through the affected section. The MTR said it had deployed additional staff to assist passengers.

World.title: Man found dead in waters off Hong Kong’s Stonecutters Island, probe under way
World.content:
Hong Kong police have found the body of a man in the waters off Stonecutters Island and believe he drowned while swimming.

The force received a report at 8.24am on Thursday that a person was floating in the water about 20 metres from a pier near Stonecutters Island in Tsing Yi.

Emergency personnel recovered the man from the sea, but he was pronounced dead at the scene. No identification documents were found on him.

The man was believed to be about 40 years old. He was around 1.7 metres tall and weighed about 80kg.

Officers later recovered his clothing at a pier near Cheung Fai Road in Tsing Yi. A preliminary investigation suggested that he might have drowned while swimming.

Police said investigations were under way to confirm his identity, while a postmortem examination would be conducted to determine the cause of death.

World.title: CUHK to integrate national education into key programme as part of new 5-year plan
World.content:
The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), the city’s second oldest university, has said it will reform its mandatory General Education programme for undergraduates by integrating national education with a global perspective, as well as concepts of innovation, entrepreneurship and sustainability, into its curriculum.

The initiative was announced on Thursday as part of the university’s new five-year strategic plan, which charts its direction and development between 2026 and 2030.

It is the first five-year plan under the leadership of president Dennis Lo Yuk-ming, a distinguished molecular biologist, who took on the role in January 2025.

In a booklet introducing the plan, CUHK said the reformed General Education programme, a mandatory course for all undergraduates, would broaden students’ knowledge by “enhancing National Education and a systematic understanding of modern China, complemented with a robust global outlook”.

Under its five-year plan, CUHK said it would focus on five strategic areas: talent attraction and development, institutional development, global and alumni engagement, education and student experience, and research and innovation.

The university would strengthen cooperation with its Shenzhen campus and other institutions in the Greater Bay Area, expand its internship programmes and “support students’ physical and mental development and lifelong learning”.

It would also start a flagship international undergraduate programme and develop initiatives to nurture talent in various fields.

World.title: 25 arrested as Hong Kong police bust loan shark ring charging up to 282% interest rate
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested 25 people, some as young as 13, in a crackdown on a loan shark syndicate that charged victims annual interest rates of up to 282 per cent.

Police said on Thursday that the crime ring had provided a total of HK$200 million (US$25.5 million) in loans to about 2,000 residents over the past year, with at least HK$8 million in criminal proceeds funnelled into the core members’ personal accounts.

During operations on Tuesday and Wednesday, officers raided three operating centres of the group in Mong Kok and Fo Tan, as well as the residences of key members.

Investigations revealed that the group promoted “no-vetting” loans and borrowing discounts through cold calls and social media.

It charged borrowers a 25 per cent handling fee and imposed heavy penalties for late repayment, with effective annual interest rates as high as 282 per cent. In some cases, the penalty amounted to 800 per cent of the original loan amount.

To enforce repayments, the syndicate recruited teenagers as young as 13 via social media to intimidate debtors, including by making threatening phone calls and splashing red paint on their homes.

World.title: ‘Lyrical Maverick’ Peter Lai, who wrote multiple hits for Cantopop stars, dies at 76
World.content:
Legendary Hong Kong lyricist Peter Lai Bei-dak, who wrote the lyrics to a string of hits for the city’s Cantopop stars in the 1980s, has died at the age of 76, triggering an outpouring of condolences from fans of “The Lyrical Maverick”.

Sports commentator Eric Chung Chi-kwong, a close friend of Lai, announced his death on Wednesday. He told the media that Lai had moved into a nursing home earlier this year after suffering a stroke and collapsing at home. He remained bedridden until his death.

Condolences flooded social media as people expressed gratitude for Lai’s contribution, calling him a “grandmaster” and a “legendary genius”.

“Thanks, thanks, thanks, thanks, Peter Lai, who can replace your place?” one user wrote, paying tribute to an iconic line written by Lai in the classic song “Monica” by the late singer Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing.

“Thank you for the outstanding performances and works you have brought us over so many years,” a user commented. “Your talent was exceptional and deeply touched our hearts. You will always be remembered, and we are grateful to have had you.”

“His lyrics made the songs of Sam Hui and Leslie Cheung well-known to everyone and deeply embedded [them] in people’s hearts,” another user wrote.

World.title: Heaps of documents, endless trials: the herculean workload of Hong Kong’s judges
World.content:
My 18-year-old summer intern is very scared of me.

She spent the entire week watching me sit in front of my computer, in complete silence, motionless except for the occasional click of the mouse to move to the next electronic document, and barely breathing. She told me this could not be further from what she imagined a barrister’s life to be. And there was one thing she was particularly puzzled by: why were there so many documents?

There were, indeed, many documents – over 40,000 pages of them, all for one case.

The number of documents involved in modern-day civil litigation is substantial. When I started practising in 2004, an average half-day court hearing – say, for an interlocutory injunction application – would involve about 300 or 400 pages of documents. Nowadays, such applications easily go into thousands of pages.

The increase in the number of documents used in litigation is not only a result of technology that enables us to capture a larger part of human interaction and turn it into tangible records. It is also a reflection of the increased complexity of the commercial activities that Hong Kong, as an international financial hub, encounters.

“Increased complexity” is often cited but not often explained, and is best illustrated by examples.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.title: The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.content:
JIANGSU, East China — “We are looking for a factory that can produce acrylic mahjong tiles.”

Hua Fangyi repeated that pitch at nearly 30 factories in Taixing, a city in eastern China’s Jiangsu province known for manufacturing mahjong tiles. “Almost every factory refused,” she says.

After quitting her job to start an export business last October, Hua, 28, spotted a surge in overseas demand for American mahjong. Believing the opportunity might last only a few months, she planned to test the market with just a few dozen sets.

But Taixing’s factories were built for large runs of traditional Chinese mahjong, not the small batches of brightly colored acrylic tiles overseas buyers wanted. Some produced only conventional melamine sets; others required minimum orders far beyond what Hua could afford.

Then Hua found a factory with 20 American mahjong sets in stock. She bought the entire batch, and it sold out almost immediately.

Within months, she had built a company shipping more than 5,000 sets a month and generating roughly $400,000 in monthly sales. Across Taixing, factories that had once turned away from American mahjong were now chasing the same overseas buyers.

“Almost every factory is now making American mahjong,” Hua says.

The shift came as rising material costs and intensifying competition squeezed margins on traditional sets. Overseas demand offered higher returns, prompting established factories to buy equipment, hire workers, and adapt their production lines to the elaborate designs sought by American buyers.

The opportunity has also drawn a new generation of entrepreneurs to Taixing: former tech workers, salespeople, and export traders hoping to manufacture the tiles and build brands of their own.

Together, they are all betting on a boom whose limits remain unclear. For now, overseas orders have given Taixing’s mahjong industry fresh momentum, sending an old manufacturing center racing to master a game it barely recognized a year ago.

Follow the dots

Growing up around her family’s garment factory and later working in international e-commerce at Alibaba, Hua had experience with both manufacturing and overseas sales. She began searching for products that could find a market abroad.

She continued using the habits she developed in product operations, tracking trends on social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook and monitoring sales performance on overseas independent websites. American mahjong stood out.

The game itself, however, has a long history in the U.S. The governing body for American mahjong, the National Mah Jongg League, was founded in 1937 with 32 members; it now has more than 350,000 members and publishes a new card of official hands and rules each year.

More recently, American brands such as Oh My Mahjong have helped recast mahjong tiles as colorful, premium lifestyle products, while influencers and social clubs have brought the game to younger players seeking in-person connection.

In April 2026, review platform Yelp reported that U.S. searches for mahjong clubs had jumped 4,467% between September 2024 and August 2025, compared with the previous 12 months. Oh My Mahjong’s sets now sell for $350 to $475, with most priced around $400 — versus the roughly 100 yuan ($15) many Chinese sets sell for in China on e-commerce platform Taobao.

But Hua initially expected the opportunity to be short-lived. Without historical data on American mahjong, she looked to previous domestic product cycles, which often peaked around specific festivals. She expected demand to surge around Christmas, just two months after she first spotted the trend.

Moving quickly to find a supplier, Hua and her father, who runs the family’s garment factory, drove several hundred kilometers from Ningbo, in neighboring Zhejiang province, to Taixing.

But many workshops had no obvious signs and appeared on maps only under broad categories such as “entertainment products.” From the road, little revealed what was being made inside.

Hua struggled to understand the local dialect, so her father asked residents and security guards where they could find factory owners. “We’d only know we’d found the right place after spotting a set or two of mahjong tiles,” she says. “They’d point us to a building and a floor, and we’d keep looking until we found the boss.”

The industry was all around them. A search for “mahjong” on Qichacha, a Chinese corporate database, returns nearly 180 businesses in Taixing, many of them small workshops specializing in a single stage of production.

The cluster grew from a household trade dating to the 1980s, when local families cut and polished tiles by hand from bamboo and ox bone. Over time, production split among specialized workshops handling tile blanks, engraving, polishing, printing, and packaging.

“If one family made money from it, the neighbors would learn too,” says Zhu Ronggen, whose father was among Taixing’s earliest mahjong makers. “One person taught another, and slowly the whole village started making mahjong.”

Zhu grew up inside that manufacturing network. After studying mechanical engineering, he returned to Taixing in 2015 and opened his own factory. By the following year, he was producing traditional sets for China’s domestic market.

So when a customer first asked him to make an American set, Zhu, now 48, assumed it would be a minor variation on a familiar product.

“Chinese mahjong designs have barely changed for decades,” Zhu says. “American mahjong is completely different. A circle tile could be a football or a bunch of grapes. One grape stands for one dot, and nine grapes represent nine dots.”

American sets also include Arabic numerals and joker tiles, while familiar symbols are constantly reworked around seasonal themes and customers’ ideas. Summer collections feature seashells and aquatic plants; Christmas designs use Santa hats and trees.

And while traditional Chinese sets are usually molded from melamine in a narrow range of colors, American buyers prefer acrylic tiles with richer palettes, sometimes built from six or seven colored layers visible along the edge.

“Every customer wants their own concept,” Zhu says. “The color palettes are also much richer than those used in China.”

Chinese players, he says, tend to value weight, legibility, and how the tiles feel in the hand. American buyers, by contrast, want sets distinctive enough to display and expressive enough to reflect their tastes.

“I gradually understood that they weren’t just buying mahjong to play mahjong,” Zhu says. “A lot of the time, they’re buying a lifestyle.”

Factory reset

Inside Zhu’s factory, traditional Chinese mahjong and its American reinvention sit side by side. Dust-covered melamine slabs are stacked near the entrance, while baskets of brightly colored acrylic tiles and export cartons crowd the corridors beyond.

By 4 p.m., Zhu is usually outside the workshop, surrounded by cardboard boxes as he seals packages and confirms overseas delivery addresses with couriers. He moves between the packing area and loading site until sunset.

After the workers leave, he returns to his office to answer inquiries that accumulated during the afternoon. His wife stays at the UV printer, often working until midnight.

At 7 a.m. the next day, Zhu unlocks the factory gate and starts again.

For years, inquiries from new buyers came weeks or even months apart. Orders from Zhu’s long-term domestic clients remained steady, but rising material costs and intensifying competition had squeezed profits. To keep costs down, he and his wife took on work once handled by employees.

Now, he receives dozens of inquiries every day — from foreign trade companies, Amazon sellers, independent online retailers, and buyers on Alibaba.

“I used to make just 20 sets of American mahjong a year,” he says. “Now, I can turn out 200 sets a day.”

Unlike traditional Chinese sets, which can be reproduced using fixed molds, each American order requires new adjustments to engraving, printing, and coloring. A batch of 300 to 400 acrylic sets takes 15 to 20 days to complete — three to five days longer than the same number of Chinese sets.

“People buy them the way they buy clothes,” Zhu says. “What’s fashionable this year may be completely different next year.”

To keep up, Zhu has invested another 1 million yuan ($148,000) in laser engravers, UV printers, and other equipment. But he has hired only two or three additional workers, leaving his family to absorb much of the extra labor.

At the center of the workshop, a giant white sack hangs above a mound of acrylic tiles. Zhu’s parents, both in their 80s, sit on opposite sides of the pile, lifting the pieces one by one and arranging them into neat rows, every face turned in the same direction. Their hands move with a steady, practiced rhythm.

They work from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., the same hours as the factory’s other employees.

“I can do 100 sets a day,” Zhu’s father says. “Workers’ wages aren’t cheap. At least the two of us can save a few hundred yuan.”

A few steps away, Jin Guihua, 62, sorts black tiles before they are colored. Their engraved patterns are barely visible against the dark surface, so she lifts each rack toward the window, tilting it until the light catches the shallow lines.

She scans the rows for matching designs, tapping each selected tile against the edge of the table before setting it aside. Sometimes she checks more than five tiles before finding the next match.

Jin once sorted about 150 sets a day. The smaller tiles and changing patterns of American mahjong have reduced her output to about 60.

“The designs are more complicated and harder to identify,” she says.

Brand new

This past March, five young entrepreneurs arrived in Taixing to start a mahjong business.

A few minutes from Zhu’s family-run factory, they turned a village house into a workshop. Machines occupied the ground floor; their bedrooms were upstairs. There were no fixed hours or weekends.

Between them, the five had experience in sales, technology, and international trade. None had ever made a mahjong tile.



Li Mingzhi, 30, leads the venture, which operates under the name SenJoy Mahjong. A former Alibaba employee, he saw American mahjong as a chance to sell a higher-value product overseas. He recruited his former colleague Wang Hao, his younger brother, and several childhood friends from northwestern China’s Gansu province to build the venture.

“I never imagined I’d move to such a remote village to start a business,” says Wang, 28.

Zhu estimates that nearly 30 new factories have sprung up in Taixing over the past year as entrepreneurs rush into American mahjong. The town’s fragmented supply chain has allowed outsiders to enter without building a factory from scratch.

“Here, you don’t need to build an entire production line yourself,” Li tells Sixth Tone. “You can outsource each step and focus on design and branding.”

In practice, however, the workshop became a crash course in manufacturing.

“Every day is unpredictable,” Li says. “Customers can call at any time, and problems can emerge at every stage — production, design, communication, quality inspection. Working until 3 or 4 a.m. is normal.”

The new equipment offered precision but no ready-made solution for mahjong production: sizes varied, hand-cut pieces did not match machine-cut ones, and every fault required another round of testing.

“Almost every step brought a different problem,” Wang says.

The UV printer proved especially difficult. Each design had to be aligned by hand, and a shift of just 1 millimeter could push the ink outside the engraved lines.

The night before Sixth Tone’s visit, all five stayed up until 3 a.m. trying to solve the problem. “Before entering the industry, I thought making mahjong would be simple,” says Wang. “Once I started, I realized American sets are closer to handicrafts.”

Despite the setbacks, the team produced and sold about 1,000 sets in its first few months, generating roughly 230,000 yuan in sales. Its customers included businesses selling on Amazon.

Li put 1.5 million yuan of his own savings into the venture. “Based on our current orders,” says Li, “we expect the business to recover that investment within six months.”

To avoid becoming another contract manufacturer in Taixing’s crowded supply chain, the team began working with outside designers to develop original sets. It also launched an independent website and overseas social media accounts.

“For us, building a brand starts with original design,” Li says. “We might become the first company in Taixing — and perhaps one of the first in China — to build a real mahjong brand instead of simply manufacturing for others.”

The team hopes to reach buyers directly through social media, influencers, online sellers, and brick-and-mortar retailers.

Their bestseller uses a coral-reef theme. Against a shimmering blue base, coral motifs represent bamboo tiles, shells stand in for circles, and small fish serve as jokers.

“As long as the designs aren’t ugly, we’re not worried about sales,” Li says. “Right now, demand far exceeds supply.”

Wang is more cautious. Today’s buyers, he says, remain a relatively small group with strong spending power. If American mahjong reaches a broader market, more manufacturers will follow, he says, adding: “Price wars are unavoidable.”

Hua, one of the first Chinese traders to bet on American mahjong, has watched competitors multiply within months.

When she launched the business, Hua handled every part of the operation herself, often staying up late to respond to customers in the U.S. and sleeping as little as two hours a night. Today, her Ningbo-based company employs about 10 people and provides customer service around the clock.

But the market that once seemed wide open has become more crowded. Designs that once sold out quickly are now easier to source, and more suppliers are competing for the same orders.

“The conversion rate isn’t as good as before,” Hua says. Her sales data show that fewer visitors become inquiries, and fewer inquiries turn into confirmed orders.

“The profit margins were much higher in the beginning, but now they have dropped significantly,” she says. “I think this is probably an inevitable stage for any viral product.”

She, too, has started developing designs of her own.

Last month, she began experimenting with AI to create early concepts before working with freelance designers to refine them. Her first ideas included themes inspired by witches, tennis, flowers, and Christmas.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Workers sort uncarved and unpainted mahjong tiles at Zhu Ronggen’s factory in Taixing, Jiangsu province, June 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018849/Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.title: Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018849/Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.content:
China has discontinued the blue exterior lights common to its vehicles equipped with autonomous driving features.

The ban, leaked by a car industry blogger on microblogging platform Weibo on July 29, was outlined in an official notice from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. According to the notice, the ban took effect as of July 27 for new vehicles, while existing vehicles are apparently not affected at this time.

The same day, the state-affiliated China Automotive Standardization Research Institute, while not directly confirming the ban, said on its public account on messaging app WeChat that the blue lights have been used excessively and improperly, and that a new national standard is under revision.

The blue lights, or advanced driver assistance system indicator lights, are usually found on the wing mirrors or lower front and back fenders of vehicles with advanced driver assistance systems. Introduced in 2022 by domestic car brand Li Auto, automakers began adopting them to indicate to other road users that intelligent driving systems were in use.

However, China’s current vehicle lighting standard does not include specific provisions for blue lights and permits only white, red, yellow, and amber for vehicle signal lights.

In its July 29 post, the China Automotive Standardization Research Institute said blue lights can cause glare for other road users at night, distracting them or interfering with their judgment of road conditions. It also noted that vehicles equipped with the lights are more likely to be cut off or followed closely by other drivers, increasing the risk of accidents.

In addition, many vehicles’ blue lights are installed in the car’s preexisting turn lamps, meaning that turn signals can sometimes glow blue.

An insider at Geely Automobile, China’s leading car manufacturer, confirmed to domestic media that they had indeed received notice of the ban but declined to disclose specific details. “We are aware of the news and will strictly comply with national regulations, awaiting further instructions from the government,” the insider said.

Zeng Qinglin, general manager of domestic car brand Yijing, listed what he sees as the reasons for the ban on his Weibo account. “First,” he said, “the brightness and flickering of various blue lights lack unified standards, affecting traffic safety and causing light pollution.”

“Second, other drivers, seeing blue lights on the car ahead, know it’s using an intelligent driving system and deliberately cut in, assuming the system will brake automatically,” he wrote. “As a result, drivers using the intelligent driving system are often startled by sudden braking. A device intended to signal safety has instead become a new source of risk.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Blue lights on a car indicating self-driving mode. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018838/How China Delivers a 14-Yuan Bouquet Over 2,000 Kilometers
World.title: How China Delivers a 14-Yuan Bouquet Over 2,000 Kilometers
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018838/How China Delivers a 14-Yuan Bouquet Over 2,000 Kilometers
World.content:
On China’s major e-commerce platforms, a bouquet of fresh-cut roses from the southwestern Yunnan province sells for just 14 yuan ($2), with free delivery to most parts of the country.

For consumers, this is an ordinary online purchase: tap to pay on a phone screen, then wait for the flowers to arrive at the door. But behind that simple transaction is a complex logistical challenge. Cut flowers are highly perishable. They lose moisture quickly and must travel more than 2,000 kilometers from Yunnan to major cities like Shanghai. Harvesting, sorting, packing, transportation, and last-mile delivery all have to happen within a narrow window.

How can a product worth less than 20 yuan cover the costs of packaging and inter-provincial delivery while remaining affordable as an everyday online purchase? The answer lies in how far China’s supply chain has evolved.

The first factor is scale.

In 2025, China’s express delivery companies handled 198.95 billion parcels, or nearly 550 million per day. Around 90% were shipped between different cities or regions.

Such enormous volumes allow logistics companies to build fixed routes, operate frequent departures, and invest in large-scale sorting centers. The costs of warehouses, vehicles, information systems, and automation equipment can be distributed across hundreds of millions of parcels.

In cities with dense order volumes, trucks can consolidate packages heading to the same areas, while couriers can complete more deliveries along compact routes. Adding another parcel does not require rebuilding the entire logistics system from scratch. Instead, existing infrastructure becomes more efficient as volume increases.

But scale alone is not enough. A huge number of parcels can also create new problems, including congested warehouses, idle vehicles, and inventory stored in the wrong places.

What has made China’s logistics system distinctive is its size coupled with the widespread application of supply chain management.

Other countries also use supply chain management, but China has applied it in a market with a combination of scale, density, complexity, and cost pressures rarely seen elsewhere. It has turned complex logistics systems into everyday services that even low-priced goods can use.

One example is demand forecasting.

As parcel volumes increase, companies need to predict not only what products consumers will buy but also where demand will come from and how much inventory and transport capacity each region will require.

This is why presales have become increasingly important, especially during China’s major shopping festivals. Rather than waiting for consumers to place orders on the day of a promotion, platforms use presales to collect advance commitments from buyers.

This gives retailers a clearer picture of expected sales volumes and buyer locations. They can prepare inventory, organize picking and packing, and adjust sales plans ahead of time. Logistics companies can reserve warehouse space and transportation capacity before order volumes surge.

Presales are only one forecasting tool. Companies also analyze historical sales, browsing trends, promotional plans, and real-time orders to estimate demand. The goal is to prepare resources before a sudden increase in orders overwhelms the system.

But predicting demand is only the first step. Goods must also be placed in the right locations — this is the warehousing question of supply chain management.

While forecasting has become increasingly sophisticated, China’s warehousing capacity has also expanded significantly. But warehousing is not simply about the size and number of facilities. Location is also crucial because it determines how far goods must travel after an order is placed and how many transfers are needed before reaching consumers. Logistics costs depend not only on how quickly goods move, but also on where inventory is positioned.

Take the major e-commerce platform JD.com as an example. In the first half of 2026, JD Logistics expanded its fulfillment network by opening new warehouses in the eastern Shandong province and other regions. Its domestic network now includes more than 3,600 warehouses across over 2,800 county-level areas, allowing merchants to stock goods closer to consumers and fulfill orders from nearby facilities.

In the past, deliveries during major shopping festivals could take weeks. Today, some presold goods are moved in advance to regional distribution hubs. Once buyers near these warehouses make the final payment, delivery can begin almost immediately, with some orders reportedly arriving within hours of payment.

For manufactured goods or everyday household items, placing inventory close to major consumer markets reduces delivery distances and logistics costs. Fresh produce, however, requires a different, more technology-intensive kind of logistics system.

Returning to Yunnan’s cut flowers, the challenge lies in speed and coordination.

At a fresh-flower cold-chain distribution center in Kunming, Yunnan’s provincial capital, five sorting lines operate at high speed. Automated equipment identifies each shipment’s destination and directs it onto the appropriate route. The center can process around 20,000 flower parcels per hour, with each parcel sorted in as little as three minutes — 1.5 times the efficiency of manual sorting.

The center began operations in 2021 and underwent a major upgrade in 2024. Its daily flower shipments increased from an initial 2 tons to more than 260 tons. After sorting, flowers quickly enter a transport network combining air freight, high-speed rail, and refrigerated trucks. Express air services can reach more than 28 cities within 24 hours, and over 90% of China’s major cities nationwide within 48 hours.

The logistics system behind fresh flowers is far more than simply transporting a box from one city to another. It is a complete chain covering harvesting, pre-cooling, sorting, packing, cold-chain transport, and final delivery. The goal of this system is to minimize transfers and reduce the time flowers spend outside controlled conditions.

Refrigeration, protective packaging, and air transport all increase costs. But for products whose value declines with every delay, faster and more controlled delivery reduces damage and extends their selling life.

This is why the key post-harvest steps, including pre-cooling, grading, and packing, must happen close to the farm, without delay. Origin-based sorting and cold-chain hubs allow flowers from multiple producers to be collected, processed, and shipped efficiently, transforming fragmented agricultural production into a reliable supply chain.

Demand forecasting, inventory positioning, warehouse placement, and AI-enabled dispatching may appear to be separate processes. In reality, they work together toward the same goal: reducing unnecessary waiting and avoiding inefficient movement.

What consumers ultimately see is often only a modest delivery fee, or simply a “free shipping” label. That price is not the result of a single cheap step. It reflects the coordination of order processing, inventory management, warehousing, transportation, and last-mile delivery.

This is the result of supply chain management applied at scale: a system that allows consumers across China to experience the increasingly ordinary reality of placing an order and receiving it almost instantly.

The 14-yuan bouquet of roses is therefore more than a cheap online purchase. It represents a shift in how people shop and access goods across one of the world’s largest consumer markets. The supply chain design behind it is what allows these expectations of convenience, speed, and choice to become an everyday reality.

Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A worker transports flower bouquets at a warehouse at the Dounan Flower Market, Kunming, Yunnan province, February 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)
