World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: High Court finds secret recording can be used as evidence in DV case
World.content:
Victim-survivors of domestic violence may now be able to use secret recordings of admissions of abuse to seek safety after a major High Court decision.

Yesterday, Australia's highest court dismissed an appeal from a man convicted of raping his wife while she slept on two occasions.

He had argued a recording of him admitting to the first rape was obtained illegally.

While most recordings of private conversations are illegal, the High Court found the recording was allowed and able to be used as evidence because it was necessary to protect the victim's "bodily autonomy and integrity".

"The covert recording was the reminder to the complainant, by replaying it to herself, to avoid being exposed to the real risk of being raped," the court said in its unanimous judgement.

" The interest of a person in not being raped is an interest deserving of the very strongest protection. "

The man, known by the pseudonym Potter, was found guilty in South Australia of raping his sleeping wife on two occasions while the jury could not reach a verdict on two further counts.

The South Australian man's appeal was knocked down in the landmark judgment. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A month before the last rape, his wife recorded a conversation on her phone where she confronted Potter about the attacks and he admitted to doing them.

The woman gave evidence that she made the recording to "convince myself never to go back to him no matter what happened".

Protecting the rights of victim-survivors to record — and use as evidence — confessions of abuse inflicted on them is a major milestone for domestic violence law in Australia, legal expert Melbourne Law School's Heather Douglas said.

"The decision is important as it explicitly recognises that a lawful interest includes a right of bodily autonomy and integrity in the context of recordings," Professor Douglas said.

"Domestic and family violence is a violation of bodily autonomy and integrity."

How perpetrators use the court system to inflict harm Jessica Seage fought for six years for the man who raped her to be convicted. Experts say her experience is a stark example of how perpetrators abuse the system to inflict more pain on their victims.

The influence of the High Court's decision could extend beyond criminal cases, potentially allowing for similar recordings to be used in protection applications, Professor Douglas said.

However, it remains to be seen how far courts will allow secret recordings to be used to as evidence against less obvious forms of abuse.

"Much of the most damaging domestic and family violence is non-physical, such as coercive control, and this form of abuse impacts autonomy," Professor Douglas said.

"I would hope the understanding extends to that."

The husband is serving a nine-and-a-half-year prison term.

AAP

World.title: No verdict in child sex abuse trial of former Mount Isa priest
World.content:
A jury has failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the trial of a former Catholic priest accused of sexually abusing a boy almost 50 years ago.

Warning: This article contains details of alleged child sexual abuse some readers might find distressing.

Neville Joseph Creen was a priest in Mount Isa during the 1970s and early '80s when he was accused of having a sexual relationship with a boy who was between 10 and 11 years old.

The 86-year-old faced trial in the Townsville District Court this week after pleading not guilty to one count of repeated sexual conduct with a child and two counts of indecent treatment of a child under 14 years old.

The prosecution told the jury that Mr Creen had allegedly sexually touched the boy and forced him to perform oral sex when they were alone in a back room in a church.

During the three-day trial, Mr Creen took to the witness box and denied ever knowing the complainant and denied the alleged acts occurred.

The jury deliberated for six hours but was unable to reach a unanimous decision.

Judge Terry Gardiner discharged the jury of six men and six women.

Mr Creen was expressionless as the jury was discharged.

Neville Creen was accused of indecent treatment of a boy in Mount Isa during the late 1970s and early '80s. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

'Nobody else was there'

During the trial, Crown prosecutor Andrew Walklate said as a priest, Mr Creen was alone with boys for duties and that there was opportunity for the alleged abuse to occur.

Before a closed court and with a screen installed to obscure Mr Creen, the male complainant, who cannot be named for legal reasons, gave evidence.

Prosecutors alleged Mr Creen had touched the complainant's penis in the back room of the church when he was in grade 5 or 6 at a Mount Isa school in the late 1970s and early '80s.

The Crown alleged the abuse occurred while Neville Creen was serving as a priest in Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The court heard on another occasion while the pair were allegedly alone in the same back room, Mr Creen allegedly forced the complainant to perform oral sex on him.

"Nobody else was there," Mr Walklate said.

Prosecutors alleged that after the two incidents, Mr Creen allegedly continued to force the boy to engage in oral sex on about 10 occasions.

"It would be done at opportune moments," Mr Walklate said.

The court heard the complainant began "playing up" at school to avoid being alone with Mr Creen.

The prosecution argued that although it had been almost 50 years since the alleged offending, the complainant was consistent in his evidence about the alleged abuse.

Mr Creen takes the stand

During the trial, Mr Creen chose to give evidence and said he did not know the complainant nor had any sexual contact with him.

"No, definitely not," he said under cross-examination.

Neville Creen pleaded not guilty in Townsville District Court to three charges. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The jury heard Mr Creen was a well-known Catholic figure in the Mount Isa community at the time and that his work included being a mine chaplain and marriage counsellor.

Mr Creen told the court no records of priest's rosters or daily movements were kept at the time.

His lawyer Jessica Horne said the prosecution case was "blurry" and that there was not enough evidence corroborating the complainant's accusations.

"You have to be really sure of [the complainant's] evidence," she said.

" There isn't any other evidence you can turn to. "

Neville Creen's matter is due to be mentioned in court on August 13. (ABC North Queensland: Rachael Merritt)

She also said there was not enough evidence to prove that the complainant had identified the correct priest.

"Keep in mind the frailty and shortcomings of memory in the context of a very long delay," she said.

"Draw on your own experiences of faulty memory recall or memory reconstruction."

A school friend of the complainant and a police officer also gave evidence.

Mr Creen was granted bail and will return to court when the matter is mentioned again on August 13.

World.title: Anti-abortion campaigner clashes with senior Liberal at meeting
World.content:
A Liberal Women's Council meeting has become a flash point for the ideological rift plaguing the South Australian party as a prominent anti-abortion campaigner clashed with the former deputy premier.

Anti-abortion campaigner Joanna Howe was invited to speak at the Liberal Women's Council's annual general meeting, in conversation with conservative Senator Alex Antic.

Professor Howe said she had been granted permission to film her address, but former Deputy Premier Vickie Chapman objected.

Joanna Howe posted a video to social media of Vickie Chapman at the meeting. (Instagram)

In a video published online by Professor Howe, Ms Chapman can be seen making a motion to block the filming.

"I've never, in the 50-odd years I've been working in the Liberal Party, known any other meetings to be [filmed]," she said.

"If that was to be recorded on an audio basis, and the meeting approve that, I think that would be quite in order but I think the meeting does need to approve it and I just ask that there be no filming of the event."

In a social media video, Professor Howe said she wanted to record her address to avoid being misquoted in the media.

"My message to Vickie Chapman might be, 'You've not seen this in 50 years, well times have changed Vickie,'" she told the meeting.

The issue was put to a vote, and Professor Howe was ultimately allowed to film the meeting.

She said Ms Chapman and a small group of women who voted with her then left.

The shift to the conservative

The Liberal Women's Council is an official organisation of the party, and the meeting on Tuesday night voted on its new leadership, and on delegates for the party's State Council, which elects the party's state president and votes on state and federal senate preselections.

At the meeting, Senator Alex Antic backed Tea Tree Gully Councillor and former Liberal candidate Irena Zagladov was elected council president.

Antic-backed candidates also won the other 12 delegate positions voted on that night.

Alex Antic is currently running uncontested to be the SA Liberal Party state president. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Professor Howe is not a member of the Liberal Party but was invited as a guest speaker.

The professor, who is an expert on labour laws, was a long-term Labor Party member until she was expelled earlier this year for campaigning against the party in the most recent state election.

In her social media video about the event, Professor Howe and her husband James Howe described Ms Chapman and her supporters as "witches" who love killing babies.

Ms Chapman led the push for abortion reform in South Australia, and ultimately succeeded in decriminalising it in 2021.

"The witch is dead is a classic call for a reason. A classic cause for celebration and we should join in these traditions as conservatives," Professor Howe said in the video.

" We should celebrate the wins and this is a win. To see Vickie Chapman, the architect of killing babies right up until birth in this state removed.' "

Ms Chapman has been contacted for comment.

Vickie Chapman served as Deputy Premier and Attorney-General in the Marshall Liberal government. (News Video)

Ms Chapman, along with other party leaders from former Premier Steven Marshall to former federal ministers Simon Bermingham and Christopher Pyne are moderately aligned.

The deputy opposition leader Josh Teague today said he did not support Professor Howe's comments.

"I don't support the remarks that have been reported about what happened at a meeting during the week and I know the leader's been very clear about not supporting those comments," he said.

"We all need to conduct ourselves in public debate with respect and with decency."

He said Ms Chapman can handle the situation.

"Vickie will be totally OK. I know Vickie very well. She'll be fine and she knows how to hold herself in the public debate. She's a tough as they come," he said.

Who will be state president?

But in more recent years, the party's conservatives have been taking over leadership roles within the administration.

Senator Antic was widely expected to become state president.

No other candidates has publicly declared they are running ahead of nominations closing for the position at 5pm on Friday.

Fellow conservative Tony Pasin has defended Senator Antic's nomination.

"There's been a level of hyperventilation around this question over the course of the last few weeks that I've never seen before," he said.

"From my perspective, I think it's interesting at the very time that One Nation seems to be attracting popular support, there's a suggestion that the right wing of the Liberal Party shouldn't exist almost in the legacy media and in the commentariat and in various places online."

World.title: Queanbeyan's own Omar Musa and why the new Miles Franklin winner told mum first
World.content:
When Omar Musa learned he had won a major literary prize he did two things:

He froze in the middle of a road in the Philippines with traffic whizzing by.

And he called his mum.

"My mother has been absolutely instrumental in helping to shape me and give me the freedom of imagination to create my art," Musa said.

"But not just me, anyone who's in the arts in Canberra or Queanbeyan would know my mother, Helen Musa."

The Malaysian-Australian grew up in Queanbeyan, close to Canberra, and on top of winning the 2026 Miles Franklin Literary Award for his novel Fierceland, he is a poet, hip hop artist, theatre performer and visual artist.

'Scallywaggery and privilege'

Omar Musa and his mother, Helen Musa, in Malaysia, where much of his novel is set. (Supplied)

Musa's mother was a magazine editor and arts journalist who met his father in Malaysia when she directed him in the role of Shakespeare's Hamlet.

He said his childhood was a dichotomy of Queanbeyan's suburban streets and Canberra's privileged arts scene.

"I mean, growing up in Queanbeyan was great fun," he said.

Omar Musa with his mother, Helen Musa, who he said cultivated his storytelling. (Supplied)

"I grew up in the flats there, spent a lot of time on the river fishing, getting up to all sorts of scallywaggery, running around the drains in the river and the streets there.

"I was [also] able to go to a lot of exhibitions, a lot of theatre shows, a lot of concerts.

"And so I had a bit of a weird upbringing in that way, because growing up in the flats in Queanbeyan, but having this privileged sort of access to the arts was really inspiring, really generative."

He said while many boys his age were encouraged to express themselves physically through sport, his storytelling was nurtured.

"My parents would give me a piece of paper and pen and tell me that I'd never be bored if I had that," he said.

"I was an only child, so I would just draw stuff or write my little dreamings and thoughts down.

"I'm still pretty much doing exactly the same thing."

21 drafts, 'tough slog'

Omar Musa has described the years-long process of researching and drafting his novel Fierceland. (Supplied: Boyz Bieber/Penguin Books Australia)

Musa said his award-winning novel Fierceland had 21 drafts over at least five years.

"It's such a long, tough slog writing a novel and you're broke all the time," he said.

" You don't necessarily know how you're going to buy your groceries and you're sort of full of self-doubt and impostor syndrome and you're wondering whether it's all worth it, whether anyone's going to read it. "

He said Fierceland followed the lives of two siblings who went to Malaysian Borneo for their father's funeral — a man who had a "rags to riches success story in modern Malaysia".

Cover image of Fierceland (2025) by Omar Musa. (Supplied: Penguin)

"But as you read on, you realise that he was one of the most corrupt logging and oil palm barons in Southeast Asia, and in fact the world, and was possibly responsible for the disappearance of people who stood in his way," Musa said.

"So it's a book about power, it's about complicity, it's about corruption, and it's about grappling with the ghosts of the past, whether it be the ghost of your father and how to mourn someone who you loved but [who] did terrible things, or the ghosts of colonialism and powerful men who tried to shape history to their will.

"I guess I was inspired to write this book by seeing the dark, complicated world of logging and oil palm and what it's done to my homeland of Malaysian Borneo."

Musa said he did a "hell of a lot of research" including speaking to people in the jungle in Borneo.

Queanbeyan's own Omar

Queanbeyan Performing Arts Centre's Jordan Best says the local arts scene is thriving. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Despite Musa's career soaring to national acclaim, he said he was "definitely a product of the Canberra-Queanbeyan arts scene".

Artistic director at the Queanbeyan Performing Arts Centre Jordan Best said she knew Musa was destined for big things.

"I'm not at all surprised," Ms Best said.

"He's so creative in such an incredibly explosive way. It's like he has to just make things ... it's like it bursts out of him.

"It's so wonderful in Omar's writing how deeply you can see how the region and community has informed his life and his creations.

"When someone from a little town like Queanbeyan wins a big award, it just proves art is everywhere."

Ms Best recently hosted a book launch for Musa's latest novel, The Vape Lord of Queanbeyan, with the night featuring a cello performance by his wife Mariel Roberts Musa.

Collins Booksellers in Queanbeyan owner Carlie Lloyd is overjoyed by Omar Musa's success. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Collins Booksellers in Queanbeyan owner Carlie Lloyd said The Vape Lord of Queanbeyan was the retailer's best selling book of the year so far.

While Fierceland has also been popular among locals and is currently sold out.

"It's so amazing. We're very proud of Omar. It couldn't happen to a nicer guy," Ms Lloyd said.

World.title: People still awaiting Census instructions less than a week out
World.content:
As Australia gears up for the Census next week, some residents across the country are saying they are confused about how to take part in the nationwide population count.

Sally Goode, a Justice of the Peace in South Australia's Riverland, said she and other JPs have been flooded with community members asking for help.

They are seeking instructions on how to fill out the online form or request a paper questionnaire for the Census, which will take place on August 11.

"People are concerned that they have not received a letter and just presume that one will hopefully come along," Ms Goode said.

"The thing I have found to be the most worrying for people is the fact they need a computer in order to do this.

" For elderly people who don't have access to a computer, it frightens them. "

Sally Goode says many elderly people are seeking assistance from JPs. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

Ms Goode said the majority of community members seeking help are older in age.

"[There has been] a rush of elderly who have come into the library where our signing room is and are completely bamboozled by the information they have received," she said.

" Many of them are not in any way computer literate, and to get a letter that says go to a website it flabbergasts them. "

She said physical Census forms should have been made available at local facilities including libraries, particularly in regional areas.

"I think it's very short-sighted to have not made printed forms readily available," she said.

Digital vs paper

While some households will be sent a paper form, most will have to request one if they do not want to fill it out online, which is the default.

Federal member for Barker Tony Pasin told 891 ABC Adelaide he believed digital forms would mean participation would be lower, and his constituents were feeling confused and frustrated.

Tony Pasin says he has not received much information that he could pass on to his constituents. (Supplied: Office of Tony Pasin)

"I just think there's a tendency in government for everyone to think digital is best, but I'm not sure in this case," he said.

"If you've got this slip, you have to use your digital prowess to convert it into an online document that you fill out."

Similar stories across the border

The story is similar in the 230-person Victorian town of Quambatook.

Quambatook General Store owner Chelle Espagne has been collecting mail from Kerang two or three times a week for the community after the local post office closed in May this year.

"No-one's got any of the forms yet," she said.

Chelle Espagne wonders how valid the information will be if not everyone is able to access a form. (ABC Central Victoria: Larissa Romensky)

"When we rang them they couldn't tell us anything, so we'd thought we'd be proactive and get some paper forms in because we're an elderly community and they gave me two, because there's two people that live in my household.

"If you get your letter today with the [telephone] number on it that lets you ring them and get a paper form … to get that paper form sent to you by Tuesday, good luck with that."

Ms Espagne had hoped to help confused community members who come into the shop.

"If we had the forms we could help the elderly who could come into the stores, or our neighbourhood house, and we would help them fill out the form or get online," she said.

Will not be fined straight away

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said it will be dropping off paper forms via field staff in areas including the Wimmera and Riverland region, with mailed forms still being delivered.

People can complete the Census after August 11 and will not be fined if they have not received their forms by this time.

If a person refuses to complete it when directed they can be prosecuted and fined up to $364 a day.

Census national spokesperson Emily Walter said there is support for people who feel confused.

"For most of the country they'll receive a letter in the mail if they haven't already," she said.

Census letters contain a unique 16-digit code to log in and complete the national survey online. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

"If people haven't received a letter in the mail or are still waiting to hear, there is a call centre.

"They can request a paper form there, or there is a very easy method through our Census website to request a paper form.

"They might also see field officers who will be carrying a bright yellow satchel and wearing an ABS identification tag, so they can request a paper form from them."

Ms Walter said if the Census is completed after August 11 it just needs to reflect the same date.

"We ask everyone to complete their Census form as soon as they can, based on who spends the night at their house on Census night, Tuesday 11 August," she said.

World.title: WA man jailed for crash that killed 15-year-old girl
World.content:
An 18-year-old has been jailed for 19 months after admitting to causing the death of a 15-year-old girl in a four-wheel drive crash in Western Australia.

Caitlyn Bragger died after the then-learner driver, who was 16 at the time, rolled a modified four-wheel drive while doing "snakies" on a gravel road near Logue Brook Dam, 200km south of Perth, in June 2025.

She was one of six teenagers in the vehicle.

The matter was set down for a week-long trial in Busselton Children's Court, but on Monday the accused changed his plea to guilty one count of dangerous driving causing death.

The 18-year-old, who cannot be named for legal reasons, also pleaded guilty to one count of dangerous driving causing grievous bodily harm and three counts of causing bodily harm.

Prosecutor James Nicholl told the court the group was camping and decided to go driving at about 8pm.

The four-wheel drive had some unauthorised modifications, with a lifted suspension, larger than normal tyres and a rooftop tent.

The court heard the driver had been doing "snakies" — veering from side to side — on a dark road.

Caitlyn called out to the driver "in alarm" just before the crash, the court was told.

Caitlyn Bragger was camping at Logue Brook Dam when the crash occurred. (ABC South West WA: Pip Waller)

As a result of these actions Mr Nicholl pushed for an immediate prison term.

He said the man had maintained he had not been doing snakies and was prepared to go to trial until it became clear that the other people in the car were going to give evidence to the contrary.

"The decision to drive dangerously was his own, with passengers urging him to settle down," Mr Nicholl said.

He accepted the offender's remorse but pointed out that Caitlyn's mother had lost her only daughter.

Defence lawyer Derek Hunter said his client's actions showed the stupidity of an inexperienced driver.

Admission to doing 'snakies'

Mr Hunter told the court the teenager accepted he had been doing snakies on the gravel road, but denied accelerating heavily or speeding.

Others in the group had been drinking alcohol, but he had not been drinking, the court was told.

"He accepts driving left to right. He doesn't know why — maybe because it was dark and fun to do," Mr Hunter said.

"[On the] last one, he lost control and a tragedy occurred. It will be something he will regret for the rest of his life."

Caitlyn Bragger was alarmed by the way the offender was driving, the court heard. (Supplied)

The offender was also injured in the crash.

Mr Hunter said his client's memory of the accident was limited and described his actions as out of character.

The teenager was struggling in the wake of the crash and had the full support of his family, the court heard.

“[It was] the greatest mistake he could make," Mr Hunter said.

Guilty plea delay 'regrettable'

Children's Court president Hylton Quail said the man's late guilty plea showed how long he took to take responsibility for his actions.

The man will serve his time in an adult prison because he continued to contest the charge after he turned 18. (ABC South West WA: Pip Waller)

"You told the person preparing the pre-sentence report you were just being an idiot," Judge Quail said.

"Finally there is that recognition you have been an idiot."

Judge Quail suspended the man's driver's licence for three years and said he would be eligible for parole in nine and a half months.

Judge Quail said the man faced adult jail instead of juvenile detention because he had continued to contest the charge until after he turned 18.

"It is very regrettable you delayed pleading guilty until after your 18th birthday," he said.

Judge Quail said the boy was employed, had previously been of good character and that the crash had a profound impact on him as well as the other survivors.

"It is clear to me that you have been devastated by her death," Judge Quail said.

" You've been described now as a broken, hurt, and sad kid. "

Sarah Highwood spoke the media after the sentencing of the man who caused her daughter's death. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Caitlyn's mother Sarah Highwood said there had been "some kind of justice".

"It's never enough, but it's something, to give him some time to reflect on what he's done," Ms Highwood said.

"Just don't know what silly driving can cause. Showing off is not worth it.

"As it's been shown … Caitlin lost her life because of [the offender] showing off."

World.title: ABC investigations boss leaves, as Four Corners probe continues
World.content:
The ABC's head of investigations and current affairs, Jo Puccini, is leaving the public broadcaster, the ABC has announced.

In an email to ABC staff, acting news director Donna Field said Puccini had shaped significant public interest journalism, leading to numerous Walkley awards.

"We wish Jo every success in whatever comes next," she said.

The announcement comes alongside a deepening investigation into the work of sacked Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal. The long-running current affairs program falls under Puccini's oversight.

Storied career for Puccini

Puccini joined the ABC in 2000 from the Seven Network, working at Media Watch as a researcher, before moving to Four Corners, where she won three Walkley Awards.

She held senior roles at Media Watch, Lateline, 7.30, the National Reporting Team and ABC Investigations.

Puccini said it was time for a new chapter in her career.

"I'm proud of the journalism I've helped produce and the impact it's had on helping our audience understand the issues and events that affect them," she said.

"It's been an adventure and a privilege to work at the national broadcaster, an institution where I've made lifelong friends. It's now time for a new chapter in my career.

"I'll be watching and cheering you all on to great success and important journalism that will continue to benefit the Australian public."

Three stories by Mahmood Fazal have been withdrawn by the ABC. (ABC News)

Accuracy concerns over Fazal's reporting

Three stories by Fazal have been withdrawn by the public broadcaster in recent weeks over concerns about their accuracy.

Other senior managers at the broadcaster at the time of Fazal's reporting have already left the broadcaster for unrelated reasons, including Four Corners executive producer Mathew Carney, news director Justin Stevens and managing director David Anderson.

Once a member of the Mongols bikie club, Fazal switched careers, becoming an award-winning journalist specialising in crime, violence, imprisonment and terrorism.

He was terminated last year after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure.

In recent weeks, the two Four Corners episodes Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway were removed by the ABC due to accuracy concerns, along with a Background Briefing episode titled "Remy was 12 when she became a drug dealer".

'Cocaine dealer' on Mahmood Fazal's Four Corners episode says she did it as 'an acting role' Further concerns over the accuracy of reporting by sacked Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal are raised on Media Watch, including that a hire car was used to mislead viewers in the profile of a purported cocaine dealer.

On Monday, Media Watch reported on claims that "Remy", who purported to be a cocaine dealer in the Background Briefing and a Four Corners episode, was self-styled Sydney rapper Charissa Habkouk, who said the core of her story was invented.

Ms Habkouk told Media Watch she considered Remy "an acting role and a favour to Mahmood".

"All of that … is a complete fable … there's no validity to [it] … [Fazal] knew I could play the part and look the part," she said.

Media Watch also alleged the Mercedes-Benz that "Remy" and Fazal drove around in the Four Corners episode was hired by the ABC and not owned by "Remy" as the program implied.

In a response to Media Watch, Fazal rejected Ms Habkouk's claims and said he stood by the "integrity of my reporting and the editorial processes that underpinned both programs".

"I reject the suggestion that I fabricated, staged or knowingly published information that I believed to be false," Fazal said in a statement.

The ABC has previously said Fazal's episodes were removed "following concerns identified about the veracity of sources used in the three programs".

"The ABC Ombudsman is already conducting an independent review of whether the Four Corners programs complied with the ABC's editorial standards," it said in a statement.

Apology to Gina Rinehart

Puccini's departure comes on the same day the ABC has apologised for a Race Around the World episode containing remarks about mining magnate Gina Rinehart, despite the ABC Ombudsman finding it did not breach editorial standards.

The episode featured contestant Kate McGuinness describing a fictional scenario that involved a violent attack on Mrs Rinehart.

Race Around the World apology The ABC apologises for a Race Around the World episode containing remarks about mining magnate Gina Rinehart AO.

Managing director Hugh Marks said the segment fell short of community expectations.

"While the Ombudsman has found that the film did not breach the ABC's editorial policies, the ABC acknowledges the episode has fallen short of community expectations," Mr Marks said in a statement.

"The ABC apologises to Mrs Rinehart and to anyone else affected or upset by the publication of the film."

Mrs Rinehart's company, Hancock Prospecting, wrote to the ABC Board on July 23 calling on the ABC to immediately remove the material, publicly apologise and investigate how the material came to be published, with full accountability for those responsible, a company statement said.

McGuinness released a statement through the ABC last week, apologising to anyone she offended and saying the sense of humour featured in her films on Race Around the World was "farcical".

"In no way was it my intention to promote violence," she said.

"My writing is cartoonish and always satirical.

"Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally."

World.title: NT police commissioner fires back at Labor MP over arrest 'politicisation' claim
World.content:
Northern Territory Police Commissioner Martin Dole says a claim from Luke Gosling's lawyer that the MP's arrest was politicised is "offensive" and part of his defence team's "strategy".

Mr Gosling, the Member for Solomon and federal Labor's special envoy for defence, veterans' affairs and northern Australia, was last Thursday arrested and charged with assaulting NT Administrator David Connolly.

The NT administrator is the Crown's representative in the NT, with the position equivalent to a state governor.

Luke Gosling's defence lawyer Marty Aust (right) claimed the matter had been politicised. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

According to a hearing in the Darwin Local Court on Friday, the charges relate to two separate incidents 30 minutes apart at the NT Thailand Grand Festival on July 18, including one in which Mr Gosling allegedly elbowed Mr Connolly.

Mr Gosling has strenuously denied the charges, with his lawyer Marty Aust SC telling the court there is no CCTV or independent witnesses.

Politicisation claim followed arrest

After Mr Gosling's arrest on Thursday, Mr Aust claimed there was a "real concern there's a degree of politicisation in relation to how this matter is being handled".

David Connolly is the former president of the NT Cattlemen's Association. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

But speaking on Darwin radio station Mix 104.9 this morning, NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole said Mr Aust's claim was "offensive".

"Quite frankly I'm sick of the attacking of the integrity of members of our police force," he said.

" The only people that are politicising this are certain members of the media and the defence who decided to use this as a strategy. "

NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro has said her office had no involvement in Mr Gosling's arrest and that "conspiracy theories" about politicisation were "completely untrue".

Lia Finocchiaro says the matter has not been politicised. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Contact timeline in question

Mr Gosling has said he was first contacted by police via a phone message last Wednesday afternoon while he was working in Queensland, before he was arrested on Thursday morning.

He also said his office had been "working to establish a meeting" with police.

Luke Gosling banned from approaching NT Government House Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been banned from approaching Government House in Darwin after facing court for the first time since being charged with assaulting NT Administrator David Connolly.

Last week, an NT Police spokesperson said officers had made "multiple attempts via phone and/or email to contact Mr Gosling in the days before his arrest".

Commissioner Dole today reaffirmed the NT Police Force's position that they had attempted to contact Mr Gosling "on multiple occasions".

"I refute the allegation that we didn't make attempts to contact him until the day before," he said.

Mr Gosling did not respond to questions from the ABC today.

No DPP advice before arrest

The NT Director of Public Prosecutions (NT DPP) yesterday confirmed Mr Gosling's matter had been referred to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions "to avoid any perceived conflict of interest".

"Immediately upon receiving the brief, the NT DPP determined that it should not have conduct of the matter and that the matter should be referred to another jurisdiction to avoid any perceived conflict of interest," a spokesperson said.

Mr Gosling is set to appear in court again on September 1. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Today, the NT DPP confirmed it did not provide any advice to police before Mr Gosling was arrested.

Under the NT Criminal Code, police do not need the NT DPP's advice before charging someone with an assault of the administrator.

Gosling 'important source of advice', defence minister says

Mr Gosling has not stood down from his special envoy role, despite calls from the opposition to do so.

Last Sunday, Health Minister Mark Butler said the envoy role was not a ministerial position and therefore Mr Gosling did not need to step down.

"It doesn't have any executive authority, any ability to make decisions that impact Australians," he said.

Asked in Darwin today whether he took advice from Mr Gosling, Defence Minister Richard Marles said the special envoy had been "a really important source of advice" for him.

Richard Marles says Luke Gosling provides advice to him on defence matters. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Special envoys are not ministers. They're not sworn into the executive, but they do play a really important role in the work of the government and Luke, as the special envoy for defence, has played a really important role in this portfolio," he said.

Mr Gosling's matter is due to return to court on September 1.

World.title: ‘I don’t feel safe anywhere’: Nicky Winmar’s victim says assault stays with her
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘I don’t feel safe anywhere’: Nicky Winmar’s victim says assault stays with her Tara Cosoleto August 6, 2026 — 5:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former AFL star Nicky Winmar has already been punished by the “erasure” of his accolades and statue, his lawyer argued, as he pushed for his client to avoid jail time for assault. Winmar, 60, was in July convicted of a May 2025 assault against a woman at Cohuna in northern Victoria. Nicky Winmar, centre, who was found guilty of assault, is pictured here with his lawyer Dermot Dann, left. AAPIMAGE The woman, who cannot be identified, told the court Winmar unexpectedly became angry at her before grabbing and twisting her arm. He then dragged the woman by the hair, pushed her up against a wall and spat in her face before repeatedly bashing her head into a wooden door.



Winmar argued the woman was lying, but Bendigo magistrate Trieu Huynh found him guilty of two counts of common law assault and one charge of unlawful assault. At Winmar’s pre-sentence hearing on Thursday, the woman told the court she no longer felt like the person she once was. “I have days where I feel so worthless and my confidence is non-existent,” she said in a statement. “I don’t feel safe anywhere. I’m always on edge.” Prosecutor Annina Tropea argued the impact on the victim had been profound as she pushed for Winmar to be jailed.



The 60-year-old had multiple opportunities during the attack to walk away and yet he persisted, Tropea said. “He needs to understand there are consequences for his decision-making,” the prosecutor said. But Winmar’s barrister Dermot Dann, KC, argued a jail term was the last resort and a community corrections order was the more appropriate sentence. Dann submitted Winmar had already suffered additional punishment since his conviction, with his statue being removed from Optus Stadium in Perth. Winmar was also stripped of his spot in the AFL Hall of Fame, Dann said.



“No one was waiting to see if he wanted to appeal – they just removed it,” he told the court. Dann conceded there had been some low points in Winmar’s life and the assault in Cohuna was one of those times. But the 60-year-old had taken steps to address his mental health struggles and issues with alcohol, Dann said. Winmar had abstained from alcohol for the past 12 months and was still seeing a psychologist to deal with his post-traumatic stress disorder and depression, the barrister said. Dann referenced the day in 1993 when Winmar stood in front of an abusive Collingwood crowd, lifted his jumper and pointed to his skin.



Moments before and after St Kilda footballer Nicky Winmar raises his jumper in response to racial taunts from Collingwood fans at Victoria Park on Saturday 17 April 1993. Wayne Ludbey “They can erase his statue,” Dann said. “What they will never be able to erase from the hearts and minds of the people who care about racism ... is the memory of his great stand that day at Victoria Park. They will never erase that.” The magistrate said he would need time to consider whether he should jail Winmar or sentence him to a community corrections order. He ordered Winmar undergo a corrections assessment ahead of his sentence hearing on August 28. Winmar, whose bail was extended, ignored questions from reporters as he left the Bendigo court.



Winmar kicked 317 goals across 251 games with St Kilda and the Western Bulldogs, and was named in the All-Australian team in 1991 and 1995. He was the first Indigenous footballer to play 200 VFL/AFL games. AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mental health is Bondi Junction’s inadequately addressed aftermath
World.content:
August 6, 2026 — 5:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mental healthcare over the world is characterised by deficiencies and weaknesses, but the Minns government has shortsightedly baulked at addressing systemic problems identified as leading to the Bondi Junction killings. A homeless Queenslander with a history of mental illness, Joel Cauchi, 40, was shot dead by NSW Police after he began his rampage in the Bondi Junction Westfield shopping centre and stabbed 16 people on April 13, 2024. Six of them died. A mourner pays tribute outside Westfield Bondi Junction after the stabbings. Dion Georgopoulos A coronial inquest determined that Cauchi, who suffered schizophrenia, was psychotic that day. The coroner recommended the government house and care for the mentally unwell, referred the killer’s psychiatrist to the watchdog over treatment “failures”, and recommended bravery awards for the heroism displayed by police, victims and witnesses to the tragedy.



The NSW government on Wednesday announced it would accept 11 of the coroner’s 13 recommendations in full. These included a new health-led response model for mental health emergencies backed by more than $270 million over 10 years, reforms to knife scanning laws after the statutory review of NSW’s wanding powers and improving emergency service communications, training and major incident response arrangements. However, the government will give only in principle support two of the recommendations, including one that proposed modelling demand for short-term accommodation services in greater Sydney to support those suffering mental health episodes and homelessness, and supporting the establishment and evaluation of long-term accommodation based on existing models. Even the government admits it not enough. Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said the government was funding accommodation initiatives but acknowledged more was required to address demand for mental health services. “I think we’re probably going to need to go beyond that. But I think it’s a really important first step,” she said.



Mental Health Co-ordinating Council chief executive Dr Evelyne Tadros said the Minns government was “all talk and no action”: four-fifths of people requiring psycho-social support in NSW were not receiving it. She described the government’s reluctance to deliver short- and long-term accommodation as “not putting your money where your mouth is”, saying investment in early intervention mental health care was essential to avoiding future crises. Tadros said some 45,900 people, one third of the total using Specialist Homelessness Services around Australia, have a current mental health issue. Meanwhile, NSW mental health emergency department presentations were up 44 per cent and too many people were already missing out on care beyond crisis, which was evident in Cauchi’s case. No one wants to stigmatise those living with mental health problems. But there is no escaping the higher risk that comes with a parlous state of mental health services, lack of support and misplaced priorities. The link between homelessness and mental health has been an ongoing and worsening issue, yet a crisis seems to be the only time it is openly discussed. The Bondi Junction tragedy was a warning. How many more will take place before government moves to make mental health services fit for purpose?
