World.title: Adam Liaw’s caramel banana tiramisu
World.content:
First make a caramel cream. Place the sugar into a small saucepan and cook over medium heat until a dark caramel forms. Add the butter and mix carefully, then add the cream and vanilla and stir until the caramel dissolves. Chill in the fridge for at least 3 hours, then whip to soft peaks.

Step 2

Place a few scoops of the caramel cream in the base of a 20cm-square serving dish. Mix the milk, sugar and rum together, then dip the savoiardi into the milk and lay in the base of the dish. Top with the sliced banana, add another layer of cream, then repeat the layers, finishing with a layer of cream. Cover and refrigerate for 6 hours, then scatter with cocoa powder to serve.

World.title: ClearVue lands Clean Energy Council green light for rooftop solar
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ClearVue lands Clean Energy Council green light for rooftop solar Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 6, 2026 — 5:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Smart building materials company ClearVue Technologies has landed a critical approval for its new rooftop solar product, securing a place on the Clean Energy Council’s (CEC) approved products list for its ClearVue-Helios panels. The listing clears a significant commercial hurdle for the company, as CEC approval is a mandatory requirement for any solar panel to be connected to the grid in Australia and is the key that unlocks access to government renewable energy subsidies. ClearVue Technologies’ Helios rooftop solar glass installation. The move comes just as the Federal Government expands its support for commercial solar installations. The changes lift the cap for up-front incentives from 100-kilowatt systems to much larger 1-megawatt installations, a move expected to significantly slash the acquisition cost for commercial-scale solar projects. timing of the approval looks impeccable, landing The CEC listing acts as a trusted benchmark in the Australian solar market, providing an independent stamp of verification that a product is safe, durable and fit for purpose. For ClearVue, it positions the company to compete in the lucrative Australian rooftop and commercial solar market.



‘Crucially these incentives will lower the acquisition cost of the whole range of ClearVue products for our customers.’ ClearVue Technologies chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt ClearVue-Helios is a unified metal-backed rooftop BIPV solar platform available in an aluminium-backed rooftop panel for lightweight large-span installations and a steel-backed rooftop panel for trafficable high-access roofs. It is designed to deliver up to 220 watts per square metre and up to 600 watts per panel. The company says the product features a fully-sealed mounting system that effectively acts as a second roof for buildings. The panels come with a Class A fire rating, a 30-year performance warranty and a 15-year product warranty. The approval is the latest in a string of successes for ClearVue, which has been steadily accumulating local and global certifications for its suite of building-integrated photovoltaic, or “BIPV” products. The company is best known for its patented, transparent solar energy-generating glass, a technology that can be used in building facades, windows and balustrades to produce power. ClearVue Technologies chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt said: “Achieving CEC listing for ClearVue-Helios is an important milestone for both our customers and our shareholders. It provides further independent verification that the product meets the quality and safety standards expected by the Australian market. We believe this strengthens the commercial opportunity for ClearVue-Helios and gives customers greater confidence when specifying our products.”



Now, with a traditional rooftop product also in its arsenal, ClearVue appears to be mounting a two-pronged assault on the building energy market. The company’s latest quarterly report for July shows it to be well-funded to continue its commercialisation strategy, with $4.6m in cash and cash equivalents on hand to continue its push. While ClearVue’s transparent solar glass has captured the imagination with its futuristic appeal, the addition of a CEC-approved rooftop panel gives the company a foothold in the massive and mature rooftop solar market. Importantly and particularly in sun-drenched Australia, ClearVue’s Helios panels can also be incorporated into carport rooftops, resulting in a lightweight, lower cost and embedded solar solution that delivers up to 605 Watts peak power per panel in a modern carpark design. According to the designs can also add functional beautification and safety benefits, such as night-lighting. The BIPV market is gaining serious traction globally as developers and building owners look for innovative ways to meet tightening energy efficiency standards and reduce operational costs. By turning passive building surfaces into active power generators, technologies like ClearVue’s are changing the very definition of building materials.



With this latest certification in the bag, ClearVue has not only validated its engineering prowess once again but has also opened a significant new commercial front in its home market, just as government tailwinds begin to blow a little stronger. World.title: Cats sponsor hit with more than 300 charges over alleged $10 million fraud
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaInsolvency Cats sponsor hit with more than 300 charges over alleged $10 million fraud Cameron Houston August 6, 2026 — 5:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Geelong Football Club sponsor Sy Giang Nguyen has been hit with more than 300 charges by police over an alleged multimillion-dollar fraud. Victoria Police said on Thursday the 59-year-old had been charged with 309 counts of obtaining financial advantage by deception over a five-year period by targeting the Geelong-based disability service provider, genU, to obtain more than $10 million. Sy Giang Nguyen. Police said their long-running investigation began in February 2023 after they “identified suspicious activity relating to accounts being wrongfully charged to the organisation”.



The former information technology manager once rubbed shoulders with some of the nation’s most prominent sporting and corporate figures, and set a Guinness World Record for drinking the world’s most expensive cocktail. The 59-year-old was once a generous benefactor of the Cats and a friend to some of Geelong’s greatest players. He had access to a private villa at Crown Casino for almost 20 years, and ingratiated himself with some of the nation’s most prominent corporate figures. Former Geelong Cats sponsor Sy Giang Nguyen. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac In Melbourne, his home base at Crown included sprawling living areas replete with a baby grand piano and a stripper’s pole, a 12-person dining table, private bar and on-call butler. Nguyen’s towels and robe were all embossed with his initials. In 2015, Nguyen consumed a $12,500 drink known as “The Winston” – made with 1858-vintage Croizet Cuvee Leonie cognac – at Crown’s former venue, Club 23.



Despite his gilded lifestyle, Nguyen was paid an average salary for his role as an IT manager at genU – one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit providers for the National Disability Insurance Scheme. He was previously employed in a similar role with the St Laurence Community Services, since the 1990s. In 2022, Nguyen was dismissed by genU. In a statement released on Thursday afternoon, genU chief executive Dr Chelsea Tobin said for someone to allegedly target a not-for-profit organisation that provides support to vulnerable members of the community was deeply disappointing. Nguyen and his lawyer, Roger Vrachnas, of Gigliotti Lawyers, declined to comment. He will appear before the Geelong Magistrates’ Court on August 25 in relation to the 309 criminal charges. World.title: Labuschagne got ahead of himself during the Ashes. Now the selectors are breathing down his neck
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Labuschagne got ahead of himself during the Ashes. Now the selectors are breathing down his neck Daniel Brettig August 6, 2026 — 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Marnus Labuschagne admits he got ahead of himself at times during last summer’s Ashes series, as he embarks upon Australia’s 12-month Test match pilgrimage with the national selectors breathing down his neck. One of the trickiest problems for Australia right now is that the two most vulnerable members of the top six on performance are arguably the two youngest players, in Labuschagne and all-rounder Cameron Green. Marnus Labuschagne wasted numerous strong starts during the Ashes. Getty Images Earlier this year, Labuschagne signed a Cricket Australia contract extension until 2029, underlining how highly he is considered within the Australian set-up, but without consistent runs from No.3, neither he nor Pat Cummins’ team are going to get very far. Last summer, after being dropped in the Caribbean, Labuschagne started the domestic season with a glut of runs in the Sheffield Shield and looked fluent at the crease against England. But he got sucked into some intemperate dismissals, twice at the hands of Ben Stokes, to finish the series without a genuinely big score.



“[It was] a little bit of lack of confidence in trusting the process, then you try to rush the process and you make errors,” Labuschagne said in Brisbane on Thursday. “There were a few dismissals last summer [against Stokes] where you’re going well, and you just rush the process. Loading “You want to get to that three-figure score, you want to get that score rather than staying in the moment. I’ve reflected a lot in the last two months on playing at my best, and it’s just letting the game come to me and being able to read what’s happening and trusting your game and technique and process, and the runs take care of itself. “It’s really important for me, we want the runs, but we want the process, and that’s what I’m looking for. The runs will come as the journey goes on, if I keep trusting my game.” Perpetually caffeinated, Labuschagne has taken time out from the game to spend more of this winter being a father, rather than poring endlessly over footage and trying to reimagine his game. He conceded that the search for batting improvements can have a mental toll, even for someone as energetic as he is.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Pretty annoying’: Inside Josh Hazlewood’s fight to keep his Test career alive “It’s hard to find long-term solutions in such a short time frame when you’ve only got three weeks between tours and things like that,” Labuschagne said. “Being on the road for so long, trying to find your feet, [you can have] a lack of confidence. When you’ve missed out a few times, you get a little greedy and start searching for runs instead of letting the game come to you. “Also, over a four or five-year period, some of those technical things just keep growing and growing. You keep trying to find short-term solutions because you know it’s not perfect, and you’re striving for perfection. “You do that over a four or five-year period and it drains you. So it’s been really nice to be in a real comfortable space with how I’m batting and how my game’s working, and now it’s just about trusting.” Ben Stokes celebrates Labuschagne’s wicket in Brisbane last summer. Getty Images



In the years before he broke through at Test level, Labuschagne was identified by state teammates as a highly talented player who was often his own worst enemy, simply by striving for too much rather than trusting in his ability to bat time. Editor's pick Australian cricket Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home “It’s about scoring runs in my areas of strength and dominating those areas like I did in 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022,” he said. “The areas where I scored predominantly were that leg-side pull shot and then getting into the ball on the off side. “They’re the key things for me when I’m playing well, scoring runs and looking to put pressure on the opposition when they miss and come into those areas. When you’re on the road playing for probably the last seven or eight years straight, this is the longest break I’ve had. “There have been times where I’ve tried to get things in order, but I just run out of time to fully commit to those small changes.”



Having never played a Test against Bangladesh, nor in Darwin, Labuschagne is trying to stay light on his feet, the better to react to the opposition and conditions. The second Test in Mackay will be a little more familiar – he made his first junior hundred there at under-14s level. Beyond this series are big-time battles with South Africa, New Zealand, India and England, adding up to as many as 21 Tests in 12 months. “It’s vitally important for us that we start really well, and take that little bit of rhythm into each series as we go,” Labuschagne said. “But making sure our focus is solely on the next series we’re playing.” Australia v Bangladesh Test series First Test: From August 13-17 at TIO Stadium in Darwin

Second Test: From August 22-26 at Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Judge lifts suppression order in Alan Jones trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former athlete who has alleged that Alan Jones sloppily kissed and groped him has denied having a financial motive for making the claims, or of inventing his story after learning that Jones had been arrested. A non-publication order preventing the public from hearing evidence from the complainant known as “J” was lifted on Thursday afternoon after two days of cross-examination by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. The cross-examination of complainant “J”, a former teen athlete who accused Alan Jones of indecent assault, can now be reported. Audrey Richardson Bashir’s questioning, sometimes terse, accused “J” of concocting claims Jones had kissed him at his properties.



Jones is standing trial in the Local Court on 22 counts of indecent assault, nine of which relate to “J”, and two counts of sexual touching without consent. He strenuously denies the allegations. Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones fusses and frowns as secrecy shrouds blockbuster trial The court heard Alan Jones paid “J”, a young athlete, hundreds of dollars a week to help with his athletic career from his late teens, in the early 2000s, to his late 20s. On Tuesday, “J” gave evidence that the payments stopped when he was not competing any more. Bashir suggested to “J” on Wednesday that the payments stopped once he was financially stable and no longer on “struggle street”. She put to him that at the time of his police report he was under financial pressure amid employment difficulties.



Asked by Bashir if he understood he could sue Jones on the basis of his claims, “J” said he believed the deadline for civil action had passed. When Bashir suggested he “saw [Jones’] arrest as an opportunity to get the money going again”, “J” replied: “I can’t control what you suggest or what you think, but it’s not true. “I don’t want anything but proper justice for this matter,” he said. Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Court on Thursday. Audrey Richardson The court heard “J”, after his athletics career came to an end, went on to become a police officer.



The court heard allegations he had issues with gambling. But “J” denied this, and the prosecution applied for a provisional non-publication order over his evidence that Judge Glenn Walsh lifted on Thursday after hearing that the matters would not arise again. Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial ‘I just want justice’: Complainant’s emotional testimony in Alan Jones trial Jones’ legal team had alleged “J” had agitated the claims against the wealthy broadcaster because he needed the money. “J” repeated the denial, that money was his motive, on Thursday. “I’ve been over this and no,” he said. “I wish there was something we could do to establish this and say [I] can not take money from the defendant, I won’t seek that, I am happy to sign a document or affirm it now.



“I don’t want to sue him, I don’t want his money.” The court on Thursday watched as “J” repeatedly closed his eyes and “put himself back there” into his memories in Jones’ home. In one flashback, “J” recalled driving Jones to his Fitzroy Falls property in 2004. Jones awoke as they went around a bend, and “J” recited line-by-line the conversation he claims to remember. Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir at an earlier court appearance for Jones. Clare Sibthorpe Then, he said, Jones put his hand on his thigh, and later down his pants and squeezed “J”’s penis “the hardest it’s ever been squeezed”.



Jones’ barrister asked what he did in response. “You were physically superior to Alan Jones?” Bashir asked “J”. “Not necessarily,” the man said, before agreeing he was “physically superior” to Jones. Bashir said “J” had concocted the story. “You were driving the car, with the brake under your foot, you had the key, you managed to slow the car down when you saw workmen on the car,” she said.



Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones used to talk for a living. He sat silently as a young man detailed his alleged crimes “Your account of what occurred in the car is not true.” “Yes it is,” the man replied. During hours of cross-examination, Bashir put to “J” that Jones had never said he would increase his weekly payments because “J” had been a “good boy”, and the payments in fact correlated with his sporting costs. She suggested “J” was “recasting these payments as something sinister”. The man disagreed. However, he acknowledged later in the questioning that his initial 2024 police statement contained some incorrect dates, and he had not received a mobile phone or a car from Jones until he had left school.



“You were trying to paint a picture of Alan Jones giving you a phone and car when you were a schoolboy, weren’t you?” Bashir asked. The man denied this. He rejected that he was “trying to fit a schoolboy narrative of sexual touching”. Earlier in the week, “J” testified that he first met Jones when he was 14 or 15 after the broadcaster interviewed him about his sporting achievements. He had said that Jones gave him a mobile phone shortly after this meeting. Sometime when he was in year 12, he told the court, Jones gave him a car. The trial continues.

World.title: ‘I don’t feel safe anywhere’: Nicky Winmar’s victim says assault stays with her
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘I don’t feel safe anywhere’: Nicky Winmar’s victim says assault stays with her Tara Cosoleto August 6, 2026 — 5:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former AFL star Nicky Winmar has already been punished by the “erasure” of his accolades and statue, his lawyer argued, as he pushed for his client to avoid jail time for assault. Winmar, 60, was in July convicted of a May 2025 assault against a woman at Cohuna in northern Victoria. Nicky Winmar, centre, who was found guilty of assault, is pictured here with his lawyer Dermot Dann, left. AAPIMAGE The woman, who cannot be identified, told the court Winmar unexpectedly became angry at her before grabbing and twisting her arm. He then dragged the woman by the hair, pushed her up against a wall and spat in her face before repeatedly bashing her head into a wooden door.



Winmar argued the woman was lying, but Bendigo magistrate Trieu Huynh found him guilty of two counts of common law assault and one charge of unlawful assault. At Winmar’s pre-sentence hearing on Thursday, the woman told the court she no longer felt like the person she once was. “I have days where I feel so worthless and my confidence is non-existent,” she said in a statement. “I don’t feel safe anywhere. I’m always on edge.” Prosecutor Annina Tropea argued the impact on the victim had been profound as she pushed for Winmar to be jailed.



The 60-year-old had multiple opportunities during the attack to walk away and yet he persisted, Tropea said. “He needs to understand there are consequences for his decision-making,” the prosecutor said. But Winmar’s barrister Dermot Dann, KC, argued a jail term was the last resort and a community corrections order was the more appropriate sentence. Dann submitted Winmar had already suffered additional punishment since his conviction, with his statue being removed from Optus Stadium in Perth. Winmar was also stripped of his spot in the AFL Hall of Fame, Dann said.



“No one was waiting to see if he wanted to appeal – they just removed it,” he told the court. Dann conceded there had been some low points in Winmar’s life and the assault in Cohuna was one of those times. But the 60-year-old had taken steps to address his mental health struggles and issues with alcohol, Dann said. Winmar had abstained from alcohol for the past 12 months and was still seeing a psychologist to deal with his post-traumatic stress disorder and depression, the barrister said. Dann referenced the day in 1993 when Winmar stood in front of an abusive Collingwood crowd, lifted his jumper and pointed to his skin.



Moments before and after St Kilda footballer Nicky Winmar raises his jumper in response to racial taunts from Collingwood fans at Victoria Park on Saturday 17 April 1993. Wayne Ludbey “They can erase his statue,” Dann said. “What they will never be able to erase from the hearts and minds of the people who care about racism ... is the memory of his great stand that day at Victoria Park. They will never erase that.” The magistrate said he would need time to consider whether he should jail Winmar or sentence him to a community corrections order. He ordered Winmar undergo a corrections assessment ahead of his sentence hearing on August 28. Winmar, whose bail was extended, ignored questions from reporters as he left the Bendigo court.



Winmar kicked 317 goals across 251 games with St Kilda and the Western Bulldogs, and was named in the All-Australian team in 1991 and 1995. He was the first Indigenous footballer to play 200 VFL/AFL games. AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ClearVue lands Clean Energy Council green light for rooftop solar
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ClearVue lands Clean Energy Council green light for rooftop solar Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 6, 2026 — 5:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Smart building materials company ClearVue Technologies has landed a critical approval for its new rooftop solar product, securing a place on the Clean Energy Council’s (CEC) approved products list for its ClearVue-Helios panels. The listing clears a significant commercial hurdle for the company, as CEC approval is a mandatory requirement for any solar panel to be connected to the grid in Australia and is the key that unlocks access to government renewable energy subsidies. ClearVue Technologies’ Helios rooftop solar glass installation. The move comes just as the Federal Government expands its support for commercial solar installations. The changes lift the cap for up-front incentives from 100-kilowatt systems to much larger 1-megawatt installations, a move expected to significantly slash the acquisition cost for commercial-scale solar projects. timing of the approval looks impeccable, landing The CEC listing acts as a trusted benchmark in the Australian solar market, providing an independent stamp of verification that a product is safe, durable and fit for purpose. For ClearVue, it positions the company to compete in the lucrative Australian rooftop and commercial solar market.



‘Crucially these incentives will lower the acquisition cost of the whole range of ClearVue products for our customers.’ ClearVue Technologies chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt ClearVue-Helios is a unified metal-backed rooftop BIPV solar platform available in an aluminium-backed rooftop panel for lightweight large-span installations and a steel-backed rooftop panel for trafficable high-access roofs. It is designed to deliver up to 220 watts per square metre and up to 600 watts per panel. The company says the product features a fully-sealed mounting system that effectively acts as a second roof for buildings. The panels come with a Class A fire rating, a 30-year performance warranty and a 15-year product warranty. The approval is the latest in a string of successes for ClearVue, which has been steadily accumulating local and global certifications for its suite of building-integrated photovoltaic, or “BIPV” products. The company is best known for its patented, transparent solar energy-generating glass, a technology that can be used in building facades, windows and balustrades to produce power. ClearVue Technologies chief executive officer and managing director Doug Hunt said: “Achieving CEC listing for ClearVue-Helios is an important milestone for both our customers and our shareholders. It provides further independent verification that the product meets the quality and safety standards expected by the Australian market. We believe this strengthens the commercial opportunity for ClearVue-Helios and gives customers greater confidence when specifying our products.”



Now, with a traditional rooftop product also in its arsenal, ClearVue appears to be mounting a two-pronged assault on the building energy market. The company’s latest quarterly report for July shows it to be well-funded to continue its commercialisation strategy, with $4.6m in cash and cash equivalents on hand to continue its push. While ClearVue’s transparent solar glass has captured the imagination with its futuristic appeal, the addition of a CEC-approved rooftop panel gives the company a foothold in the massive and mature rooftop solar market. Importantly and particularly in sun-drenched Australia, ClearVue’s Helios panels can also be incorporated into carport rooftops, resulting in a lightweight, lower cost and embedded solar solution that delivers up to 605 Watts peak power per panel in a modern carpark design. According to the designs can also add functional beautification and safety benefits, such as night-lighting. The BIPV market is gaining serious traction globally as developers and building owners look for innovative ways to meet tightening energy efficiency standards and reduce operational costs. By turning passive building surfaces into active power generators, technologies like ClearVue’s are changing the very definition of building materials.



With this latest certification in the bag, ClearVue has not only validated its engineering prowess once again but has also opened a significant new commercial front in its home market, just as government tailwinds begin to blow a little stronger. World.title: Cats sponsor hit with more than 300 charges over alleged $10 million fraud
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaInsolvency Cats sponsor hit with more than 300 charges over alleged $10 million fraud Cameron Houston August 6, 2026 — 5:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Geelong Football Club sponsor Sy Giang Nguyen has been hit with more than 300 charges by police over an alleged multimillion-dollar fraud. Victoria Police said on Thursday the 59-year-old had been charged with 309 counts of obtaining financial advantage by deception over a five-year period by targeting the Geelong-based disability service provider, genU, to obtain more than $10 million. Sy Giang Nguyen. Police said their long-running investigation began in February 2023 after they “identified suspicious activity relating to accounts being wrongfully charged to the organisation”.



The former information technology manager once rubbed shoulders with some of the nation’s most prominent sporting and corporate figures, and set a Guinness World Record for drinking the world’s most expensive cocktail. The 59-year-old was once a generous benefactor of the Cats and a friend to some of Geelong’s greatest players. He had access to a private villa at Crown Casino for almost 20 years, and ingratiated himself with some of the nation’s most prominent corporate figures. Former Geelong Cats sponsor Sy Giang Nguyen. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac In Melbourne, his home base at Crown included sprawling living areas replete with a baby grand piano and a stripper’s pole, a 12-person dining table, private bar and on-call butler. Nguyen’s towels and robe were all embossed with his initials. In 2015, Nguyen consumed a $12,500 drink known as “The Winston” – made with 1858-vintage Croizet Cuvee Leonie cognac – at Crown’s former venue, Club 23.



Despite his gilded lifestyle, Nguyen was paid an average salary for his role as an IT manager at genU – one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit providers for the National Disability Insurance Scheme. He was previously employed in a similar role with the St Laurence Community Services, since the 1990s. In 2022, Nguyen was dismissed by genU. In a statement released on Thursday afternoon, genU chief executive Dr Chelsea Tobin said for someone to allegedly target a not-for-profit organisation that provides support to vulnerable members of the community was deeply disappointing. Nguyen and his lawyer, Roger Vrachnas, of Gigliotti Lawyers, declined to comment. He will appear before the Geelong Magistrates’ Court on August 25 in relation to the 309 criminal charges. World.title: Labuschagne got ahead of himself during the Ashes. Now the selectors are breathing down his neck
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Labuschagne got ahead of himself during the Ashes. Now the selectors are breathing down his neck Daniel Brettig August 6, 2026 — 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Marnus Labuschagne admits he got ahead of himself at times during last summer’s Ashes series, as he embarks upon Australia’s 12-month Test match pilgrimage with the national selectors breathing down his neck. One of the trickiest problems for Australia right now is that the two most vulnerable members of the top six on performance are arguably the two youngest players, in Labuschagne and all-rounder Cameron Green. Marnus Labuschagne wasted numerous strong starts during the Ashes. Getty Images Earlier this year, Labuschagne signed a Cricket Australia contract extension until 2029, underlining how highly he is considered within the Australian set-up, but without consistent runs from No.3, neither he nor Pat Cummins’ team are going to get very far. Last summer, after being dropped in the Caribbean, Labuschagne started the domestic season with a glut of runs in the Sheffield Shield and looked fluent at the crease against England. But he got sucked into some intemperate dismissals, twice at the hands of Ben Stokes, to finish the series without a genuinely big score.



“[It was] a little bit of lack of confidence in trusting the process, then you try to rush the process and you make errors,” Labuschagne said in Brisbane on Thursday. “There were a few dismissals last summer [against Stokes] where you’re going well, and you just rush the process. Loading “You want to get to that three-figure score, you want to get that score rather than staying in the moment. I’ve reflected a lot in the last two months on playing at my best, and it’s just letting the game come to me and being able to read what’s happening and trusting your game and technique and process, and the runs take care of itself. “It’s really important for me, we want the runs, but we want the process, and that’s what I’m looking for. The runs will come as the journey goes on, if I keep trusting my game.” Perpetually caffeinated, Labuschagne has taken time out from the game to spend more of this winter being a father, rather than poring endlessly over footage and trying to reimagine his game. He conceded that the search for batting improvements can have a mental toll, even for someone as energetic as he is.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Pretty annoying’: Inside Josh Hazlewood’s fight to keep his Test career alive “It’s hard to find long-term solutions in such a short time frame when you’ve only got three weeks between tours and things like that,” Labuschagne said. “Being on the road for so long, trying to find your feet, [you can have] a lack of confidence. When you’ve missed out a few times, you get a little greedy and start searching for runs instead of letting the game come to you. “Also, over a four or five-year period, some of those technical things just keep growing and growing. You keep trying to find short-term solutions because you know it’s not perfect, and you’re striving for perfection. “You do that over a four or five-year period and it drains you. So it’s been really nice to be in a real comfortable space with how I’m batting and how my game’s working, and now it’s just about trusting.” Ben Stokes celebrates Labuschagne’s wicket in Brisbane last summer. Getty Images



In the years before he broke through at Test level, Labuschagne was identified by state teammates as a highly talented player who was often his own worst enemy, simply by striving for too much rather than trusting in his ability to bat time. Editor's pick Australian cricket Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home “It’s about scoring runs in my areas of strength and dominating those areas like I did in 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022,” he said. “The areas where I scored predominantly were that leg-side pull shot and then getting into the ball on the off side. “They’re the key things for me when I’m playing well, scoring runs and looking to put pressure on the opposition when they miss and come into those areas. When you’re on the road playing for probably the last seven or eight years straight, this is the longest break I’ve had. “There have been times where I’ve tried to get things in order, but I just run out of time to fully commit to those small changes.”



Having never played a Test against Bangladesh, nor in Darwin, Labuschagne is trying to stay light on his feet, the better to react to the opposition and conditions. The second Test in Mackay will be a little more familiar – he made his first junior hundred there at under-14s level. Beyond this series are big-time battles with South Africa, New Zealand, India and England, adding up to as many as 21 Tests in 12 months. “It’s vitally important for us that we start really well, and take that little bit of rhythm into each series as we go,” Labuschagne said. “But making sure our focus is solely on the next series we’re playing.” Australia v Bangladesh Test series First Test: From August 13-17 at TIO Stadium in Darwin

Second Test: From August 22-26 at Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Judge lifts suppression order in Alan Jones trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former athlete who has alleged that Alan Jones sloppily kissed and groped him has denied having a financial motive for making the claims, or of inventing his story after learning that Jones had been arrested. A non-publication order preventing the public from hearing evidence from the complainant known as “J” was lifted on Thursday afternoon after two days of cross-examination by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. The cross-examination of complainant “J”, a former teen athlete who accused Alan Jones of indecent assault, can now be reported. Audrey Richardson Bashir’s questioning, sometimes terse, accused “J” of concocting claims Jones had kissed him at his properties.



Jones is standing trial in the Local Court on 22 counts of indecent assault, nine of which relate to “J”, and two counts of sexual touching without consent. He strenuously denies the allegations. Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones fusses and frowns as secrecy shrouds blockbuster trial The court heard Alan Jones paid “J”, a young athlete, hundreds of dollars a week to help with his athletic career from his late teens, in the early 2000s, to his late 20s. On Tuesday, “J” gave evidence that the payments stopped when he was not competing any more. Bashir suggested to “J” on Wednesday that the payments stopped once he was financially stable and no longer on “struggle street”. She put to him that at the time of his police report he was under financial pressure amid employment difficulties.



Asked by Bashir if he understood he could sue Jones on the basis of his claims, “J” said he believed the deadline for civil action had passed. When Bashir suggested he “saw [Jones’] arrest as an opportunity to get the money going again”, “J” replied: “I can’t control what you suggest or what you think, but it’s not true. “I don’t want anything but proper justice for this matter,” he said. Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Court on Thursday. Audrey Richardson The court heard “J”, after his athletics career came to an end, went on to become a police officer.



The court heard allegations he had issues with gambling. But “J” denied this, and the prosecution applied for a provisional non-publication order over his evidence that Judge Glenn Walsh lifted on Thursday after hearing that the matters would not arise again. Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial ‘I just want justice’: Complainant’s emotional testimony in Alan Jones trial Jones’ legal team had alleged “J” had agitated the claims against the wealthy broadcaster because he needed the money. “J” repeated the denial, that money was his motive, on Thursday. “I’ve been over this and no,” he said. “I wish there was something we could do to establish this and say [I] can not take money from the defendant, I won’t seek that, I am happy to sign a document or affirm it now.



“I don’t want to sue him, I don’t want his money.” The court on Thursday watched as “J” repeatedly closed his eyes and “put himself back there” into his memories in Jones’ home. In one flashback, “J” recalled driving Jones to his Fitzroy Falls property in 2004. Jones awoke as they went around a bend, and “J” recited line-by-line the conversation he claims to remember. Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir at an earlier court appearance for Jones. Clare Sibthorpe Then, he said, Jones put his hand on his thigh, and later down his pants and squeezed “J”’s penis “the hardest it’s ever been squeezed”.



Jones’ barrister asked what he did in response. “You were physically superior to Alan Jones?” Bashir asked “J”. “Not necessarily,” the man said, before agreeing he was “physically superior” to Jones. Bashir said “J” had concocted the story. “You were driving the car, with the brake under your foot, you had the key, you managed to slow the car down when you saw workmen on the car,” she said.



Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones used to talk for a living. He sat silently as a young man detailed his alleged crimes “Your account of what occurred in the car is not true.” “Yes it is,” the man replied. During hours of cross-examination, Bashir put to “J” that Jones had never said he would increase his weekly payments because “J” had been a “good boy”, and the payments in fact correlated with his sporting costs. She suggested “J” was “recasting these payments as something sinister”. The man disagreed. However, he acknowledged later in the questioning that his initial 2024 police statement contained some incorrect dates, and he had not received a mobile phone or a car from Jones until he had left school.



“You were trying to paint a picture of Alan Jones giving you a phone and car when you were a schoolboy, weren’t you?” Bashir asked. The man denied this. He rejected that he was “trying to fit a schoolboy narrative of sexual touching”. Earlier in the week, “J” testified that he first met Jones when he was 14 or 15 after the broadcaster interviewed him about his sporting achievements. He had said that Jones gave him a mobile phone shortly after this meeting. Sometime when he was in year 12, he told the court, Jones gave him a car. The trial continues.

World.title: Jon Adgemis seeks to block probe into $1.8 billion bankruptcy
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesPubs Jon Adgemis seeks to block probe into $1.8 billion bankruptcy Kishor Napier-Raman August 6, 2026 — 5:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Failed pub baron Jon Adgemis has made a last-ditch bid to dodge a public examination into the $1.8 billion collapse of his hospitality empire. Lawyers for the former KPMG partner argued that a seven-day examination into Adgemis’ financial affairs, which kicked off in the Federal Court on Thursday, would amount to an abuse of process. They also sought to block public access to the hearings. Jon Adgemis arriving at court in Sydney on Thursday. Dominic Lorrimer Federal Court registrar Susan O’Connor referred the matter to be heard by a duty judge on Friday morning, further delaying the prospects of getting answers about how Adgemis’ businesses unravelled. “What you’re asking for is exceptional,” she said.





Thursday’s hearings would have given both Adgemis’ liquidators and his bankruptcy trustee, Andrew Yeo of Pitcher Partners, an opportunity to pick through the wreckage of Adgemis’ business and personally question him about his financial affairs. Ahead of the examination, the Federal Court published orders requiring a lengthy list of former associates, lenders and ex-girlfriend model Cheyenne Tozzi to produce documents in the hearings. Also named in the order are billionaire Alex Waislitz, Adgemis’ former chief financial officer and Woollahra councillor Alexander Andruska, prominent racehorse owner and MaxCap founder Brae Sokolski, music pioneer Tom Misner, and Adgemis’ former business partner Ben Madsen. But on Wednesday night, a Federal Court registrar made an order that a summons to appear in the action brought by the bankruptcy trustee “be adjourned to a date to be fixed”. While the liquidators’ examination was slated to begin on Thursday, that process was also frustrated. Dressed in a tailored navy suit and wearing tinted sunglasses indoors, Adgemis spent just minutes on the stand and did not face a single question, before his lawyers requested a lengthy adjournment.



When the matter resumed, his legal team, led by Miles Condon SC, requested that the hearings be held in secret – a move which was tentatively supported by lawyers representing liquidators – with ERA Legal director Blake O’Neill telling the court that his client wanted “to get on with things”. Later, Condon told the court that Adgemis’ team contended that the entire examination constituted an abuse of process. They are also seeking to stop ERA Legal from acting for the liquidators. The abuse of process application will be heard by a Federal Court judge on Friday morning. If that fails, Adgemis’ team will seek to have the examination held in secret. Lawyers representing media outlets including this masthead are set to oppose that application. The Tax Practitioners’ Board is also opposing attempts to keep the examination secret. The court adjourned the examination proceedings until next week. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Peter Dunne believes Luxon's frustration with NZ First, ACT behind MMP referendum call
World.content:
Former United Future leader Peter Dunne does not believe there is enough public appetite for a referendum on MMP, saying it is likely the prime minister's call was down to his frustrations with his current partners rather than a genuine desire to change the electoral system.

Christopher Luxon announced on Newstalk ZB that if re-elected, he would look at a referendum on MMP.

The idea caught both of his coalition colleagues off-guard.

Luxon's caucus colleagues have defended his call, saying the prime minister was reflecting conversations he had had with constituents.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters has poured scorn on the idea, saying nobody had raised the issue with him during his extensive travels around the country.

Dunne, who served as a minister under both Labour and National governments in his 33-year Parliamentary career, told Checkpoint there was always a "measure of frustration" with the electoral system, because people saw it as not giving them the result they wanted.

Former minister Peter Dunne weighs in on MMP referendum Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

But he did not think there was any more frustration now than there was usually.

"I worked with people I didn't always agree with, but part and parcel of the MMP system was finding the compromises necessary to make things work, and not just sort of throwing your arms up in horror when you can't get your own way,

In 2011, a referendum saw 57.8 percent of people vote to keep the MMP system. Following the referendum, a review into the system was carried out by the Electoral Commission.

Dunne said some of the recommendations from that review had still not been implemented, and so another referendum was premature.

"I don't really think there's a need at this point. I don't think sufficient deficiencies have been identified to require one. Having said that, we should never assume the electoral system is set in stone. We should always be prepared to review it."

Winston Peters has dismissed Luxon's idea. RNZ

Dunne said Luxon had not made it clear whether he wanted a referendum on getting rid of MMP, or if he had an alternative in mind.

He believed it was more down to Luxon's own frustration with New Zealand First and ACT.

"I don't think he imagined three years ago that he would be run rings around by his two coalition partners the way he has been so often, and he's in a tough international situation, which perhaps wasn't foreseeable at the time as well, so I think it's a measure of that frustration, rather than a deep sense that the ecosystem has caused all of this."

World.title: Nelson businesses offered rates deferral amid ongoing city centre roadworks
World.content:
The Nelson City Council has agreed to defer rates for businesses affected by city centre infrastructure works.

The $78 million Bridge to Better project, jointly funded by the council and government, involves the replacement of three waters infrastructure through the city centre. Work began in 2025 and will be complete by 2027.

At a council meeting on Thursday, elected members agreed to allow affected businesses to defer rates from the current year, with repayments split over the next three years.

It comes after several struggling businesses asked the council for financial help.

RNZ / Samantha Gee

Longstanding cafe and food store Prego Mediterranean Foods & Comida Cafe shut its doors in June, and the owners said the roadworks were one of the factors in its closure.

Co-owner Claudia Kern previously told RNZ that roadwork adjacent to Bridge Street meant there was a six-foot fence across the cafe entrance for several months in the lead up to last Christmas and she estimates they lost around $50,000 in revenue during November and December.

Mayor Nick Smith said the proposal to defer rates came after he and the deputy mayor met with a number of "very distressed" business owners who were feeling the pressure of the ongoing roadworks.

He said it was unusual for councils to offer a rates referral or discount during infrastructure works and said it was with "some trepidation" that the council were considering it.

RNZ / Samantha Gee

Staff had gone to "tremendous effort" to try and minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses, he said.

"It is unfortunate the combination of economic downturn, the additional financial pressure from the oil crisis, as well as this work which really does have this group of businesses under pressure and so I do think it is worth council considering it."

Smith acknowledged the work was "incredibly disruptive" but said it was essential to renew and upgrade infrastructure that in some places, was over 100 years old.

The council said it would only consider rates remission if landlords agreed to provide the equivalent financial relief to the tenant.

RNZ / Samantha Gee

Deputy mayor Pete Rainey said it relied on landlords "coming to the party".

Property owners must apply on behalf of an affected tenant, and sign a declaration that the tenant would receive the equivalent financial relief.

Councillor Lisa Austin said she had spoken to a couple of Bridge St landlords about a potential rates deferral and had positive feedback.

RNZ / Samantha Gee

"The tenants are going to have to prove they have had a loss and [the landlords] said that will not be hard to do, most of their tenants are really suffering right now."

Applicants from eligible businesses along Bridge Street between Collingwood and Rutherford Streets must show a reduction in turnover for the quarter ending 30 June 2026 against the same quarter in 2025 to qualify for the deferral.
