World.content:
RNZ is tracking the money flowing to the parties this election year and where it is coming from.

In an update on Thursday, August 6, National’s tally of officially recorded donations had increased by $440,000 since the start of July, taking its total to $1.26m so far this year.

The boost includes the party’s single largest donation of the year of $250,000 from Graeme Hart’s Rank Group.

National remains second behind ACT, which has $1.73m from large, declared donations.

In the same period, ACT recorded another $203,120.91, the Green Party $179,880, Opportunity $176,140, and NZ First $23,000.

The largest donors to those parties in the update were Opportunity board member Alan Wilderland, who gave $176,140 to his party and Stephen West who gave $100,000 to the Greens. Wilderland and West were co-founders of Serato Audio Research.

Here’s where things stand across all parties for declared donations of over $20,000.

When the donations made to the parties in the governing coalition are combined, the spread looks as below.

Who are this election's big donors?

The following donors have given $100,000 or more so far in 2026.

Not all donors are individuals. Companies, trusts and unions also give to political parties. The chart below shows the split between organisational and individual giving over $20,000 for each party.

In the 2023 election, unions gave $335,000 to Labour. National received no donations from unions, but did receive more than $1m from businesses.

Farah Hancock looks into political donations Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Exploring the data in the below chart shows where donors have focused on a single party or donated to more than one party.

Each line represents a donor with wider lines indicating larger amounts.

How the money grew

Donations of $20,000 and more made from the start of the year are captured on the below chart.

If someone makes numerous donations under $20,000, once the cumulative total tops $20,000 it must be declared.

How much bigger could the donation pot grow?

The below chart shows the 2023 annual total of donations over $20,000, compared to the current 2026 total.

Some who donated in 2023 haven't given more than $20,000 so far in 2026 to the same party. The table below identifies who these donors are.

Each row represents a party. A donor may appear more than once if they gave to multiple parties in 2023.

The following donors haven't donated before 2026.

How we analysed the data

All original data comes from the Electoral Commission website. RNZ's analysis normalises names which may appear more than once, but with different treatment. For example a John Smith and J Smith with the same address are updated to both be John Smith. In some instances where people have given individually as well as jointly their names are collated. If Joan Smith had the same address as John Smith and had donated individually, as well as made a joint donation with John Smith, the name is updated to John and / or Joan Smith.

Donation dates are taken from the "date received by party" information. In some cases one donation entry will consist of several donations made over time. The date received is the date on the donation return and should be the date the total donated by the donor tipped over $20,000.

World.title: Primary school students sway Wellington City Council on road safety measures
World.content:
A group of primary school students have achieved something in minutes that many adults have attempted for decades - quick change through council on a contentious issue.

The Year five and six students at Lyall Bay School visited Wellington City Council on Wednesday to deliver their submission on a trial that had made going to and from school safer for them.

A low-traffic area was trialled on Freyberg St, outside the school, making it easier for the children to cross at drop-off and pick-up times.

Schools across the country struggle with dangerous drivers, with a pilot programme launched in Auckland to curb the growing issue, while other schools have had to close roads during peak hours.

Minutes after the students' submission, the council committee voted to make the road-safety changes a permanent fixture.

Lyall Bay principal Melanie Dean told Checkpoint the students were ecstatic to have made a difference.

"[There were] huge grins and fist pumps, they were excited that they'd had some influence."

Dean said she was incredibly proud of the students' submission, which all came from them.

Primary school students prompt quick change from the council Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

The trial first began, after safety concerns were raised by the school around traffic speeds, volumes and the use of local streets as rat runs.

Dean said parts of the road had been blocked off to create a cul-de-sac outside the school, meaning cars could travel one way down the street, before having to turn around.

"Cars can come up from the beach, drop the children at school and turn around, or cars can come from the town area, drop the children, and then turn around and go back out again."

While there hadn't been any accidents before the trial, Dean said the children had noticed the dangers of the busy road.

"Cars were speeding down Freyberg Street, they were using it as a rat run to get from town to the beach," she said. "It was never safe to be out on the footpath.

"After school, people would be gathering around the crossing, waiting to cross the road, but it was very difficult to ever get across the road."

In their submission to the council, the students made it clear to the council why it was so important to keep the crossing, which they said had made them much more confident to cross the street.

Lyall Bay School students support their peers in the Wellington City Council chambers. Supplied

To get all their thoughts across, the children presented to the council in a reporter-and-interviewee style, asking the questions they thought everyone would wonder about why the crossing needed to stay.

Others who weren't so keen on presenting came along to support their peers with handmade signs.

While 36 percent of the submitters strongly opposed or opposed making the changes permanent, Dean said the students understood the reasons why not everyone would be on side.

She said the kids felt they had had a huge impact on the final decision.

"They said that the submission team were all smiling and laughing, and enjoying their submission, so they felt very proud and positive about themselves."

Dean said the students were incredibly excited that they were involved.

"They were surprised that they were allowed to be part of the democratic process at first, but they thought that they brought a lot to the table and that the committee must have liked what they did, because it had gone through.

"It was a really important thing to them and so they should be able to have as much say as possible in something that really does affect them."

World.title: Industry leaders praise nine new secondary school subjects
World.content:
Industry leaders are enthusiastic about nine new secondary school subjects announced on Thursday, but the teachers' union warns the timeline to develop and introduce them is extremely tight.

The government says industry skills boards will develop the subjects for introduction in 2029, when a new qualification replaces the NCEA.

The subjects are:

Next-Gen manufacturing

Applied intelligent systems

Construction and built environment

Energy and infrastructure

Engineering technology

Food and fibre systems

Health services and care

Hospitality, food and beverage

Tourism

Education Minister Erica Stanford launched the subjects with Finance Minister Nicola Willis at Meridian Energy's Mākara windfarm, overlooking Cook Strait.

New proposed subjects may sway number of early leavers Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

She said it was critical that industry helped write the new content.

"They are the people on the ground who know what the skills and knowledge are that they will need for the future," she said. "That is being built into the curriculum, so these young people, when they leave school, will have relevant knowledge and skills to be able to.. walk into either jobs, further training, apprenticeships or through to university."

Stanford said the new subjects would vary less than NCEA subjects, and would better equip teens with skills and knowledge that employers wanted.

She said more industry-led subjects may be added.

Stanford said not all schools would be able to offer all nine subjects, and some might work together or with local trades academies to provide them.

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge was enthusiastic about the new subjects. RNZ/John Gerritsen

"There will, of course, always be some in-school provision as well, and that's why we're working with the likes of the PPTA and the Teaching Council to make sure that we can get those people the pay that they require to be able to teach," she said.

Industry leaders at the launch were enthusiastic and said one of the main effects of the new subjects would be to open students' eyes to potential careers in industries they had never heard of, many of which faced serious workforce shortages in future.

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge said the energy and infrastructure subject would bring entirely new courses to schools.

"This is new," he said. "In my sector - energy and infrastructure - there's nothing at school.

"There's a bit of geology, a bit of physics, but really there's nothing about energy and infrastructure."

Aldridge said the board wanted to see the subject offered in all schools.

He said whether the subject would be taught in schools or in trades academies run by polytechnics or other tertiary providers was yet to be determined.

Some of the new subjects, such as tourism and building, already existed in some form in schools.

Construction and Specialist Trades industry skills board chair David Kelly said letting industry have a hand in what's taught would have several advantages over the current system.

"One is it raises the status of some trades, so that it gives it equal status within the secondary schools," he said. "Secondly, it does give recognised skills across the country, so when students come out of secondary school, they've got something to show that is a nationally accepted standard that they've achieved.

"It will be more comprehensive and more linked-up, so it's connected to potential employment. At the moment, there are some good courses, but they're not consistent right across the country and really depend on the individual school."

Rotorua Girls High School principal Sarah Davis was seconded to the Education Ministry to work on the subjects.

Naenae College students Lydia Campbell, Daytona Falwasser, and Reagan Cronje said the subjects provided good opportunities for future generations, but were not sure they would study them. RNZ/John Gerritsen

She said the involvement of industry would ensure the subjects created real pathways to jobs.

Davis said some teachers already had industry qualifications and might be able to teach the new subjects.

"That's not going to be the case across the board and, in some cases, I'm thinking for my school Rotorua Girls', we might look to Toi Oho Mai, our local polytechnic, to support us with the delivery of those courses it kind of depends," she said.

Teacher union vice-president Kieran Gainsford said the PPTA supported industry-led subjects, but there was a lot to work out before 2029.

Construction and Specialist Trades industry skills board chair David Kelly. RNZ/John Gerritsen

"In some cases, schools are going to need very technical learning spaces or technical equipment," he said. "They're going to need specialist staff often from industry and those people are going to have to be recruited... and then we have to keep them in schools.

"There's a lot of work to happen between now and then, and unless we get the details pretty pronto, that timeline does start to look a little bit unrealistic."

Gainsford said who would teach the subjects was not clear.

"We're desperately keen to know exactly what the government's plan is for the delivery of these subjects, because until we see that, we can't get started on making it work for the kids," he said.

Gainsford said some of the subjects could be offered by schools and already were, but others, like applied intelligence systems, would require more teachers.

World.title: New season New Zealand wool market cools, but still booming for growers
World.content:
A long-awaited recovery in prices for New Zealand wool is easing, as buyers become reluctant to spend top dollar on the clip this new season.

However, a North Island auctioneer believes the mid-winter market might have hit its floor, after a strong lead-up.

Buoyant prices, including premium clips even cracking the $7 a kilogram mark, have been enjoyed by wool growers this year.

Morning rural news Rural News Download MP3 4m

But subdued demand from buyers had calmed prices across most wool types at the last few wool auctions.

Last month's auction at Hawke's Bay's last remaining wool auction house, Kells Wool in Napier, was a "tough day", due to buyer interest and fewer orders affecting prices, the firm said.

But owner Richard Kells said prices firmed at this week's auction on Tuesday, with long wool types attracting the greatest competition.

The average greasy price hit 375 cents versus 488c clean, with the average price per bale reaching $562.87.

This compared to the same time last year when the average greasy price was 285c, 342c clean, with the average bale nabbing $417.72, Kells said.

"We had a big turnout, a full bench of buyers and the bidding was brisk, so they all wanted some wool," he said.

"That's what gives us confidence that we've seen the worst of this correction."

PGG Wrighton South Island wool auctioneer, Dave Burridge with its general manager of wool, Rachel Shearer. RNZ/Monique Steele

Kells said there was some reluctance from Chinese buyers in particular to pay top dollar again, but he expected the bottom had been hit.

"We've gone through a very sharp peak, but we're still ahead of last year," he said.

"The prices at our auction equalled the national sale in Christchurch.

"In fact, the fleece and the occupants were slightly firmer. So we think the bottom of the slide has been reached and we can look forward to some improvement in the coming months."

Prices for second shear, crossbred fleeces and oddments were particularly hit at PGG Wrightson's last national auction in Christchurch last week.

Here, 95c fell off the strong wool indicator and only 69 percent of the offering sold.

Its national auction manager, Dave Burridge, said although the market had eased considerably, the fundamentals of reduced wool supply into the next few months remained unchanged.

"Exporters have struggled to secure new sales following the elevated buying levels seen at the end of the season in June, while many overseas buyers are waiting for prices to stabilise before re-entering the market," he said in PGG's latest wool market report.

Kells said this week's wool supply was "more of a dribble" than a flow, disrupted by cold and wet weather and time of year on farm.

He said ewe wool was effectively finished, and with lambing beginning for some, it was now down to trading lambs for the next couple of months.

Meanwhile, PGG said it was expecting tighter supplies to support the market, though it forecasts expected price volatility to continue.

World.title: Tax, gambling and migration fights ahead for Labor
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Gina Rushton is filling in for Courtney Gould to get you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Parliament is yet to resume but the battlelines have been drawn for political fights set to play out next week when the winter break ends and the prime minister settles back in after his holiday in Tasmania.

The gambling debate has kicked off, the government is readying to unveil its new immigration policy and the treasurer has been tinkering with his tax overhaul.

On Tuesday night Jim Chalmers released four pieces of draft legislation with the next round of tweaks to his capital gains tax and negative gearing reforms that passed parliament in late June.

The draft promises to fix what critics have dubbed a "widow's tax" (the loss of existing negative gearing access for people who inherit an investment property from their spouse) and so-called "death tax" (taxing disbursements from discretionary trusts established at death).

Chalmers has said the changes reflect the government's "commitment to consult" on the tax reforms announced in the budget while acting opposition leader Jane Hume wasn't buying it, saying Labor was "still trying to clean up a mess of its own making".

The treasurer will be under pressure next week as the Coalition, One Nation, independent David Pocock and the Greens are planning a joint push to force the abolition of the "widow tax" in the next sitting.

The treasurer will be under pressure next week as the Coalition, One Nation, independent David Pocock and the Greens are planning a joint push to force the abolition of the 'widow tax'. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Gambling companies won some, lost a bit more at Senate inquiry

You win some, you lose a bit more if you're one of the gambling companies that appeared at this week's Senate inquiry into Labor's wagering laws.

Representatives from Sportsbet, Tabcorp and Responsible Wagering Australia appeared before the inquiry to defend an industry that makes Australians the biggest gambling losers per capita with some $32 billion lost annually, including from pokies, according to an Equity Economics report commissioned by anti-gambling advocates last year.

Labor could shelve gambling crackdown Labor is unlikely to entertain major changes to its gambling ad crackdown despite the bill being friendless in parliament.

"Publicity-seeking extremists" was how Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V'landys described the senators leading the inquiry. But the companies spent a decent chunk of time defending their own forms of self-promotion, whether it was answering questions about pictures of children wearing Bet365 shirts, or about gambling ads playing between Disney songs on Spotify.

It was tough going too for the department officials responsible for Labor's legislation, as they appeared unable to provide the basis for advertising restrictions.

The legislation would restrict gambling television ads to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm, with a complete ban during live sport in those hours — but a question about the reasoning behind these time frames was taken on notice.

Former rugby league player Luke Bateman gave evidence about his personal experience losing "tens of thousands of dollars a month" to problem gambling.

Bateman, who last month told Australian Story his gambling meant he could barely afford to feed himself while earning $400,000 playing for the Canberra Raiders, said there was "absolutely zero duty of care" from the gambling companies.

He described being flown interstate for race days where he says he was given alcohol and offered his choice of drugs.

Former rugby league player Luke Bateman gave evidence about his personal experience losing "tens of thousands of dollars a month" to problem gambling. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Bateman did not disclose during the inquiry that he had been previously employed in the gambling industry, but on Wednesday confirmed to the ABC he had worked for Southern Cross Bet for six months shortly after he left the NRL. He said he was still struggling with problem gambling and quit the position to go into rehab.

Alliance for Gambling Reform chief advocate Reverend Tim Costello also told the inquiry TAB and Sportsbet had funded travel, escorts and drugs for a high-spending gambler who was now in Silverwater prison on charges related to the theft of about $12.3 million.

The companies have denied claims they offered customers access to illicit drugs and sex workers to encourage continued gambling, and implored advocates to present evidence to authorities.

After the two days of sensational evidence, the Coalition has said the government is ignoring gambling inducements which are causing "immeasurable harm to some Australians". The Greens and crossbench have also pushed for amendments aimed at further protecting children and vulnerable Australians and some of Labor's own MPs are pushing for a stronger plan.

But as the ABC's Clare Armstrong reported this morning, Labor is unlikely to entertain major changes to its gambling ad crackdown despite the bill being friendless in parliament and claims it would in fact consider shelving the gambling advertising crackdown altogether rather than substantially changing it.

That's one way to negotiate.

Tony Burke was scheduled to appear at the National Press Club today to unveil a new immigration policy but the home affairs minister cancelled as some elements were not going to be finalised before the speech. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Labor loiters on immigration

Tony Burke was scheduled to appear at the National Press Club today to unveil a new immigration policy but the home affairs minister cancelled as some elements were not going to be finalised before the speech.

Labor has one big political test on migration If stopping asylum seeker boats was the great immigration challenge in decades past, achieving a lower Net Overseas Migration (NOM) figure has become the new political test.

As the ABC's Tom Crowley reported, the measures are expected to include a crackdown on asylum seeker work and appeal rights, a ban on visitors applying for family visas while in Australia, and a reduction of the number of backpackers allowed to extend their visa stays beyond a year.

The government's political rivals seized on Burke's cancellation, with Pauline Hanson claiming he was "fighting his own cabinet, the unions and the Greens", and the Coalition accusing Labor of "coming late to the party" on lowering migration.

Labor is acutely aware of the role One Nation's immigration stance has played in its rise, as David Speers wrote in his column this morning, but the government is also aware of the political sensitivities and the backlash any change to the migration program will attract.

"If stopping asylum seeker boats was the great immigration challenge in decades past, achieving a lower net overseas migration (NOM) figure has become the new political test," Speers wrote.

When he appeared at the National Press Club last year Clive Palmer said that if he successfully sued Australia for almost $300 billion, he would spend it better than the government. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

We all just saved about $300 billion

When he appeared at the National Press Club last year Clive Palmer said that if he successfully sued Australia for almost $300 billion, he would spend it better than the government.

I guess we'll never find out if the billions of dollars could have revived his defunct dinosaur park Palmersaurus into something more Spielbergian, as the former politician has lost his legal fight.

Palmer will instead have to pay the Commonwealth $13 million court costs after he failed to classify himself as a foreign investor when on Wednesday a Swiss Federal Supreme Court upheld a previous finding.

His case argued the government had breached a trade agreement in blocking his company's mining proposal in Western Australia.

It is the latest development in Palmer's ongoing legal woes — accounts of his mining company found he's lost more than $160m in royalties as he remains in a separate legal battle with his mining tenants.

Loading

One Nation v the media

And finally, last week we flagged that Pauline Hanson would be announcing her candidates for the Victorian election. Unfortunately she banned the ABC, Guardian Australia and The Age from the press conference where she revealed the candidates.

She told Melbourne's 3AW the trio of outlets were "left leaning like your judges" and she's "not interested".

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

The ABC still reported on the new candidates from afar, as well as a protest of about 200 people outside the party's fundraiser.

In May, ahead of the Farrer by-election, One Nation's chief-of-staff James Ashby ejected two journalists working for the ABC's rural service.

In a National Press Club speech broadcast on the ABC in June, Hanson called for the national broadcaster to be a subscription-only service.

Still, it isn't quite as extreme as her desires for SBS, which she'd like to be axed altogether.

"There's no need for it anymore," she said, days after SBS began its FIFA World Cup coverage.

World.title: Dockers not treating trip to MCG any differently as AFL finals loom
World.content:
Since Justin Longmuir took the reigns at Fremantle ahead of the 2020 AFL season, the Dockers have only played at the MCG 12 times.

On Saturday afternoon they face Melbourne at the venue, in what presents as the perfect preparation for the grand final in late September. Unless you're Longmuir, that is.

"I just don't get caught up in dress rehearsals," he said.

"We feel like we've played there enough, had good experiences, had some average experiences there, but beaten teams that have been on top of the ladder.

"We feel like it's not a burden going to the MCG now. [We] go to Melbourne every second week, nearly, so we feel like that's not a burden either."

Justin Longmuir has overseen a record-breaking season for Fremantle, but the ultimate prize is still up for grabs. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The game is at 1:15pm on Saturday, comparable to the grand final start time of 2:30pm, but Longmuir won't look that far ahead.

"We're going over there to give our best and all we've got, to play and improve our footy against Melbourne, who we know have played some really good footy there," he said.

"[It would] be disrespectful to this game if we got ahead of ourselves.

"It's not the be-all and end-all either. We've had plenty of experiences at MCG and it shouldn't hold any fears for us."

Graham's future no distraction

As the Dockers prepare for the finals, Jaymie Graham will balance his role of assistant coach with the lure of being a potential head coach of a different AFL side.

Graham has reportedly advanced to the final round of interviews for both the vacant Essendon and Carlton jobs, but Longmuir is confident he won't be distracted by that as Fremantle enter the season's home stretch.

Jaymie Graham is fielding considerable interest in his skills from clubs on the east coast. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

"I've spoken to him regularly about it … we're colleagues, we're pretty good mates away from work, so yeah, of course I've spoken about it," Longmuir said.

"I haven't had to speak to him about getting the balance right. He's professional, he understands his responsibilities at the club, and he's done a great job of managing that.

"The way he's around the club, you wouldn't even know that he's occupied with anything else outside of it."

Battle-worn Freo fans dare to dream flag within reach Hard-bitten Dockers supporters won't want to say it out loud, but hope is slowly turning to expectation that a first premiership could be on the cards.

Should Graham be offered either the Blues or Bombers job, Longmuir said a decision on whether he would remain at Fremantle until the end of its campaign would be made in due course.

"We'll cross that bridge when it comes," he said.

"[I've] got a lot of faith in Jaymie to be able to walk and chew at the same time. I've also got a big understanding that he wants to see this through, and he's enjoyed his time here, he's enjoyed his work here and he loves working for the club.

"If he got a job elsewhere and they announced it and he wanted to see it through, I'd be happy for him to do that."

Longmuir confirmed he had no plans to rest large numbers of players in the run into finals, following a warning from the AFL, although he did say he was slightly surprised by the memo.

Fremantle won't rest large numbers of players in the run to finals, but some may still be managed. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

"I understand that they want to make sure the integrity of every game is there and I get that," he said.

"I also think that it's the club's responsibility to make sure that we're as best prepared to go as long in the season as we can.

"The teams in the top six get a week off. So it's probably not directed at us as much."

World.title: 'Menacing' threats left me terrified, Brooke Boney tells racism inquiry
World.content:
Former Today show presenter Brooke Boney has told the federal racism inquiry she was forced to leave the media industry after receiving "menacing" threats, including the doxxing of her email and home address.

Ms Boney said the public backlash she received for voicing her perspective on changing the date of Australia Day was one factor in her decision to walk away in 2024, although the harm she experienced from racism accumulated over many years.

"I wasn't trying to impose my view on anyone else, I was just offering another perspective, not trying to shout over the top of everyone saying, 'I'm right and you're wrong,' it's 'this is an alternative view that some Australians hold,'" she told the hearing in Naarm/Melbourne.

"I received threats, physical threats, and I think some of the things that happen when you're a broadcaster and you have an obligation to being public-facing every day … is that people engage with you in a way that feels quite personal.

"Sometimes that extends to showing up physically where you are and sometimes it means that your account details get doxxed, so your email accounts and where you live."

She said it was "absolutely terrifying when those threats are realised".

Ms Boney said racism was forcing First Nations people to weigh up the cost of speaking up, leading to fewer perspectives in public debate.

"Repeated exposure to racism, including in response to doing that work, has contributed to my decision to be less vocal on issues where I might have otherwise contributed to public discourse," she said.

"That withdrawal is in and of itself a public harm … Silence should not be the price of participation."

Narelda Jacobs called for anti-racism training in newsrooms. (ABC: Compass)

Network Ten journalist Narelda Jacobs told the inquiry news coverage in Australia often perpetuated negative stereotypes.

"When talking about Indigenous people, stories will often use our vision of squalid living conditions, communities littered with rubbish, Aboriginal people in handcuffs, camping out in a park.

"Such is the entrenched racism in the media. I have been complicit."

Ms Boney said media reporting on issues like youth crime often relied on "racial narratives" which depicted Aboriginal children as "symbols of disorder".

"Racism doesn't require an explicit slur. It can operate through disproportionate images, unverified claims, crime reporting without trend data and portraying a whole group of children as a threat."

Narelda Jacobs said the current system of media regulation provided very little accountability for outlets that are "spouting hate and racism".

"There are no consequences. If you do lodge a complaint, it's seen by those media organisations as engagement that fuels their purpose.

"And they continue publishing articles or opinion pieces because … it sells."

She said she had long experienced racism in the industry but it became "acute" during the 2023 Voice referendum.

"'Both sides-ism' meant I was forced to platform disinformation because for every yes we had to give air time to a no," she said.

"Networks make it a priority to train reporters and producers on their legal obligations but they don't undertake anti-racism training."

SBS/NITV national Indigenous affairs editor John Paul Janke said he had witnessed "an alarming escalation of online racial slurs, of delegitimising First Nations history and expertise, coordinated online pile-ons, and sustained abuse aimed at First Nations voices".

He said NITV was forced to leave X (formerly Twitter) after a barrage of racist abuse directed at its reporting and its staff.

"Racism is being left in plain sight. It's amplified by social media algorithms and tolerated by platforms and publishers that have both the capacity and the responsibility to do better."

Public broadcasters give evidence, other outlets decline

Committee chair Jana Stewart said the media organisations Sky News, News Corp, Nine Network, 7 West and Channel 10 were all invited to appear before the committee but declined.

ABC director of First Nations strategy Kelly Williams told the inquiry the ABC was making changes after the 2024 independent review into racism in the organisation.

"Things are moving, but as you know the ABC is a 90-year institution, what I will say is that there is goodwill to make that change," Ms Williams said.

The Listen Loudly, Act Strongly report, led by Dr Terri Janke, found current and former ABC employees experienced systemic racism within the workplace and from external parties.

Ms Williams said the ABC had accepted all 15 recommendations in principle and had addressed all "to some extent", including the rollout of anti-racism training to staff and a formal apology from the former managing director David Anderson.

In a written submission, national First Nations broadcaster NITV said it recorded a 300 per cent increase in negative comments on its Facebook and Instagram pages between January 2024 and April 2026.

Director for First Nations Tanya Denning-Orman said the organisation had to pay an external provider to moderate online content to protect First Nations staff from exposure to the racist comments.

"To see and deal with the consistent hate, even if it's a story on the cost of living or the fuel crisis … the staff needing to see it day in and day out causes harm," she said.

She urged the government to impose greater obligations on social media platforms to remove harmful content.

"The more these violent, hurtful statements stay online, the more they travel."

Athletes 'fighting for fair go' on and off the field

Earlier in the day, the inquiry heard elite sporting organisations were not culturally safe for First Nations athletes and their complaint procedures not fit for purpose.

Former Olympic boxer Marissa Williamson Pohlman told the inquiry Indigenous athletes carried the load of racism both on and off the sporting field.

"I'm not only dealing with the racism I experience whilst I'm trying to be an athlete in the arena, but also the systemic failures that are going on for me and my family outside of sport," she said.

"I don't think that I'll ever actually get to witness myself what I could have become as an athlete because all my energy has been wasted on fighting just for a fair go."

Marissa Williamson Pohlman says she has experienced racism in and out of the ring. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Ms Williamson Pohlman, the first Aboriginal woman to represent Australia in Olympic boxing, said she had frequently been on the receiving end of racist slurs during her sporting career.

She also said a Boxing Australia official had called her home coach and threatened "repercussions" if she carried the Aboriginal flag at an Olympic Games qualifier in Solomon Islands.

"Institutions celebrate Blak excellence when it is convenient, but abandon us when it matters most," she said.

"So it's all good when I put some deadly artwork on the uniform, but cultural safety and practice is another thing."

Ms Williamson Pohlman said she had faced many roadblocks trying to pursue complaints against former national head coach Jamie Pittman.

Mr Pittman is currently employed as Boxing Australia's acting high-performance manager, despite having withdrawn from the Paris Olympics after admitting to sexual misconduct.

Ms Williamson Pohlman wants an independent investigation into the organisation.

"Through my trials and tribulations I've come to understand that sporting federations investigate themselves," Ms Williamson Pohlman said.

"Sport Integrity Australia, despite their name, they can only investigate individuals, not the actual organisation.

"The National Sports Tribunal can only take complaints if the federation agrees to it. So they're all just looking out for each other."

The ABC has contacted Boxing Australia for comment.

'You're not in our shoes'

Representatives of Melbourne football and netball club the Fitzroy Stars told the hearing they had experienced racism at the hands of competitors, coaches and umpires, with little recourse.

Esme Bamblett says racism complaints must be adjudicated by people with lived experience. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Club president Aunty Esme Bamblett said racism complaints should not be adjudicated by all-white sporting tribunals and must include people with lived experience.

"You can't be impartial [if] you don't know what it feels like to be an Aboriginal person," she said.

"You don't know what it feels like in this country to be an Aboriginal person who has racism directed at them. You don't know because you're not in our shoes."

Torres Strait Islander and former AFL executive Tanya Hosch told the inquiry the responsibility of dealing with racism should not be placed on those who experience it.

"I can't think of a single workplace that I have worked in where I haven't experienced racism and depending on your circumstances in that workplace, [it] drastically impacts your ability to stand up to it," she said.

Ms Hosch said it was "beyond disappointing" that few state and territory government departments across the country had accepted the committee's requests to appear in person.

"It would seem to me that governments of all persuasions are seeking to avoid fronting up to this conversation for fear that they may be politically wedged."

She said the federal inquiry was "one of the few glimmers of hope" among the "ongoing assaults of racism".

Independent senator and committee member Lidia Thorpe said the AFL and NRL had both declined the committee's requests to appear.

The parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence against Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people was announced in the wake of the alleged terror attack on an Invasion Day rally in Perth in January and a violent neo-Nazi attack on Camp Sovereignty in Melbourne last August.

The final report is due to be tabled in parliament by the end of the year.

World.title: Court asked to jail disgraced AFL great Nicky Winmar for assaulting woman
World.content:
The future of disgraced AFL great Nicky Winmar hangs in the balance, with prosecutors calling for him to be jailed for assaulting a woman.

Winmar, who was recently removed from the league's Hall of Fame, was last month found guilty of bashing the woman in the town of Cohuna in 2025.

Winmar smashed the woman's head against a door, pulled her hair and twisted her arm during the attack.

She said the assault left her "a shadow of the person I once was".

Bendigo magistrate Trieu Huynh said he had not decided whether to impose a jail term.

Annina Tropea (left) told the Bendigo court Nicky Winmar needed to be sent to jail to learn the consequences of his actions. (ABC News: Nate Woodall)

Prosecutor Annina Tropea said Winmar had prior convictions for violence and said jail was needed to make him understand that there were consequences for his actions.

"Engaging in that conduct was a conscious and persistent choice," she said.

However, Winmar's barrister, Dermot Dann KC, said his prison should be a punishment of "last resort", and a community corrections order was more appropriate.

A sentencing date has been set for August 28.

Winmar was found guilty last month of assaulting a woman in northern Victoria last year. (ABC News: Nate Woodall)

Winmar, who sat alone, slumped forward and covered his ears as the victim read out a statement about how the crime affected her life.

The woman said she felt "extreme pain" in her arm, leaving her unable to complete daily duties or simple tasks.

She said the attack also had an "immense impact" on her mental health and that she constantly felt paranoid, scared and frightened.

"The visions and reminders of being overpowered and powerless are so detailed," she said.

"Not being able to stand up for myself — I was so helpless."

Former AFL great Nicky Winmar found guilty of assaulting woman The woman previously told the court she was "fearful" for her life on the night of the incident last year.

Winmar pleaded not guilty during the case; however, the magistrate found the charges guilty beyond reasonable doubt after hearing evidence from the victim and other witnesses.

Mr Dann, for the defence, said his client had a storied AFL career whose most important achievement was standing up to racism, when he famously lifted his jumper and pointed to his skin in a match against Collingwood in 1993.

After Winmar was found guilty, he was stripped of numerous playing accolades and a bronze statue of him outside Perth Stadium was taken down.

"They can erase his statue and they can erase his names from their hall of fames," Mr Dann said.

"What they'll never be able to erase … in the hearts of minds of the many, many people who care about racism and intolerance and injustice, is the memory of his courageous stand that day at Victoria Park."

Winmar endured a difficult upbringing in WA and currently struggled with depression, PTSD and alcohol disorders, Mr Dann said.

"This is a man who's had plenty of highlights but also plenty of lowlights," he said.

"Of course, this proceeding is one of the real lowlights.

"He has undergone significant efforts towards rehabilitation."

Mr Dann said his client suffered numerous concussions in his playing days and investigations were under way to determine whether he had acquired a brain injury or developed CTE.

Winmar's priors include multiple convictions for assault, including an attack on a taxi driver in 2019, the court heard.

Winmar made no comment outside court.

World.title: Birthday boy Popyrin wins in Montreal
World.content:
Alexei Popyrin has celebrated turning 27 by booking his place in the Montreal Masters' round of 32 for the third year running.

The shock 2024 champion progressed in just 76 minutes, beating the 32nd-seeded Belgian Raphaël Collignon 6-4, 6-3 on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Former world number 19 but currently ranked 139, Popyrin beat fellow Australian Thanasi Kokkinakis to earn his place in the main draw and saw off Román Andrés Burruchaga in round one to notch his first ATP-level win since May.

And with another crack looming at the US Open in New York — where he beat Novak Djokovic in 2024 en route to his best finish at Flushing Meadows — Popyrin can largely credit another win in Canada to his booming serve.

Popyirn fired down 10 aces, won 84 per cent (27/32) of first-serve points and did not face a break point, while also converting three of nine break-point opportunities of his own.

The Sydneysider will next face another Argentine in Thiago Tirante, who upset world number 9 and seventh-seeded American Taylor Fritz 7-5, 6-3.

At the women's WTA event in Toronto meantime, Australian world number 61 Daria Kasatkina suffered a lengthy, 6-3, 5-7, 6-4 loss to second seed Elena Rybakina.

The two-time grand slam champion from Kazakhstan survived after a two-hour and 22-minute scare to progress and tee up a clash with 28th seed Anna Li of the US.

Later on Wednesday, 20-year-old Aussie qualifier Maya Joint beat 14th-seeded Romanian Sorana Cîrstea 6-4, 6-4 to join compatriot Talia Gibson in the third round.

AAP

World.title: Geelong under scrutiny over player concussion deal
World.content:
AFL club Geelong is under scrutiny over an alleged deal with a player with a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

The secret agreement has been slammed by the AFL Players' Association (AFLPA), which was unaware of it, along with concussion campaigners and experts.

A bombshell report in News Corp newspapers on Thursday morning said a Victorian AFL club had the unnamed player sign the agreement in a bid to exonerate itself and its medical staff from future court action.

Loading...

The report said the club, confirmed by AAP to be Geelong on Thursday afternoon, viewed such an agreement as the only way the player could continue his career, given his history of multiple concussions.

The deal with the unnamed footballer, who is still an active AFL player, was signed two years ago.

The disclosure agreement reportedly required the individual to "take upon yourself the physical and legal risk of loss, damage or injury" arising from future concussions.

It also acknowledged the player was at higher risk of more concussions and could face more serious damage if they suffered further head knocks.

The Geelong Football Club has been contacted for comment.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

"Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and Standard Playing Contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws," AFLPA boss James Gallagher said in a statement.

"Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so.

"We are in discussions with AFL to better understand the circumstances of this case and ensure this issue is not replicated further at the elite level."

'I have lost basically everything': Ex-AFL player opens up on compensation fight Head trauma ended Aiden O'Driscoll's promising AFL career before he could play his first game. Now, like many former footballers affected by brain injuries, he faces an uncertain future as he fights for compensation.

Concussion campaigner Peter Jess said those involved with the drafting of the contract must step down.

"The people who are responsible must resign immediately, the whole chain of command that has given this," he said.

"Even if the chairman of the commission knew, he must go. There is no place for these people in our sport."

Mr Jess said the intent behind the contract appeared to prioritise the club above the welfare of the player.

"If you are trying to limit your duty of care, if you are trying to limit your responsibility to that player, knowing full well that if he's been damaged to such an extent he may not have the ability to make an informed decision, it's frightening," he said.

Daniel Schram, special counsel at Margalit Injury Lawyers, said the player in question was likely incredibly vulnerable due to repeated brain trauma.

"Whether the player is in a position to sign a document like this is a particularly pertinent question," he said.

"I think it's horrifying that a club would ask a player to enter into an agreement like this about any physical injury, let alone a brain injury."

Mr Schram said he was unsure as to whether the contract would hold water legally but noted the statutory rights of players were inviolable.

"It's very difficult to say whether this type of agreement would hold up in court, these matters turn on their facts," he said.

"But what I would say is, you cannot contract out of legislation."

Melbourne coach and former Cats assistant Steven King, who spoke before Geelong was identified as the club in question, was asked about the report on Thursday morning.

"All I'll say about that is that, as a club and me personally, I'd never do anything or ask my players to put themselves at risk," King said.

"Their health and safety is paramount."

Former West Coast premiership coach Adam Simpson was in disbelief.

"From a coach's eye, it's hard to really fathom how you would get to the conclusion that this is a good thing to do. And how it goes up the chain?" Simpson told SEN.

"From a father point of view and a coach point of view, I can't see how you would accept that is the right thing to do for your son or your player."

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley and Shane Tuck, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

AAP

World.title: Netball's uniform debacle hints at bigger problem for women in sport
World.content:
The Diamonds' 2026 Commonwealth Games campaign may well go down in history for all the wrong reasons, remembered not only for a shock semi-final loss to Jamaica but also for the dress controversy that preceded it.

After the Diamonds' 99-38 demolition of Tonga, media coverage focused not on the lopsided result but on the ill-fitting dresses players tugged at throughout matches.

Players like Sophie Garbin may have insisted the outfits were fine, but as ABC journalist Britt Carter put it, "if a shooter has to pull it down more than 10 times in a quarter, how much of that energy could be re-directed?"

Loading Instagram content

For elite women athletes, the problem is not just the impact poor-fitting uniforms have on performance.

Research shows that many adolescent girls drop out of sport citing body image issues, while concerns about uniforms have also been identified as a barrier to participation.

These are not just problems for younger people or community sport.

The ABC and Deakin University's recent survey of elite Australian athletes in women's sport found that 25 per cent have negative feelings about their body image, while 44 per cent have experienced an eating disorder and/or disordered eating.

The latter figure is much higher than what the Butterfly Foundation, a national charity for anyone affected by eating disorders and body image issues, estimates at 17 per cent for the general population.

Teigan O'Shannassy wants to see women and girls feel more comfortable in their bodies on the netball court. (Getty: Sanka Vidanagama)

Sydney-based netballer Teigan O'Shannassy is one of those who lives with a history of eating disorders and disordered eating.

She argues more awareness about the struggles elite female athletes face is key.

Dresses an issue during Super Netball season

O'Shannassy, who the ABC interviewed before the Commonwealth Games, admitted having issues with the Swifts' dress in the most recent Super Netball season, with teammates seen adjusting them during some matches.

"When you're playing in a dress in front of thousands of people, you want to be able to perform, and don't want to have to think about how you look or how you feel in the dress," she told the ABC.

" If you're struggling with your body image, having to do that and put on something that you don't want to wear, or you don't feel comfortable in, is really hard. "

Teigan O'Shannassy (left) has played for the Canberra Giants and the Sydney Swifts in her netball career. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

O'Shannassy, 27, has previously been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa and remembers vividly the moment her career came to a crossroads.

If you or someone you know needs help: The Butterfly Foundation: National helpline 1800 ED HOPE (1800 33 4673)

She was playing for the Giants at the time, in the middle of COVID-19 lockdowns, and was about to leave with the team for a Queensland hub.

O'Shannassy was called into a meeting with her head coach, assistant coach, dietitian, doctor and physio and told she would be staying behind so she could see a dietitian and therapist weekly.

"Looking back, I think that was probably the best decision they could have made," she said.

"I think it was one of the best things that could have happened to me. But obviously I was absolutely gutted. I thought my career was over."

Those feelings intensified when the Giants told her they would not offer her another contract, but invited her to stay on as a training partner.

The Swifts called with the same offer before O'Shannassy decided to leave.

Netballer Teigan O'Shannassy has struggled with body image throughout her career in the national league. (Getty: James Worsfold)

"Something needed to change," she said.

"I just felt like I was stuck in this constant cycle of injuries and under-fuelling because I felt like I wasn't training [enough] and I didn't deserve to eat."

'The more we can talk about it, the better'

Given her personal experience, O'Shannassy says she was "unfortunately not surprised" by the results of the ABC and Deakin survey.

"When I was really struggling, I honestly thought I was the only person that was struggling with my body and food and having all these negative thoughts around it," she said.

"But since I've spoken up about it, people have come to me and said 'oh, I struggle with this too', which in a way I think is helpful, that we're so open about it.

"I think the more we can talk about it, the better. Even for me, talking about my body in a positive way is still something that I need to work on, and I think everyone can do that every day."

Teigan O'Shannassy now teaches other women about nutrition and health. (Getty: Brett Hemmings)

O'Shannassy, who has since trained as an associate nutritionist and runs a business called Tossed Together, is passionate about building community understanding of the unique challenges athletes face.

These include, in a team sport like netball, the pressure to be more like your teammates or competitors.

She remembers first coming through competitive pathways at 17 and having her body compared unfavourably to others by her coaches.

"We got told, 'you should be lifting this amount of weight, you should all look like this player, you should be able to do what certain players can do,'" she said.

"That stuck so much in my head. I'd have niggle after niggle and just felt like my body was never good enough.

"I just wanted to be like the other netballers who were so strong and looked like athletes."

By contrast, O'Shannassy described her younger self as "tall, lanky and uncoordinated", and says she "never felt like I looked like an athlete".

Teigan O'Shannassy began playing for the Canberra Giants in her late teens. (Getty: Mark Nolan)

The requirement to undertake body composition testing, including skin folds and DEXA scans, also bred unhealthy comparisons.

"I remember being 19, 20, and hearing some girls saying what body fat [percentage] they were, and thinking 'oh god, I'm a bit higher than them' and just freaking out about it," O'Shannassy said.

Social media exposes further body scrutiny

Danni Rowlands, the Butterfly Foundation's director of education initiatives, is a former state netballer herself and shares a similar story to O'Shannassy.

She was diagnosed with an eating disorder at age 21 and remembers skin fold testing significantly influencing how she felt about her body as a junior athlete.

A former netballer herself, Danni Rowlands now advocates for a shift in sporting cultures through the Butterfly Foundation. (Supplied.)

"I was identified as being too high in body composition, so I was supported through a dietitian to reduce body fat," she said.

"I went on to make the state team and play nationals, which was amazing, but unfortunately played the entire tournament with a stress fracture in my ankle, which was later identified as being caused by under-nourishment and over-training.

" That just kicked off this whole cycle at a very vulnerable age where I connected my weight to my worth and success as an athlete. "

Since retiring from sport, she has worked to shift sporting cultures, heading Butterfly Foundation's BodyKindSports initiative, which recognises adolescence as a vulnerable time for athletes' relationship with their body, particularly young girls.

"We want to protect and support athletes in those early pathways so that they can thrive, and that the consequence of participating in sport isn't a lifelong struggle with eating, training and poor body image," Rowlands said.

The Diamonds claimed the bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. (Getty: Lintao Zhang)

She holds particular concerns for contemporary women athletes who are more accessible to the public than ever on social media.

"This idea that athlete bodies are commodities and we can all have a piece of them, and critique as we want [online], absolutely adds a layer of pressure for athletes that makes it more intense than ever before," Rowlands said.

" There are intense appearance pressures on women athletes to look pretty, and feminine, but not too muscular, or too thin. They just can't win, which is tough. "

She added that when players do have issues with their uniforms, as in the Commonwealth Games example, this can generate further unwanted attention on their bodies.

"Looking at women across a lot of sports, there's much more exposure of body parts compared to men," she said.

"I think we have to ask: why is this the case? Is it because it's going to help them perform better, or is it because we're treating female bodies differently in sport?"

Uniforms a factor in girls dropping out of sport Studies show a large percentage of girls drop out of sport when they become teenagers. One of the contributing factors is the clothes they have to wear.

O'Shannassy admitted being under the spotlight, and being photographed or filmed constantly, added a layer of discomfort for those with body image issues.

"For a female, that can be really triggering. You're always being watched, and I think that's something that can be kind of daunting," she said.

"As an athlete, obviously it's such a cool job, and there's so many positive things that come out of it, but the highs are high, and the lows are low.

"If you've never done it, you just really don't know what it can be like."

Athletes 'not immune' to body image issues

Moving forward, both O'Shannassy and Rowlands shared messages of support for women in sport.

Rowlands encouraged athletes who might be struggling to "seek support sooner rather than later".

"Being an athlete doesn't make you immune to any of those pressures. If anything, it intensifies them further. So be kind to yourself, and if you are struggling, reach out," she said.

All Teigan O'Shannassy ever wanted to do in her life was play netball. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

O'Shannassy, meanwhile, hopes sharing her story will continue to inspire others who may be experiencing something similar.

Although her worst days are well behind her, she says it can help to acknowledge that an eating disorder is not "something you can just turn off, or wake up and you're fine".

"You might have that voice in your head forever," she said.

"For me, it's just, I hear that voice and I acknowledge it, but I don't let it control me anymore."

She says it is important to find the thing that motivates you to keep fighting, which for her has always been her chosen sport.

"For me it was netball, all I ever wanted to do was play netball," she said.

"And I knew that if I didn't eat or didn't fuel myself I was never going to get there."

World.title: FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA says it has apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to sell commercial rights linked to the World Cup, as the governing body's leadership reaffirmed its support for president Gianni Infantino after a crisis meeting in Morocco.

Following the meeting in Rabat, attended by Mr Infantino, secretary general Mattias Grafström and members of FIFA's management board, FIFA said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for the president while acknowledging that the handling of the withdrawn FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal should have been different.

In a statement, FIFA said a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologising for the errors and promising a review.

It added that, with the proposal withdrawn, FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process" and would take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Vehicles believed to be carrying Mr Infantino and Mr Grafström were seen leaving FIFA's Africa office in Sale after the meeting, which came amid mounting criticism of Mr Infantino's leadership ahead of next year's presidential election.

The meeting followed last week's withdrawal of a proposal to sell a 20 per cent stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion for football development.

The proposal, which also drew scrutiny because of the involvement of a company with family links to US President Donald Trump, prompted fierce criticism from European soccer's governing body UEFA and other stakeholders, who accused FIFA of poor governance and a lack of consultation.

Gianni Infantino's closeness to US President Donald Trump has been criticised. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

The apology underscored FIFA's acknowledgement that mistakes had been made in the handling of his proposal for a new commercial rights body, which has become the most serious challenge to his leadership since he became FIFA president in 2016 after triggering a torrent of criticism from UEFA, several member associations and senior FIFA officials over governance and consultation.

His backdown last Friday has done little to assuage those critics, most notably UEFA, which accused him of selling the soul of the game and has said it no longer has confidence in his leadership.

That has cast a shadow over Mr Infantino's re-election for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco in March, which had looked like a foregone conclusion two months ago.

A handful of European federations have withdrawn their backing for the Swiss Italian, but perhaps more damaging are the messages coming from Infantino's FIFA colleagues.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also questioned Mr Infantino's leadership on Wednesday, saying he has lost confidence in the FIFA president after learning senior advisers had not been consulted on the abandoned proposal.

"I don't have confidence in Mr Infantino," Mr Carney told reporters, adding that failing to inform senior executives and fellow board members of such a significant proposal "should be fatal" for any leader.

Mr Grafström had sent an internal memo to staff lamenting the "sad and reproachable series of events" that led to the project being "permanently abandoned", two sources told Reuters.

"Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue," the Swede added in the letter, which made no mention of Mr Infantino by name.

His words echoed those of FIFA's Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour, who said last week that staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned in protest at the plan last week. Arsene Wenger, FIFA's chief of Global Football Development, said he had not been involved in drafting the proposal, and called the decision to withdraw it "absolutely necessary".

Former Portugal great Luis Figo, who had planned to run for the FIFA presidency in 2015, said Infantino should resign over the affair, while UEFA Vice-President Laura McAllister told Reuters the controversy surrounding the abandoned proposal had brought the FIFA president's leadership to a crisis point.

Mr Infantino has spent the past week in Morocco, which will co-host the World Cup in 2030 and whose football association has announced its continued support for him.

Gianni Infantino has garnered the support of FIFA's executive, but many national governing bodies are sharpening their knives. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The meeting was widely seen as an effort to reinforce support for Mr Infantino and ensure that he emerges from the crisis with enough backing to remain the favourite for re-election in March.

An Extraordinary Congress could be called if 43 or more FIFA member associations make a formal written request for one.

Qatar, which hosted the 2022 World Cup, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Indonesia and the Philippines have declared their loyalty to Mr Infantino.

Mr Infantino has always enjoyed a lot of support away from the traditional heartlands of the game, where impoverished football associations rely on FIFA's largesse to operate.

But European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect clubs, players and fans.

It also criticised the "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Leading African football administrators have sent messages of support as Mr Infantino looks to the continent's 54 members for backing. The African confederation (CAF) has yet to take a stance.

The executive committee of the smallest and least wealthy regional confederation, Oceania, will meet next Wednesday to discuss their approach.

Under FIFA rules, the vote of San Marino, whose men's team are ranked 211th and last in the world rankings, counts as much as that of World Cup winners like Brazil, Germany, Argentina and Spain.

One clear advantage for Mr Infantino as he looks to extend his presidency until 2031 is that no clear candidate to stand against him in March's election has yet emerged.

Jordan FA President Prince Ali bin Hussein has twice stood for the post, and he made his position clear on Tuesday when he accused FIFA of "blackmail", saying it had offered to help solve problems in exchange for endorsing Mr Infantino.

"We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now," Prince Ali wrote on social media.

A FIFA spokesperson rejected reports that Mr Infantino had made promises over the host of the 2030 World Cup final.

"It is false and misleading to claim the FIFA president has made any promise in relation to hosting the FIFA World Cup 2030 Final. A decision will be made by FIFA in due course," the spokesperson said.

Reuters

Tech.title: Elon Musk’s attempt at an AI Wikipedia hasn’t been updated in months
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

xAI’s Grokipedia, an online encyclopedia with AI-generated articles that Elon Musk once promised would be a “massive improvement” over Wikipedia, apparently hasn’t been updated since April 24th, according to a report from Lawfare. “As far as we can tell, no entry has changed in more than three months,” Lawfare said.

Grokipedia launched in v0.1 in October 2025 with an initial batch of 885,000 articles, and is now on v0.2 (released in November 2025) and has more than 6,000,000 total articles, according to grokipedia.com/live. But that live page also has a section titled “Recent changes to…” with a message under it that reads “No live edits available right now.”

You can still suggest articles for Grokipedia to cover and edits to individual pages. But Lawfare looked at both popular and unpopular pages on Grokipedia and found that they weren’t updating. “In our subsequent analysis of 34,519 pages with at least one suggested edit in our sample, containing a total of 225,496 recommended edits, we found no accepted or rejected corrections dated within the past three months,” Lawfare said.

xAI didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Users on Reddit and X have wondered if Grokipedia is “dead.” Lawfare also noted that Musk’s last X post mentioning Grokipedia was from February.

Tech.title: X product chief Nikita Bier is leaving after one year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

X head of product Nikita Bier is stepping down and says he will move into a role as an advisor, writing that “it’s time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster.” He shared the update just over a month after celebrating his one-year anniversary on the job, and just weeks after Elon Musk’s combined SpaceX / X / xAI companies went public.

He says that “almost every aspect of X” has been rebuilt while he was head of product, including its timeline, Android app, chat, and notifications. Going forward, the “next leaders” mentioned are Benji Taylor leading design with iOS lead Jonah Katz and Mridul Singhai leading the product team.

Bier also called out the long-delayed and recently-launched X Money, which Elon Musk at one point expected to launch by the end of 2024. During his tenure, X has continued to focus on incentivizing native posts and login requirements for access to features, and last month Bier said that missing data from the X algorithm had made the platform feel like a “battleground.”

Bier previously co-founded the startups tbh (acquired by Meta) and Gas (acquired by Discord). He was appointed to lead product just days before former X CEO Linda Yaccarino stepped down, and has been a public face of the company ever since.

Tech.title: Two of Ring’s latest video doorbells are a lot cheaper than usual
Tech.content:
Ring’s Wired Doorbell Pro and Battery Doorbell Plus are two of the brand’s most well-rounded video doorbells, whether you’re looking for a hardwired model or one that runs on a battery. Right now, its Wired Doorbell Pro is down to $199 ($50 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, while the Battery Doorbell Plus is on sale for $119.99 ($60 off) at Amazon and Best Buy. Both deals are the second-best prices we’ve seen, just $20 shy of their Prime Day lows.

Aside from how they’re powered, the main difference between the two comes down to video quality. The Wired Doorbell Pro records sharper 4K video, and it can automatically respond to visitors with prerecorded messages. The Battery Doorbell Plus has fewer features and can capture video in slightly less sharp 2K resolution. Beyond that, the two doorbells share many of the same core features.

Both can provide a head-to-toe view of your doorstep and support motion detection, two-way talk, and support for color night vision. If you’re willing to pay $4.99 for a monthly subscription, you also get more specific alerts for people, packages, and vehicles. Upgrading to the $19.99 Ring Pro plan, meanwhile, grants access to extra AI features like facial recognition and text-based activity summaries, all of which are free for the first month. Both also work well with Amazon Alexa, allowing you to view a live feed on a compatible Echo Show smart display and receive audible announcements when someone rings your doorbell.

Tech.title: Uber CEO brushes off reports of a Waymo break-up
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After Uber and Waymo ended their partnership in Phoenix earlier this year, experts and robotaxi watchers wondered whether the companies’ improbable bromance was fraying. Not so, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said today. The two companies are committed to continue working together in Atlanta and Austin, and the partnership remains “very strong.”

“Waymo is a very important partner of ours, and we continue to operate in Austin and Atlanta,” Khosrowshahi said in an earnings call today. “We believe we’ll continue to operate next year in those marketplaces. It’s a terrific product, and the on-the-ground partnership continues to be very strong.”

There’s been plenty of evidence that points to a weaker relationship than Khosrowshahi would like to admit, like Uber’s CTO tweeting about a “scary Waymo moment” and an Uber white paper that emphasizes a hybrid model of human- and robot-powered rides over an AV-only model. Last month, the two companies found each other on opposite sides of a bill in Washington, DC, that would legalize robotaxi services, with Waymo supportive and Uber pushing for a hybrid model.

Khosrowshahi didn’t address any of those incidents, but did note that Waymo isn’t Uber’s only robotaxi partner.

“We want to make sure that we’re not dependent on one partner,” he said on the call. “We’re absolutely seeing a plethora of newer players in the AV ecosystem, just like you see in the foundation model space. While we continue to provide a great service with Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, we’ll continue to build our services with our other players as well.”

Indeed, Uber has made a big to-do about linking up with a variety of AV partners, including Zoox, Wayve, Avride, Nuro, Motional, and Waabi. Basically, if you’re a startup with some autonomous driving experience and a few vehicles in the field, chances are you’ve received a call from Uber. The company has said it plans on spending upwards of $10 billion to build out its robotaxi business over time.

But Waymo is really the only one doing it at scale. And since the company has shown it can work in markets both with and without Uber’s imprimatur, it really seems like Uber needs Waymo more than vice versa.

But while Khosrowshahi doesn’t sound ready to break up with Waymo any time soon, he also wasn’t willing to concede that robot-driven cars would quickly become the norm. In fact, Khosrowshahi’s next move was to downplay the significance of robotaxi rides on the company’s platform, noting that they only account for “less than 0.5 percent of our overall trip volume.” Physical AI — which is industry lingo for real-world AI like robots and driverless cars — is moving at a slower pace than large-language models like ChatGPT. And in time, a Waymo competitor may emerge to challenge the Alphabet-owned company’s dominance.

“We have time to develop the partnerships with our other set of partners to create a competitive playing field with attractive commercials,” Khosrowshahi added.

Khosrowshahi’s reticence is understandable. Uber and Waymo may be partners in a couple of markets, but the companies are mostly competitors. And early data suggests that Waymo is taking away market share from traditional rideshare players like Uber and Lyft. The two companies may still need each other now, while robotaxis are in their infancy, but the future is more of an open question.
